: Opens the orifices and awakens the spirit: for wind-stroke
and phlegm collapse or qi constraint with sudden collapse.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, and neutral, Benzoinum (an xi xiang) opens
the orifices and invigorates the movement of qi and blood
by virtue of its fragrant, dispersing aroma. The seventh.
century Tang Materia Medica, the earliest Chinese text to
record its properties, says that it "governs noxious qi in
the Heart and abdomen." Less than a hundred years later!
the Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Zi provided a more detailed
account: "treats blood pathogens, sudden turmoil disor.
der, wind pain, and in women, clenched jaw and coma
due to blood [stasis rushing upward]." The gynecological
symptoms refer to such biomedically-defined disorders
as eclampsia, for which Treasury of Words on the Materia
Medica recommends combining Benzoinum (an xi xiang)
(3g) and Trogopterori Faeces (wi ling zhi) (15g) as a pow)
der, in a dose of 3g taken with tea made from dry-fried
ginger: "Treats postpartum coma, [abdominal] distention

15 / Aromatic Substances that Open the Orifices
due to stagnant blood, and clenched jaw [while] sinking
toward death."
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang Bing
Cheng mentions its revivifying action, saying that Ben
zoinum (an xi xiang) "treats sudden collapse from wind.
stroke, and all pain in the Heart and abdomen." Encoun.
tering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica concurs: "Stops suddenly-occurring Heart pain, nausea, and
rebellion." The Thoroughly Revised Materia Medica adds
"Promiotes the movement of qi and blood. Taken ground
[into powder] it promotes the movement of blood and
directs the qi downward, calming the spirit."
Description of the Materia Medica expands its indica
tions to other types of pathogenic wind: "treats wind.
stroke, wind painful obstruction, wind convulsions, crane's
knee wind, lower back pain, and tinnitus."
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. STYRAX (su he xiang)
Both substances open the orifices and treat loss of consciousness. Styrax (su he xiang) uses its warmth and pierc.
ing fragrance to transform phlegm and clear away filth, and
thus is especially useful for wind-stroke with collapse due
to phlegm. The aromatic, orifice-opening power of Benzoinum (an xi xiang) is similar in strength to Styrax (su he
xiang), but it lacks that substance's warmth. On the other
hand, it invigorates the blood and is therefore used to treat
pain in the chest and abdomen and postpartum coma.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
"Contraindicated in those with qi deficiency, loss of appe
tite, yin deficiency and excessive fire." (Encountering the
Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "pacifying extinguishing fra
grance"
Benzoin is a balsamic resin derived from Styrax benzoin
known internationally as Sumatran benzoin, or from S
tonkinensis, known as Siam benzoin. The latter is also produced in southern China. Benzoin is not a natural product
of the tree, but only develops after incisions are made in the
bark. It takes about eight weeks before the exuding whitecolored resin becomes firm enough to collect.
The word benzoin is devived from the Arabic word
ben, meaning fragrant, or the Hebrew ben, meaning a
branch, and zoa, meaning exudate: literally, the juice of the
bran ch.
Li Shi-Zhen explained the origin of its Chinese name:
"This aromatic clears away evil, pacifying the noxious and
951
extinguishing all pathogens an exi zhu xie,
hence the name. Another explanation is that an xi is the
name of a country; Sanskrit books call it the fragrance of
Zhuobeilou ( zhuo bei luo xiang). The Sanskrit
word for benzoin is lobana,or lubanhowever,the name of
the tree is karbura, which is closer to Li Shi-Zhen's transliteration.

Kidney yang deficiency with such symptoms as impotence,
male.or female infertility, premature ejaculation, urinary
frequency, incontinence of urine, irregular menstruation,
cold and painful lower abdomen, and a weak and sore
back.

Semen (tu si zi) for impotence, spermatorrhea, and premature ejaculation from Kidney yang deficiency.
-- With Ginseng Radix (ren shen) and Dioscoreae Rhizoma

Sweet and warm, such that it tonifies, but acrid and warm.
such that it disperses, Morindae officinalis Radix (ba ji
tian) enters the Kidney channel to warm the Kidney yang.
augment the essence, fortify the sinews and bones, and
disperse wind, cold, and dampness. Yet its nature is soft
and moistening, so that while it is warm, it is not overly
drying, and its tonification is not cloying. In addition, as a
tonic it is rather modest, and it is also considered to have a
minor action in augmenting the blood. It is typically used
with similar herbs for such problems as impotence due to
Kidney yang deficiency, infertility, irregular menstruation.
and abdominal pain due to cold in the Womb, and pain
in the lower back and knees due to invasion of pathogenic
wind-dampness taking advantage of Kidney yang defi.
ciency. Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia
Medica notes that this herb
does not wither in the winter; it is an herb of the Kidney
channel blood level and of the Penetrating vessel... its
nature both tonifies the primal yang and disperses pathogens. When the primal is tonified, how can a pathogen
linger?
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica observes that,
according to the books [it] is an important herb for Kidney
tonification, because it is moist in nature. However, with an
acrid, warm flavor, it also expels wind and dampness, so it
is even better for symptoms such as pain in the lower back
And knees, wind qi, leg qi, and edema.

780 12 / Tonifying Herbs
The Grand Materia Medica confirms that it "treats leg qi
expels wind illnesses, and tonifies the sea of blood." The
'sea of blood' here refers to the Penetrating vessel.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH CISTANCHEs HERBA (rou cong r6ng)
Both herbs tonify the Kidney yang, and are special ir
that neither is overly drying. Cistanches Herba (rou cong
rong) is particularly moistening, and within its ability to
tonify the yang is the capacity to augment the essence and
moisten the Intestines. Morindae officinalis Radix (ba jr
tian) is not moistening as such, but is less drying than other
Kidney yang tonics, and its gentle, acrid flavor moderates
the potential for cloying that exists in Cistanches Herba
(rou cong rong). Hence this is an excellent combination for
tonifying the yang without injuring the yin, and can also be
used for constipation in the elderly, by increasing the dosage of Cistanches Herba (rou cong rong).

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
A variety of names have been coined to emphasize certain
desirable qualities in this herb, such as morinda flesh (E$k
ba ji rou) or fat morinda (E E#k fei ba ji), after the high
quality, large, fleshy roots.
Without further preparation, this herb tonifies the
Kidney yang, and also expels wind-dampness. It is best
in its unprepared form when treating wind-damp painful
obstruction with concurrent Kidney yang deficiency.
>SALT-PREPARED MORINDA (E#kyan baji)
The root is mixed with salt water, then thoroughly steamed.
which facilitates removal of the heartwood. It is then sliced
into sections and dried in the sun. This method of preparation enhances its ability to enter the Kidney channel, and
while it augments the primal yang, it also replenishes yin
water, and is thus appropriate for the treatment of impotence or spermatorrhea due to the depletion of Kidney
essence.
>PROCESSED MoRINDA(#E#k zhi baji)
The roots are boiled together with Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan
cao) until soft, then the heartwood is removed while the
roots are still hot. Once cooled, but still moist, they are
cut into sections and dried. This method of preparation
is traditionally considered to moderate its nature so that
it tonifies fire but does not unduly dry yin, and so is quite
popular.

englishReference.actions:
- Promotes the movement of qi, transforms dampness, and
strengthens the Stomach: for dampness obstructing the
middle burner as well as damp-warmth. Symptoms include
a stifling sensation in the chest, fullness in the epigastrium,
lack of'appetite, and a very greasy tongue coating.
- With Amomi Fructus (sha ren) for fullness and a stifling
sensation in the chest, vomiting, diarrhea, and a thick

482 7 / Aromatic Herbs that Transform Dampness
tongue coating from cold-dampness encumbering the
Spleen and obstructing the movement of qi.
With Citri reticulatae Pericarpium (chen pi) for fullness and discomfort in the chest and abdomen, belching,
nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea due to Spleen and Stomach
deficiency with a subsequent accumulation of turbid
dampness.
-With Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) and Coicis Semen
(yi yi ren) for headache, stifling sensation in the chest,
fatigue, dark urine with reduced output, diarrhea, and usually accompanied by a white, greasy tongue coating, as in
the early stages of damp-warmth. See Three--Nut Decoction
(san ren tang)
-With Scutellariae Radix (huang qin), Talcum (hua shi)
and Polyporus (zhu ling) for damp-warmth in the middle
burner, with more heat than dampness, marked by recurring fevers, body aches, dark urine, and a yellow tongue
coating, as in Scutellaria and Talcum Decoction (huang qin
hua shi tang).
-With Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) and Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) for distention due to qi obstruction or cold-dampness in the Spleen and Stomach.
Warms the middle burner and causes rebellious qi to
descend: for vomiting due to cold from deficiency of the
Spleen and Stomach, Stomach cold, cold-dampness, or
food stagnation.
-With Pogostemonis/Agastaches Herba (huo xiang) and
Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) for nausea and
vomiting, epigastric discomfort, and reduced appetite due
to either cold-dampness or food stagnation. This combination can also be used for morning sickness.
-With Caryophylli Flos (ding xiang) for belching due te
Stomach cold.
-Powdered together with Amomi Fructus (sha ren) and
Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao) and placed inside an infant's
mouth for spitting up of milk.
englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, warm, and aromatic, Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai
dou kou) enters the Lung, Spleen, and Stomach channels.
It warms, disseminates, and pierces through turbidity by
virtue of its aroma, and can mobilize stagnant qi within
the Triple Burner, while opening the middle and easing
the Stomach. It is particularly effective for dredging and
dispersing Lung qi blockage. It can warm the middle,
transform dampness, awaken the Spleen, and restore the
appetite. In this way it treats phlegm-dampness obstruct
ing the Lungs and qi stasis which causes a stifling sensation
in the chest; it does this by its warming transformation of
phlegm-dampness and its ability to disseminate the Lung
qi. It also treats cold-dampness obstructing the middle
with nausea, vomiting, hiccough or reflux, and Stomach
and Intestinal qi constraint with epigastric and abdominal
distention and pain.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica observes that
this herb
has a wonderful kind of clear, refreshing qi; it enters the
Lung channel qi level in the upper body, so it is an important qi-dispersing herb for Lung patients. Its acrid, warm
aroma expedites, dredges, and mobilizes the Triple Burner.
warming the Spleen and Stomach, and eliminating all cold.
damp distention, malarial disorders due to deficiency, nau.
sea and vomiting, upset Stomach, abdominal pain, and alsc
eye disorders such as superficial visual obstructions and
redness of the canthi.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH AMOMI FRUCTUs (sha ren)
Both herbs are aromatic and warming, which enables them
to transform dampness, and both enter the middle burner
to awaken the Spleen, mobilize the qi, and ease the middle.
Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou) has a light, clear
aroma, with only mild drying properties; it tends to regulate the Stomach qi, alleviate nausea, and stop pain. Amomi
Fructus (sha ren) has a more intense aroma and a slightly
stronger drying action, so that it more strongly warms and
transforms dampness, thereby awakening the Spleen and
easing the middle.
Together the aroma of these herbs pierces through tur
bid dampness and reduces the heavy, congealing yin qualities that characterize cold-dampness, thereby increasing
the local yang activity that raises and disperses pathogenic
yin influences. Thus this combination is ideal when colddampness encumbers the Spleen and movement of the
yang qi is obstructed, resulting in a thick tongue coating,
loss of appetite, epigastric pain and fullness, stifling sensation in the chest, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

following comparison:
Because it warms the Stomach and awakens the Spleen.
it has the same efficacy as Tsaoko Fructus (cao guo) and
Myristicae Semen (rou dou kou via a different means.This
is why it shares the name dou kou.Yet Amomi Fructus
rotundus (bai dou kou) has a clear aroma and intense acrid.
ity which can be regarded as superior to theirs: it has no
astringent taste in the mouth, and its fragrant aroma excels
in raising upward, opening and draining upper burner qi
stagnation, which is different from [the effects of] Tsaoko

"Acrid, hot, and intensely drying, it promotes movement
in the Triple Burner; it should not be included [in a prescription] whenever nausea and vomiting are not due to
cold or yang deficiency." (Harm and Benefit in the Materia

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "white cardamon"
The standard name for this product in the pharmaceutical
literature is simply # dou kou, while the standard name
in the practitioner literature is bai dou kou,which
we use here.
The herb is generally used in its raw (unprepared) form.
Penetrating the Mysteries of the Materia Medica explains
why:
The functions of Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou)
reside completely in its fragrant aroma: dry-frying only
reduces this effect. Before using in a decoction, it should be
crushed finely, then-for even better results--added at the
very last roll of the boil before drinking.
>ROUND CARDAMON KERNELS
=bai doukou ren
When the fruit husks (the papery pericarp) are removed
by pounding and sifting the fruit, the seed kernels are left
These are ground further before using, and are also known
simplyas=bai kou ren or#=dou kou ren.The
seed-kernels without the husks are more potent at promot.
ing the flow of qi and transforming dampness, warming the
Stomach, and alleviating nausea. They are thus often used
in the treatment of symptoms such as nausea, vomiting
abdominal pain, and diarrhea due to Stomach cold and qi
stasis.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH EPHEDRAE HERBA (md huang)
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) lightly clears and raises,
specifically dredging the Lungs, dispersing and draining
obstructions to the qi dynamic in order to treat cough and
wheezing. Ginkgo Semen (bai guo) has a strong flavor, with
an astringent nature that restrains and inhibits the Lung qi
to settle wheezing.
Together the two herbs are complementary, one disseminating, the other restraining, so that the Lung qi is
controlled in its dissemination. Each herb controls the
other, so that the inhibition of Lung qi is not excessive, nor
does its spreading dissemination weaken the Lung qi itself.
In this way the combination has a strong effect in calming
wheezing.
Because Ginkgo Semen (bai guo) restrains, it is most
suited to protecting the Lung qi in cases of long-term
deficient cough and wheezing. However, the combination

13 / Herbs that Stabilize and Bind
is rarely used by itself, but rather as the foundation for
other herbs, depending on the clinical presentation and the
accompanying symptom patterns. For example, see Arrest
Wheezing Decoction (ding chuan tang), which is designed
for phlegm-heat smoldering in the interior, with wind-cold
constraining the exterior.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. SCHISANDRAE FRUCTUS (wu wei zi)
Both herbs restrain the Lungs to treat cough and wheezing. However, Ginkgo Semen (bai guo) primarily restrains
the Lungs to arrest wheezing, and is most appropriate for
wheezing due to Lung heat with profuse phlegm. By contrast, Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi) primarily restrains
the Lungs to stop coughs, but its nature is warmer and
thus better suited to chronic cough due to Lung deficiency,
or cough and wheezing due to Lung cold with profuse
phlegm.
Again, both herbs treat lower burner pathology, but for
Ginkgo Semen (bai guo), this is limited to turbid vaginal
discharge, especially that due to predominant dampness,
while Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi) secures the lower
burner and enriches the Kidney water, and is mainly used
for leakages such as enuresis, urinary frequency, spermatorrhea, and also diarrhea. Furthermore, Schisandrae
Fructus (wi wei zi) generates fluids and restrains the Heart
qi, enabling it to treat injury to both the qi and yin leading
to such symptoms as insatiable thirst, excessive sweating,
irritability, and insomnia.

englishReference.keyCharacteristics: enriches the Lung yin, drains heat from the Heart, stops coughs, quiets the spirit
englishReference.dosage: 9-30g CAUTIONS AND CONTRAINDICATIONSNone nOted See ToxICITY below.
englishReference.actions:
833
- Moistens the Lungs, clears heat, and stops coughs: for dry
Lung or Lung-heat coughs and sore throat. Especially use
ful when a chronic cough due to Lung heat has injured the
yin.

834 12 / Tonifying Herbs
--With Mori Cortex (sang bai pi), Asteris Radix (zi wan),
and Fritillariae Bulbus (bei mu) for phlegm-heat clogging
the Lungs and injuring the fluids, leading to cough and
wheezing.
-With Platycodi Radix (jie geng), Armeniacae Semen
(xing ren), and Farfarae Flos (kuan dong hua) for coughs
in children marked by phlegm clogging the chest and dys.
function of the throat.
--With Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang), Rehmanniae
Radix preparata (shu di huang), and Scrophulariae Radix
(xuan shen) for cough with blood-streaked sputum, hot
palms and soles, and nightsweats from Lung and Kidney
-- yin deficiency, as in Lily Bulb Decoction to Preserve the
Metal (bai he gu jin tang). This is one type of Lung consumption.
-With Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao), Asteris Radix (zi
wan), and Peucedani Radix (qian hu) for wind-heat cough
contracted during pregnancy.
-With Farfarae Flos (kuan dong hua) and Stemonae
Radix (bai bu) for chronic Lung heat cough that is marked
by blood-streaked sputum.
- Clears the Heart and calms the spirit: for such symptoms
as intractable low-grade fever, insomnia, restlessness, and
irritability in the aftermath of a febrile disease. Also for
palpitations brought on by insufficiency of qi and yin.
-With Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) for palpita
tions, irritability, insomnia, and dark, scanty urine due to
lingering heat, as in Lily Bulb and Rehmannia Decoction
(bai he di huang tang).
-With Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) for irritability
and mental disorientation due to yin deficiency or lingering
heat in the late stages of a febrile disease, as in Lily Bulb and
Anemarrhena Decoction (bai he zhi mlu tang).
englishReference.commentary:
Sweet and moistening, Lilii Bulbus (bai he) enriches the
Lung yin; slightly bitter and cold, it clears the Heart, drains
and clarifies while directing downward. It is best for moist--
ening the Lungs to stop coughs, and clearing the Heart
to quiet the spirit. Rectification of the Meaning of Materia
Medica says that it is
slightly sweet, bland and neutral; moderate in effect.
Because it is sweet and moderate,it can tonify and augment
the qi and blood, moisten the Lungs to eliminate cough.
settle the corporeal soul, quiet the spirit, drive out anxiety.
and stop palpitations.
It is used to treat dry cough due to Lung dryness or cough
ing of blood due to deficiency consumption. It also treats
mental disorientation, palpitations, insomnia, and an inde.-
finable feeling of constraint due to yin deficiency, or to
disharmony of the nutritive and protective qi following an
externally-contracted illness.
In the earliest record of its properties, the Divine
Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica states that it is
"sweet, neutral, governs pathogenic qi, abdominal distention and Heart pain, facilitates [passage of] stool and urine,
tonifies the middle and augments qi." The Miscellaneous
Records of Famous Physicians adds that it "eliminates
edema, abdominal distention, focal distention, chills and
fever, pain all over the body, difficult lactation, and painful
obstruction of the throat."
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica,
Zhang Shan-Lei explains:
Lilii Bulbus (bai he) is sweet and cold, and also a bitter,
slippery, and moistening substance. Although the Classic
of the Materia Medica calls it sweet and neutral, its main
indications, ancient and modern, suggest that its nature is
to clear heat, drain, and direct downward. When the Classic
of the Materia Medica and Miscellaneous Records state that
it governs pathogenic qi' andgoverns chills and fevers
they are referring to a heat pathogen that has collected. [As
to its treatment of the other symptoms] they are all due to
its slippery, moistening ability to open up areas of clumping, and its unblocking, facilitating, draining, and guiding
actions. The Classic of the Materia Medica also says that it
tonifies the middle and augments the qi, and when texts
like the Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Zi state that it also quiets
the spirit and strengthens the resolve, this refers to elimination of pathogenic heat and recovery of normal qi-it does
not mean that sweet, cold substances tonify the qi.
The most well-known application of this herb is illustrated
in Essentials from the Golden Cabinet in relation to what is
called lily bulb disorder ( bai he zheng), characterized by mental disorientation, irritability, insomnia,
palpitations, bitter taste, and dark, scanty urine. This usually
occurs following an externally-contracted disease. Rectifi
cation of the Meaning of the Golden Cabinet explains:
This pattern is a result of a pathogenic influence interacting with the nutritive level of the Heart and the protective
level of the Lungs. The Heart governs the hundred vessels.
the Lungs govern the transformation of qi throughout the
body. ... The reason that Lilii Bulbus (bai he) is chosen in
the treatment method... is that the qi of Lilii Bulbus (bai
he) is extremely clearing, and enters the Lungs; its flavor is
slightly bitter, and enters the Heart; so it is most capable of
clearing the upper burner, and thus serves as the chief.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH REHMANNIAE RADIX (sheng di huang)
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) both cools heat in the
blood, which disturbs the spirit, and nourishes the Kidney
yin, which supports the Heart yin and prevents Heart fire
from blazing. Lili Bulbus (bai he) nourishes the Lung yin,

12 /. Tonifying Herbs
while draining pathogenic heat from the upper burner.
This combination cools the Heart and treats both qi
and blood, as the Heart governs the nutritive qi, which
moves inside the vessels with the blood, while the Lungs
govern the protective qi, which moves outside the vessels.
If pathogenic heat disturbs the vessels, for example, following a warm pathogen disease, the spirit, which relies on the
blood for its residence, can also be disturbed. This combi.-
nation can restore harmony.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GLEHNIAE/ADENOPHORAE RADIX (sha shen)
Because both herbs nourish the yin and clear the Lungs,
moisten dryness, and stop the coughing, each of them
is often used in the treatment of dry coughs. However.
between them, Glehniae/Adenophorae Radix (sha shen) is
better for augmenting the Stomach, generating fluids, and
stopping thirst, while also clearing the Lungs and expelling
phlegm to stop the cough. By contrast, Lilii Bulbus (bai he)
moistens the Lungs and-stops the coughing of blood due
to deficiency consumption, but also clears the Heart and
quiets the spirit.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
"Excels at unblocking stool and urine, [thus] should not be
taken by those with cold in the middle sinking downward."
(Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)
"In the early stage of coughs one should not be overly hasty
to use it." (Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica)
"Wind-cold fettering the exterior with cough due to the
inability of the Lung qi to disseminate: this is a particularly
forbidden herb [for that]." (Rectification of the Meaning of
Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "hundred meetings"
Both wild-crafted and cultivated, the bulb of several related
Species of Lilium are used as this herb (see
englishReference.alternateSpecies:
below). The small and thick sections of the wild-crafted plant are preferred for medicinal
purposes, as it is rather bitter flavored; the larger, thinner.
and sweeter sections of the cultivated plants are preferred
for culinary purposes. The former is called wild lily (f
835
ye bai he), but it grows slowly, and the supply is limited
Without further preparation, the bulbs are called unprepared lily sheng bai he.Usually the herb is
presented as curved sections of the bulb, which are called
lily slices(Hbai he pian),or dry lilygan bai
he). Because it is sweet, it is not an uncommon food item,
and is known as sweet lily ( tian bai he). In the past,
lilies produced in the north were used as food, while those
produced in the south were used for medicinal purposes.
The white-flowered lilies grown in Xuanzhou were preferred. Hence the names southern lily(nan bai he
white flower lily ( bai hua bai he), and Xuan lily
( xuan bai he. However, some commentators feel
that no matter whether wild-crafted or cultivated, as long as
the bulbs are big, white, fleshy, and heavy, they are good for
medicinal use, although they should not be stored too long.
These qualities have given rise to the names large lily (
da bai he and new lily(#xin bai he.
>HONEY-PREPARED LILYmi zhi bai he
Honey is first slowly brought to a boil, and the froth and
any residual wax or extraneous material scraped from the
surface. The honey is then poured through a filter, returned
to the wok, and again brought to a boil, which is main.
tained at 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles and the
honey no longer stretches between the fingers.
Boiling water is then added to thin the honey, which
is slowly poured over the bulb sections, and briefly left
covered. They are then dry-fried at a low temperature until
deep yellow and no longer sticky to the touch. This is also
known as prepared lilyzhi bai he,honey lily
mi bai he), or dry-fried lily (k chao bai he): This
method of preparation strengthens the ability of the herb to
moisten the Lungs and stop the coughs, as well as its ability
to tonify the Lung qi. It is therefore particularly appropriate
for chronic cough due to Lung deficiency.

englishReference.keyCharacteristics: cools the blood, stops bleeding, clears heat in the Lungs and Stomach, promotes urination
englishReference.cautions: Use with caution in those with cold from deficiency of the Spleen and Stomach.
englishReference.actions:
Cools the blood and stops bleeding: for the chaotic movement of hot blood with such symptoms as nosebleed, vomiting blood, coughing of blood, and blood in the urine.
- With Nelumbinis Nodus rhizomatis (ou jie) and Cirsii
Herba (xido jl) for heat-induced nosebleed, bloody urine.
or coughing of blood. Most effective if the fresh juice of
these herbs is used.
- With Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) and Poria (ft
ling) for blood in the urine due to heat, even with significant underlying deficiency.
along with thirst and dark urine in the later stages of warm
pathogen diseases.
englishReference.commentary:
Sweet and cold, Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mao gen) enters
the Lung, Stomach, Small Intestine, and Bladder channels
to clear latent lurking heat, cool the blood, and stop bleed.
ing. It also benefits the Stomach and alleviates thirst, cools
heat, and promotes urination. Its sweetness is not cloying, its coldness is not harmful to the Stomach, and when
it promotes urination, this does not injure the yin, but
rather leads heat downward and out of the body through
the urine. For all of these reasons it is an excellent herb for
treating bleeding in the upper or lower body due to heat,
cough due to Lung heat, and damp-heat leading to painful
urinary dribbling. The primary types of bleeding for which
it is used include vomiting blood, nosebleed, and blood in
the urine, for which it is especially effective.
Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mdo gen) is cold, cooling, and
very sweet in flavor, able to clear heat in the blood aspect
without injuring with dryness, and is also neither cloying
nor sticky. It cools the blood without any worry that it will
cause accumulation or stagnation--it can also unblock
blocked urination due to painful urinary dribbling and treat
blood in the urine. (Rectification of the Meaning of Materia
Medica)
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting
the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun observed:

580 10 / Herbs that Regulate the Blood
[Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mdo gen)]is sweet in flavor, cool.
ing by nature, holiow in the center with nodes; and the
most excellent thing for venting and bringing out heat con
strained within the Organs, drawing out the
englishReference.toxicity:
of pox
and rashes to the exterior. It is also excellent for facilitating
urine that is painful and difficult to pass, and scanty due
to heat, with abdominal distention and generalized edema.
Moreover, it enters the Lungs and clears heat to alleviate
cough and calm wheezing. Because its flavor is sweet, and
when the fresh root is chewed it is full of juice, it is able to
enter the Stomach and enrich the yin in order to generate
fluids and alleviate thirst. It treats heat in both the Lungs
and Stomach, coughing of blood; spitting up of blood,
nosebleed, and blood in the urine, but for marked therapeutic effect, the fresh root must be used.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is acrid, sweet, and very cold,
cooling heat in the Lungs and Stomach, while also releasing the muscle layer at the exterior to encourage the venting of the pathogen. Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mao gen) is
sweet and cold, cools heat, generates fluids, and also helps
vent constrained heat deep in the blood aspect and in the
organs. It can also cool blood and promote urination.
Together they complement each other to provide a
very cooling effect which reduces irritability, generates
fluids, and stops thirst. The advantage of this pair is that in
cooling, the yin is not injured, and in generating fluids, the
Stomach is not encumbered by greasy substances.
This pair is often used for a persistent fever from ?
warm pathogen disease, or the later stages of warm pathogen diseases with remnants of fever, thirst, and dark urine
It can also be used for excessive heat in the summertime
opening the pores such that sweating injures the fluids,
leading to thirst, irritability, and darkish urine.
> WITH PHRAGMITIS RHIZOMA (lu gen)
Both substances are sweet, cold, and moistening, and both
enter the Lung and Stomach channels.Phragmitis Rhizoma
(lui gen) is hollow and moist, and tends to clear qi-level heat;
it enriches the fluids and clears Lung heat in order to stop
coughs, while also cooling the Stomach, generating fluids.
and alleviating nausea. Together they form a strong heatclearing pair, since heat in both the blood and qi aspects are
addressed. Both herbs also support the fluids
This combination is admired because, while clearing
heat, the yang is not injured, and while generating fluids;
they do not cause pathogenic influences to be retained
Both herbs are mild in nature, and although cooling
they are not cloying. This combination is widely used for
various types of heat disorders, and can be used either as a
stand-alone pair, or as the basis of a small prescription, if
the condition is not too severe. It will be even more effec.
tive if both herbs are fresh.
> WITH REHMANNIAE RADIX (sheng di huang);
see page 122

see page 591

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
This is inappropriate if the bleeding results from cold from
deficiency. The same applies if there is diarrhea due to cold,
or vomiting of phiegm-dampness due to cold in the center,
or fever from stasis of thin mucus. (Harm and Benefit in the
Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
The unprepared herb is best for heat disorders with Iack
of fluids.
>FRESH IMPERATA (###R xian mao gen)
The newly-harvested imperata is cleaned and sliced. In the
past it was called unprepared imperata ( # #& sheng mdo
gen), but this phrase now refers to the unprepared dried
herb. The fresh herb is sweet, cold, and moistening, with
all of its properties fresh and strong. It is therefore stronger
than the dried herb at cooling heat and generating fluids,
cooling the blood, and stopping bleeding. It can be used for
bleeding of any type from the Lungs, Stomach, or Bladder.
If the fresh herb is pulped and pressed for juice, it is
called imperata juice ( bai mao gen zhiFine
Formulas for Women recommends the fresh juice alone as a
treatment for nosebleed due to blood heat.
>CHARRED IMPERATA(##R mao gen tan)
The herb is placed in a calcining container and cooked
with high heat until black. It is then sprayed with water to
quickly cool it, then dried. This increases its ability to stop
bleeding, but reduces its ability to cool heat.
>IMPERATA FLOWER (# mao hua)
The flower of this plant is sweet and cold; it cools heat
in the blood and stops bleeding. It is primarily used for
blood heat patterns with bleeding from the upper part of
the body, such as nosebleed and coughing or vomiting of
blood. It is both taken internally and applied topically

englishReference.commentary:
Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shdo) is bitter, sour, and cool
it enters the Liver channel where its sourness inhibits the
yin. The Liver favors dispersal, and this quality is, in effect,
tonified by an acrid flavor which encourages dispersal;
conversely; a sour-inhibiting action has the effect of drain
ing the Liver. At the same time, Paeoniae Radix alba (bai
shao) also cools and nourishes the blood; thus, it could be
classified with equal validity as an herb that extinguishes
wind, owing to its ability to nourish Liver blood and soften
the Liver, thereby preventing the floating ascent of Liver
yang. Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
observes:
The slight bitterness of Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shdo
tonifies yin, while its slight sourness restrains and inhibits.
Because sourness travels to the Liver, short-term use will
tonify the Liver; [but] because the Liver's nature favors dis
persal and is averse to inhibition, this sourness is also used
to curb the Liver. This is why it is said that Paeoniae Radix
alba (bai shdo) both tonifies and drains.
The Liver governs the sinews, which cramp and spasm
if unsupported by the Liver blood. This herb tonifies
the Liver blood and thereby relieves pain due to acutely
cramped sinews, or other pain associated with Liver blood
deficiency, such as in the flanks and abdomen. The Liver
stores the blood, and reduced blood storage can affect

754 12 / Tonifying Herbs
other important blood organs, such as the Heart, and the
sea of blood', which refers to the Womb and its associated vessels. If the Heart lacks the support of Liver blood,
palpitations and insomnia may result; if the sea of blood
lacks the support of Liver blood, menstruation can become
irregular and cause infertility or dysmenorrhea. All of these
disorders are appropriate for treatment with Paeoniae
Radix alba (bai shao). Thus, one could look at the softening
aspect of this herb as having an "unwinding" function, due
to its dual tonification and drainage, that allows the Liver
to soften up enough to accept the blood and store it, much
like a sponge soaks up water.
This herb also enters the Spleen channel and sup.
ports the Spleen when it is accosted by rebellious Liver qi.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes that it
"tonifies the blood and augments the true yin of the Liver
and Spleen. In order to inhibit and contain the chaotic
dispersal of the Spleen qi, or the unrestrained transverse
rebellion of the Liver qi, Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) (is
the herb to use]." It goes on to say that this herb is "bitter
and slightly sour, [so that it] augments the yin of the greater
yin Spleen, while holding in lax and dispersed great qi (
da qi), and also augmenting the Liver yin and quieting
its transverse rebellion."
Because of its ability to cool, nourish, and restrain the
yin, this herb is often used as an assistant in the treatment of
sweating from various causes, such as spontaneous sweating from disharmony at the nutritive and protective levels,
and nightsweats due to yin deficiency. Seeking Accuracy in
the Materia Medica notes that, "together with Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gul zhi), it inhibits sweating due to wind (pathogen]; together with Astragali Radix (huang qi) and Ginseng
Radix (ren shen), it restrains sweating from deficiency."
englishReference.combinations:
>WrTH GLYCYRRHIZAE RADIX (gan cao)
The Liver is a hard, "edgy' organ and its qi has a tendency to
rebel transversely. Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) preserves
the yin, softens the Liver, and alleviates pain. It is effective
in moderating the wayward inclinations of the Liver qi and
preserving the Liver yin; this is what is meant by softening of the Liver. Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao) tonifies and
augments the qi of the middle burner, especially that of
the Spleen. Together these herbs regulate the relationship
between the Liver and Spleen and nourish the sinews.
>WITH SCUTELLARIAE RADIX (huang qin)
This combination was first cited in a formula from Discussion of Cold Damage, Scutellaria Decoction (huang qin
tang), to treat dysenteric disorders with abdominal pain
due to heat entering the interior. Scutellariae Radix (huang
qin) is bitter and.cold, and drains heat in the Large
Intestine, while Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) is bit.

Literal English translation: "white peony"
This herb is produced from cultivated Paeonia lactiflora,

12 / Tonifying Herbs
with the bark removed; the same species is used for
Paeoniae Radix rubra (cht shao), which is wild-crafted, and
the bark is generally retained. Without further processing, the herb is known as unprepared white peony (#.
sheng bai shao) or just white peony( bai shao. In
general, thicker, larger, and cleaner roots are considered
superior. For this reason, large white peony ( da bai
shdo) is often specified.
DRY-FRIED WHITE PEONY chao bai shao
The sliced roots are dry-fried until slightly yellow, or dry
fried in heated bran. It is then also known as processed
white peony root ( zhi bai shao). This method of
preparation reduces its cold property, but enhances its
ability to nourish the blood, harmonize the functioning of
the collaterals, moderate the Spleen, relax the Liver, and
alleviate pain. Transforming the Significance of Medicinal
Substances observes:
Its flavor is bitter and sour, its nature cold--not originally
a Spleen channel herb. The process of dry-frying eliminates
its [cold] nature: if the Spleen qi disperses, it can restrain it,
if the Stomach qi is hot, it can inhibit it; this is used to drain
pathogenic Liver [activity], in order to moderate the Spleen
qi in the middle burner.
It is often used for diarrhea with abdominal pain due to
either Spleen deficiency or Spleen and Liver disharmony.
>EARTH FRIED WHITE PEONY(k tu chao bai shao)
Finely powdered Terra flava usta (zao xin tu) is heated in
a wok, then slices of the herb are added and stirred until
their surface turns earth-colored; the earth is then sifted
out. This method of preparation leads it directly into the
Spleen and Stomach, quieting the Spleen, stopping diarrhea, harmonizing the Stomach, and alleviating nausea. It is
often used for nausea or diarrhea with abdominal pain due
to Spleen and Stomach deficiency.
>WINE-FRIED WHITE PEONYjiu chao bai shao
or i jiu bai shao
The sliced roots are mixed with yellow rice wine, left cov
ered briefly as the wine is absorbed, then dry-fried at a
medium temperature until dry. This method of prepara
tion moderates both its cold nature and its sour flavor,
and gives it a mild ability to invigorate the blood, so that
within its tonification is the idea of moving dispersal. Zhu
Zhen-Heng (also known as Zhu Dan-Xi) observed, "In the
winter months it must be used wine-fried, and also for any
abdominal pain, as this is usually due to congealed binding
in the blood vessels."
Wine-fried white peony is therefore usually used when
blood deficiency is coupled with blood stasis, or blood
755
deficiency is found with cold, which slows the movement
of blood.
>VINEGAR-FRIED WHITE PEONY
(* cu chao bai shao)
The sliced roots are mixed with rice vinegar, left covered
briefly as the vinegar is absorbed, then dry-fried at a medium temperature until dry. This method of preparation
enhances its ability to relax and soften the Liver, alleviate
pain, and inhibit bleeding, and so is often used to nourish
the blood and tonify the Liver, or combined with other
herbs that stop bleeding in order to treat disorders such as
irregular or continuous uterine bleeding due to Liver agita
tion destabilizing the Penetrating and Conception vessels.
As a variant method of dry-frying, it is interesting to
note that in the Convenient Reader of Materia Medica,
Zhang Bing-Cheng stated that "when it is soaked in a
decoction of Cinnamomi Cortex (rou gut) and then fried
until dry, it greatly calms the Liver.
>CHARRED WHITE PEONY(bai shao tan)
The sliced roots are dry-fried until the surface is blackened
and the interior is scorched yellow. Charred white peony
is best for restraining the blood and stopping bleeding
but also helps reduce diarrhea in dysenteric disorders. It
is somewhat stronger in its ability to stop bleeding thar
is vinegar-fried white peony, but is less able to relax and
soften the Liver.

englishReference.commentary:
Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) enters the Lung, Stomach.
and Kidney channels. It is bitter, but not drying, so it directs
downward; it is salty, and can thus enter the blood, and also
cold, enabling it to clear heat. These actions are performed
without injuring the yin or blood. And because blood-level
heat is cleared, the yin and blood are protected by this
herb, which is uivalent to replenishing these substances.
It cools both the heat of yin deficiency as well as that due to
pathogen
the surface wher
g the pathogenic influence toward
leased. This is useful in such cases
as prolonged low-grade fever due to a residual pathogenic
inffuence in the lat es of a febrile disorder: heat in the
blood is cooled directly and also by venting.
This herb cools the Lungs and facilitates the passage of
urine, enabling it to treat painful urinary dribbling in which
the urine is scanty and burning. Its functions in treating
urinary disorders and sores are of secondary importance,
however. Heat from deficiency following childbirth, painful urinary dribbling with blood in the urine, early periods
due to heat in the blood--all of these conditions are appropriately treated with this herb. It also can be used for cough
due to Lung heat, especially if associated with a low-grade
fever.

2 I Herbs that Clear Heat
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica elaborates on the nature of this herb:
The Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica
states that the nature of Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) is
neutral, but because it primarily treats warm and febrile
pathogens, thisneutral' should be cold'.Miscellaneous
Records of Famous Physicians does in fact call it greatly
cold'this should be its basic nature.... All bitter-cold
herbs tend to be drying, except Cynanchi atrati Radix
(bai wei). Although cold, it does not harm the yin fluids,
essence, or blood. Thus, its main indications all relate to
heat at the blood level rather than to any damp-heat disor.
der. It can be regarded as possessing a mild, inherent yinenriching quality within its main heat-clearing actions. This
is why ancient formulas used it so often for women.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH LYCII CORTEX (di gu pi)
Cynanchi atrati Radix (bdi wei) is bitter, salty, and very
cold, clearing heat and cooling the blood. It can be used for
cooling heat from deficiency, but also for pathogenic heat
from excess in the interior. Lycii Cortex (di gu pi) is sweet,
bland, and cold in nature, and is best for cooling steaming
bones and heat from deficiency. Both herbs enter the blood
Ievel.
There are differences between them, however. Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) moves into the yang brightness
channel and is thus best at clearing heat from the earthlevel tissues (the muscles) from which the heat is vented
toward the surface. It also enters and cools the blood in
the Penetrating and Conception vessels. Materia Medica
Arranged by Channel says that Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai
wei) is "bitter, salty, and cold; an herb of the yang brightness, Penetrating, and Conception vessels. Facilitates yin
qi, clears blood heat, adjusts menstruation." Lycii Cortex
(di gu pi), on the other hand, travels in the Lung and Kidney
channels, cooling the Lungs and clearing internal heat.
Together these two herbs vent and clear internal heat.
strongly reducing heat from deficiency. Thus, the pair is
often used for tidal fevers and steaming bones due to yin
deficiency. This combination makes an excellent foundaton for prescriptions designed for patients with low-grade
fevers from unidentified causes, and no other symptoms.
englishReference.comparisons:
> Vs. MoUTAN CoRTEX (mu dan pi) and LYCII CoRTEX
(di gu pi)
All of these herbs cool the blood and reduce heat from
deficiency, making them suitable for treating the heat from
yin deficiency associated with consumptive disorders with
low-grade fever. The differences are that both Moutan
225
Cortex (mui dan pi) and Lycii Cortex (di gu pi) are also able
to reduce heat from excess at the blood level--not just
heat from deficiency; they are often used for bleeding in
the upper or lower body due to heat from excess causing
chaotic movement of blood. Moutan Cortex (mu dan pi)
dispels blood stasis, which the other two herbs cannot do,
and is also appropriate for steaming bones and consumptive heat disorder without sweating, while Lycii Cortex (di
gu pi) treats the same heat disorders with sweating.
The ability of Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) to cool
the Lungs is similar to that of Lycii Cortex (di gu pi), but
Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) can vent residual pathogenic heat injuring the yin in the later stage of a febrile
disorder, which the other two herbs cannot do. While it
does not have the blood-invigorating properties of Moutan
Cortex (mu dan pi), it can facilitate urination.
>Vs. STELLARIAE RADIX (yin chai hu) and
ARTEMISIAE ANNUAE HERBA (qing hao)
The ability of Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei) to vent
pathogenic heat is similar to that of Artemisiae annuae
Herba (qing hao), but the latter herb cannot cool the Lungs,
nor does it facilitate urination. Stellariae Radix (yin chai
hu) does not vent heat, and thus can only cool the blood
internally--it does not have the ability to vent blood heat
outward like Cynanchi atrati Radix (bai wei).
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
In New Compilation of Materia Medica, Chen Shi-Duo cautions: "This is an important assistant or envoy herb, but is
not suitable for chief or deputy status. ... The dose should
not exceed two qian [6g] to avoid injuring the Stomach
with its intense cold." Dry-fried cynanchi can be used for
patients with a weak Spleen and Stomach.

highest quality, and are known as eastern cynanchi (*
# dong bai wei).

226
>FRESH CYNANCHI (# xian bai wei)
2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
The newly-harvested roots are cleaned and immediately
dispensed. The actions of the fresh herb are somewhat better for cooling heat toxin and reducing scrofula. It is often
applied externally by itself as a pulped herb.
>HONEY-PREPARED CYNANCHI(zhi bai wei)
This is fried or baked with cooked honey until dark yel
low, then sprayed with water to cool it. This method of
preparation focuses its actions on the Lung channel in the

>DRY-FRIED CYNANCHI (# chao bai wei)
Here the herb is baked or dry-fried with moderate heat
until scorch marks appear or the herb turns a burnt yellow color. This method somewhat moderates its cooling
nature, rendering it more appropriate for yang-deficient
patients or those with Spleen and Stomach weakness.

[It] expels dampness to augment the qi, harmonizes the
middle to tonify the yang, reduces illness, drives out water,
generates fluids to alieviate thirst, stops diarrhea and dysen.
teric disorders, and reduces swelling of the legs and calves
due to dampness.
The reference to its ability to generate fluids is drawn from
the Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica
and seems puzzling, but Hidden Aspects of Materia Medice
explains:
Since Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (baf zhu) is
drying, how can the {Divine Husbandman's] Classic of the
Materia Medica say that it generates fluids? It is because the
Spleen is averse to dampness. Once Spleen dampness pre.
vails, the qi is unable to transform: from where might fluids
be generated? Thus it is said: the Bladder is the dwelling
of the yin fluids and yang fluids, from which they exit [by
virtue of] qi transformation. [This function of qi transformation explains] the present usage of Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (baf zhu) to dry dampness and allow the
qi to circulate, so that the fluids, following qi transformation, might be generated.
This may also explain a modern usage of this herb in which
a large dose of Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai
zhu), either by itself or combined with Rehmanniae Radix
(sheng di huang) and Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma), is
used to improve the transportive function of the Spleen in
the treatment of constipation, by unblocking the bowels.
The dosage for this purpose is 60-120g.
This herb has other notable qualities: it halts spontaneous sweating, and calms the fetus in pregnancy. Most
materia medica texts agree that the spontaneous sweating referred to here is the result of dampness obstructing
the flesh and preventing the harmonious interaction of
the nutritive and protective qi; the interstices and pores
then become disordered, and sweating occurs randomly
This herb clears earth dampness--the earth includes the
muscles and flesh--and thereby restores harmony and
halts the sweating.

28 12 I Tonifying Herbs
Regarding the ability of this herb to calm the fetus
in pregnancy, Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica
explains: "Fetal qi is linked to the Spleen; if the Spleen is
deficient then the Girdle [vessel] has no support. Thus
miscarriage readily occurs." Atractylodis macrocephalae
Rhizoma (bai zhu) is usually combined with Scutellariae
Radix (huang qin) for this purpose, as that herb deals with
the other major cause of miscarriage--heat.

englishReference.comparisons:
> DIFFERENT TYPES OF ATRACTYLODES
There are three herbs known as atractylodes (# zhu) in
Chinese medicine. One is Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang
zhu), literally "dark atractylodes." The other two are types
of Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu): "white
atractylodes" (regular white atractylodes) and "winter
white atractylodes." All three herbs dry dampness and
strengthen the Spleen. However, Atractylodis Rhizoma
(cang zhu) more powerfully dries dampness and induces
sweating, and is used for externally-contracted cold-dampness causing headache, a heavy sensation in the body,
lethargy, aching limbs and joints, chills and fever but no
sweating; and also for wind-dampness painful obstruction
when dampness predominates. Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu), on the other hand, more powerfully
tonifies the Spleen qi, stops sweating, and calms the fetus.
Winter white atractylodes does dry dampness, but is also
moistening, such that the dryness is not extreme; it does
not, however, alleviate diarrhea as well as the usual prepa
ration of Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu).
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica,
Zhang Shan-Lei observes:
Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (baf zhu) and
Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) were not differentiated in
ancient times, but now they are separate. As a result, whenever the ancients discussed drying dampness and driving
out water [in connection with this herb], we must now
use Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) from Maoshan [Mt.
Mao in Jiangsu province] as a substitute;to tonify and aug
ment the Spleen and Stomach, Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu) should be used. As for that [herb]
known presently as winter white atractylodes, it is moist in
texture and aromatic, so that it has considerable power to
strengthen the transportive aspects of the Spleen yang while
nourishing the Stomach yin. This aroma prevails, [so that]
it does not cause epigastric fullness, and is truly a specific
remedy for strengthening the Spleen and augmenting the
Stomach.
> Vs. JUJUBAE FRUCTUS (da zao); see page 731
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
The five organs are all yin. However, all the average person
knows is that to tonify the Spleen, which is a damp earth
organ, dampness must be dried, and that when dampness
is expelled the Spleen is strengthened, and that this is toni.
fication. They do not know that to use [this herb] when the
Spleen does not have pathogenic dampness is to adversely
dry the yin and yang fluids of the Spleen patient, which
injures the Spleen yin. What kind of tonification is that?
Because this is such an easy mistake to make, it is especially
posted here to make it known. (Harm and Benefit in the
Materia Medica)

: Nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit: for irritability.
insomnia, forgetfulness, and palpitations with anxiety due

from deficiency, vertigo, forgetfulness, and insomnia

due to blood or yin deficiency.

Semen (he tao ren) for constipation in the elderly or in

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet and neutral with a gentle, harmonious nature, the
sweetness of Platycladi Semen (bai zi ren) enriches and
Heart channel, it nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit;
entering the Kidneys it tonifies the true yin and moistens
Kidney dryness; entering the Large Intestine, it moistens
the Intestines and unblocks stool. It is commonly used for
anxiety, palpitations, and insomnia with dream-disturbed
sleep due to Heart blood deficiency failing to nourish the
spirit. It is also important for dry stools and constipation
due to yin and blood deficiency. When the Kidney yin is
exhausted, with sensations of heat, weakness in the knees
and lower back, and amenorrhea due to yin and blood
deficiency, Platycladi Semen (bai zi ren) can be used as an
assistant herb
The Grand Materia Medica states that it
has a nature that is neither cold nor drying; its sweet flavor
tonifies, its acrid flavor moistens, with a clear, fragrant
aroma that penetrates the Heart and Kidneys, and aug.
ments the Spleen and Stomach---[for all of these reasons]]
it is considered in the top grade of herbs [in the Divine
Husbandman's categories]. It should be used in prescriptions for enriching and nourishing.
Zhang Jie-Bin, however, points out that the herb's tonifying
actions are limited. As an advocate of warm tonification
he describes Platycladi Semen (bai zi ren as sweet and
neutral, with a slightly cooling nature." In Rectification of
the Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang notes:
In sum, it is cooling and aromatic with a moistening, slip
pery nature, and although it is excellent for enriching the
yin and nourishing the blood, if one wishes to'cultivate and
tonify the fundamentals, this is not the strong point of a
cooling herb.
Because the herb enters both the Heart and Kidney channels and moistens,it has been used as an aid to hair growth
particularly in those cases associated with blood deficiency
and exhaustion of essence. One of its preparations involves
combining it with Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui)
grinding both herbs into a powder, and adding honey to
make pills which are taken in doses of 6-9g, three times a
day.

yin and blood and stopping nightsweats. This combination

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
When the unprepared seeds are desired, for example, for
their intestinal moistening action, this is specified in the
prescription by the term unprepared biota seeds (-7
[= sheng bai zi ren). The raw seeds have an oily aroma
however, that may cause nausea in patients with weak
digestion. For these patients, dry-fried biota seeds (%h # -7
= chao bai zi ren) are recommended.
>DRY-FRIED BIOTA SEEDS (k#6 71= chao bai zi ren)
The seeds are dry-fried at a moderate temperature until the
oil turns yellow and a slightly scorched aroma is perceived.
This method of preparation moderates and harmonizes
the herb's intestine-moistening action, and eliminates its
tendency to cause nausea.
> DEFATTED BIOTA SEED, lit. biota Seed frost
(+-= bai zi ren shuang)
The seeds are crushed into a paste, then placed between
layers of absorbent cloth or paper which are wrapped up
tightly. After steaming thoroughly, the package is pressed
to extract the oil, then the cloth or paper is replaced and the
procedure is repeated until no more oil can be extracted,
and the seeds fail to adhere together in the shape of a small
cake. They are then finely ground. This method of preparation completely eliminates their tendency to cause loose
stools or nausea, and is most often used in the treatment of
insomnia or disturbance of the Heart spirit in patients with]
Spleen deficiency. These are also known as defatted biota
kernels ((=# bai ren shuang).

Glehniae Radix (bei sha shen) is heavy, firm in texture.
sweet, cooling, and rather greasy. It tends to clear Lung

and parched throat due to Lung dryness or heat injuring

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GLEHNIAE RADIX (bei sha shen),ADENOPHORAE
RADIX (nan sha shen),and ADENOPHORAE RADIX
RECENs (xian sha shen)
These herbs are considered the three main varieties of
sha shen. All are sweet and cold, clear heat, nourish the
yin, and generate fluids; all enter the Lungs and Stomach.
817
However, Glehniae Radix (bei sha shen) is heavier in weight
and firmer in texture and thus more strongly enriches the
yin, especially of the Stomach. Adenophorae Radix (nan
sha shen) is lighter in weight, less dense in texture, with
a slight bitterness, and thus is better at expelling phlegm,
but it still nourishes the yin and cools heat, particularly of
the Lungs. Adenophorae Radix recens (xian sha shen, lit.
fresh sha shen), is Adenophorae Radix (nan sha shen) that
has just been harvested or maintained in a fresh state. It is
thus very juicy, and especially good for clearing heat and
generating fluids.
Accordingly, for chronic cough due to Lung yin deficiency,use Adenophorae Radix (nan sha shen),particularly
if there is phlegm. If the warm or febrile disease has injured
the fluids or led to Stomach yin deficiency with intense
thirst, then Glehniae Radix (bei sha shen) is best. The two
are often combined.

Summary of
Comparative Functions
Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) and Aconiti Radix lateralis
preparata (zhi fu zi) are both used to rescue devastated yang
from collapse. Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang), however,
is more specifically indicated for treatment of cold from
deficiency of the Spleen and Stomach, and has a relatively
long-lasting effect. Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zht fu
zi) focuses more on warming and assisting the Heart and
Kidney yang; its actions are less localized, more penetrating, and more immediate.
Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zhi fu zt) is by far
the most commonly used form of aconite in present-day
Chinese medicine, as it revives the yang, tonifies the fire at
the gate of vitality, and strongly disperses cold while being
quite safe if used correctly. Aconiti Radix preparata (zht
chuan wu) is more focused on eliminating wind; its use
is limited to severe pain, as in severe painful obstruction.
Aconiti kusnezoffi Radix preparata (zhi cao wu) at present
is almost exclusively used topically for cold-damp painful
obstruction.
Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zht fu zi) and Cinnamomi Cortex (rou gui) both warm and tonify the fire at the
gate of vitality. They are used in treating yang deficiency
and cold from deficiency of the lower burner. However,
Cinnamomi Cortex (rou gul) is milder in action, more specifically indicated for treatment of lower burner disorders,
leads the fire at the gate of vitality back to its source, and has
some dispersing (i.e., diaphoretic) action. Unlike Aconiti
Radix lateralis preparata (zhi fu zi), it is therefore not used
to rescue the yang from collapse.
Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang), Evodiae Fructus (wu
zhu yu), and Alpiniae officinarum Rhizoma (gao liang
jiang) all disperse cold from the middle burner and are used
for pain and a feeling of coldness in the epigastrium. The
differences among them are that Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan
jiang) also warms the Lungs and can be used to transform
phlegm and stop coughs, while Evodiae Fructus (wu zhu
yu) also warms the lower burner and is used for cold bulging disorders or diarrhea due to cold in the lower burner.
Locally, Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) primarily warms
the Spleen and is thus used for pain and diarrhea, while
Alpiniae officinarum Rhizoma (gao liang jiang) warms the
Stomach more and is used for epigastric pain and coldness
with belching or vomiting. Evodiae Fructus (wu zhu yu)
is used more for belching and vomiting when the Liver is
involved.
Litseae Fructus (bi cheng qie), Piperis longi Fructus (bi
ba), and Zanthoxyli Pericarpium (hua jiao) all treat cold
from deficiency disorders of the middle burner. Piperis
lonigi Fructus (bi ba) is hotter and is used for cold that has
sunk deeply into the middle burner leading to abdominal
pain, nausea, and vomiting. Litseae Fructus (bi cheng qie) is
less hot, but more acrid, such that it has a strong dispersing
action which unblocks areas of qi stagnation. It is used for
qi stagnation causing pain in the trunk, or the various signs
of rebellious qi due to Stomach cold. In addition to treating
middle burner cold, Zanthoxyli Pericarpium (hua jiao) also
dries dampness and kills parasites, making it useful when
parasites are part of the clinical picture.
Both Caryophylli Flos (ding xiang) and Foeniculi Fruc.
tus (xido hut xiang) warm the middle and lower burners.
and tonify the Kidney yang. Both herbs have a signifi.
cant action in regulating the flow of qi. However, while
Caryophylli Flos (ding xiang) directs qi downward, stop
ping hiccough, Foeniculi Fructus (xido hui xiang) regulates
the flow of qi through the Liver channel, treating bulging
disorders and stopping pain.
Piperis Fructus (hu jido) is more restricted in its thera.
peutic scope than either of the two preceding herbs, as it
is limited to warming the middle burner and dispersing
Stomach cold with symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, and
abdominal pain. On the other hand, it is far more widely
used in its culinary role as pepper---both black and white.

Tonifying Herbs
ONIFYING HERBS, also called tonics, are those which
strengthen or supplement an area or physiological process of the body that is weakened or insufficient.
They also strengthen the body's defenses against disease.
Clinically, they are used in combination with herbs that
expel external pathogenic influences for disorders in which
the pathogenic influence is strong and the normal qi is
weak, a strategy called "supporting the normal and expel.
ling the pathogenic (#iE fu zheng qu xie. These
herbs assist in the recovery of those who have been ill with
chronic or degenerative disorders by strengthening the
various physiological processes of the body and supple.
menting substances which are depleted.
Tonics are used in treating patterns of deficiency of the
qi, blood, yin, and yang. For purposes of discussion, they
are presented here in accordance with which of these four
aspects they tonify, yet it is important to remember that
in the clinic, depending on the patient's presentation, the
herbs are often combined. For example, a patient with yang
deficiency usually suffers from qi deficiency as well, and the
same process may also involve yin deficiency. Moreover,
patterns of qi deficiency may evolve into yang deficiency.
The practitioner must therefore be flexible when using
these herbs.
A few words of caution should be made with regard to
tonics. It is important to remember that herbs are only one
part of the healing process. There is a tendency to suggest
to debilitated patients that taking a tonic is all that is needed
for recovery. This is not true; physical and breathing exer
cises and diet are also important, and of course sufficient
rest. What is more, tonifying herbs strengthen the pro
cesses of the body, including pathogenic processes, such
as those associated with external pathogenic influences
Thus, unless they are combined with herbs that release the
709
1
exterior, tonifying herbs should not be prescribed in case
where there are still signs of an exterior disorder. If they are.
the exterior disorder will linger on.
The practitioner should also be aware of a condition
referred to as deficient yet unable to accept tonifica
tionn xu er bu shou buThis refers to an
individual who regularly develops problems after taking
tonics. The most common are digestive problems such
as nausea, bloating, or loss of appetite. Signs of fire from
deficiency, including dry mouth and lips, irritability, and
insomnia, can also appear. These problems are usually due
to underlying stagnation, which must be dealt with before
tonification can be successful. In addition, if a tonic is given
to a patient who is not primarily deficient, a wide range
of problems can occur including indigestion, rashes, and
irritability.
Section 1
HERBS THAT TONIFY THE QI
The herbs in this section are used in treating patterns of qi
deficiency, disorders in which the functional aspects of the
body, or of a particular organ, are weak. The most common disorders are found in the Spleen and Lungs. This is
because these two yin organs are primarily responsible for
the extraction of qi from food and air, as well as the transportive functions of qi within the body.
The major symptoms of Spleen qi deficiency are lethargy, weakness in the extremities, lack of appetite, abdominal distention or pain, and loose stools or diarrhea.

10 12 / Tonifying Herbs
Furthermore, because the Spleen qi is the main component
of the middle qi---which both holds in the fluids and holds
the structures of the body in place-qi deficiency often
underlies such problems as generalized superficial edema
and prolapses.
The major symptoms of Lung qi deficiency are shortness of breath, shallow breathing, dyspnea on exertion,
weak voice, pallid complexion, and spontaneous sweating.
Because the qi is responsible in part for the generation and
movement of blood, these herbs are also often used in treating patterns of blood deficiency.
Herbs that tonify the qi are generally sweet and rich ir
nature. Excessive or chronic use can readily lead to a sense
of fullness in the chest and diaphragm, or sensations of
heat. Clinically speaking, it is therefore important that they
be combined with small amounts of herbs that move and
regulate the qi.

englishReference.commentary:
Trionycis Carapax (bie jia) is salty, slightly cold, and
heavy in weight. Because it is derived from an animal, it is
considered to be 'a substance of sympathy between blood
and flesh# xue rou you qing zhi pin),and
thus strongly tonifies the yin fluids. Being heavy in weight
it subdues the yang. And because it is slightly cooling, it
clears heat. For these reasons it excels at enriching the yin
to anchor the yang and eliminate heat from deficiency
and is thus used to treat yin deficiency leading to steaming
bones or ascendant Liver yang, either due to injury to the
yin and blood following a warim-heat pathogen disease, or
chronic illness injuring the yin and blood. It is also used
for internal stirring of wind from deficiency, resulting from
the inability of the Liver and Kidneys to nourish the sinews.
leading in mild cases to tremor of the hands and feet, and
in more severe cases, to convulsions. Traditionally, for the
purpose of enriching the yin and subduing the yang, it
should be used in its unprepared form.
When vinegar-fried, it enters the blood level of the
Liver channel with an enhanced ability to promote movement, and its salty quality endows it with the ability to
soften areas of hardness and clumping, such as mobile and
fixed abdominal masses or painless clumping in the flanks.
The New Compilation of Materia Medica says that it "excels
in attacking hard [areas], and does not deplete the qi, so it
should be used for any stubborn focal stagnation, internally
or externally, in the upper or lower [body]." Thus, traditionally, to soften areas of hardness and disperse clumps,
the vinegar-fried variety should be used.
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang Bing.
Cheng says that its "nature is fundamentally salty and cold,
enters the Liver channel and thrusts out to the collaterals
with the effect of promoting movement in stagnant lumps,
reducing heat, and subduing the yang." He goes on to
explain that it
enters the Liver because its color is green; it is salty, cold,
and nontoxic. It unblocks the channels and collaterals,
disperses stagnant blood, and is a medicinal of the terminal
yin blood level. All aquatic shells benefit the yin and subdue
the yang, and their salty, cold nature is similar--what is different is the places they enter.
The Materia Medica of Combinations states that it "travels
through the Penetrating vessel."

>Vs.OsTREAE CONCHA (mu li)
Both are heavy substances that anchor floating yang or sub
due ascendant yang. Both are salty so that they soften areas
of hardness. And both benefit the yin. However, Ostreae
Concha (mu Ii) more strongly anchors and subdues the
yang, and is astringent so that it prevents leakage of fluids
such as sweat, seminal emissions, and vaginal discharge. It
also quiets the spirit. By contrast, Trionycis Carapax (bie
jia) more strongly tonifies the yin, and is cooling at a deeper
level, treating steaming bones and nightsweats by strongly
enriching the yin, while Ostreae Concha (mu li) primarily
treats sweating through its astringent, inhibiting quality,
supported by its cool nature.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
If there is no preparation beyond being dried in the sun, it
is called unprepared soft-shelled turtle shell ( sheng
bie jia). Another common name for the soft-shelled turtle
is "round fish', hence it is also called round fish shell (
I tuan yu jia).
An ancient adage says that "The best come out of the
Yuan River in the Yue prefecture, and have nine ribs." For
this reason, ancient formulas occasionally used the term
nine ribbed soft-shelled turtle shell jiu lei bie
jia).
> VINEGAR-FRIED SOFT-SHELLED TURTLE SHELL
cu chao bie jia
Iron filings are heated in a wok at a high temperature, then
the shells are added and the temperature reduced to medium. Sand can be substituted for the iron filings. The shells
are cooked until slightly yellow, then they are removed, and
the iron filings or sand are sifted away. The shells, while hot.
are then briefly soaked in (or sprayed with) rice vinegar
rinsed with water, then dried in the sun until dry. Also
known as prepared soft-shelled turtle shell (& zhi bie
jia), this method of preparation directs the shell's actions
into the Liver, and strengthens its ability to soften areas of
hardness and disperse clumping. It is therefore appropriate
in the treatment of abdominal masses and accumulations
It also reduces the somewhat unpleasant taste of the shell.
and makes it more crisp and friable, facilitating pulveriza.
tion. Hence the name crisp soft-shelled turtle shell (
su bie jia). This method increases the solubility of the shell
in decoctions by as much as four times.

englishReference.commentary:
Arecae Semen (bing lang) is a herb of the arm and leg
yang brightness channels (Large Intestine and Stomach)
with a bitter flavor that directs downward; an acrid flavor
that disperses, and a warmth that unblocks and promotes
movement. Overall it directs the qi downward, guides out
stagnation, promotes the movement of pathological water,
and kills parasites. Poor function of the Stomach and Large
Intestine can generate dampness, phlegm, or pathogenic
water, or damp-heat can accumulate and provide fertile
ground for parasite growth. This herb is well-suited to deal
with such pathologies in these two organs

17 / Herbs that Expel Parasites
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica states that it
enters the chest and abdomen to break up stagnant qi without ceasing: it enters the Intestines and Stomach to drive
phlegm lumps directly downward. It can regulate all herbs
to travel downward, driving out water and attacking leg qi
.- because its nature drives downward and sinks, it can]
drive out parasites and travel downward.
Disseminating, unblocking, and promoting movement.
Arecae Semen (bing lang) acts on accumulations of many
types, dispersing qi stagnation, promoting movement in
blood stasis, transforming phlegm, facilitating elimination
of pathogenic water, reducing food stagnation, unblocking
stool, and driving out parasites.
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang BingCheng remarks:
This substance specifically and primarily directs the qi
downward. It can be used whenever the qi of any of the
Organs in the body is congealed, stagnant, and fails to dis.
seminate--there is no need to be confined by 'enters the
Stomach and Intestines'.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Generally cultivated, this herb was previously imported
into China from south and southeast Asia, hence the alter.
niative name, southern ocean seeds (# # -7 hai nan zi). It
is now grown in southern China. Collected in winter and
spring when ripe, the seeds are soaked in water until thoroughly moistened, then sliced and dried in the sun. This is
known as areca slices (# H bing lang pian) to differentiate it from the also common practice of simply crushing the
seeds into chunks. The red veins visible against the white
matrix inthe slices give it the name fiowery areca (t#p
hua bing lang)
Some varieties of Areca yield a smaller pointed seed
known as chicken heart areca ($# ji xin bing lang)
or pointed areca (# jian bing lang or jian bing)
Some consider these to be of better quality, although the
official drug is Areca catechu. In Convenient Reader of
Materia Medica, Zhang Bing-Cheng explains:
There is one type with a long and pointy shape called
pointed areca or chicken heart areca, and another type that
is round and flat called big belly areca (# da fu
bing lang)... Although the nature, flavor, and therapeutic
actions are the same, the pointy one is superior.
>WHITE ARECA (4 bai bing lang)
The growing season for Areca catechu is quite long, and
generally divided into three periods: early autumn, early
winter, and mid-winter. White areca are the fresh, tender
fruit of early autumn, boiled in water, baked dry, then
sliced. They are also known as large white slices ( H da
bai pian). White areca is particularly effective in driving qi
downward and promoting urination, but its ability to kill
parasites is relatively weak. As the adage says, "The white
seeds are acrid and mostly disperse qi.
>FRESH ARECA (# # # xian bing lang)
When the newly-collected fresh seeds are used (during any
growing period), their special characteristic is that they

1008 17 / Herbs that Expel Parasites
promote the movement of qi and resolve food stagnation
without injuring the yin. They also have a better parasitekilling action than the dried form. However, because they
are fresh, their use is limited to areas of Areca production.
>DRY-FRIED ARECA(k## chdo bing lang)
The sliced herb is dry-fried at a moderate temperature until
the color changes. This method of preparation slightly
reduces its strength, and is thus more appropriate for use in
older or weaker patients.
>ScORCHED ARECA (##& #F jiao bing lang)
The sliced herb is dry-fried at a high temperature until
scorch marks appear. When prepared in this manner, the
herb primarily reduces and guides out to harmonize the
Stomach qi, and is generally used for middle burner food
stagnation. In ancient times this method was discouraged. As Grandfather Lei's Discussion of Herb Preparation
explains: "When Arecae Semen (bing lang) is to be used,
first remove the base with a knife and slice it thinly. Do not
expose it to fire for fear that it will lose its power. If applied
when cooked, one might as well not use it. Modern
research has shown that the alkaloid content is indeed
higher when it has not been dry-fried or scorched.
>DATE ARECA(## zao bing lang)
These are the immature dried betel areca which resemble
dried and withered dates. They are also known as date
child areca($## zao er bing lang or # zao er
bing). They are bitter and astringent, and have the ability to
digest food stagnation, revive-from drunkenness, unbind
the chest, and stop nausea. Note that they are not considered to be therapeutically equivalent to Arecae Semen (bing
lang). Rather, they are primarily used in the treatment of
food accumulation with qi stagnation, nausea, and stifling
sensations in the chest and diaphragm.

englishReference.combinations:
> WITH ARISAEMATIS RHIZOMA PREPARATUM
(zhi tian nan xing)
Both herbs pierce and penetrate, Borneolum (bing pian)
through its concentrated acrid aroma that mobilizes and
penetrates to open the orifices and unblock closure, Arisaematis Rhizoma preparatum (zhi tian nan xing) through its
intensely acrid properties of opening, draining, penetrating, and drying, without conserving.
Together these qualities create a strong reviving combination that wakens the brain, expels wind, and opens what
is closed. This combination can be used by itself, applied
externally as a powder rubbed on the gums for wind-stroke
with clenched jaw, or in conjunction with other herbs taken
internally.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. MosCHUs (she xiang)
Both substances are acrid, aromatic, mobile, and piercing, and both open the orifices and awaken the spirit.
The two are often combined in situations involving Ioss
of consciousness, such as delirium associated with febrile
diseases, fainting due to summerheat, or wind-stroke.
Moschus (she xiang), however, more powerfully opens the
orifices and awakens the spirit; Borneolum (bing pian) has
a supporting role.
The two substances are also often used for swollen sores
due to heat toxin, but the action of Moschus (she xiang) is
in invigorating the blood, unblocking the collaterals, and
reducing and dispersing qi and blood stagnation. Hence
it is often used for hematomas or traumatic injury, or for
abdominal masses or amenorrhea due to blood stasis.
Borneolum (bing pian), on the other hand, dissipates and
disperses fire constraint so as to reduce swelling and stop
pain, and is thus used in treating sore red eyes, mouth
ulcers, and toothache.
