Zhang Xi-Chun describes the actions of this herb:
Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he) leaves are similar in
flavor and temperature to Borneolum (bing pian): they
excel at penetrating the orifices. Their strength reaches
internally to the organs, sinews, and bones, exteriorly to the
pores, interstices, skin, and hair. Everywhere they vent and
penetrate, thus enabling the herb to treat aching bones and
sinews in warm pathogen disease. If you regard the herb as
light and clear, suitable only for bringing out sweat on the
skin, you are viewing it in too shallow a manner.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH SCHIZONEPETAE HERBA (jing jie)
Schizonepetae Herba (jingjie) is acrid,warm, and also enters
the blood; it has a strong wind-expelling action, especially if
Schizonepetae Spica (jing jie sut), with its intense aroma, is
used. Although Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) is warm by
nature, it is not excessively drying. Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) is acrid, cool, and disperses wind-heat, tending to enter the qi level. Combined, both the qi and blood
are affected, and the wind-expelling and sweat-inducing
actions are very strong. This pair is therefore ideal for treating wind-heat obstructing the exterior.
>WITH STELLARIAE RADIX (yin chai hu)
Stellariae Radix (yin chai hu) is sweet, bitter, and slightly
cold. It enters the Liver and Stomach channels to cool heat
from deficiency and eliminate the fever resulting from
childhood nutritional impairment. Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) disperses wind-heat and also cools the Liver.
Together they cool and drain pathogenic heat from the
Liver and reduce steaming heat in the bones from consumptive heat.
>WITH UNCARIAE RAMULUS CUM UNCIS (gou teng)
Uncariae Ramulus cum Uncis (gou teng) is sweet and slightly
cold, pacifying the Liver and cooling Liver heat, extinguish.
ing wind and alleviating spasms. Uncariae Ramulus cum
Uncis (gou teng) tends to clear, while Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) tends to disperse. Together they expel windheat, soothe the throat, and calm Liver wind. The pair can
be used to prevent children's febrile convulsions where
there is fever; for chills, Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) can
be added for even greater effect. Neither Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he) nor Uncariae Ramulus cum Uncis (gou
teng) should be decocted for very long.
>WITH CICADAE PERIOSTRACUM (chan tut)
The acrid, dispersing coolness of Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) can reach from the bones to the exterior
driving out wind and venting unexpressed rashes. Cicadae
Periostracum (chan tui) is also acrid and cool. The Grand
Materia Medica notes that it "focuses on treating all wind.
heat disorders." Together the strengths of these two herbs
are complementary, a powerful pair for expelling wind.
heat and venting rashes.

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
In addition, Cicadae Periostracum (chan tut) is salty
and.enters the blood, allowing it to search out and expel
wind from within the blood. It leads Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) into the blood to strengthen the action of
expelling wind and stopping itching. A simple yet effective
remedy for skin disorders such as the itching of eczema is
to powder Cicadae Periostracum (chan tui) and Menthae
haplocalycis Herba (bo he) together and take 3g with wine.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica warns that
Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he) is acrid, aromatic, and
injures the qi; overconsumption impairs the Lungs and
damages the Heart--it should be kept away from deficient
patients. It should not be taken soon after recovering from
an illness, for if the exterior qi is weak it will cause con
tinuous sweating. It is also forbidden for cough from cold
lodged in the Lungs without any heat symptoms. Yin defi.
ciency with fever is another circumstance in which exces.-
sive sweating from Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he)
may readily injure the yin and yang fluids.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:

Light with a mild aroma, the leaves are best for mobilizing the exterior to disperse wind and vent rashes. Zhang
Xi-Chun obseryes that "The best leaves are green and
tender. ... If they are not green, but greyish-green, they are
especially weak. With tender green leaves, 9g in a formula
is sufficient."
>MENTHA STALKs(###E bo he geng)
The stalks are heavier in nature and best for bringing down
the qi and easing the middle. Zhang Xi-Chun notes: "As tc
the stalks, these should be used with qi-regulating herbs; if
they are used with the intention of inducing sweating, that
effect is reduced by half [compared to the entire plant].
> DRY-FRIED MENTHA(k## chao bo he)
Briefly fried over a low flame, its acrid flavor is reduced
and thus its sweat-inducing action is moderated. This is
best used when sweating is already present in patterns such
as exterior wind-heat, to avoid injuring the qi and fluids
through excessive sweating. This method is uncommon at
present.
>CHARRED MENTHA(### bo he tan)
Frying over a low flame until slightly scorched enables
Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he) to enter the blood and
disperse blood-level heat. This method is uncommon at
present.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, and very warming, Psoraleae Fructus (bu gu
zhi) tonifies the yang of both the Spleen and Kidneys, and
has an astringent nature that acts on the Kidneys to secure
the primal yang, and on the Spleen to stop diarrhea. It
is often used to treat impotence, spermatorrhea, urinary
frequency, and pain due to cold in the lower back and legs,
as well as diarrhea associated with Spleen and Kidney yang
deficiency. It also assists the Kidneys in grasping the qi, and
can be used in the treatment of cough and wheezing due to
cold from deficiency. Soaked in wine and applied topically,
it is used to treat vitiligo.

WITH JUGLANDIs SEMEN (he tao ren)

Psoraleae Fructus (bu gu zhi) is acrid, bitter, and very
warm, with a hard, yang nature. Juglandis Semen (he tao

Psoraleae Fructus (biu gu zhi) is usually taken together

Pericardium meet and connect with the fire at the gate of

blood. Blood is yin,and is averse to dryness, thus oil can

This book, and a number of other materia medica texts,

>DRY-FRIED PsORALEA(k### chao bu gu zhi)
The sliced herb is dry-fried until yellow, aromatic, and

> SALT-FRIED PsORALEA (* HE yan chao bu gu zhi)
The fruit is mixed with salt water, left covered briefly, then
dry-fried or baked until dry. This is also known as pre.
pared psoralea (li zhi bu gu zhi). It has the effect of
directing the actions of the herb into the Kidney channel.
enhancing its ability to tonify and secure the lower burner
primal yang. It is often used in the treatment of urinary
frequency, incontinence, impotence, and Kidneys failing
to grasp the qi.
>WINE-FRIED PsORALEA k#i jiu chao bu gu zhi)
The herb is mixed with yellow rice wine, left covered overnight to absorb the wine, then dry-fried or baked until dry.
This method of preparation exploits the acrid-dispersing
qualities of the wine to enhance the acrid flavor of Psoraleae
Fructus (bu gu zhi), strengthening its ability to treat painful
obstruction due to wind-dampness. Nowadays, however, it
is rarely used.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, warm, and drying, aromatically dredging and
dispersing, Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) dries Spleen
and Stomach dampness, strengthens and harmonizes the
middle burner, while dispersing externally-contracted
wind-cold, venting and releasing the exterior, and inducing sweating. Rectification of the Meaning of the Materia
Medica notes that "Its aroma clears away filth, and prevails
over seasonal abnormal qi, thus it is often used for seasonal
epidemic disorders."
The Spleen prefers warmth and dryness, and is averse
to dampness. Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) matches
this profile perfectly by virtue of its warm and aromatic
dryness. Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) can therefore
be used whenever turbid dampness has encumbered the
Spleen, impairing its transportive function, and leading to
such symptoms as epigastric fullness and nausea, abdominal pain and diarrhea, edema, and abdominal distention
and fullness. It is also appropriate for externally-contracted
cold-dampness causing headache, heavy lethargy, aching
of the limbs and joints, chills and fever without sweating:
and for wind-damp painful obstruction when dampness is
predominant.
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
provides a detailed description of this herb's actions:
It governs the treatment of dampness in the three sections
[of the body]: Dampness in the upper burner readily gener
ates phlegm-dampness; this [herb] is used to dry dampness]
and mobilize phlegm. Dampness in the middle burner stag
nates qi and causes diarrhea; this is used to ease the middle
and strengthen the Spleen. Dampness in the lower burner
atrophies and weakens the legs and knees; this is used with
Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai) to treat the atrophy, helping the legs and knees regain power.
In Rectification of the Meaning of the Materia Medica
Zhang Shan-Lei describes a wide range of symptoms associated with dampness and the constrained transportive
functions of the Spleen within the scope of Atractylodis
Rhizoma (cang zhu). He concludes by saying that "As long
as the tongue coating is white, thick, turbid, and greasy
[this] is the single most requisite herb.
Finally, Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) is noted in a
number of materia medica texts for its efficacy in treating
night blindness. This may, however, be due to the traditional pairing of this herb with pig or goat liver when treat.
ing this condition.

7 / Aromatic Herbs that Transform Dampness
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH MAGNOLIAE OFFICINALIS CORTEX (hOu po)
Both herbs are aromatic and transform dampness, but
Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) raises by nature and
assists the transportive functions of the Spleen, while
Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) directs downward
and eliminates sensations of fullness. In this combina
tion, Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) is the chief, while
Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) serves as assistant
by promoting the flow of qi. Mutually supportive, they are
much stronger together in transforming turbid dampness
and strengthening the Stomach and Spleen than is either
one by itself. Because one raises and the other directs
downward, the rise and fall of the qi dynamic is restored.
This combination is best used in the treatment of dampness encumbering the Spleen yang with such symptoms as
epigastric fullness, distention of the abdomen and epigastrium, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, loss of taste, and
a thick greasy tongue coating.

middle and induce sweating, but as for tonifying the middle

>MAOSHAN ATRACTYLODES (##t mdo cang zhu or
# i mdo shan cang zhu)
This is the southern form of atractylodes (see
englishReference.additionalProductInformation:
.below) which is produced in the
Maoshan (Mt. Mao) area of Jiangsu province. And because
the largest commercial center for supplying this herb is the
nearby city (and former capital) Nanjing, it is also known
as capital atractylodes ( i jing cang zhu).
This variety is highly valued for its clear aroma that
49
is not excessively acrid; it dries dampness without harming
the Stomach, and strengthens the Spleen while still expelling dampness. Rectification of the Meaning of Materia
Medica observes: "That produced in Maoshan is compact
and firm in texture, with a flavor like sweet liquor; its tonifying and augmenting actions are far greater than those of
other Atractylodes." Unfortunately, the supply of this par.
ticular variety is limited, and most of this herb is produced
elsewhere.
>PREPARED ATRACTYLODES(&f zhi cang zhu)
After soaking in rice water, the rhizome is steamed until
black, then sliced and dried in the sun. This method of
preparation weakens its acrid-drying qualities, and ren
ders its medicinal effects gentle and harmonious; it also
removes most of its exterior-releasing properties. It is most
appropriate for older or weaker patients, when the Spleen
is encumbered by dampness.
>DRY-FRIED ATRACTYLODES (k# chao cang zhu)
Rhizome slices are dry-fried with bran until slightly yellow,
then the bran is sifted out. The rhizome slices can also be
dry-fried directly without bran, until they appear slightly
scorched and highly aromatic. This is known as scorched
atractylodesijiao cang zhu.Alternativelythey
can be dry-fried with earth (especially reddish-colored or
brownish-yellow-colored earth) until yellow or scorched,
after which the earth is sifted out. This is known as earthfried atractylodes (* tu chao cang zhu).
All of these methods of preparation reduce the acriddispersing properties of the herb, however each method
adds its own special quality. Dry-frying with bran trans.
forms dampness and harmonizes the middle. Scorching is
considered best for warming the Spleen and stopping diarrhea. Dry-frying with earth enhances the Spleen-strength
ening effect so as to alleviate nausea and vomiting, and
drive out phlegm and pathogenic water.

Acrid, dispersing, and warm, qualities which enable it to
unblock, the clear aroma of Alpiniae katsumadai Semen
(cao dou kou) is ideal for treating constrained clumping
of cold-dampness in the middle burner, which disrupts
the normal ascent and descent of qi. Symptoms include
epigastric and abdominal cold pain and distention, nausea,
epigastric discomfort, acid reflux, and a white, slippery
tongue coating. This function also allows it to treat phlegm
dampness constraining the Lungs and affecting breathing.
causing fullness and a stifling sensation in the chest.
Supplement to the Extension of the Materia Medica
observes that this herb is
warm by nature, disperses stagnant qi, and reduces phlegm
above the diaphragm. If it is obvious that the body has
contracted pathogenic cold,[or the patient] consumes cold

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.AMOMI FRUCTUS ROTUNDUS (bai dOu kOu)

Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou), nor does it effectively disseminate the Lung qi, but it is warmer and better

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "grass cardamon"
Historically the term dou kou was widely used to refer to
a number of similarly aromatic, cardamon-like fruits (see
Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou]). Nowadays it is
recommended that a particular fruit be specified in the
prescription, and in general, when only dou kou is written,
Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou) will be dispensed.
>KATSUMADA's GALANGAL FLESH ( cdo kou rou)
or KERNELs(#=cao kOu ren)
Because the outer fruit pericarp is removed in the initial
processing, only the inner flesh of the fruit-which is primarily composed of seeds---is used. This provides a more
strongly concentrated aromatic aspect.
Nowadays this herb is generally used in its raw (unprocessed) form. However, earlier texts refer to roasted Katsumada's galangal seed wei cao kou), a process
which involved wrapping the whole fruit in flour and
baking until cooked; the pericarp was then removed. This]
method of preparation somewhat moderates its piercing
aroma.

- Cools the blood and stops bleeding: widely used for various bleeding disorders including vomiting blood, bleed.
ing gums, coughing of blood, blood in the stool or urine,

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, astringent, slightly cold, Platycladi Cacumen (ce
bai ye) enters the Liver, Lung, and Large Intestine channels. Bitterness dries dampness, astringency inhibits and
restrains, and its slight coldness cools what is hot; thus, this
herb cools the blood and inhibits bleeding. It also promotes
hair growth and dries dampness to stop vaginal discharge.
It can be used when heat in the blood leads to the coughing
or expectoration of blood, blood in the stool or urine, and
for irregular uterine bleeding. It cools the Lungs and expels
phlegm, and applied topically can assist in the healing of
burns, and promote the regrowth of hair in cases of balding, for which it is also taken internally.
Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians states that
this herb "governs the vomiting of blood, nosebleed, bleeding dysenteric disorder, continuous vaginal bleeding and
vaginal discharge; expels damp painful obstruction and
generates flesh."

58 10 / Herbs that Regulate the Blood
englishReference.combinations:
>WrTH REHMANNIAE RADIX (sheng di huang)
Combined, the blood-cooling actions of these two herbs is
greatly enhanced. Platycladi Cacumen (ce bai ye) contributes its ability to stop bleeding, while Rehmanniae Radix
(sheng di huang) contributes its ability to replenish the
yin injured by heat. It is thus an excellent combination for
treating all types of bleeding due to heat in the blood. Its
sole shortcoming is that the bitter-coldness of Platycladi
Cacumen (ce bai ye) plus the greasiness of Rehmanniae
Radix (sheng di huang) is hard on the digestion, so the
combination should only be taken for short periods of
time. One way of mitigating this problem is to use charred
Platycladi Cacumen (ce bai tan): although this method of
preparation reduces its blood-cooling action, it improves
its ability to stop bleeding, and simultaneously assists in its
digestion.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ECLIPTAE HERBA (mo han lian)
Both herbs cool the blood to stop bleeding and both pro
mote hair growth and color. However, Platycladi Cacumen
(ce bai ye) governs hair growth when blood heat is the cause
of the hair loss. Ecliptae Herba (mo han lian), by contrast,
nourishes the yin and promotes the growth of healthy hair
and is thus best for hair loss associated with deficiency of
the Liver and Kidneys.
>Vs.SANGUISORBAE RADIX (di yu); see page 572
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Cold and drying by nature, (Platycladi Cacumen (ce bai
ye)] greatly cuts down Stomach [qi]; although it can stop
bleeding, it has no power to generate yang, therefore defi.
cient patients who have lost blood should not take it without prescription. (Encountering the Sources of the Classic of
Materia Medica)

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
Raises and lifts the yang qi, specifically the clear qi of the
Stomach and Gallbadder: for prolapse, sensations of drag.
ging downward, hemorrhoids, vaginal discharge, bleeding or exhaustion. All of these symptoms can indicate an
abnormal descent of qi with an inability to rise.
--With Astragali Radix (huang qt) to raise the clear yang
due to abnormal descent of qi.
-With Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) and
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) for symptoms associated

englishReference.commentary:
Entering the Gallbladder, Liver, Pericardium, and Triple
Burner channels, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is bitter, acrid,
cool, and light in weight so that it raises and disperses to
vent the exterior and drain heat. This raising action also
raises the clear qi of the Stomach and Gallbladder, and in
conjunction with its acrid dispersal, restores the normal
movement of Liver qi in order to relieve Liver qi constraint.
Materia medica texts both ancient and modern seem
to be equally divided on the question of whether to classify
Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) as neutral or cool. The problem
appears to have begun with the Divine Husbandman's
Classic of the Materia Medica, which listed it as "bitter
and neutral," while most of its application's in the equally
revered but slightly later Discussion of Cold Damage involve
heat. Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica puts
the case as follows:
The use of Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) lies in its cooling dis.
persal, which pacifies Liver heat. Because its nature is cool,
it thus releases alternating chills and fever, tidal heat in
the muscle layer and exterior, fire blazing in the Liver and
Gailbladder, painful clumping in the chest and flanks, and
also treats sores and heat in the blood chamber.
Because of this division of opinion, most texts choose one
side, then note an authority which states the other; or, like
the Materia Medica Arranged According to Pattern and
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica, opt for both and
simply say "neutral and slightly cool."
As to its other effects, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) has
a rising, spreading, and draining nature with a relatively
good heat-clearing action, particularly for eliminating a
pathogen at the lesser yang half-interior, half-exterior
level. It also lifts the yang qi and regulates Liver qi to relieve
constraint
The range of symptoms that this herb addresses is
remarkably broad, including the alternating chills and fever
15
associated with a lesser yang stage pathogen, prolapse or
diarrhea resulting from the sinking of yang qi, distending
pain in the chest and flanks plus menstrual irregularity due
to Liver qi constraint, skin conditions, and diseases of the
eye and ear.
In addition to the most common uses of Bupleuri Radix
(chai hu) discussed above, a few others deserve comment.
> HEAT FROM DEFICIENCY
There are two common ways that Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu) is used for this purpose. The first is for treating deficiency consumption with steaming bones and tidal fever,
where Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is used because of its
broad cooling effect on the Liver, Gallbladder, Heart, and
Pericardium. The second is for raising yang and dispersing fire so as to spread and expel heat in the muscle layer
and skin; this is referred to in the adage, "Constrained fire
should be discharged." Li Shi-Zhen noted that "when there
is deficiency consumption in the Spleen and Stomach with
heat, or yang qi sinking downward, then Bupleuri Radix
(chai hu) is the only herb to guide clear qi and reduce fever:
it is absolutely necessary." Usually, it will be combined with
Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma), Puerariae Radix (ge gen),
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng), Paeoniae Radix alba
(bai shdo), and Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao), as in Raise
the Yang and Disperse Fire Decoction (sheng yang san huo
tang).
> GYNECOLOGICAL DISORDERS
This herb is very commonly used in treating women's
disorders. Li Gao pointed out that it "focuses on blood
in the yin organs, while in the channels it focuses on qi,
which makes it a perfect choice for gynecological disorders.
where qi and blood regulation is paramount. It can regulate menstruation, treat heat entering the blood chamber
relieve qi constraint, cool puerperal fever, and accomplish
miany other tasks, if properly assisted. In gynecology, great
emphasis is placed on differentiating qi and blood pathologies and determining the degree of heat or cold; thus,
herbs to assist Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) will also be chosen
according to these criteria.
For example, for Liver qi constraint, Cyperi Rhizoma
(xiang fu), Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong), or Citri
reticulatae Pericarpium (chen pi) might be selected, while
for blood stagnation, Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui),
Persicae Semen (tao ren), or Carthami Flos (hong hua)
would be best. If the constraint generates heat, Gardeniae
Fructus (zhi zi), Moutan Cortex (mu dan pi), Scutellariae
Radix (huang qin), or Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi shao) can
be used. If cold .is involved, Zingiberis Rhizoma recens
(sheng jiang), Evodiae Fructus (wu zhu yu), Cinnamomi

6 1/ Herbs that Release the Exterior
Ramulus (gui zhi), or Zanthoxyli Pericarpium (hua jiao)
would be selected. For blood deficiency, Bupleuri Radix
(chai hu) might be combined with Rehmanniae Radix
preparata (shu di hudng), Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao),
Lycii Fructus (gou qi zi), or Corni Fructus (shan zhu yu).
And if there is qi deficiency, Ginseng Radix (ren shen),
Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu), Poria (fu
ling), and Glycyrrhizae Radix preparata (zhi gan cao) would
be the herbs of choice.
Y OTHER USES
For boils and furuncles, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is used
to disperse clumped qi and blood in all the channels. Li
Gao notes that it is similar to Forsythiae Fructus (lian
qiao) in that way, but must be accompanied by reducing
and dispersing herbs. Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is a commonly used herb for eye and ear diseases, because it enters
the lesser yang and terminal yin channels to disperse heat
and fire, and can be used as a guiding herb into those
areas. Important Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold Pieces
combines Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) with Cassiae Semen
(jue ming zi) to treat blurry vision, while Secrets of the
Orchid Chamber combines it with Citri reticulatae viride
Pericarpium (qing pi), Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu),
Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui), and Rehmanniae
Radix (sheng di huang) in several eye disease formulas. For
early stage deafness and tinnitus, Unblock the Qi Powder
(tong qi san) uses equal amounts of Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu) and Cyperi Rhizoma (xiang fu), with Chuanxiong
Rhizoma (chuan xiong) at half the amount.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ScUTELLARIAE RADIX (huang qin)
This combination is a pillar of the clinical strategy of harmonizing, exemplified in the Discussion of Cold Damage
formula Minor Bupleurum Decoction (xiao chai hu tang).
Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is bitter, cool, clear, and light,
with a rising nature that excels at forcing a pathogen at
the half-exterior level of the lesser yang out to the exterior
where it can be dispersed, and relieving qi level constraint.
Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is bitter and cold, and excels
at cooling Liver and Gallbladder qi-level heat, internally
resolving a half-interior pathogen.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica notes:
For cooling the muscle layer and reducing fever, Bupieuri
Radix (chai hu is best, but despite this,without Scutellariae
Radix (huang qin), it will not be able to cool the muscles or
reach the exterior, because it only addresses half the problem. Combined, one spreads the lesser yang's half-exterior
pathogen, one cools the lesser yang's half-interior heat, and
both enter the lesser yang Liver and Gallbladder, restoring smoothness to their pivotal functions; [they] generally
represent an ideal team for harmonizing lesser yang stage
disorders and dredging Liver and Gallbladder heat from
constraint.
This combination is also frequently used for the gynecolog.
ical condition known as heat entering the blood chamber
(#Af. re ru xue shi). This can occur if there is exposure
to an external pathogen during menstruation, leading to
fever, chills, and the characteristic delirium.
> WITH PAEONIAE RADIX ALBA (bai shao)
The Liver stores blood but also spreads and drains, thus
its form is yin while its function is yang. The nature of
Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is acrid and dispersing, and it
mainly enters the qi aspect. The nature of Paeoniae Radix
alba (bai shao) is sour and soft, and it mainly enters the
biood aspect. Therefore, while Bupleuri Radix (chai hu)
dredges and spreads Liver qi, harmonizing its function, at
the same time Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) nourishes the
Liver blood, thereby tonifying the Liver's yin aspect and
moderating its hard yang aspect. With the Liver softening
providedby Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shdo), the qi-mobilizing action of Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) can soothe the Liver
without excessive dispersal. and drainage, which might
otherwise injure the Liver yin and blood. In fact, some
physicians make it a rule to never use Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu) without adding Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shdo) to the
prescription.
Movement and stillness each play a part in this combination, and form and function are both considered. It is
therefore frequently prescribed for the extremely common
clinical presentation of Liver blood deficiency with Liver qi
constraint. This is also why it is the foundation for so many
formulas addressing Liver constraint: Rambling Powder
(xiao yao san), Bupleurum Powder to Dredge the Liver
(chai hu shu gan san), and Frigid Extremities Powder (si nt
san) being three classic examples.
>WITH PEUCEDANI RADIX (qian hu)
The aroma of Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) frees constraint,
and it is very light in weight, enabling it to ascend; it raises
and disperses, draining heat and dredging the exterior.
Peucedani Radix (qian hu) is bitter, acrid, and slightly
cold, specializing in directing qi downward and expelling
phlegm, while also dispersing wind and relieving fever.
Together, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) lifts and opens up areas
of constraint, while Peucedani Radix (qian hu) quells rebellious qi and directs it downward. One rises while the other
descends; this regulates the rise and fall of the qi dynamic.
regulating.the clear dissemination of Lung qi, while also
dispelling wind-heat. A far better result is thereby achieved

1/ Herbs that Release the Exterior
than would be the case from using only herbs that direct the
Lung qi downward.
Thus, the combination has a pathogen-expelling.
cough-alleviating action which is commonly used when
wind-heat constrains the Lungs, leading to a stifling sensation in the chest and a productive cough. It is so frequently
used that physicians will sometimes simply write the two
hu (literally "two barbarians," - er hu) in their prescriptions.

englishReference.toxicity:
One case of allergic reaction was reported after oral administration; the symptoms included pruritus and papular rash, accompanied by dizzines, headache, a sense of
oppression or even pain in the chest.
This herb should not be given intramuscularly as this

>NoRTHERN BUPLEURUM(Sb##H bei chai hu)
This is the root (and the occasional stem) of B. Chinense,
which has been cleaned and sliced. It is produced in the
northern provinces of Liaoning, Hebei, and Henan. Its root
is larger and firmer with less twists, thus it is also called hard
bupleurum (ying chai hu). Because it is usually harvested
in autumn, another name is autumn bupleurum (qiu chai
hu.
Northern Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is generally thought
to have a stronger harmonizing and heat-clearing action
that is best in its unprepared form; it is most often used for
diseases of externally-contracted heat. Treasury of Words
on the Materia Medica observes: "In the major and minor
Bupleurum formulas from Discussion of Cold Damage,
Zhang Zhong-Jing used northern bupleurum."
>SoUTHERN BUPLEURUM(##nan chai hu)
This is the root or whole plant of B. scorzonerifolium,
cleaned and sliced. It is produced in Sichuan, Hubei, and
Jiangsu provinces; that from Sichuan can be specified as
Sichuanese bulpeurum (chuan chai hu). Its root is thinner and more pliable than the northern variety, with more
twists and turns, and is therefore also called thin bupleurum (xi chai hu) or soft bupleurum (ruan chai hu). Some
places will only ask for the root with a brownish red surface
which is called red bupleurum (hong chai hu).
Southern bupleurum is generally 'regarded as bet.
ter for spreading Liver qi and releasing constraint, and
would therefore be most appropriate in formulas such as
Rambling Powder (xiao ydo san) and Bupleurum Powde
to Dredge the Liver (chai hu shu gan san).
>SPRING BUPLEURUM#chun chai hu
This is the young whole plant of southern Bupleuri Radix
(chai hu), picked in springtime; the wholesale trade name
is sprouted bupleurum (ya hu). Its effects are similar to
those of southern bupleurum, but as a young sprout, it
has a heavy perfumed aroma and a light, clearing texture,
qualities which embody the lifting and spreading nature
of springtime qi. Its dispersing and draining actions are
strong and particularly well-suited to encouraging the
spreading penetration of Liver qi.
>DRY-FRIED BUPLEURUM#chao chai hu
In this form, the herb is dry-fried until slightly scorched,
sometimes with wine or bran. Once fried, its cooling action
is reduced, but its ability to lift the clear yang is enhanced.
It is thus most appropriate for formulas such as Tonify
the Middle and Augment the Qi Decoction (bu zhongyi qt
tang).
VINEGAR BUPLEURUM( cu chai hu
Mixed with vinegar, then fried over a moderate flame until
the liquid is absorbed, this method of preparation focuses
the actions of the herb on the Liver channel and enhances
its ability to soothe the Liver, harmonize the blood, and
stop pain. This is most appropriate for formulas such as
Revive Health by Invigorating the Blood Decoction (fu
yuan huo xue tang).
Note: The term chai hu covers all types and forms of this
plant, such as root only or the whole plant, although some
regard it as a shortened name for northern bupleurum.
Stellariae Radix (vin chai hu) is a completely different herb;
See Chapter 2.

Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica explains the
differences between these herbs:
The use of Dichroae Radix (chang shan) is basically
to unbind phlegm, drive out water, wash away dampness, and transform accumulations, thus both the Divine
Husbandman and Miscellaneous Records list it as a pri
mary herb for malarial disorders. Later, people became
obsessed with [Zhang] Zhong-Jing's Minor Bupleurum
Decoction (xiao chai hi tang) method, so that many knew
that Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) governed malarial disorders.
but few knew that Dichroae Radix (chang shan) governed
malarial disorders. Did they not know that when Bupleuri
Radix (chai hu) treats malarial disorders, it only governs
the pathogen when it is in the channels and collaterals
and cannot manage stagnant accumulation of phlegm and
dampness? It is only appropriate for cases in which the
onset and disappearance of symptoms is gradual. Used too
early or too late, it will be unsuitable.
On the other hand, when Dichroae Radix (chang shan)
treats malarial disorders, it dredges and unblocks accumulated clumping in the interior, severing the root of the

englishReference.commentary:
Aquilariae Lignum resinatum (chen xiang) sinks and directs
downward, but is not overly draining, nor is its warmth
overly drying. Thus it can warm the middle and direct
rebellious qi downward, while also warming the Kidneys to
grasp qi. Because it promotes the flow of qi, disperses cold.
ness, directs downward and stops nausea, it is often used
in the treatment of cold constraint with clumping qi which
leads to a stifling sensation in the chest and abdominal distention, belching, hiccough, nausea, and vomiting. Because
it assists the Kidneys in grasping the qi, it calms wheezing
due to Kidney deficiency. The Kidneys also store essence
and control lower body elimination; thus, when the Kidney
yang is deficient, the essence lacks warmth, urination can
become difficult, and stools become loose. For these con
ditions, too, Aquilariae Lignum resinatum (chen xiang) is
appropriate. On the other hand, it is also frequently used
for constipation due to qi stagnation or Liver qi constraint
(particularly in young women) when combined with such
herbs as Aucklandiae Radix (mu xiang), Arecae Semer
(bing lang), Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shi), and
Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang), as in Six Milled-Herb
Decoction (liu mo tang), and for constipation due to
Kidney yang deficiency.
Penetrating the Mysteries of the Materia Medica observes
that this herb is
warm without being drying, promo ent withoutuiave
draining, supports the Spleen so that transportation is not
fatigued, and reaches the Kidneys to guide fire back to its
base.Its action in directing downward does not break up
the qi and [thereby] cause harm. It is truly a fine substance
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH AUCKLANDIAE RADIX (mu xiang)
This combination is used for rebellious middle burner
qi with belching, hiccough, nausea and vomiting; or for
urinary difficulty due to forced retention of urine or excessively repressed sexual activity. It has a strong qi-regulating
action, particularly appropriate for directing rebellious
537
middle burner qi downward, and is often used in the
treatment of epigastric and abdominal distention, stifling
sensation in the epigastrium, with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, belching, and hiccough. It is often combined with
herbs that otherwise regulate the qi, or those that tonify the
Spleen and Stomach.
There was also an interesting ancient application for
this combination. Excessive repression of sexual urges, or
extended forced retention of urine, was believed to cause
twisting of the bladder'(# bao zhuan), which in turn
led to urinary difficulty. Customary herbs for facilitating
urination could not resolve the disorder. This combination
was therefore prescribed, taken as a powder on an empty
stomach with boiled water, to disperse the clumping and
guide the qi downward and outward, thereby unblocking
the Bladder.
englishReference.comparisons:
> Vs. LINDERAE RADIX (wu yao)
Both herbs warm the Spleen and Kidneys, mobilize the
qi, disperse cold, and treat distention and fullness of the
chest and abdomen with wheezing due to rebellious qi.
However, Aquilariae Lignum resinatum (chen xiang) is
bitter so that it drains and drives downward, directing
rebellious qi downward, and helping the Kidneys accept qi.
It warms the Kidneys more than Linderae Radix (wu yao)
but Linderae Radix (wu yao) has a mobile, masculine qual.
ity that reaches everywhere and is thus appropriate for any
pathogenic rebellious disorder, whether it be pathogenic
cold in the Triple Burner, qi blockage, or congealed blood
due to cold.
>Vs.CINNAMOMI CoRTEX(rdu gut)
Both herbs are effective in treating lower abdominal pain
associated with obstruction of the qi and blood due to cold
from deficiency. The effect of the former is attributed more
to its action in regulating the qi, and the latter to warming
the yang.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
For cold qi, rebellious qi, qi constraint, or clumped qi, this
is an especially important herb. Despite that, if middle qi is
deficient, or qi does not return to its base, or qi is deficient
and sinks, it's use is forbidden. For a pathogenic excess in
the Heart channel, it is forbidden. For those who do not
have debility of the true fire at the gate of vitality, it should
not be added to herbs for the lower burner; for those with
flourishing fire from yin deficiency, it definitely should not
touch their lips. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:

Because of its heavy, aromatic secretions, this herb is heavi.
er than most woods, and tends to sink somewhat in water
hence the nickname sinking-[in]-water fragrance (iK
chen shui xiang)
Under most conditions the wood does not contain
large amounts of sap. It is only when the wood is dam
aged or deteriorating that the sap begins to flow, and this
creates the material used for this herb. The richer the sap
content, the better the quality. The best quality is known as
top aquilaria (E. shang chen xiang). There is very little
high-quality product available, and not infrequently one
encounters counterfeits as obvious as balsa wood painted
black being offered for sale as Aquilariae Lignum resinatum
(chen xiang).
Because the herb is generally pulverized or ground into
powder before use, the terms aquilaria scraps (t / chen
xiang xie) or aquilaria flour ( chen xiang mian) are
used. When the wood is steamed until soft, then sliced, it is
called aquilaria slices (i # H chen xiang pian).

blood.

and impeded blood flow.

.. Add detoxifying herbs, such as Lonicerae Flos (jin
yin hua) and Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao), for pain and

cal problems associated with hot blood.

englishReference.commentary:
Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi shao) and Paeoniae Radix alba
(bai shao) were not differentiated in the earliest materia
medica texts. Almost all classical texts tend to discuss their
properties under the single heading of paeoniae (& # shad
yao), while recognizing that the white and red varieties are
quite distinct in the quality of their therapeutic actions (see
CoMPARISoN below). Indeed, Tao Hong-Jing first made
this differentiation in the sixth century
Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi shao), however, is strictly
draining due to its bitterness, so that it invigorates the
blood, expels stagnation, and stops pain; its slight sourness
retains its affinity for the Liver so that it enters the blood
aspect of the Liver, where its coldness cools heat in the
blood. It is thus used for rashes due to warm pathogen disease causing heat in the blood, and swollen toxic sores, as
explained in Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and
Respecting the Western: "[It] is superior for transforming
stasis, thus those who treat sores and abscesses often use
it for its ability to transform toxic hot blood stasis without
causing the formation and perforation of pus."
Essentials of the Materia Medica notes that it
Specifically drains Liver fire and disperses noxious blood.
It treats abdominal pain, firm accumulations, blood painful obstruction, bulging disorders, and mobile abdominal
masses, amenorrhea, Intestinal wind, swollen sores, and
reddened eyes-all these are the effects of dispersing and
draining.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PAEONIAE RADIX ALBA (bai shao)
Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shdo) restrains while Paconiae
Radix rubra (chi shao) disperses; Paeoniae Radix alba (bai
shdo) tonifies while Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi shao) drains;
Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) nourishes the blood and
harmonizes the nutritive,while Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi
shdo) promotes the movement of blood and dispels blood
stasis. All of these actions are present when the two herbs
are used together. The combination is often used when
623
deficiency of blood and nutritive qi is coupled with imped.
ed blood flow, causing spasms and cramping pain.
Note, however, that because both herbs are cold, they.
are best used in disorders involving heat, unless other
warming herbs such as Cinnamomi Ramulus (gut zhi) or
Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gut) are used as well, or
they are prepared by dry-frying or baking, to lessen their
cooling effect.
>WITH RHEI RADIX ET RHIZOMA (da hudng)
While Paeoniae Radix rubra (chi shao) breaks up blood
stasis, Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) drains heat toxin
and breaks up accumulation and stagnant blood. Not
only is this a rather powerful combination for breaking up
obstruction within the blood, it also has the ability to drain
heat and stop pain. A formula from Important Formulas
Worth a Thousand Gold Pieces uses just these two herbs for
"chronic suffering of accumulation within the abdomen,
blockage of urine, constipation, qi rushing upward to the
Heart, abdominal distention and fullness, and rebellious
damage from food and drink." This combination forms
an excellent foundation for a strong stagnation-remoying prescription; it must be used with caution, however.

englishReference.commentary:
Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu) cools and transforms phlegm-heat, stops coughs, and disperses clumps,
while also moistening the Lungs. It is most commonly
indicated for dry heat in the Lungs with a nonproductive
cough. However, it also directs Heart fire downward and
thus treats constraint.
The use of Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei
mu) for relieving constraint is not well-represented in the
modern literature, despite its long history. The late Han
dynasty physician Zhang Zhong-Jing prescribed it for two
conditions marked by constraint. The Song dynasty workDivine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica

englishReference.actions:
o Clears heat and transforms phlegm: for many types of
cough, chiefly chronic cough, cough with signs of fire due
.to yin deficiency, cough with slight sputum that is difficult
to expectorate, or cough with blood-streaked sputum. It
is most effective in treating cough accompanied by con.
strained qi, manifested in a reduced appetite and a stifling
sensation in the chest and upper abdomen.
-With Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu for cough with
minimal or difficult-to-expectorate sputum due to fire
from yin deficiency burning the Lungs, as in Fritillaria and
Anemarrhena Powder (er mu san).
-With Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) for cough and
wheezing with copious sputum.
--With Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye), Ophiopogonis
Radix (mai men dong), and Polygonati odorati Rhizoma
(yu zhu) for chronic cough presenting with fatigue, irritability, excessive or bloody sputum, stifling sensation and
distention in the chest, and lack of appetite.
--With Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi), Poria (fu ling), and
Trichosanthis Fructus (gua lou) for painful obstruction of
Alternative Statements in Materia Medica specifically notes
that "Fritillariae Bulbus (bei mu) can disperse constrained
qi in the Heart and chest." In Seeking Accuracy in the
Materia Medica, Huang Gong-Xiu concurs: "Presently it is
used with good results in treating those with uneasiness in
the Heart, anxiety, and constraint." This ability to relieve
constraint and direct Heart fire downward is cited as an
explanation for actions attributed to the herb in the earliest
materia medica, for example, its efficacy in treating painful
urinary dribbling.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica provides the
following discussion:
Fritillariae [cirrhosae] Bulbus ((chuan] bei mu) is an herb
which opens constraint, directs qi downward, and dissolves
phlegm in order to alleviate cough and calm wheezing.I
is indicated for clumped fire from deficiency conditions.
Therefore use it with:
: Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) to clear the qi and nour
ish the yin;
- Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian) and Scutellariae Radix
(huang qin) to direct fire and phlegm downward;
Ginseng Radix (ren shen) and Astragali Radix (huang qi) to
tonify without accumulation
- Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) and Paeoniae Radix
alba (bai shao) to harmonize the nutritive qi;
- Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao) to release constrained toxins
and treat goiter.
It can also be used as a substitute for Pinelliae Rhizoma
preparatum (zhi ban xia) in Two-Cured Decoction (er chen
tang) to tonify the Lungs, eliminate phlegm, harmonize the
middle, and direct fire downward.
For all of the above uses of Fritillariae Bulbus (bei mu), one
should use Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu) to
achieve outstanding results.

380 6 / Herbs that Transform Phlegm and Stop Coughing
Wang Ji, however, warns that substituting Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu) for Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) cannot be done indiscriminately.
In Thoroughly Revised Materia Medica, he is quoted as
follows:
They say that Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia)
is acrid and toxic, and one should substitute Fritillariae
cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu-do they not know that
Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei muis cold,moist
and mainly for Lung patients with dry-phlegm, whereas
Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) is warm,dry
ing, and mainly for Spleen patients with damp-phlegm?
How could they be used interchangeably?
Because of the relative expense of Fritillariae cirrhosae
Bulbus (chuan bei mu), it is often administered as a powder
to be taken together with the strained decoction of other
herbs that alleviate cough. Traditionally, more prescriptions call for its use in powder or pill form than as a decoction.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ANEMARRHENAE RHIZOMA (zhi mu)
Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu) is a Lung chan.
nel herb which cools, moistens, and transforms phlegm
The action of Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is not
limited to the Lungs, but cools and tonifies the yin of the
Kidneys and Stomach as well. Because this pair of herbs
emphasizes cooling and moistening over the transformation of phlegm, it is best suited for the heat from deficiency
associated with Lung consumption disorder leading to
cough with scanty sputum. It is not so cloying that it gen.
erates additional phlegm, nor is it so bitter and cold that
it will further injure the yin. This combination addresses
four different aspects of the condition simultaneously: deficiency, heat, phlegm, and dryness.
>WITH ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
The sweetness of Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei
mu) moistens dryness, its bitterness transforms phlegm,
and its coolness clears the Lungs and eliminates heat.
Together these actions transform phlegm-heat and restore
the Lungs' ability to disseminate qi. The bitterness of
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) directs rebellious qi downward, while its gentle warmth disperses constraint and stagnation. Its focus is thus on restoring the descent of Lung qi,
which will thereby alleviate the wheezing and cough.
When used together, Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) acts
primarily on the qi, Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei
mu) on the phlegm; the joining of warmth with coolness
results in a harmonious quality that is further benefitted by
the moistening qualities of each of the constituent herbs.
This pair is frequently prescribed for a variety of respiratory conditions: wheezing and cough from externally-contracted Lung disorders, long-term nonproductive cough
from Lung deficiency disorders, and coughing of thick
yellow sputum due to phlegm-fire constraint.

was the first text to distinguish Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus

thunbergii Bulbus (zhe bei mu), calling it elephant mountain fritillariaxiang shan bei mu.It can thus be
inferred that all references to Fritillariae Bulbus (bei mu) in
materia medica prior to the Grand Materia Medica were to
Fritillariae cirrhosae Bulbus (chuan bei mu).

honey.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, cold, and slightly toxic, Toosendan Fructus (chuan
lian zi) cools heat, regulates and directs qi downward, kills
parasites, and clears damp-heat by guiding it out through
the urine. It has a marked ability to relieve qi constraint and
ated with pathogenic heat. The Grand Materia Medica
observes that, because it is
bitter and cold, it can guide out heat in the Small Intestine
and Bladder, and because it leads Pericardium ministerial
fire downward, it unblocks and facilitates urination, and is
an important herb for bulging disorders.
Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting

[It] is slightly sour and slightly bitter in flavor, and cool.
ing in nature. Sour things enter the Liver, bitter things
direct downward, [thus] it can guide heat in the Liver
and Gallbladder downward and out through the urine

accumulation of Gallbladder fire causing pain in the hypochondrium, and also pain due to qi constraint in the epigastrium, as wood can dredge earth. Although it is cooling
in nature, when it treats bulging disorders it is commonly
used as a guiding herb, as its virtue of directing downward
guides the other herbs to reach the afflicted location.

Bulging disorders and mobile masses are all due to cold

(xiao hut xiang).

englishReference.commentary:
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) enters the Liver channel to warm and unblock the blood vessels, yet its acrid
flavor and its relatively light material substance enable it to
promote the movement of qi at the blood level. This also
allows it to disperse qi stagnation and externally-contracted
wind. In so doing, it reaches upward to the head and eyes,
outward to the muscles and skin, and laterally to the joints
of the limbs. The famous twelfth-century writer Zhang
Yuan-Su summarized its special characteristics: "Above,
it moves through the head and eyes, while below, it moves
through the sea of blood." The Treasury of Words on the
Materia Medica exclaims:
Flavor acrid, nature yang, qi-moving and piercing with no
yin-congealing, sticking, or blocking attributes--although
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) enters the blood, yet it
eliminates wind of all types and regulates qi of all kinds!
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica explains its dual
effect on the qi and blood, and then extends this action to
pathogenic wind:
If the qi is constrained by blood, the movement of qi should
be promoted to disperse the blood. If the blood is con.
strained by qi, the blood should be invigorated to unblock
the qi. Promoting the movement of qi requires Chuanxiong
Rhizoma (chuan xiong); blood can return [to its normal
circulation] and thereby is supplemented and invigorated,and the qi of the blood is therebv further assisted by
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong.This reaches upward
to the head and eyes, and downward to the sea of blood.
Its acridity is most able to disperse pathogens, so when
the blood is constrained by wind, the use of Chuanxiong
Rhizoma (chuan xiong) naturally invigorates the blood, and
the wind is naturally reduced.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica states that
the herb has a strong warming quality and acrid fiavor, and
that it
acts on the qi, with a particularly intense power to raise and
discharge. It reaches upward to the head and eyes,directly
venting the vertex and crown. Yet its physical substance is
not solidly hard, with many empty gaps, so that it travels
laterally to the joints of the limbs, linking and unblocking
the channels and collaterals, penetrating through the interstices and pores to open and drain the muscles and skin.
Zhang Shan-Lei, the author of this work, proceeds to
warn:
Still, we need to consider that, for disorders like headaches
due to wind-heat or Liver yang attacking upward, one cannot recklessly try warm, rising, acrid-dispersing [herbs].
[Li] Dong-Yuan said that Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan
xiong) must be used for headaches, meaning especially
wind-cold headaches, but his language is too unspecific. It
has been taken up by vulgar books such as Ode of Medicina
Properties [for Four Hundred Herbs], which has the single
sentence [for] headaches, use Chuanxiong Rhizoma
(chuan xiong)', a general treatment for all headaches! What
reply can be made to the damage this has caused?
As shown above, when combined with other appropriate
herbs, this herb can be used for headaches from a variety
of causes.

englishReference.commentary:
Halloysitum rubrum (chi shi zhi) is sweet and warm and
thus augments the qi; heavy in weight, such that it enters
the lower burner; reddish in color, such that it enters the
blood level; and sour, such that it stablizes and binds.
These characteristics also enable it to generate flesh, and
thus assist in the healing of chronic sores; it is also applied
externally for this indication. Its main areas of application.
however, are in the treatment of chronic diarrhea and uterine bleeding associated with deficiency disorders.
Although because of its crimson color the earlier materia medica texts associated this substance with the Heart
and with blood, in the Grand Materia Medica, Li Shi-Zhen
says that
All five stone resins are medicinals of the hand and foo
yang brightness channels. They are sweet and warm, heavy
in weight, with an astringent nature. Astringent and heavy
they therefore inhibit dampness, stop bleeding, and stabilize the lower [body]; sweet and warm, they augment the
qi, generate flesh, and adjust the middle. The 'middle' here
means the Intestines, Stomach, flesh, muscles, palpitations
with anxiety, and jaundice; the lower [body]' means blood
in the stool, dysenteric disorders, incessant uterine bleeding, vaginal discharge, and spermatorrhea.
Li goes on to say that the separation of attributes by color
in Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians is rather
forced, but "of the white and crimson colored, the white
enters the qi level while the red enters the blood level."
Li Gao says that this medicinal expels retained placenta
but many commentators have disagreed, pointing out that
this would require an ability to transform blood stagnation.
Others suggest that Li was probably referring to women
whose Spleen and Stomach qi is so exhausted following
childbirth that they lack the strength to expel the placenta
normally. For them, the warm sweetness of Halloysitum
rubrum (chi shi zhi) can augment the qi, and thereby assist
in the elimination of the placenta.
englishReference.combinations:
>WrTH LIMONITUM (yu yu liang)
Because these two medicinals have similar actions, there
is a synergistic binding and securing effect when they are
combined. They are often used together for chronic dysenteric diarrhea with incontinence, and incessant uterine
bleeding without clotting. At the same time, the neutral
nature of Limonitum (yu yu liang) modifies the warmth of
Halloysitum rubrum (chi shi zhi), so that the combination
can still be used in slightly warm conditions.
Chronic' is the primary indicator for using this combination, yet this remains a branch, not a root, treatment.
Other substances must be added to address the underlying
deficiency.
In some cases, however, the chronic diarrhea is not
the result of deficiency, but is iatrogenic in origin. Equal
amounts (30g) of each substance are prescribed in the
Discussion of Cold Damage formula Halloysitum and Limonite Decoction (chi shi zhi yu yu liang tang), which is
designed for incessant diarrhea following repeated (and
improper) downward-draining treatments of the patient.
According to Zhang Zhong-Jing, "If it does not stop [after
administering this prescription], one should then facilitate
urination."

Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica compares these
three herbs:
Halloysitum rubrum (chi shi zhi), Limonitum (yu yu liang)
and Papaveris Pericarpium (ying su ke) are all remedies
that restrain, bind, and stabilize conditions of abandon.
ment. However, Papaveris Pericarpium (ying su ke) is light
in weight and slightly coldwith an action that enters the qi
level and preserves the Lungs, while Halloysitum rubrum
(cht shi zhi) is sweet, warm, heavy in weight, and red in
color [so that it] enters the lower burner blood level to
stabilize abandonment. It also closes up sores which have
perforated, and generates flesh. Limonitum (yu yu liang)
is sweet,neutral, and astringent,heavier in weight than
Halloysitum rubrum (chi shi zhi),and strictly binding in its
effect. In terms of sedating and pressing down, the others
are inferior to Limonitum (yu yu liang. Thus the warmth
of Halloysitum rubrum (chi shi zhi) augments qi to generate
flesh, its sourness stops bleeding and stabilizes the lower
body.
By contrast, Limonitum (yu yu liang) only binds, and has
no ability to augment the qi or generate flesh. Papaveris
Pericarpium (ying su ke) is light in weight rather than

heavy, which enables it to enter the upper burner where it
addresses the qi level of the Lungs rather than the blood

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "crimson stone resin"
This substance resembles kaolinite in that both are clay
substances which are similar in composition, both being
hydrous aluminum silicates. Kaolinite is also known as
kaolin (china clay), long used medicinally in treating diarrhea as an ingested absorbent powder, which, it is sug
gested, binds and inactivates poisons that may be in the
intestines. Kaolin is also used for industrial purposes such
as porcelain and the manufacture of coated paper. In their
pure form, both halloysite and kaolin are white in color,
and although in contemporary times the reddish colored
clay-crimson stone resin ( chi shi zhi)-is preferred for medicinal use in Chinese medicine, Li Shi-Zhen
noted that the properties of the various colored stone resins
shi zhi) are basically similar. He did say, however,
that "regarding the white and crimson colored, the white
enters the qi level while the red enters the blood level."
This substance is quarried, cleaned of extraneous mate.
rial, and the red-colored clay, which is slippery and greasy
like resin, is then collected. When wet, it gives off the smell
of fresh clay, and being quite absorbent, it sticks a bit to
the tongue when licked. Without further preparation, it is
known as unprepared halloysite (# sheng chi shi
zhi), and is sweet, sour, astringent, and warm, with a strong
ability to restrain dampness and generate flesh. In this
form, it is often applied externally for chronic ulcers that
fail to heal over, or for bleeding from wounds.
>CALCINED HALLOYSITE (#T duan chi shi zhi)
The substance is mixed with vinegar, rolled like dough.
then cut into sections. These are placed inside a calcining container, then heated until red hot in a charcoal fire.

Prepared in this manner, it is sweet, astringent, and warm.
Its restraining and inhibiting nature is enhanced, and its
ability to stop bleeding, vaginal discharge, and diarrhea
is increased. The calcined form is generally preferred for
internal use, although the raw form is used in some places
in decoction. In either case, it is best placed in a cotton bag
before decocting

- Sedates the Heart and settles tremors and palpitations: for
palpitations, childhood convulsions, and seizures. Also
used for disharmony of the Heart and spirit wherein the
patient is easily frightened or angered.
- With Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren), Platycladi
Semen (bai zi ren), and Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi) for
irritability and insomnia from Heart deficiency with heat.
-With Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui), Rehmanniae
Radix preparata (shu di huang), and Ginseng Radix (ren
shen) for continuous palpitations and insomnia from Heart
and Liver blood deficiency.
With Succinum (hu po), Arisaematis Rhizoma preparatum (zhi tian ndn xing), and Cinnabaris (zhu sha) for palpi.
tations with anxiety, seizures, or childhood convulsions.
-With Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zht ban xia), Uncariae Ramulus cum Uncis (gou teng), and Poria (fu ling)
for continuous palpitations or palpitations with anxiety as
well as disorientation.
With Bovis Calculus (niu huang) and Coptidis Rhizoma
(huang lian) for childhood convulsions, as in Calm the
Palace Pill with Cattle Gallstone (an gong niti huang wan).
- Clears the Liver and eliminates superficial visual obstructions: for blurred vision due to pterygium or other superficial disorders of the eyes. Often used topically as a powder.
With Bovis Calculus (niu hudng) and Borneolum (bing
pian) for red eyes or superficial visual obstructions. This
combination is also used for severe pain, swelling, and
ulceration of the throat. It is generally applied topically as
a powder and can be used for severe, chronic, nonhealing
Ulcerations anywhere on the body.
With Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) and Haliotidis Concha
(shi jue ming) for wind-heat affecting the Liver channel
with red, dry, and painful eyes along with superficial visual
obstructions.
Promotes healing and generates flesh: used topically as a

14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
powder for chronic, nonhealing ulcers or macerated areas
(usually throat or gums)
- With Borax (peng sha), Indigo naturalis (qing dai), and
Borneolum (bing pian) as a powder applied topically for
sores in the oral cavity and face, including those affecting
the teeth, throat, and ears.
englishReference.commentary:

Heart and Liver channels to clear heat from these two
channels, and to calm the spirit, calm the Liver, and
reduce superficial visual obstructions. It augments the
yin and resolves

It is generated endowed with the essential qi of the greater

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Both salt water pearls from salt water oysters, and freshwater pearls from freshwater clams are used as Margarita
(zhen zhu). For internal use the pearls are finely ground,
and often aqueous trituration is then used to obtain the
finest powder possible. Zhang Jie-Bin cautions that "If fine
powder is not used, it will injure the internal organs." The
powder is placed in an appropriate grinding vessel, cold
water or distilled water is added, and the mixture is stirred.
The material that becomes suspended in the water is immediately poured off and retained, while the coarser material
sinks. This is further ground, water added, and the process
repeated several times. Finally, the material which cannot
be suspended is discarded. The products of the pouringoff are combined and allowed to settle, the water poured
off, and the powder is then dried.. This gives an extremely
fine powder that is most amenable to use. Some references
note that this process is best done in the winter and spring.
as the pearls processed in the summer and autumn tend to
ferment, impairing quality.
Pearls previously used for jewelery must be thoroughly
cleaned of their oily covering, often done by boiling the
washed pearls in a cloth bag immersed in bean curd (250g
of bean curd for 300g of pearls) for two hours. The pearls
are then removed, washed, dried, and powdered, then subjected to aqueous trituration, as described above.
englishReference.qualityCriteria:
Good quality consists of large, pure, round, fine, hard,
lustrous pearls with distinct concentric layers in cross
section.

englishReference.commentary:
Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) is acrid, warm, and enters
the Lung and Stomach channels to release the exterior and

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
induce sweating in the very early stages of externally-contracted exterior disorders, especially that of wind-cold. It is
best at spreading and unblocking the yang qi in either the
upper or lower body, in the exterior or deep in the interior.
In the exterior, it disperses wind-cold and can release the
exterior, but its sweat-inducing action is relatively weak
The Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica
describes its original indications: "As a soup, Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) treats cold damage chills and fevers
attack by wind, and edema and swelling of the face and
eyes. It can induce sweating.
In the interior, Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) unblocks
the yang qi. This use is particularly interesting in the con.
text of a lesser yin-stage disorder characterized by diarrhea,
lassitude, cold extremities, flushed face, and a faint pulse
This is a special situation in which the yin is increasing and
accumulating in the lower part of the body, forcing the
weakened yang to the upper body. In this context, a flushed
face is the key sign indicating that Allii fistulosi Bulbus
(cong bai) is needed to unblock the qi. This is reflected
in the notes following the Discussion of Cold Damage formula Unblock the Pulse Decoction for Frigid Extremities
(tong mai si ni tang), where Zhang Zhong-Jing states: "For
patients with a crimson face, add 9 stalks of Allii fistulosi
Bulbus (cong bai). For those with abdominal pain, remove
the Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) and add Radix Paeoniae
shao yao [6g].
Extensive Annotations to the Differentiation of Patterns
in the Discussion of Cold Damage explains the relationship
of Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) to the face:
Its flavor is acrid, it enters the arm greater yin, and thus
guides all the herbs to unblock the pulse, since both pulses
of the arms belong to the arm greater yin Lung channel.
Furthermore, it also enters the leg yang brightness channel,
and thus travels upward to the face and unblocks the yang
qi, since the leg yang brightness channel skirts the nose and
ascends anterior to the ears, all of which is on the face.
For external application, the use of Allii fistulosi Bulbus
(cong bai) for urinary blockage dates back to the Materia
Medica of Food Therapy, where it "treats wind-water and
swollen pain in the skin ... and facilitates the fiow of urine."
It is repeatedly recommended in many materia medica
texts for emergency treatment of urinary blockage. For
this purpose it can be applied warm to the lower abdo
men, testicles, or umbilicus, or with the addition of moxa
or combined (again externally) with other herbs such as
Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) and Phellodendri Cortex
(huang bai), or with salt, ginger, and Sojae Semen prepara.
tum (dan dou chi).
Internally, both the Materia Medica of Food Therapy
and the later Formulas of Universal Benefit from My Practice
35
note the effectiveness of this herb for treating blood in the
urine. The latter text says to use one handful of Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) and 30g of Curcumae Radix (yu jin)
decoct, and drink warm to unblock this orifice and stop the
bleeding.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH SOJAE SEMEN PREPARATUM (dan dou chi)
The key to this combination lies in its mild and harmoni.
ous action. Acrid and warm, but without parching dryness.
it induces sweating, but not excessively. This preserves the
fluids, which should always be a consideration when using
sweating as a treatment method.
This combination is appropriate for elderly or weakened patients, pregnant women and children, during any
season, and for either hot or cold pathogens. During influenza epidemics, it can be used for prevention. This pair of
herbs is the basis for the formula Scallion and Prepared
Soybean Decoction (cong chi tang). Miso and scallion soup
is an easy, delicious, and only slightly less effective alternative.
Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) is acrid, warm, opens
up the circulation of yang, and releases the exterior. Sojae
Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) is acrid and sweet, opens
up obstruction in the chest to relieve pent-up distress, and
releases the exterior.
This is thus an ideal combination for early-stage
wind-cold which has constrained the protective yang and
obstructed the Lungs and skin, causing chills, absence of
sweating, headache, nasal congestion, and sneezing. The
strong sweat-inducing action of Ephedra Decoction (md
huang tang) may be too extreme at this stage, whereas
Cinnamon Twig Decoction (gui zhi tang) releases the
muscle layer, meaning that sweating is already occurring.
so it too would be inappropriate.
>WITH EpHEDRAE HERBA (md huang)
This herb is lightweight, acrid, and warmly dispersing. Its
actions are focused on the exterior to expel wind-cold. Allii
fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) is acrid and warm, and although
its sweat-inducing action is much milder than Ephedrae
Herba (ma huang), it has a strong yang-unblocking quality
that assists the protective qi in expelling wind-cold from
the exterior.
Used as a pair, they complement each other, Allii fis.
tulosi Bulbus (cong bai) supporting Ephedrae Herba's (ma
huang) sweat-inducing and cold-dispelling strengths with
its own ability to unblock the yang. There is an ancient
adage that goes so far as to say that "without Allii fistulosi
Bulbus (cong bai), Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) is unable

36 1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
to release the exterior." This is an exaggeration, but it does
serve to emphasize the importance of Allii fistulosi Bulbus
(cong bai). Clinically, the pair is most frequently used for
exterior wind-cold patterns where the yang qi is severely
constrained and blocked, requiring a relatively strong
induction of sweating.
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) also disseminates and
unblocks the Lung qi, and dredges the interstices and
pores in order to help the upper burner disseminate qi and
transform fluids, in the treatment of fluid retention and
edema. Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) is able to thoroughly
unblock the flow of yang qi above and below in the treatment of urinary difficulty resulting from the failure of the
Bladder to transform qi.
Therefore, as a pair, these two herbs have a definite
ability to eliminate fluid retention and promote urination,
especially in the treatment of wind-water, a type of edema
marked by swelling of the face, head, and upper body
resulting from the failure of the Lung qi to transform qi,
allowing fluids to accumulate.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. ALLII MACROSTEMI BULBUS (xie bai)
These two herbs are related by form and nature. Both of
them enter the Lungs, and both are warm and acrid. The
main difference is the slipperiness of Allii macrostem
Bulbus (xie bai), which facilitates the orifices, specifically
for unblocking the Large Intestine in dysenteric disorders
brought on by cold stagnation. It is also bitter, warmer, and
better able to move the qi, which enables it to drive out cold
from the chest, scour turbid phlegm, and thereby unbind
chest painful obstruction with pain that penetrates to the
back, accompanied by wheezing and shortness of breath.
Alii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai), on the other hand
releases the exterior with a mild sweat-inducing action that
is lacking in Allii macrostemi Bulbus (xie bai), and enters
the leg yang brightness channel rather than the arm yang
brightness channe -the Stomach instead of the Large
Intestine. However, while it is also used for diarrhea, e.g.!
in the lesser yin stage of a cold damage disorder, this is not
the severe diarrhea associated with dysenteric disorders
brought on by stagnation, but rather that associated with
accumulated cold and lack of yang movement in the lower
burner. Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong bai) is also not bitter, not
as warm as Allii macrostemi Bulbus (xie bai), and does not
scour turbid phlegm.

ity plunders the yin; also there is the problem of deficient

lions will cause people to become confused, will damage

taken together with honey, it will cause diarrhea and lead qi
to accumulate with great injury. Eaten with dates will also
inake one sick. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)

dampness or other processes obstructing the middle and

when these disorders are accompanied by incomplete and

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid and warm, Arecae Pericarpium (da fu pi) enters
the Large Intestine, Small Initestine, Spleen, and Stomach
channels. Unblocking because of its warm nature, and
dispersing because of its acrid flavor, it transforms damp.
ness which has clumped and obstructed the flow of qi.
thus restoring normal qi and fluid circulation. It eases the
middle, drives qi downward, promotes fluid metabolism
and flow, and reduces edema. When the fluids flow in a
regular fashion, urination is natural and easy. By this means

526 9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
it treats abdominal distention and fullness, incomplete
bowel movements, urinary difficulty, edema and leg qi due
to pathogenic dampness obstructing the qi dynamic.
This herb is particularly noted for its ability to treat
pathogenic influences with or without form: it can dis.
perse formless qi stagnation, but also drain dampness and
edema, which do have form. Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Z
notes that it "drives all qi downward, stops sudden turmoil disorder, unblocks the Large and Small Intestines,
strengthens the Spleen, unbinds the Stomach, and regulates
the middle." The Grand Materia Medica lists the following
actions:
directs rebellious qi downward, reduces water qi, floating
edema in the muscles and skin,accumulated rebellious
leg qi, focal distention and fullness, fetal qi [disturbance],
morning sickness, and stifling sensations in the chest [during pregnancy].
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH ATRACTYLODIS MACROCEPHALAE RHIZOMA
(bai zhu)
In this commonly used combination, Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu) tonifies the Spleen while
Arecae Pericarpium (da fu pi) reduces obstruction in the
qi dynamic and fluid metabolism. Thus the actions of each]
enhance the overall effect of the combination: tonifying the
normal qi to eliminate the pathogen, and eliminating the
pathogen to assist tonification. This combination strength
ens the Spleen, assists transportation, dredges clogged
stagnation, facilitates the removal of pathogenic water and
dampness, and reduces edema. It is often used in the treatment of Spleen qi deficiency which has allowed dampness
and water to accumulate and obstruct the qi dynamic, lead
ing to such symptoms as loss of appetite, and epigastric and
abdominal distention and fullness with edema. It is also
good for Spleen deficiency which has allowed pathogenic
water to accumulate and spread through the skin, leading
to floating edema; in this case, Atractylodis macrocephalae
Rhizoma (bai zhu) serves as the chief herb, and Arecae
Pericarpium (da fu pi) as an assistant.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ARECAE SEMEN (bing lang)
The two herbs are similar in nature and action, in that they
both drive qi downward, facilitate the removal of pathogenic water, and reduce edema. In fact, they are different
parts of the same fruit. However, Arecae Pericarpium (da
fu pi) is acrid, lightweight, and has a moderate nature that
more slowly drives qi downward, and tends to disperse
formless qi stagnation. While it is capable of dispersing a
formed pathogenic influence, this refers to the relatively
easily-moved dampness and swellings of edema.
By contrast, Arecae Semen (bing lang) is bitter, acrid.
and heavy, with a strong sinking nature that violently
drives qi downward, breaks up qi stagnation, and drains
accumulated obstruction that does have form. It also.kills
parasites.
The Detailed Materia Medica compares them this way.
The actions of Arecae Pericarpium (da fu pi) are the same
as Arecae Semen (bing lang), but its nature is slower and
moderate, and slightly less powerful, unlike the violent
nature of Arecae Semen (bing lang). [Arecae Pericarpium
(da fu pi), however,] also dredges and unblocks excess
phlegm in the'Spleen and Stomach; if there is qi deficiency.
add Ginseng Radix (ren shen) when using it.
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang BingCheng draws attention to its structure as an external shell:
"While it does not have the [violent] downward-directing
action of Arecae Semen (bing lang), it does have the effect
of mobilizing the skin, disseminating and discharging, and
thus treats edematous swelling in the skin."
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:

because it can drain true qi." (Seeking Accuracy in the
Materia Medica)
