englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, cold, and with a strong downward-directing action,
Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) strongly mobilizes
and reaches directly into the lower burner. Entering the
yang brightness, it washes away accumulated obstruction due to heat from excess; entering the terminal yin, it
clears heat from excess in the blood level, and eliminates
blood stasis. In this way it is useful for a wide variety of
conditions including constipation due to clumped heat
in the Intestines; diarrhea due to collected blockage in
the Intestines; jaundice; epistaxis, red eyes, and swollen throat due to ascendant fire and heat compelling the
blood upward; heat toxin sores and abscesses. It is alsc
used for amenorrhea due to stasis and stagnation, postpartum obstruction, and injury and hematoma from trauma
Unprepared Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) can also be
ground into a powder and used externally to cool heat and
remove toxins.
Materia Medica for Decoctions notes:
Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) is a yin-within-yin herb
which drains fullness, pushes out the old to create the new,
and expels old fith in order to quiet the five yin organs,
exactly like suppressing turmoil and rebellion to bring
about great peace, which is why it is called the genieral' (#
T jiang jun).
Zhang Shan-Lei elaborates on the actions of this herb:
The twelve characters from the Divine Husbandman's
Classic of the Materia Medica that sayl *pushes out the old
to create the new, regulates the middle to transform food.
and quiets the five yin-organs' relate to the application of
Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang), and should be taken
most seriously. This is because unblocking is equivalent
to tonification, both in the digestion of the Intestines and
Stomach, and in the total circulation of the blood vessels.
If there is dormant foulness lodged in stagnation, turbid
237
filth wili not be expelled, and then even the newly gener
ated blood will readily accumulate into stasis. Only washing
away this old putrefaction will create freshness, so that the
middle qi will be harmoniously regulated, food will not be
hindered in its transformation, and the five yin organs will
rest in peaceful harmony.
Zhang goes on to lament that some materia medica texts
characterize its strong effects as "toxic," thereby scaring the
average practitioner from using it in the clinic, "when even
doctors in Western countries extol it as a marvelous tonic
for the Stomach!
Nonetheless, Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) is a
strong purgative, and must be used with care during, for
example, menstruation or for deficient patients. Inform
the patient that it tends to turn the urine and sweat yellow.
It also passes through to the breast milk--which may turn
yellow---and can cause diarrhea in an infant. Note also that
the herb has a peculiar double action: while a large dose
(10g or more) will promote bowel movement, as expected,
a small dose may have the opposite effect. If a strong effect
is needed, the herb should be added separately later in the
process of cooking a decoction because over-cooking will
reduce its effect.
What is less known is that this herb can be used with
excellent effect to expel phlegm-heat through the Intestines.

>WITH NATRII SULFAs (mang xiao)
This is a very commonly used combination. Rhei Radix
et Rhizoma (da huang) attacks, Natrii Sulfas (mang xiao)
softens and moistens. The combination thus works well to
eliminate the obstruction within the Intestines, draining the
excess heat out with the stool. Once the old fetid material
is expelled, the Stomach and Intestines are purified; when
pathogenic heat is removed, the Stomach and Intestines
can function smoothily. This is the reason that this combination is found in most of the formulas that purge heat
accumulation. In biomedical terms, Rhei Radix et Rhizoma
(da huang) stimulates peristalsis, while Natrii Sulfas (mang

bowel, increasing fluids in the intestines, and thus leading
to passage of watery stool.
Natrii Sulfas (mang xiao) and Rhei Radix et Rhizoma
(da huang) can also be combined in the treatment of
abscesses, swellings, and toxic sores, as they clear fire and
reduce swelling.
> WITH CINNAMOMI RAMULUS (gui zhi)
This combination has a broad clinical application, and is an
excellent example of the subtleties involved in the strategy
of combining hot and cold herbs, Due to the strong exterior-releasing and channel-warming actions of Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gui zhi), and the purging and blood stasis-reducing actions of Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang), this combination has a very intricate clinical action:
- Utilizing the exterior-releasing effect of Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gui zhi) with the draining of internal excess accu
mulation by Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) to treat a
combined exterior and interior condition which presents
with chills, headache, fever and sweating, together with
abdominal fullness and pain. This is called "sweating and
purging used together.
Utilizing Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) to drain
downward, and the warmth of Cinnamomi Ramulus (gul

et Rhizoma (da huang). This is often the remedy for a situation in which purging has been used too soon in an externally-contracted exterior disorder, causing the exterior
pathogen to sink into the interior and obstruct the Spleen,
Stomach, and Intestines, with such symptoms as abdominal fullness and pain with constipation.
Utilizing the ability of Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da
huang) to enter the blood and remove stagnation, as well
as its ability to cool the blood, as the primary approach,
and Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) to warm the blood and
thereby encourage the restoration of normal blood flow
after the stagnation has been removed. This is reflected in
the formula Peach Pit Decoction to Order the Qi (tao he
cheng gi tang)

Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da huang) is bitter and cold. I

englishReference.commentary:
16 / Substances that Extinguish Wind and Stop Tremors
According to some traditional sources, this substance
Bitter, cold, and heavy in weight, Haematitum (dai zhe shi)
cools heat and suppresses rebellion, relying on its heaviness
to sedate the Liver fire, and to calm and direct the rebellious
qi downward. Encountering the Sources of the Classic of
Materia Medica observes: "The heaviness of Haematitum
(dai zhe shi) is used to sedate rebellious qi."
It is thus used for dizziness, tinnitus, and deafness due
to Liver yang ascendancy. When there is tranverse rebellion of Liver fire affecting the Lungs and Stomach, leading
to nausea, vomiting, belching, and acute wheezing from
phlegm, Haematitum (dai zhe shi) can be used as a chief
medicinal. Its heaviness sedates trepidation, jitteriness, and
fright causing the qi to float upward, and it is used in the
treatment of convulsions in both adults and children.
Because the Liver stores the blood, and Haematitum
(dai zhe shi) excels at clearing Liver. fire, it also cools the
blood and stops bleeding associated with heat in the blood,
whether it manifests as nosebleed, vomiting of blood, or
continuous uterine bleeding.
As explained in Essays on Medicine Esteeming the
Chinese and Respecting the Western:
It can generate blood while cooling blood; its weighty
mass excels at suppressing rebellious qi, directing phlegm
downward, stopping nausea and vomiting, and unblocking
dry clumps-when used adroitly it can achieve marvelous
results.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. INULAE FLOs (xuan fu hua)
Both substances direct rebellious Lung and Stomach qi
downward to stop nausea and vomiting and to stop wheez
ing, but while Haematitum (dai zhe shi) relies on its mas.
sive weight to sink the rebellious qi, and its bitter coldness
to cool Liver fire, Inulae Flos (xuan fu hua) has a more
complex action involving its bitter, salty, warm, and acrid
properties. Saltiness softens hardened areas of clumped
phlegm, which are then dispersed by its warm acridity, and
then directed downward by its bitterness. Inulae Flos (xuan
fu hua) is thus most appropriate when clumped turbid
phlegm accumulates internally and obstructs the ascent
and descent of the qi dynamic, leading to nausea, vomiting, and wheezing. Haematitum (dai zhe shi), on the other
hand, can sedate Liver yang ascendancy, cool the blood and
stop bleeding, which Inulae Flos (xuan fu hua) cannot do.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "red stone from Dai county
Hematite gets its name from a Greek word meaning bloodlike' because of the color of its powder, which has long been
used as a pigment. In Chinese, too, the stone is named
for its color, as Li Shi-Zhen explains: "[The character] #
(zhe) means reddish." The word dai was the name of an
ancient prefecture which supplied large quantities of the
ore, and H shi simply means stone.
This mineral is also known as red stone ( T fi hong
shi tou. The term nail-head hematite (# ding tou
zhe shi) refers to chunks of hematite studded with protrusions that appear to have been beaten outward with a
punch; this is considered to be the best quality. When used
without calcining, it is known as unprepared hematite (#
+# sheng dai zhe shi), which is cold and most appropriate for calming the Liver, subduing the yang, directing
downward, stopping nausea, cooling the blood, and stopping bleeding. If calcined, these properties are somewhat
diminished.
>CALCINED HEMATITE (+# duan dai zhe shi)
The ore is placed inside a calcining container and heated
until red hot all through, then plunged into vinegar to cool
down. This process is repeated until the ore is friable, after
which it is removed and pulverised. This process reduces
its cold, bitter nature, while enhancing its ability to restrain
inhibit, and stop bleeding. It is thus most often used in the
treatment of nosebleed, vomiting of blood, and continuous
uterine bleeding.
Li Shi-Zhen describes the purpose behind this:
It is calcined red hot and cooled in vinegar either three
times or seven times, pulverized, then used after aqeous
trituration. This relies on the mutual control [between the
ore and the vinegar], and also leads it into the blood level of
the Liver channel.
Not everyone agrees with this form of processing, however.
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting
the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun--who, it must be said, generally prefers unprocessed substances--says that: "For
directing the Stomach [qi] downward, this is truly the most
effectived substance ... but if it is calcined, it no longer has
this effect.

16 / Substances that Extinguish Wind and Stop Tremors
Be that as it may, the high temperature involved in the
process of calcining (over 500C) has the beneficial effect
of reducing the level of arsenic salts contained in the ore, as
well as the tendency of raw hematite to irritate the intestinal
tract.

englishReference.commentary:
Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) is lightweight and
floating in nature, with good venting, dispersing, and disseminating actions. Not only does it vent and disperse
exterior pathogens, it can also spread and clear constrained
heat in the interior. Its sweat-inducing action is very subdued, and is therefore said to "bring out sweat without
a superior medicinal for venting constraint."
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica elaborates:
Since its flavor is bitter and its temperature cold, one would
expect it to be a bitter, downward-directing herb without
any power to ascend or lead upward. However, after it is
Steamed, and despite its bitter flavor, it is aromatic, and
although it is cold, it has lifting and dispersing properties.
This is why, combined with Allii fistulosi Bulbus (cong
bai), it can induce sweating, with salt it can induce vomit
ing, with wine it can treat wind, with Chinese leeks (#
jiu cai) it can treat dysenteric disorders [Allii macrostemi
Bulbus (xie bai) was noted for this indication in the Grand
Materia Medica], with garlic it can stop bleeding, and when
dry-fried until cooked it can stop sweating. Likewise when
there is a pathogen in the upper body causing symptoms of
irritabilityrestlessness,headachestifling sensation in the
chest,vexation, insomnia,expression of rashes, and nausea
when combined with Gardeniae Fructus (zhi zi) it can lead
the pathogen upward to be vomited out. This prevents it
from descending internally and causing symptoms of internal clumping.
One of the controversies surrounding the combination
of Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) and Fructus
Gardeniae Jasminoidis (zhi zi) is whether, when it first
appeared as the formula Gardenia and Prepared Soybean
Decoction (zhi zi chi tang) in Discussion of Cold Damage, it
was meant to induce vomiting. The question arose because
of a note following the formula which states ambiguously
that if a person vomits after taking it, they should not be
given any more. The most reasonable explanation is that
this means if a person vomits they should stop taking
the formula, not that it is intended to induce vomiting
However, through the ages many writers have characterized the formula as an emetic. Because the formula following this one in Discussion of Cold Damage uses the same
combination plus Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang)
to stop nausea and vomiting, this reading would seem dif.
ficult to defend. Nonetheless, some patients do vomit, and
many do feel better having done so. When this occurs, as
Discussion of Cold Damage points out, the patient should
stop taking the herbs.
Some insight into the use of Sojae Semen preparatum
(dan dou chi) can be gleaned from writings about how it
is used to treat lurking pathogens. An example is Liu BaoYi's discussion in Encountering the Sources of Warm-Heat
Pathogen Diseases about how to treat lurking pathogens in
the lesser yin channel of the Kidneys:t
In my humble opinion there is nothing better than using
Scutellaria Decoction (huang qin tang) plus Scrophulariae
Radix (xuan shen) and Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
chi). It is the most appropriate method by far, with littie
need for alteration. This is because Scutellaria Decoction
(huang qin tang) is specially designed to drain and cool
internal heat. Scrophulariae Radix (xuan shen) tonifies
Kidney yin. Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) is made
from black soybeans, which themselves enter the Kidney
channel, and is made by steaming in a pent-up container--just like the pathogen itself before it begins to emerge.
Because its nature and flavor is harmonious and neutral,
without the drawback of strong diaphoresis or damage to
the yin, it is just right for assisting the expression of a deep.
lying pathogen in the lesser yin.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH GARDENIAE FRUCTUS (zhi zi)
This herb is bitter and cold. It drains heat by directing fire
downward and out through the urine. Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) is acrid, bitter, and cool, ascending
and dispersing, with the ability to disseminate constrained
heat. When used together, Fructus Gardeniae Jasminoidis
(zhi zi) guides heat downwa'rd, cooling and draining the
irritability from the heat constrained in the chest and diaphragm, while Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou chi) vents
the heat toward the exterior and releases the constraint.
Each supports the other, one venting and releasing, the
other guiding downward and out. The pair is therefore
commonly used for exterior heat as it first enters the interior, as well as for later stage residual heat trapped in the
chest and diaphragm. This combination is called Gardenia
and Prepared Soybean Decoction (zhi zi chi tang)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Unless other exterior-releasing herbs are used in the fermentation process, the venting and dispersing quality of
this herb is extremely weak. However, various ingredients
are used in different parts of China to prepare this herb.
some of which are cold and others hot. Most commonly.
Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao) and Mori Folium
(sang ye) are made into a decoction which is then used to
steam the black soybeans until they are thoroughly soft.
The beans are then covered with the dregs of the decoction, left to ferment, and finally dried to form Sojae Semen
preparatum (dan dou cht). This is known as aromatic prepared soybean ( xiang dou chi or simply # xiang
chi), or clearing prepared soybean ( qing dou chi).
This is the type that is most appropriate for the Discussion
of Cold Damage formula Gardenia and Prepared Soybean
Decoction (zhi zi chi tang), which treats heat constrained
in the chest.
The product known as Sojae Semen preparatum (dan
dou chi) from Shanghai is prepared quite differently. The
juice is pressed from fresh Polygoni hydropiperis Herba
65
(la liao), Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao), Eupatorii
Herba (pei lan), Perillae Folium (zi su ye), Pogostemonis/
Agastaches Herba (huo xiang), and Nelumbinis Folium (he
ye). Separately, Ephedrae Herba (ma hudng) is cooked until
a concentrated decoction remains. The black soybeans are
mixed with these liquids, steamed, fermented, and dried
This produces a preparation which is warmer than that dis.
cussed in the previous paragraph. It is suitable for treating
exterior wind-cold patterns, and is the type called for in the
formula Scallion and Prepared Soybean Decoction (cong
chi tang), variously called bland prepared soybean (
dan dou chi), warming prepared soybean (i wen
dou chi) or even (confusingly) clearing prepared soybean
(#i qing dou chi). It is best to consult one's supplier to
determine whether the Sojae Semen preparatum (dan dou
chi) that they sell has been prepared with Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang).
DRY-FRIED PREPARED SOYBEANS chao dOu chi)
Here the soybeans are dry-fried over a moderate flame until
aromatic or slightly scorched. Historically, most materia
medica texts record that fried Sojae Semen preparatum
(dan dou chi) can stop sweating. For example, the Grand
Materia Medica notes that, "fried well, it can stop sweating, just like the roots and nodes of Ephedrae Herba (md
huang)." The present view is that, after dry-frying, its abil
ity to release the exterior is weakened, and it only reduces
food stagnation and harmonizes the middle.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter and slightly cooling, Salviae miltiorrhizae Radix (dan
shen) enters the blood level of the Heart, Pericardium, and
Liver channels to invigorate the blood, transform stasis,
and tonify the blood. It cools the blood, reduces swelling,
clears heat from the nutritive level, and eliminates irritability. Salviae miltiorrhizae Radix (dan shen) is a primary
herb for gynecological disorders involving blood stasis and
blood heat, and is also used in the treatment of joint pain
and sores.
Materia Medica of Combinations states that it "nour
ishes the blood, invigorates the blood, generates new
blood, and expels retained blood ... it cures fever and chills
due to consumption, and stops pain in the joints." The
Thoroughly Revised Materia Medica adds that it "also treats
red eyes, bulging disorder pain, sores, scabies, and toxic
swellings, expels pus, and generates flesh."
Regarding the ability of this herb to calm irritability due
to heat, Materia Medica of South Yunnan says that it "tonifies the Heart and settles the emotions, quiets the spirit
and makes tranquil the Heart." It is used for restlessness,
irritability, palpitations, and insomnia due to heat entering
the nutritive level.
Many later materia medica texts contain the statement
that "the single herb Salviae miltiorrhizae Radix (dan shen),
powdered, has effects equal to those of Four-Substance
Decoction (si wu tang) and therefore treats all women's
disorders. However, this statement was roundly criticized
by such writers as Zhang Shan-Lei. In Rectification of the
Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang says that even this
famous formula cannot, by itself, treat all women's disorders, and "even more, a single-herb formula--is this not a
huge joke? ... Mediocre physicians and vulgar practitioners
all thrill to its simplicity, memorize it, and use it indiscrimi.
nately!?" Zhang goes on to place the blame squarely at the
feet of Li Shi-Zhen, who (he says) uncritically quoted the
passage from an earlier work in his Grand Materia Medica.
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang BingCheng says that it
may have the character (shen) [which is in the name of
Ginseng Radix (ren shen)] as part of its name, but its blood.
tonifying action is rather weak, while its blood-invigorating
action is very strong; it is a capital herb for regulating the
blood level. The reason [earlier materia medica said that] it
603
treats wind painful obstruction and expels clumped accumulations is that when the blood moves, wind is naturally
extinguished, and accumulations are naturally mobilized.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH SANTALI ALBI LIGNUM (tan xiang)

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Although it can tonify the blood, it is best at promoting
blood movement. If menstruation is early in its course, o
obstructed due to lack of blood, or if the blood is limited
and unable to nourish a fetus causing the fetus to become
restless,or after giving birth the blood flows smoothlyin
none of these cases should (Salviae miltiorrhizae Radix
(dan shen)] be used; if it is used it will cause continuous
bleeding. Whenever during a warm or febrile disorder the
pathogen is in the qi level, if Salviae miltiorrhizae Radix
(dan shen) is mistakenly used, it will lead [the pathogen]
into the blood or the nutritive level: one must be cautious.
Long-term consumption often leads to reddened eyes, thus
it should be [called] warm in nature; the Materia Medica

Unless there is good cause, its use is contraindicated for

>DRY-FRIED SALVIA (#chao dan shen)
The root is dry-fried until slightly scorched, which modifies its nature to slightly warming and more moderate in
its actions, allowing it to both nourish and invigorate the
blood with less of a blood-cooling effect. This is best for
cases of blood deficiency or blood stagnation without any
Signs of heat.
>WINE-FRIED SALVIA (jiu chdo dan shen)
The root slices are mixed with yellow rice wine, left covered briefly as it is absorbed, then dry-fried until deep
yellow in color. This method of preparation utilizes the
acrid-dispersing quality of the wine to increase the root's
ability to invigorate the blood and dispel stasis. It is mainly
used to treat disorders such as dysmenorrhea, postpartum
abdominal pain, and abdominal masses.
>TURTLE-BLOOD SALVIA
bie xue ban dan shen)
The fresh blood of the Chinese soft-shelled turtle (Amyda
sinensis) is mixed with the herb until the roots are saturated; they are then dried in the sun. This method has the
effect of better guiding the herb into the Liver blood and
also moderating its adverse bitter and drying qualities. It
is used primarily for cases of blood stasis associated with
Liver blood or Liver yin deficiency.
>CHARRED SALVIA (F dan shen tan)
The root slices are dry-fried at a high temperature until the
exterior is blackened, then cooled by spraying with water.
This method retains the herb's property of invigorating the
blood, but enables it to stop bleeding. In this ability to both
invigorate the blood and stop bleeding, it is quite similar
to Notoginseng Radix (san qi), but inexpensive and more
readily available.

englishReference.commentary:
Lophateri Herba (dan zhu ye) is bland, sweet, and cold. Its
ability to leach out dampness and facilitate urination is very
strong, while at the same time it cools the Heart and thus
eliminates irritability. It is usually prescribed for febrile
diseases, irritability, thirst, scanty dark urine, and painful
urinary dribbling. Because it is lightweight with a thin qi, it
is also used to treat upper burner qi-level heat. Harm and
Benefit in the Materia Medica notes, however, that "Its therapeutic strength is rather weak. It cannot serve as the chief
herb, but it can serve as an assistant." The Grand Materia
Medica was the first book to identify Lophateri Herba (dan
zhu ye). It comments briefly that the herb "expels irritable
heat, facilitates urination, and cools the Heart." Lophateri
Herba (dan zhu ye) has a greater diuretic action than actual
bamboo leaves, which are better for heat in the upper burner causing cough, irritability, and thirst.

englishReference.commentary:
The sweetness of Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) toni
fies and moistens, its acrid flavor disperses, its bitterness
drains, and its warmth unblocks. These properties make
it the most appropriate herb for harmonizing the blood,
which means that it both invigorates and tonifies the blood,
and is suitable for all blood patterns involving stasis, deficiency, dryness, or cold. When the blood is sufficient and
moves harmoniously, the qi will also circulate properly;
the Grand Materia Medica therefore calls this an herb "for
the qi within the blood." Proper movement of both qi and
blood eliminates pain, expels wind, restores normal men--
strual flow, assists healing, and moistens dryness. The type
of dryness it particularly addresses is that in the Intestines
causing constipation, as noted in Essentials of the Materia
Medica, which says that it "moistens dryness and lubricates
the Intestines.
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun notes that this herb

0 12 / Tonifying Herbs
is sweet, slightly acrid, rich in fluids, and warm in nature. It
is the primary herb for generating blood and invigorating
blood, but it also disseminates and unblocks the qi aspect,
inducing the qi and blood to return [to their proper place],
hence the name state of return. Its power can raise because
it is strong and steady in action, and warm; it can direct
downward because its flavor is rich and acrid; internally,
it moistens the organs because of its concentrated fluids
and sweetness; externally, it thrusts out to the muscle layer
because of its acrid, warm nature.
Although Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) is warm,
it can still be used if there is heat with blood deficiency,
because, as it can generate blood,it enriches the yin,and
by enriching the yin, it can reduce heat. Although its exte
rior-dispersing property is rather weak, it actually excels
at expelling wind, because when wind contacts the body
it tends to cause painful obstruction of blood, and blood,
once invigorated, unblocks the area of obstruction, so that
wind naturally departs.
Cheng Wu-Ji, one of the earliest commentators on the
Discussion of Cold Damage, is quoted in the Grand Materia
Medica as saying that
The vessels are the dwelling of blood, and all blood belongs
to the Heart. In order to unblock the vessels,one must first
tonify the Heart and augment the blood. Therefore, Zhang
Zhong-Jing treated those with hands and feet that are
extremely cold and a pulse that is [so] thin that it is about
to be cut off by using the bitter warmth of Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) to assist the Heart blood.
Zhang Yuan-Su observed:
Blood that is clogged and thus unable to flow causes pain,
the sweet warmth of Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui)
harmonizes the blood, its acrid warmth disperses internal
cold, and its bitter warmth assists the Heart and disperses
cold, making qi and blood each return [to normalcy].
Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) is well known as the
premier herb in gynecology due to its harmonious warmth,
which is not drying, its tonification, which is not cloying,
and its gentle invigoration of the blood,which is not exces
sive. Nonetheless, during pregnancy, it should only be used
with considerable caution, and only after the practitioner
has a firm grasp of its clinical use.

>DRY-FRIED TANGKUEI( chao dang gui)
The sliced herb is dry-fried until yellow or scorch marks
appear. Dry-frying reduces the oil content of the herb,
which renders it less able to moisten the Intestines, but it
retains its ability to harmonize the blood and adjust men
struation. It is particularly appropriate for gynecological
patients who have diarrhea.
> WINE-FRIED TANGKUEI (&# jiui chao dang gui)
The herb slices are sprayed with yellow rice wine, left covered briefly to absorb the wine, then dry-fried until dry. If
it is baked dry rather than fried, it is called wine-washed
tangkuei ( jiui xi dang gut), which retains a slightly
stronger Intestine-moistening quality. Both methods of
preparation rely on the acrid, dispersing qualities of the
wine to greatly enhance the herb's ability to invigorate the
blood. It is therefore most appropriate for patterns of blood
stasis accompanied by blood deficiency.
>EARTH-FRIED TANGKUEI(tu chdo dang gui)
Finely powdered Terra flava usta (zao xin tu) is heated in
a wok, then slices of the herb are added and stirred until
the surface turns earth-colored; the earth is then sifted out.
This is also known as earth tangkuei ( tu dang gui)
This method of preparation reduces its oil content, and
leads it directly into the Spleen and Stomach. It is com-

monly used for tonifying the blood in patients with diarrhea or loose stools.
>VINEGAR-FRIED TANGKUEI(k#cu chdo dang gui)
The herb is mixed with rice vinegar, left covered briefly to
absorb the vinegar, then dry-fried or baked until dry. This
method of preparation is not commonly used nowadays,
although there are some who regard vinegar-fried tangkuei
as superior for entering the Liver channel, and its sour,
inhibiting quality as superior for restraining bleeding. In
Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang Bing-Cheng
advised: "To treat nosebleed, use vinegar-fried tangkuei."
>CHARRED TANGKUEI(dang gui tan)
The sliced herb is dry-fried until the surface is blackened
and the interior is scorched yellow. This method of preparation is best for stopping bleeding while still reducing
blood stasis, and is thus commonly used in the clinic.

englishReference.actions:
- Cools the blood and reduces steaming: This herb specifi.
cally drains Kidney fire, eliminates lurking heat, and clears
heat from the bories. It is used for such symptoms as night
sweats, steaming bone disorder with sweating, chronic lowgrade fever, irritability, and thirst. Also for floating fire in
the Kidney channel marked by toothache.
- With Stellariae Radix (yin chai hu) for blood deficiency
steaming bone disorder, or other types of recurrent after.
noon fevers. Add Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) and
nels. It eliminates heat from excess in the blood by cooling
it, and is therefore indicated for bleeding associated with
chaotic circulation due to heat. It also treats blood heat
from deficiency, and is very effective in treating sensations
of heat from yin deficiency and steaming bone disorder
with sweating. In addition, it clears and directs Lung fire
downward to stop cough, thirst, and restless irritability. It
is often used for the flushing associated with heat from deficiency, nightsweats, cough, and wheezing from Lung heat,
and for nosebleeds in wasting and thirsting disorder.
According to the Grand Materia Medica, Lycii Cortex
(di gu pi) tonifies yin deficiency. While this is disputed by
other writers, by eliminating the injurious effects of heat on
the blood and yin, Lycii Cortex (di gu pi) is able to preserve
their integrity, and thus, in effect, to tonify them.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes:
"This substance is cool but not intense. It can regulate
deficient and consumptive disorders. Its aroma is light and
acrid, thus cooling the Lungs." Wang Hao-Gu adds that
Lycii Cortex (di gu pf) "directs lurking fire in the Lungs
downward."
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and
Respecting the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun explains his under
standing of the origin of these qualities:
This ... root drives deep into the earth, and is full of yin
qi, so it is cool by nature and is excellent at reducing heat.

2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
Because its vigor tends downward, it has the power to restrain and inhibit, and this is why it treats steaming bones
with sweating. It can stop the spitting up of blood and
nosebleeds, and especially directs downward and clears
Kidney heat. It unblocks.and facilitates both bowel movements and urination, and treats bleeding due to heat ir
both the stool and urine. Furthermore, its ability to restrain
and drive downward can clear and direct downward the
heat that floats and drifts in the upper burner, thus curing
cough due to heat in the Lungs. This is why most of the
materia medica [texts] mention that it treats cough. Yet it is
forbidden for cough due to pathogenic wind in the Lungs,
as its nature is restraining.

englishReference.comparisons:
> Vs. ARTEMISIAE ANNUAE HERBA (qing hao)
Both herbs clear heat, cool the blood, and treat steaming
bone disorder. Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao), however, is bitter, cold, and tends to clear heat of the Liver and
Gallbladder, as well as heat at both the yin and blood levels.
It induces lurking, latent heat that is deep within the yin' to
vent outward and be released, and also resolves summerheat and malarial-like disorders. By contrast, Lycii Cortex
(di gu pi) is sweet, bland, and slightly cold. Its sweet, moist,
and cold-clearing properties act primarily on the Lungs,
Liver, and Kidneys, treating heat from yin deficiency. While
Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao) treats steaming bone
disorder where there is no sweating, Lycii Cortex (di gu
pi) treats it where there is sweating. And where Artemisiae
annuae Herba (qing hao) treats malarial-like disorders,
Lycii Cortex (di gu pi) treats wasting and thirsting disease.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ARISAEMA CUM BILE (dan nan xing)
Both substances cool heat and settle jitteriness and convul.
sions; both are used for restlessness and convulsions due
to high fever, as well as cough and wheezing due to fire
and heat in the Lungs. Pheretima (di long), however, more
strongly clears heat and calms the Liver, Arisaema cum
Bile (dan nan xing) more strongly expels wind, transforms
phlegm, and settles convulsions. In the Lungs, Pheretima
(di long) is more often used for asthma, and the dyspne?
of bronchiolitis, while Arisaema cum Bile (dan nan xing)
is more frequently used for spasmodic cough and wheez
ing due to hot phlegm blocking the Lungs, for example, in
childhood pneumonia or acute bronchitis.
Both medicinals are also used for impaired limb move.
ment as a sequela of wind-stroke or hemiplegia. Pheretima
(di long), however, tends to unblock the collaterals, while
Arisaema cum Bile (dan nan xing) tends to expel wind
and transform phlegm; hence the former mainly treats the
paralysis, while the latter is used for phlegm-heat causing
loss of consciousness in wind-stroke.

>MALE CLOVE (T gong ding xiang)
Generally cultivated, the flowerbud is collected in winter
when the buds change color from green to red. This is also

To emphasize the best quality, the terms large flower clove

>MoTHER CLOVE(#Tmu ding xiang)
This is the dried mature clove fruit, also known simply
as #T mu ding. One explanation for its name is that the
small spikes were considered male and thus more powerful.
hence the term gong, which means male (among other
things); the larger round fruits were considered female
and thus less powerful, hence the term # mu, meaning
mother. As they often split in two, and then resemble the
tongue of a chicken, they are also known as chicken tongue
fragrance ( ji she xiang), a term used as early as the
Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians.
Mother i0ve are less fragrant in aroma, and more
bland in flavor, with less ppower to direct rebellious Stomach
qi downward. However, their effect Iasts longer than the
buds (male cloves), and thus they are often combined to
achieve a more powerful and lasting effect than either used
alone. Furthermore, the mother cloves enter the blood
aspect to invigorate the blood and induce labor. Extension

sheath filled with powdered mother clove and inserted into

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid-dispersing, bitter-drying, and warming in nature
to expel pathogenic cold and promote qi and blood flow,
Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du hu) dispels wind, pre.
vails over dampness, disperses cold, and unblocks painful
obstruction. Entering the Kidney channel, which governs
the interior and the lower body, Angelicae pubescentis
Radix (du hu6) tracks down lurking wind and is used for
painful obstruction in the feet, aching heaviness of the
lower back, lurking wind headache, and swollen gums and
toothache due to wind. One of the hallmarks of this herb is
that it can be used for both chronic and acute disorders.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.NOTOPTERYGII RHIZOMA SEU RADIX (qiang huo)
Both herbs are very similar in action in that they dispel
wind and eliminate dampness, disperse cold, and relieve
painful obstruction. They are thus often used together in
the treatment of painful obstruction disorders due to wind
cold, and dampness.
However, Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo)
mainly enters the greater yang and is best for dispersing
the pathogenic influences of wind, cold, and dampness in
the greater yang by promoting sweating and releasing the
exterior. Thus, it is better suited to an attack on the upper
body reffected in such symptoms as pain and stiffness of the
upper back, neck, occiput, and head. By contrast, Angelicae
pubescentis Radix (du huo) tends to have a stronger action
on the lesser yin channel, and is thus better suited for winddaimpness in the lower body with pain in the lumbar region
legs, calves, and feet.
Both herbs treat headache, but of different types: Noto.
pterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) treats greater yang
headache in the vertex and occiput, while Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo) treats lesser yin headache involving
the teeth and cheeks.
These differences are best remembered.through their
channel tendencies: the actions of Notopterygii Rhizoma
seu Radix (qiang huo) are more superficial, treating recently contracted wind in the upper body, which are greater
yang. The actions of Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo)
are deeper, focusing on chronic lurking wind in the interior
and lower body, and are thus lesser yin.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang
Shan-Lei emphasizes that Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du
huo), and for that matter Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix
(qiang huo), are best suited to very cold climates like that
of northern China. In warmer climates, extremely cold and
damp winds are less likely to be the sole cause of headache
and other pains:
325
Acrid and warm [qualities] are not suited to the southeast
[of China], and this applies to more than seasonal disorders. Even though Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang
huo and Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo) are excel
lent medicinals for wind-cold-damp pathogens, painful
obstruction, and atrophy disorders, in these provinces the
yin and blood are constitutionally frail, and even if people
do suffer from any of these disorders, half of the cause is
blood deficiency.There might be wind-cold,but it is blood
deficiency that generates the wind, and qi deficiency that
generates the cold. This is vastly different from the wind
painful obstruction of northwest [of China], all of which
is due to bandit wind and extreme cold; the nature of the
disorder is simply not the same. Thus, [in more clement
climates] the use of even one acrid-warm and rigorously
drying herb must be attended with caution at all times.

>WITH GINSENG RADIX (ren shen)

for patterns involving yang deficiency associated with]
insufficiency of essence, blood, and marrow.
An adage drawn from the Inner Classic states that if the
form is insufficient, warm it with qi, and if the essence
is insufficient, tonify it with flavor. In this combination,
Ginseng Radix (ren shen) strongly tonifies the primal qi,
and Cervi Cornu pantotrichum (lu rong) warms the fire
at the gate of vitality to generate qi. Cervi Cornu pantotrichum (lu rong) also has a strong flavor to augment the
essence and marrow, strengthening the sinews and bones,
which is complemented by the fluid-generating property
of Ginseng Radix (ren shen). Thus while qi, blood, yin, and
yang all benefit from this combination, it goes deeper to
powerfully fortify the primal yang. Since ancient times it
has been regarded as an unrivaled supplement for congenital insufficiency, or post-natal depletion due to consumption. However, it is more appropriate for yang deficiency
or weakness of the fire at the gate of vitality than it is for
yin deficiency.
This combination should also be taken in small doses
over a long period of time, rather than trying to get quick
results by taking large and frequent doses. As explained by
the early modern physician Cao Bing-Zhang:
If one is taking Ginseng Radix (ren shen) and Cervi Cornu
pantotrichum (lu rong),use small amounts over many days
it will augment the qi and nourish the bloodall benefit
and no harm, even if [the patient] has some heat, it still will
not harm. If the person is yang deficient with dry yin, and
also suddenly takes large doses, this will simply reinforce
the dryness and burn the yin.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Deer antler velvet refers to the early stage of antler growth.
and is formed from cartilage that later rapidly converts
into bone, after which all blood supply is lost. Antlers are
deciduous. Each spring, male deer form new antlers on the
base of the previous year's antlers. Antlers grow rapidly, up
to 10kg within two months.
If not removed, the antlers are naturally shed in winter
to allow the growing cycle to begin again the following
spring. In all farmed deer, the antlers are removed for
safety reasons, whether they are used medicinally or not.
The optimal time for surgical removal of the deer velvet is
between 55 and 60 days after the new antlers have begun tc
grow. This is done under anesthetic.
Generally, the soft, tender slices are regarded as supe.

12 / Tonifying Herbs
rior in quality, hence the term tender deer velvet (t #t #
nen lu rong), but other terms refer to the level of antler from
which the slice was taken. If cut closer to the tip (the best)
where the texture is tender, oily, and moist, it is called deer
velvet blood slices (##H lu rong xue pian) or blood
velvet slices (f # H xue rong pian). If cut further from the
tip (not as good) where the texture is tougher, less oily
and the slices are of a whitish color, it is called deer velvet
powder slices (##H lu rong fen pian). This, however.
should not be confused with the actual processed powder
called deer velvet powder (# lu rong fen), which is
suitable for capsules, pills, or direct consumption.

China; see

englishReference.commentary:
Tonics derived from animals are considered a step closer to
humans than those derived from plants. As such, they are

12 / Tonifying Herbs
thought to be particularly effective, and are described as
sympathetic substances between blood and flesh (fu #
xue rou yo qing zhi pin). Asini Corii Colla (e jiao) is
one of the most commonly utilized, as it not only replenishes the Kidney essence, moistens Lung dryness, and nourishes the Liver blood, but also stops bleeding. By enriching
the yin, it directs the fire from yin deficiency downward,
and so can be used in the treatment of blazing fire from yin
deficiency, which causes irritability and insomnia, as often
occurs following a febrile disease.
The Grand Materia Medica lists the common indications of this medicinal:
vomiting of blood, nosebleeds, painful bloody urinary drib
bling, blood in the urine [without pain], Intestinal wind,
dysenteric disorders [due to heat], pain in women due to
blood, blood dryness, irregular menstruation, infertility,
continuous uterine bleeding, vaginal discharge, and ali disorders of pregnancy and birth.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica observes that it
incorporates the beneficial pure yin water from the [Dong]
E [area] welis, and also incorporates the yin tonification
of the pure black donkey hide. Its nature and flavor are
both yin, so that it enters the Liver channel to nourish the
blood, then enters the Kidney channel to enrich the water
Tonification of water naturally controls heat. As a gelatin, it
is moistening and not drying, and gelatin [made from hide]
by nature moistens the Lungs.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH CoPTIDIS RHIZOMA (huang lian)
There are two aspects to this combination: one is cool.
ing heat and quieting the spirit, the other is fortifying the
yin and alleviating dysenteric disorders. Thus it is both a
supplementing and a heat-clearing combination
Asini Corii Colla (e jiao) enriches the Kidney water
and supplements the Heart blood, while Coptidis Rhizoma
(huang lian) drains the Heart fire and expels irritability
and heat. Similarly, when the Kidney water is replenished,
it too can ascend and benefit the Heart; when Heart fire is
directed downward, the Kidneys obtain warmth. In this
way, the mutual support between fire and water is restored,
and the spirit is naturally quiet. This is known as tonifying
the north (Kidneys) and draining the south (Heart). This
combination is the foundation for the Discussion of Cold
Damage formula Coptis and Ass-Hide Gelatin Decoction
(huang lian e jiao tang).
Furthermore, Asini Corii Colla (e jiao) has the ability
to stop bleeding and enrich the blood, and can also dredge
heat toxin from the Intestines and guide it out of the body.
The Grand Materia Medica notes:
[D]ysenteric disorders often come from lurking heat following injury by summerheat. Asini Corii Colla (e jiao)
is an important herb for the Large Intestine: if heat toxin

remains and obstructs the Large Intestine, Asini Corii Colla
(e jiao) can dredge and guide it out; if there is no obstruction from heat toxin, Asini Corii Colla (e jiao) can pacify
and quiet.
Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian) is extremely cold, clearing
and releasing heat toxin within the Intestines, and because
it is bitter, it also fortifies the yin. Together these medici
nals treat heat toxin accumulating into clumps within the
Intestine, injuring the blood collaterals and thereby causing
the passage of blood and pus in the stool. The pair is eyen
more appropriate for blood in the stool associated with
deficiency of nutritive qi and blood, such as might occur
during pregnancy or in the immediate postpartum period.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Preparation of the gelatin is generally done in winter, as
summer temperatures prevent proper gelling. The process
involves three steps:
1.PREPARING THE MATERIALS: The hide is washed and
soaked, changing the water once or twice each day, until
the hairs can be scraped off. It is then cut into small squares
and washed in clean water, and boiled for 15 minutes until
the skin curls.
2. TRANSFORMING THE HIDE: The curled squares are
placed in a large wok filled with water, and stewed at a high
temperature, adding water as needed, for about 15 to 16
hours until thickened into a sauce-like consistency. The
liquid is poured off and retained, and the skin stewed again
in the same manner, with the resulting thick liquid added
to the first batch. The liquid is then strained, and alum is
added to make it precipitate.
3. PREPARING THE PASTE: The clear liquid above the
precipitated sediment is collected, placed in a large wok,
and concentrated into a gelatinous paste. Two hours before
the gelatin forms, rock sugar, yellow rice wine, and soybean
oil or peanut oil is added to form the proper consistency
of thick glue. This is then poured into a trough where it is
allowed to congeal naturally.
The gelatin is then cut into squares and thoroughly
dried.
The product which utilizes the water from the wells of
the Dong E area in Shandong province is traditionally considered to be of superior quality, and is given the name F]
H e jiao. And that which uses the hide of black donkeys is
regarded as the very best, called black donkey hide gelatin
( hei lu pi jiao). Because there are many substitutes to be found on the market, the term true ass-hide glue
(# T zhen e jiao) is used. The aged product is also valued, and is called aged ass-hide glue (* chen e jiao)
In its unprepared form, it is better at nourishing the blood;
prepared, it is more effective at stopping bleeding, and its
greasy, cloying properties are somewhat reduced.
Meretricis/Cyclinae Concha (ge qiao) powder is heated in
a wok. When it is hot, small pieces of Asini Corii Colla (
jiao) are added and fried until they soften and form smal
pearl-shaped balls. This is also known as clam-powder
fried ass-hide glue (*y ge fen chao e jiao, or
simply fried ass-hide ( FT chao e jiao). Prepared in this
manner, ass-hide glue can better nourish the Lung yin to
moisten the Lungs, and also stops coughs and transforms
phlegm. This method of preparation is frequently used for
dry cough and wheezing due to Lung dryness, or consump.
tive cough when the yin has been injured and fire is overabundant. It is particularly appropriate if there is coughing
of blood.
> TYPHA POLLEN FRIED ASS-HIDE
#*Tpuhuang chaoejiao
Typhae Pollen (pu huang) is heated in a wok, then Asini
Corii Colla (e jiao) is added and fried until soft. It is then
formed into small yellow balls. Prepared in this manner
ass-hide glue nourishes the blood and moistens dryness
but also invigorates the blood, transforms stasis, stops
bleeding, and harmonizes the collaterals. This method of
preparation can tonify blood without being cloying, and
can stop bleeding without leading to stasis. Because it tonifies and mobilizes simultaneously, it is a very commonly
used method of preparation for gynecological disorders,
where it is used in the treatment of such things as threatened abortion or continuous uterine bleeding.

englishReference.cautions: Contraindicated in cases of exuberant fire from yin deficiency, spasms from blood deficiency, or in the absence of pathogenic wind, dampness, or cold. See ToxiCITY below.
englishReference.actions:
- Releases the exterior and expels wind: for headache, chills.
and body aches due to externally-contracted wind-cold.
-With Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) for patterns of
exterior excess or pruritic rash, as in Schizonepeta and

: Expels wind-dampness and alleviates pain: for exterior

englishReference.commentary:
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) expels wind, but has a
moderate, gentle nature, slightly warm but not parching,
sweet and not at all harsh. It is known as the most moist of
the wind herbs, although this simply indicates that it is less
drying than most wind-expelling herbs. It can be used for
all wind patterns, hot or cold, upper or lower body, exterior
or interior. This ability to reach the deeper interior levels of
the body to track down and expel wind is one of its special
characteristics.
By expelling wind it treats headaches, general body.
aches, and spasms, although its ability to relieve muscular
tetany is too weak for it to serve as a chief herb for this problem. In the treatment of wind-damp painful obstruction,
for which it is particularly appropriate when the patient is
weak or blood deficient, it can eliminate wind-dampness.
This is because.its effects are less drying than many other
herbs used in the treatment of painful obstruction.
Another valued quality of Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang
feng) is its ability to relieve Intestinal wind, reduce tenes.
mus, and reduce diarrhea. According to Rectification of the
Meaning of Materia Medica, it lifts the yang qi and stops
Intestinal wind and bleeding from the bowels. The Medical
Discourses of [Zhang] Ju-Ren concurs, saying it raises the
Spleen yang and alleviates diarrhea.

18 1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
In New Compilation of Materia Medica, Chen-Shi-Duo
observes:
Surprisingly, Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) can be used
when pathogenic wind is not present; if used with Astragali
Radix (huang qi) it can shut out wind from entering the
skin. However, this combination cannot be used once the]
wind pathogen has alreadv entered.There is always a deer
significance when the ancients name something; by ponder.
ing the name, one obtains comprehension.
Chen here is referring to the literal Chinese meaning of fang
feng (the herb's name): to guard against wind.
englishReference.combinations:
> WiTH SCHIZONEPETAE HERBA (jing jie)
This combination is less warming than Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang) and Cinnamomi Ramulus (gul zhi), and thus
can be used for exterior patterns in any season. It can
even be used with pathogenic wind-heat if other wind
heat dispersing herbs are added, such as Mori Folium
(sang ye), Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he), Forsythiae
Fructus (lian qiao), and Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua). A
detailed comparison of Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) and
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) is provided under the
entry for Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) above.
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) is considered a
'moistening' wind-expeller, meaning only that it is not as
drying as most wind-dispersing herbs, while Schizonepetae
Herba (jing jie) is neutral in nature. They can therefore be
used together to expel wind and stop itching in dermatological complaints.
If these herbs are cooked until charred, their wind-dispersing effect is lost, but they can be used to stop bleeding.
This is especially true of charred Schizonepetae Herba (jing
jie tan).
> WITH GENTIANAE MACROPHYLLAE RADIX (qin jiao)
This herb is acrid, bitter, and slightly cold; the acrid flavor
disperses, while the bitter flavor drains. It also enters the
Liver channel to relax the tendons and stop pain, which
adds to its effect when expelling wind and removing dampness. Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) is acrid, sweet, and
slightly warm, lifting and bringing out to disperse. It is
therefore appropriate for all types of wind disorders, and is
also able to overcome dampness and stop pain.
The two herbs have similar actions and are thus mutu.
ally supportive. They are an indispensable combination in
prescriptions for the treatment of wind and dampness.
Furthermore, among herbs that expel wind, both of
these herbs are considered to be relatively moistening. One
is slightly warm, the other slightly cold, so the temperature
is balanced. This pair can therefore be used regardless of
whether the pattern is excessive or deficient, long-term or
recent, as long as there are symptoms of wind-damp painful obstruction, spasms of the tendons, or numbness of the
limbs.
>WITH ATRACTYLODIs RHIZOMA (cang zhu)
When used together, the effect of these two herbs is focused
on expelling wind and treating dampness. Saposhnikoviae
Radix (fang feng) is best at dispersing wind-dampness in
the exterior, Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) for parching interior dampness; it also has a certain sweat-inducing
action.
This pair is commonly used for externally-contracted
pathogenic wind, cold, and dampness leading to chills with
no sweating, headache, heavy head, lethargy and heavy
limbs, as well as stifling fullness in the chest and gastric
cavity. It is also useful for relieving the symptoms of painful obstruction: aching joints, heavy limbs, and generalized
aching discomfort.
A third use derives from an appreciation of Saposhni
koviae Radix's (fang feng) ability to "lift the yang and
regulate the Spleen." Together, Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang
feng) enhances the dampness-drying and Spleen-regulating
effect of Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) in order to treat
diarrhea when dampness has obstructed the Spleen and
Stomach, preventing the clear yang from properly ascending so that dampness pours down.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ANGELICAE PUBESCENTIs RADIX (du hu6) and
NoTOPTERYGII RHIZOMA SEU RADIX (qiang hu6)
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica notes that "Compared to Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo) and Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo), Saposhnikoviae
Radix (fang feng) is somewhat lighter in weight and its
nature is also somewhat more neutral." As this implies,
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) is less drying and less
aromatic than either of the other two herbs, which means
that it is less able to disperse a heavy accumulation of turbid
dampness, but is more gentle in its effect. This suggests, for
example, that it will not injure the yin as rapidly.
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) is also useful for treating
Intestinal wind or painful diarrhea, which is not true of the
other two herbs.
>Vs.SCHIZONEPETAE HERBA (jingjie)
Both herbs eliminate wind, release the exterior, and disperse wind-cold and wind-heat, but Schizonepetae Herba's
(jing jie) wind-expelling and exterior-releasing actions are
weaker and more superficial than those of Saposhnikoviae

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
Radix (fang feng). Because Schizonepetae Herba's (jing jie)
nature is light and spreading, its ability to disperse wind.
heat from the blood is derived from its spreading nature
Its wind-expelling action is limited to the skin, muscles,
and blood.
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng), on the other hand
is stronger at expelling wind that is deep in the body, and
can also overcome dampness. It is appropriate for all types
of wind. As noted by Li Zhang-Zi: "Wind under the skin
but outside the membranes: Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie)
masters it. But Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) cannot enter
the bones and flesh like Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng)
can." Because of this, when treating wind disorders, the two
herbs are often combined to great benefit.

Lungs, while on the other, it facilitates the water pathways,
unblocks the orifices, and expels pathogenic heat. Its
particular characteristic is harmony in both tonification
and in promoting urination, supporting the normal while
expelling the pathogenic, and is therefore especially appropriate when the Spleen is deficient and there is a simultaneous overabundance of dampness with such symptoms as
phlegm and thin mucus, diarrhea, and edema. This harmonious set of functions, which allows the herb to promote
urination without injuring the qi, makes it an important
choice for promoting urination and leaching .out dampness. It can be used whenever there is urinary difficulty,
edema, phlegm, or thin mucus, regardless of whether the
condition is hot or cold, deficient or excessive.
When the Spleen functions harmoniously, both the
Heart and Lungs benefit directly from this source of generative transformation. This is why the herb is often used
to treat insomnia and palpitations due to insufficiency of
the Heart and Spleen. Yet its ability to leach out dampness,
ease the orifices, and dispel pathogenic heat also makes it
useful for accumulation of damp-heat in the lower burner
causing painful urinary dribbling with ministerial fire blazing in the Kidney channel.
englishReference.combinations:

This is a frequently used combination to facilitate the
removal of water and leach out dampness. The bland flavor
of Poria (fu ling) leaches and promotes urination, while
its sweetness tonifies the Spleen's transportive and transformative functions. Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) is sweet,
bland, and cooling, and it excels at driving out water in the
three burners and the Bladder.
Together their ability to eliminate water and dampness
is greatly strengthened, because the transportive function in the middle burner initiates movement throughou
the water pathways, and excessive pathogenic fuids are
directed downward and expelled through the Bladder.
Meanwhile, the Spleen qi is protected from the harmful
effect of this downward-leaching by the sweet, tonifying
action of Poria (fu ling).
This combination is appropriate whenever water and
dampness become stagnant and gather, leading to disorders such as edema, jaundice, diarrhea, turbid painful urinary dribbling, and scanty, difficult urination with
abdominal distention. The consensus is that this combination is most appropriate for fluid disorders of the middle
and lower burners.
> WITH CINNAMOMI RAMULUS (gui zhi)
This combination has a strong ability to drive out water and
dampness, and is widely used clinically. Water and dampness disorders generally originate from a middle burner
disharmony. The sweetness of Poria (fu ling) tonifies the
Spleen, and its blandness facilitates the removal of water
and dampness; thus it tonifies, but not harshly, and facilitates, but not violently, gently treating the source of the
dampness. Water and dampness are moist, yin pathogens
which impede the yang qi. The acrid flavor of Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gui zhi) pierces through and disperses the heavy
occluding quality of the yin pathogens, while its sweetness
prevents this dispersal from occurring too quickly or from
being too short-lived. The sweet warmth of Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gut zhi) assists the expansion of the yang to
transform the yin pathogens, breaking up their congealing.
yin quality. Together with Poria (fu ling), it can focus its
qualities on transforming dampness rather than mobilizing
the exterior, while Poria (fu ling) gains greater impetus to
unblock the yang, promote urination, and thereby expel
the dampness and water.

and perfectly conform to the ancient adage, "Disorders of

herbs." Thus, this combination can be used whenever
symptoms of water and dampness disorders appear, be it

Pouch of Pearls describes the actions of this herb:
The uses of Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) are four [in
number]. First, it unblocks and assists the Heart yang.
Second, it expels stubborn sunken cold in the organs.
Third, it disperses cold qi in all the channels. Fourth, it
treats abdominal pain due to externally-contracted cold.
When fried black, it enters the Kidneys and acts at the
blood level. Prepared in this manner, Zingiberis Rhizoma
preparatum (pao jiang) is no longer acrid, but has become
bitter; its nature is warm and harmonious, and its primary
actions are warming the middle, stopping diarrhea, and
stopping bleeding due to yang qi deficiency. Because of
this warming, consolidating, and moderate effect, Zhang
Yuan-Su said that it "conserves without mobilizing." In

If overabundant yin separates from yang so that fire cannot
return to its base, or deficient yang is unable to contain the
blood, causing spitting up of blood, nosebleed, or bleeding from below, then [dried ginger] should be thoroughly
dry-fried (yet not to the extent of losing its form) and used:
it is the most important herb for stopping [this kind of]
bleeding.

Whenever there is cold from deficiency of the Stomach.
and the primal yang is about to be cut off, use [Zingiberis

the yang. This is why textbooks all include the sentence
Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zht fu zi) without

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter and cold, Kansui Radix (gan sui) directs downward
drains and expels heat, unblocks both the Intestines and
urination, and is a powerful herb for draining pathogenic
water and thin mucus. When the transportation and transformation of fluid metabolism slows, the movement of
water stops; it will then accumulate and can congeal into
thin mucus, leading to edematous swelling and distention.
The initial approach would normally be to restore transportation and transformation through warming, tonification, and the facilitation of urination. When, however, the
thin mucus has accumulated deep within the body and the
yang qi is unable to circulate, the pathogen can gather into
a hard, excessive clump that resists more gentle treatment.
The pathogen must then be expelled. Essentials from the
Golden Cabinet explains:
If the patient's pulse is hidden, and there is an urge to
move the bowels, after which there is some relief but still
a sensation of hard fullness in the epigastric region, this is
lingering thin mucus wanting expulsion. The main formula
should be Euphorbia Kansui and Pinellia Decoction (gan
sui ban xia tang).
Pouch of Pearls explains that it "directly reaches the loca.
tion where water qi has clumped, and is thus a sage-like
herb for draining water. When water has clumped within
the chest, without this, it cannot be expelled."
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PHYTOLACCAE RADIX (shang lu)
Both of these herbs have similar properties, however Kansui Radix (gan sut) has a stronger ability to drive pathogenic water and thin mucus downward, as it tends to mobilize
the Intestines to drain water outward; it is best used for
draining edema in the chest and abdomen. This is confirmed in Pouch of Pearls: "When water has clumped within
the chest, without this [formula], it cannot be expelled."
Phytolaccae Radix (shang lu) tends to facilitate urination,
and is best for reducing edema and swelling while also
directing rebellious qi downward to drain heat.
Together these herbs strongly expel water, eliminate
plugged accumulation, and unblock the water pathways to
treat edema or thin mucus in the upper, middle, and lower
burners. This combination can be used to treat edema in
the abdomen or limbs, and ascites. However, the toxic
nature of the two herbs requires that one exercise great caution in prescribing them.

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Its nature is toxic yin; although it excels at driving water
downward and expelling dampness,it can harm and injure
the true yin and exhaust the yin and yang fluids. Those who
are deficient in primal qi (except for those with cold damage and pathogenic water causing clumping in the chest
disorder, for whom there is no other method of treatment)
should not use it. This includes those with edematous,
drum-like abdominal swelling and frequent urination due
to Spleen yin deficiency, in which deficiency of earth is
unable to control the fluids, which then spread and flood.
Liu He-Jian [Liu Wan-Su] says that all damp swelling and
fullness belongs to Spleen earth: the standard method
should be to tonify the Spleen and firm the earth, add.
ing [herbs] that facilitate urination.-If, conversely, Kansui
Radix (gan sut) is used to drive downward, this doubly
weakens the patient's foundation. Even if the [pathogenic]
water temporarily leaves, on relapse the patient will surely
die. Thus, it is crucial to ascertain that the disorder pertains
to damp-heat, that thin mucus or pathogenic water is pres.
ent, and that the primal qi is still strong--only then can it
be used for a short-term treatment. It should be ground
and used in pills or powders. (Harm and Benefit in the
Materia Medica)

englishReference.actions:
- Discharges exterior conditions and disperses cold: for
externally-contracted wind-cold, and especially for headsensation in the mouth, excessive saliva, dull aching in the

englishReference.commentary:
Ligustici Rhizoma (gdo ben) has acrid, warm, ascending.
and dispersing properties with a powerful aroma that is
quite drying. Numerous texts record its ability to enter the
Governing vessel as well as the Bladder channel, thus it is
particularly good for reaching the vertex of the head and
treating all wind disorders involving the upper posterior
aspect of the body.
The relationship of the Bladder channel and Governing
vessel with the Kidneys, however, also allows Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) to treat lower backache and gynecological
masses, vaginal swelling, or pain from wind-dampness

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
in the interior of the body, as well as relieving headaches
involving the teeth. It also relieves acute abdominal pain
and diarrhea associated with lower abdominal wind-dampness. Its wind-expelling quality is best expressed in the
upper body, while its ability to dry dampness comes more
into play in the lower body.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica observes
that "Whenever using Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) to
treat headaches at the vertex, it should be combined
with Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) plus wine-fried
Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma) and Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu)." Wine-frying the latter two herbs enhances their abil.
ity to lift the clear yang.
When considering Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) in the
treatment of headache at the vertex, remember that pain in
this area can also occur secondary to a terminal yin disorder, for which this herb would be inappropriate. Additional
signs and symptoms of a terminal yin disorder include dry
retching, vomiting of thin sputum, cold hands and feet, and
sometimes diarrhea. The treatment should be to warm and
soothe the Stomach and Liver, which will dispel the excess
yin that is preventing the clear yang from rising. Evodia
Decoction (wu zhu yu tang) is the appropriate treatment.
As Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) works at the vertex to eliminate pathogenic wind-cold, rather than dispel excess yin, it
should be avoided in these circumstances.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.OTHER HERBS FOR HEADACHES
Materia Medica of Combinations notes that without assistant herbs to guide into the proper channels, no treatment
for headache will be effective. It further states that Ligustici
Rhizoma (gao ben) is best for headaches at the vertex,
Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) for headaches
at the back of the head, Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai zhi)
for frontal headaches, and Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan
xiong) for lateral headaches or any headache involving
blood stagnation.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica compares
Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) and Chuanxiong Rhizoma
(chuan xiong):
One might say that the nature of Ligustici Rhizoma
(gao ben) is really quite similar to Chuanxiong Rhizoma
(chuan xiong), since they both treat headache. However,
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) focuses on the Liver
and Gallbladder, and although it moves to the head and
eyes, it does not reach the vertex. Ligustici Rhizoma (gao
ben focuses on the Bladder and Governing vessel,following them and unblocking both above and below;
but the difference is that it does not reach the Liver and
Gallbladder.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PUERARIAE RADIX (ge gen)
This combination is designed to reach a very specific
25
location. While both herbs are acrid and enter the yang
brightness, Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai zhi) is warm
while Puerariae Radix (ge gen) is cool. Together they excel
at relieving chills and fever from the level of the exterior
muscles and interstices. This level of the exterior pertains
to earth and is known as the "exterior of yang brightness."
When wind-cold invades and penetrates (usually rapidly)
to this depth, it can become stuck, produce heat, and lead
to chills, fever, lack of sweat, stiff neck, headache, restless6e
anxiety in the chest,and a floatingtight pulse
level, however, it is inappropriate to use skin-At this
level herbs like Ephedrae Herba (ma huang), or muscle
level herbs like Cinnamomi Ramulus gui zhi, nor do
learing herbs such as Mori Folium (sangye) orwind-heat cle
Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) achieve the desired result. This
is because the root pathogen is wind-cold, despite the heat
resulting from its confinement in the exterior membranes
and interstices. Only the use of two dispersing yang bright.
ness channel herbs---one warm, one cool-can produce
the effect of dispersing at the proper level to free the pentup pathogen, ushering it out through the exterior.
While Puerariae Radix (ge gen) disperses and cools
the heat from constraint and frees the pathogen from the
exterior membranes and interstices, the warming Angelicae
dahuricae Radix (bai zhi) increases the local yang qi activ.
ity to expel the obstructing cold pathogen out through the
skin.
>WITH CHUANXIONG RHIZOMA (chuan xiOng)
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) is acrid and warm
and enters the lesser yang channel; its nature is expressly
dispersing and ascending, which enables it to move around
the eves and head.It is a superior herb for eliminating wind
and relieving pain. Extension of the Materia Medica notes:
"Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) is a very commonly
used herb at present, but when it fails to completely clear
wind from the fac
to assist it
and head, other herbs should be added
Thus, when Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai
zhi) is added for this urpose, its wind-expelling and pain.
relieving actions supplement those of Chuanxiong Rhi.
zoma (chuan xiong), and it leads the actions of Chuanxiong
Rhizoma (chuan xiong) into the yang brightness channel.
For these reasons, this pair is most often prescribed for
headaches involving both the lesser yang and the yang
brightness areas of the head, especially those chronic
headaches which are aggravated by exposure to wind
and cold and involve a sharp, stabbing pain. Although
resulting from wind, these chronic headaches differ from
recently contracted exterior wind headaches, as the former
usually involve repeated encroachment by wind on the
clear orifices of the head. Such long-term disorders enter
the collaterals and obstruct the flow of qi and blood, for

26 1 I. Herbs.that Release the Exterior
which the usual wind-cold expelling herbs are inadequate.
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) is required because of
its ability to both expel wind and move the blood. In more
severe cases, the addition of other herbs to move the blood
is warranted.
>WITH BOMBYX BATRYTICATUs (bai jiang can)
Bombyx batryticatus (bai jiang can) is salty, acrid, and neutral, and like Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai zhi), it has a
strong ability to expel wind and relieve pain. The two herbs
combine their strength in this area, and so are commonly
used for frontal headaches associated with pathogenic wind
in the yang brightness channel. This combination is then
adjusted according to the nature of the wind pathogen: for
wind-heat, use relatively more Bombyx batryticatus (bai
jiang cdn), and vice versa for wind-cold.
In addition, because both herbs can dry dampness
while Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai zhi) also raises the
yang and Bombyx batryticatus (bai jiang can) also transforms phlegm, they are useful together in the treatment of
continuous vaginal discharge from the downward-pouring
of turbid dampness. For this purpose they generally serve
as ancillary herbs within a prescription.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid and very warming, Alpiniae officinarum Rhizoma
(gao liang jiang) specifically disperses pathogenic cold in
the Spleen and Stomach to warm the middle, stop pain,
in the Stomach.
>WITH TROGOPTERORI FAECES (wu ling zhi)
While Alpiniae officinarum Rhizoma (gao liang jiang)
enters the Spleen and Stomach channels, Trogopterori
Faeces (wu ling zhi) enters the Liver and Spleen; Alpiniae
officinarum Rhizoma (gao liang jiang) enters the qi level
to promote the movement of qi and stop pain, while
Trogopterori Faeces (wu ling zhi) enters the blood level to
invigorate the blood, unblock the collaterals, and stop pain!
Together, qi and blood are both addressed, and warmth
assists the movement of blood, thus the combination
strongly invigorates both the qi and blood and eliminates
stagnation to alleviate pain. When cold invades the Spleen
and Stomach, the channels are injured; first, there will be
qi stagnation, and afterward the blood will stagnate in the
collaterals. This situation worsens as qi fails to promote the
movement of blood, and the blood can no longer support
the movement of qi. This results in increasing epigastric
pain that worsens with cold and improves with heat. This
combination is ideal for this situation, and it is often used
for the pain involved in peptic ulcers when associated with
symptoms of cold, qi, and blood stagnation.

(sheng jiang) is a sage-like herb for nausea because its acrid

Puerariae Radix (ge gen) is thin in nature and flavor, light
