englishReference.combinations:
>WITH BUPLEURI RADIX (chai hu)
Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) is light, clear, lifting, and dispers.
ing; these are qualities which enable it to vent the exterior
and drain heat. Puerariae Radix (ge geri) raises, disperses,
and releases muscle layer heat. Together, their power is
augmented to release muscle layer heat, and thus the combination is quite popular for exterior patterns where, as
the chills gradually improve, the fever gradually increases,
along with stiffening of the neck and upper back, and
the absence of sweating. This combination is the foundation for the formula Bupleurum and Kudzu Decoction to
Release the Muscle Layer (chai ge jie ji tang). The contemporary physician Liu Feng-Wu explained the combination
this way:
It uses Puerariae Radix (ge gen) to release the muscle layer
and cool heat to mobilize the yang brightness exterior.
On this basis, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) can fully elaborate
its dredging-releasing action to support the exiting of the
pathogen outward. .. Without Puerariae Radix (ge gen) to
release the muscle layer and unblock the movement of the

2 1/ Herbs that Release the Exterior
pathogen, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) has not the slightest
ground upon which to do battle.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
If a pathogen has not yet entered the yang brightness stage.
this [herb] can lead the pathogen inside--it [therefore]
cannot be used. Only if the pathogen is in the greater yang
stage and there are already a few symptoms of the yang
brightness stage, then the important thing is to defend the
yang brightness. Puerariae Radix (ge gen) must be used to
cut off the pathogen's route of attack. (Seeking Accuracy in
the Materia Medica)
Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica repeats this warning, and then elaborates:
Also, if rashes and sores have already expressed red spots.
Puerariae Radix (ge gen) should not be used for fear that
the exterior will be further weakened and the lesions will
worsen. People with exhaustion, or excess in the upper
body and deficiency in the lower, should not take it, and it
should not be taken in the summer,even if there are Spleen
and Stomach disorders; this is especially true for those
already sweating excessively. When it is used, it should be
in small doses to avoid injuring the Stomach qi from its
excessive raising and dispersing.
Puerariae Radix (ge gen) is a wind herb, all of which are
drying. When Divine Husbandman's Classic says that it
generates fluids and stops thirst; this is a misprint for
'raises fluids.' It is not that Puerariae Radix (ge gen) itself
can alleviate thirst; it all depends on its raising the Stomach
qi up into the Lungs so that fluids can be generated. So if
the thirst does not result from the inability of clear vang to
ascend, but rather from fire drying and exhausting the fluids, then mistakenly consuming this wind herb will find the
wind fanning the flames and boiling away the source qi.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
>UNPREPARED KUDZU (M#R sheng ge gen) or
DRIED KUDZU (#$# gan ge gen)
Here the herb is simply cleaned, soaked in water to soften,
sliced, and then dried. Some feel that the powdery aspect of
the dried root is better, and that it should therefore not be
soaked prior to slicing. Others emphasize the desirability
of its sweetness by calling it sweet kudzu (# # gan ge
gen).
Unprepared kudzu is used to release the muscle layer,
raise fluids and alleviate thirst, and vent rashes. Formulas

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
for which it would be most appropriate include Kudzu
Decoction (ge gen tang) or Cimicifuga and Kudzu Decoction (sheng ma ge gen tang).
> ROASTED KUDZU ( tR wei ge gen)
The herb is enveloped in two layers of wheat bran, and
roasted until the outer layer is scorched. Then the bran and
the herb are dry-fried together until the kudzu is a deep yellow color. Some just dry-fry the kudzu with the bran, which
is called fried kudzu (chao ge gen)
Both the roasting and frying process reduce the cooling.
dispersing nature of this herb so that it then specifically
raises and brings out the clear yang qi of the Spleen and
Stomach. Its ability to raise the yang and alleviate diarrhea
is therefore much stronger than in its unprepared form. In
addition, the wheat bran endows the kudzu with a Stomach
harmonizing action. In this form it is even more appropriate
for use when diarrhea results from Spleen deficiency. The
Convenient Reader of Materia Medica explains: "Roasting
thoroughly eradicates its dispersing nature, then it moves
from the Stomach to the Intestine, no longer mobilizing the
yang brightness exterior, but only entering the yang brightness interior: its function is to raise the clear."
>KUDZU STARCH(ge fen)
The unprocessed root is ground with water and then
allowed to settle in order to extract the starch. The nature
of the starch is somewhat different from kudzu itself: it is
very cold, its power to generate fluids and alleviate thirst is
stronger, and it is more effective at cooling heat and elimi
nating irritability.
The Materia Medica of the Kaibao Era says that kudzu
starch "expels irritability and heat, facilitates the passage of
stool and urine, and alleviates diarrhea." Traditionally, it
was combined with millet in a porridge to treat stifling heat
in the chest with thirst, irritability, and restlessness.

englishReference.commentary:
Lycii Fructus (gou qi zi) nourishes the blood in the Liver
to brighten the eyes, and tonifies the Lung and Kidney
yin, while also mildly augmenting the Kidney yang. The
Grand Materia Medica states that it "enriches the Kidneys.
moistens the Lungs, and brightens the eyes." It goes on to

760 12 / Tonifying Herbs
note that "the fruit is sweet, neutral, and moistening, with
a nature that enriches and tonifies: it cannot eliminate heat
[as the root-bark of this plant, Lycii Cortex (di gu pi), can];
it only tonifies the Kidneys and moistens the Lungs, generates essence and augments the qi."
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun takes issue with the
ability of this herb to cool heat, stating that the fruit "defi.
nitely has the effect of reducing heat, and this is not empty
talk: I have personally examined this carefully. He then
describes how, at fifty years of age, he would feel hot when
waking from sleep, and over the course of a night would
drink a full pitcher of water. If he chewed 30g of this herb
before sleeping, the water intake was reduced by half,]
and he would awaken without heat. He rhetorically asks
whether this is heat from deficiency, or from excess, then
proceeds to explain that, as he is rather fat,
there is no lack of yin. This is clearly not heat from defi.
ciency [in the normal sense]. Likewise, there is no heat
sensation during the day, nor at night when not asleep; it is
only when just waking from sleep that heat emerges from
the area of the Heart. This heat is generated during sleep,
and is clearly not the same as the flushing of heat from
excess. It comes about because, during sleep, the Heart and
the Kidneys naturally connect and generate heat, a manifes.
tation of the flourishing of vigorous congenital primal yang
Because only Lycii Fructus (gou qi zi) can tonify and enrich
the primal yin so that it mutually aids the congenital primal
yang, it has this effect.

englishReference.commentary:
Uncariae Ramulus cum Uncis (gou teng) is sweet, slightly
cold, and enters the Liver and Pericardium channels. The
Liver governs wind, and the Pericardium governs fire!
Wind and fire can provoke each other to cause such disorders as childhood convulsions, dizziness, and headaches.
Because this herb is light, clearing, and cooling, not only
draining fire, but also settling wind, it can treat such patterns as extreme heat generating convulsions and Liver

16 / Substances that Extinguish Wind and Stop Tremors
channel heat, or ascendant Liver yang leading to dizziness,
headache, and red eyes. It is particularly appropriate for
childhood convulsions. Because of its light, clearing, and
draining nature, it is also used for externally-contracted
headache and red eyes, or for spots and rashes that fail to
surface.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica states that it
is swift and sharp by nature; in an instant it can expel wind.
phlegm, open blocked qi, or quiet down childhood con.
vulsions ... however, if decocted for long it has no power
After the other herbs have boiled sufficiently, put it in and
immediately lift [the pot from the stove] so it will be at its
strongest.
Chen Shi-Duo warns that it should be used with an eye
to treating the root of the condition, explaining in New
Compilation of Materia Medica that it
very quickly eliminates wind, and must be used for [internall wind patterns.However,the generation of wind-fire
is usually caused by insufficiency of Kidney water,which
leads to dryness of wood and fire blazing. Using a little bit
of Uncariae Ramulus cum Uncis (gou teng) among herbs
that tonify the yin readily disperses the wind-fire. If one
does not tonify the yin, and only uses Uncariae Ramulus
cum Uncis (gou teng) to eliminate wind and disperse fire,
the wind will not be extinguished and the fire will flare even
more!
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica, the early
twentieth-century writer Zhang Shan-Lei says that it was
considered an excellent herb for children in the earlier
materia medica texts, and that it is in fact quite well-suited
for this by nature: "It is light and clearing, with a sweet,
cold nature that is most appropriate for constitutions with
the not-yet-filled childish yin and the readily exuberant
childish yang." He goes on to explain its ability to treat
childhood convulsions:
The reason that it can treat convulsions is that seizure dis
order is an illness caused by Liver blazing and generating
wind, qi, and fire flaring upward and surging into the neurons of the brain. This substance is light in weight, clearing
and cooling, able to drain fire and also to settle wind.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, salty, and pure yin, Testudinis Plastrum (gui ban)
tonifies the Kidneys, enriches the yin, and unblocks the
Conception vessel: In Case Records as a Guide to Clinical
Practice, Ye Tian-Shi says that it is "yin by nature and travels through the Conception vessel." By strongly tonifying
the yin, it treats steaming bones, consumptive heat, and
nightsweats; when yin is fortified, it can control the yang
and extinguish internal wind, thus subduing the ascendant
Liver yang that could lead to vertigo and tinnitus, and the
internal wind that causes spasms and convulsions. As a
bone-like substance, it strengthens the bones and sinews,
and is thus used for weakness of the lower back and legs,
as well as delayed closure of the fontanel in infants. By
unblocking the Conception vessel, it treats spermatorrhea,
continuous uterine bleeding, vaginal discharge, and excessive menstrual bleeding.
Supplement to the Extension of the Materia Medica says
that "the lower plate tonifies the yin, and governs insuf
ficiency of yin and blood ... treating consumptive exhaus.
tion [causing] lack of power in the extremities. Essentials
of the Materia Medica says that it
enriches yin, strengthens the resolve, and treats yin and
blood insufficiency, consumptive heat, steaming bones,
long-term cough, malarial disorder, mobile and fixed
abdominal masses, continuous uterine bleeding, the five
[types of] hemorrhoids, difficult labor, and patterns of yin
deficiency and frail blood.
The Detailed Materia Medica elaborates:
The ancients used the dorsal shell and the ventral shell
interchangeably, only the [Materia Medica of] Ri HuaZi started to use the ventral plate. Now, the turtle is yin.
and the ventral plate is extreme yin within yin, with a
very strong Kidney-tonifying action, such that the illnesses it governs are all those caused by Kidney deficiency.
Generally, medicinals that enrich the yin and direct fire
downward are cold and injure the Stomach, yet Testudinis
Plastrum (gui ban) has the sweet flavor of the middle
regions---a truly fine substance.
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang Bing
Cheng notes:
The turtle (@ gui) is the spirit of the north, black in color.
sweet, salty, and cold, entering the Kidney channel, with
a head that often hides in its abdomen, thus it unblocks
the Conception vessel ... fortifies Kidney water, eliminates
steaming bones, subdues deficient yang--its primary
therapeutic effects are not apart from these. It is even better
when boiled into glue.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.TRIONYCIs CARAPAX (bie jia)
Both are shells that enrich the yin, subdue the yang, and
soften areas of hardness. However, Testudinis Plastrum
(gui ban) primarily enters the Kidneys, and because it is
sweet, it has a superior ability to enrich the yin so as to
anchor the yang, while also unblocking the Conception
vessel in the treatment of such gynecological conditions
as continuous uterine bleeding. By contrast, Trionycis
Carapax (bie jia) primarily enters the Liver channel, with
a stronger ability to cool heat and soften areas of hardness.
It is therefore used for such gynecological conditions as
abdominal masses and clumping around the flanks. It is
not sweet, but only salty and cold.
The Detailed Materia Medica explains that
Trionycis Carapax (bie jia) is green in color so it enters
the Liver, and the illnesses it governs are all those of the
Liver channel blood level. Testudinis Plastrum (gui ban) is
black in color so it enters the Kidneys, and the illnesses it
governs are all those of the Kidney channel blood level; it
also unblocks the Heart, Both are shelled animals in the yin
category, and primarily treat yin channels, each according
to its type.
The Materia Medica of Combinations notes that
Trionycis Carapax (bie jia) enters the Liver, tonifies the yin.
expels heat, disperses clumping and softens areas of hardness; it treats Liver channel blood level disorders ... [and]
travels the Penetrating vessel. Testudinis Plastrum (gui ban)

12 I Tonifying Herbs
unblocks the Heart, enters the Kidneys, tonifies the yin.
cools heat, and treats all yin deficiency and blood weakness
patterns, and can unblock the Conception vessel.
This view is consistent with the relationship between the
Liver channel and the Penetrating vessel, as well as the
Kidney channel and the Conception vessel.
>Vs. CERVI CoRNU PANTOTRICHUM (lu rong)
Both substances augment the Kidneys and fortify the
bones, and treat atrophy and weakness of the sinews and
bones. However, Testudinis Plastrum (gui ban) augments
the Kidney yin and unblocks the Conception vessel, and,
by nourishing the yin, can subdue the yang, tonify the
blood, and stop bleeding. It is therefore best for heat
associated with yin deficiency or blood heat causing continuous uterine bleeding. By contrast, Cervi Cornu pantotrichum (lu rong) reinforces the Kidney yang and tonifies
the Governing vessel; it warms the Kidney yang, but also
generates essence and augments the marrow. It is used in
treating uterine bleeding due to yang deficiency. However
because Testudinis Plastrum (gui ban) tonifies the yin and
Cervi Cornu pantotrichum (lu rong) fortifies the yang, they
can be combined when there is deficiency of both yin and
yang.
The Detailed Materia Medica states that
The head of the turtle often hides in its abdomen, unblock
ing the Conception vessel, so the lower plate is used to
nourish the yin. The nose of the deer often turns toward its
tail, unblocking the Governing vessei, so the antlers on the
top [of its head] are used to nourish the yang.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Blood turtle plate (n f t& xue gui ban) is the ventral plate
of the turtle which has been slaughtered upon capture,
the flesh scraped away, and the shell washed and then
843
dried in the sun. This is considered to be of better quality
than decocted turtle plate (r #& tang gui ban), which is
derived from killing the turtle by boiling it, which tends
to reduce the gelatinous content of the shell, and thereby
reduce its quality. In either case, without further preparation, it is called unprepared turtle plate ( @ sheng
gui ban) or primal warrior plate (it a#& yuan wu ban).
Defeated turtle plate (# bai gui ban) refers to the shell
of a naturally deceased turtle, and was a name commonly
used in ancient texts, as many regarded it as the best quality. Other commentators disagreed, however, pointing
out that the cause of death may leave undesirable residual
toxins. The term is rarely used nowadays, but appears in
ancient formulas.
>VINEGAR-FRIED TURTLE PLASTRON
( ky s t cu chao gui ban)
Sand is heated in a wok at a high temperature, then the
shells are added and the temperature reduced to medium.
The shells are cooked until slightly yellow, and are then
removed, and the sand sifted away. At this point the shells,
while hot, are soaked (or sprayed) briefly in rice vinegar,
rinsed with water, then dried in the sun. Also known as
prepared turtle plastron (%# #& zhi gui ban), this method
of preparation directs the medicinal actions into the Liver
channel, and enhances its ability to subdue yang. It is most
appropriate for Liver yin deficiency leading to ascendant
Liver yang, as well as uterine bleeding due to the failure
of the Liver to store blood. It also reduces its somewhat
unpleasant taste, and makes the shell more friable, facilitating pulverization.
Yellow rice wine can be used instead of vinegar in the
processing; this is called wine-fried turtle plastron (
# jiu chao gui ban. This method of preparation adds
movement to its tonification and is most often used in
the treatment of atrophy and weakness of the bones and
. sinews.
In its prepared form, the shell becomes crisp and fri.
able, hence it is also known as crisp turtle plastron (
& su gui ban). These methods of preparation increase the
solubility of the substance in decoctions by as much as four
times.

englishReference.commentary:
Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) ranks with Ginseng Radix
(ren shen) as the subject of the most learned discussions in
the Chinese medical literature. This is because of its place as
the chief herb in Cinnamon Twig Decoction (gui zhi tang)
the premier formula in Discussion of Cold Damage. That
book demonstrates, with elegant efficiency, the various
permutations of this formula, how Cinnamomi Ramulus
(gui zhi) can be used from the upper to the lower body
and from the exterior to the interior. In Discussion of Cold
Damage, and its companion text, Essentials from the Golden
Cabinet, Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) is cited one-hun
dred-thirty times in seventy-seven different formulas.
An essential point in understanding Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) is to realize that it does not induce sweating
in exterior-releasing formulas; it releases the muscle layer.
The distinction between inducing sweating and releasing
the muscle layer is one of depth and affiliation. The Lungs
govern the skin and pertain to mobilizing protection (as in
the protective qi), while the Spleen governs the fiesh and
pertains to the supply of nutrition (the nutritive qi). The
method of inducing sweating relies on the opening, dispersing actions of the herbs themselves, as with Ephedrae
Herba (ma huang), to vent and drive the pathogen outward
through the pores of the skin to exit the body. Inducing
sweating is the approach used when cold has constrained
the most superficial level of the exterior.
Releasing the mtiscle layer, on the other hand, should
be used when the pathogen is not constrained in the skin,
but is slightly deeper. Usually the pathogen is wind, which
is faster than cold at penetrating the exterior. The skin is
not blocked, so sweating may already be present, and what
is required to eliminate the pathogen is a more gentle suffusion of normal qi, the harmonized nutritive and protective
qi, which escorts the pathogen outward through the exterior. In this--the outward-releasing of the pathogen---the
two methods are similar, but the different mechanisms of
action should not be confused.
This is how Li Shi-Zhen described it in the Grand

which draws Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) to the level of
the muscles and flesh.

englishReference.commentary:
In the ancient work Divine Husbandman's Classic of the
Materia Medica, Sargassum (hai zao) is said to
govern goiter, clumped qi, disperse hard painful nodules on
the lower neck, swollen sores, mobile and fixed abdominal
masses and areas of hardened qi, thundering sounds in the
upper, middle, and lower abdomen, and all types of edema.
It is still used for all these problems, except for "thundering
sounds."
Sargassum (hai zao) is a salty, bitter, cold, moisten
ing herb that enters the Liver channel. Its major functions
are reducing phlegm, softening areas of hardness, and
mobilizing fluid metabolism. It is especially indicated for
goiter and nodules of phlegm, both of which are frequently
caused by Liver and Gallbladder fire drying and thickening
the fluids until they form phlegm and obstruct the collaterals. Sargassum (hai zao) is both cooling and softening in
nature, and thus addresses both the fire and the dry, hardened phlegm clumps.
Because it is cooling and clears the accumulation of flu--
ids, it can also treat damp-heat, and is often used for swelling and pain of the testicles (a form of bulging disorder)
or leg qi with fluid retention. As noted in Encountering the
Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica, "The pathogen is
expelled through the urine."
>Vs MERETRICIs/CYCLINAE CoNCHA (ge qiao)
Both substances are salty and cold with the ability to soften
areas of hardness, reduce phlegm, and facilitate the move.
ment of fiuids to reduce edema. However, Sargassum (hai
zao) enters the Liver channel and is stronger at softening
hardness and dispersing clumps; it is thus better for goiter, testicular pain and swelling, and enlargement of the
liver and spleen. By contrast, Meretricis/Cyclinae Concha
(ge qiao) mainly enters the Lungs, and its ability to cool
and direct phlegm-heat downward is better than that of
Sargassum (hai zao). Meretricis/Cyclinae Concha (ge qiao)
is therefore more appropriately indicated for cough and
chest pain due to phlegm-fire.
>Vs.ECKLONIAE THALLUS (kun bu); see page 402
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Thoroughly Revised Materia Medica notes that "patients
with Spleen cold and dampness should not take it." And
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica observes:
If the disorder is not due to excess pathogenic clumping, it
is definitely contraindicated... furthermore, [because] it
drives qi downward very rapidly, long-term consumption
makes people thin. As to those island peoples who eat it
frequently [without ill effect], this is because their environment differs.
Traditionally, both Sargassum (hai zao) and Eckloniae
Thallus (kun bu) were thought to be incompatible (& fan)
with Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao), and therefore were not
to be joined in the same prescription. Nevertheless, they
were combined in several traditional formulas, as far back
as Li Gao. And despite the frequent use of this combination at present, there has been only one reported case of a
possibly significant adverse reaction. This prohibition was
therefore removed from the official Chinese Pharmacopoeia
beginning in 1977.

englishReference.actions:
- Clears heat and drains fire: for high fever, irritability, and
thirst from heat in the qi level. Especially useful for warm
pathogen diseases that occur during the summer.
--With Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) and Talcum (hua
shi) for high fever, thirst, and irritability associated with
heat in the qi level, as in Cinnamon and Poria Sweet Dew
Used for burns and sores: applied topically for burns and

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, salty, and very cold, Glauberitum (han shui sht)
enters the Stomach channel to.clear fever and expel pathogenic heat, especially that of summertime warm pathogen
disease where the pathogen is at the qi level accompanied
by high fever, insatiable thirst, and yellow tongue coating.
It is also used externally for inflamed eyes due to wind-heat,
or for scalds and burns.
The acrid, mobilizing, dispersing nature of this mineral
promotes urination and reduces edema, while its saltiness
allows it to enter the Kidneys and blood, direct fire downward, and soften areas of hardness in treating symptoms
such as swelling and pain of the throat and gums, clumping
massed in the abdomen, edema, and anuria.
Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians says that
this substance "expels seasonal predominant heat, latent
heat within the five yin organs, heat in the Stomach, sensations of irritating fullness, thirst, edema, and painful
obstruction in the abdomen." The Grand Materia Medica
notes that "its quality is very cold, its flavor is acrid and
salty, it enters the Kidneys and travels the blood. Its capacity to cool heat is the same as all the salts." Li Shi-Zhen
noted that Glauberitum (han shui shi) is usually quarried
from land that is very alkaline and salty, and has the (now
rarely used) name: essence of salt stone (# yan jing
shi).
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Both medicinals clear yang brightness qi-level heat from
excess and its attendant symptoms of high fever, insatiable
thirst, and a large, strong pulse; they are often used together
for just this purpose. However, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao)
also enters the Lung channel, and is thus used for cough or
wheezing due to heat, or for releasing pathogenic heat from
the skin and muscle layers. Glauberitum (han shui shi), on
the other hand, is salty as well as acrid, and thus enters the
Kidneys to treat edema. It also softens, mobilizes, and disperses areas of hardness.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
The Materia Medica of Combinations cautions that it is "not
to be used for patients with weak Stomachs."

2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
There are two minerals used as calcitum (#k han shut
shi), which was called congealing water stone (# ak ning
shui shi) in the Grand Materia Medica. One is Gypsum
rubrum, or red gypsum hong shi gao, whose
constituents are basically those of gypsum (CaSO4-2H,O)
Because this is the form mainly used in northern China, it
is also known as northern calcitum (t zk bei han shui
shi). The other mineral is calcite (CaCO,), known as
A fang jie shi. This is primarily used in the southern part
of China, and is thus also known as southern han shui shi
(##k& nan han shui shi). This is the more standard
product and the one that is generally available outside of
China.

englishReference.commentary:
Nelumbinis Folium (he ye) is bitter, sweet, and neutral. It is
aromatic and blue-green in color, entering the Liver, Heart,
and Spleen channels. It is best for clearing heat, resolving
summerheat, raising and discharging clear yang, and also
stops bleeding. It is often used for excessive summerheat
leading to splitting headache, stifling sensation of the chest,
nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. It can also be used for any
type of bleeding.
The Renewed Materia Medica says that it can "cool,
clear, and resolve summerheat, alleviate thirst, generate
yang fluids, treat diarrhea and dysenteric disorders, while
also resolving fire and heat."
Penetrating the Mysteries of the Materia Medica notes
that it can "open the Stomach, reduce food [stagnation],
stop bleeding, and secure the essence."
In the Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang
Bing-Cheng explains its properties:
Nelumbinis Folium (he ye) is bitter, neutral, aromatic,
blue-green in color, the leaves are shaped like the trigram
(# zhen) [symbolizing wood and the east] so that it
enters the Liver channel. Liver stores the blood, thus this
herb disperses blood and has the ability to raise yang.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
This herb is also called dry lotus leaf (#t# # gan he ye). If
it is collected after the weather has turned frosty, it is called
fallen-down-after-frost lotus leaf (## ## jing shuang
bai he ye) or simply fallen-down lotus leaf (k tr # bai he

>FRESH LOTUS LEAF (# ## xian he ye) or RAW LOTUS
LEAF#shenghe ye
Once the stem is removed the fresh leaves are simply tied
up in preparation for use. If the tender young leaves are
used, they are called tender lotus leaf ($# # nen he ye)
The fresh leaves are stronger for cooling summerheat, and
can also be used for alleviating the bleeding that results
from heat in the blood. The fresh product is specific for
nosebleeds and spitting up of blood.
>CHARRED LOTUS LEAF (# he ye tan)
These are dry-fried or baked with high heat until black
ish yellow, then sprayed with cool water to extinguish any
glowing embers. Another method traps the leaves between
two woks, seals the outer gap with mud, then places the
woks over heat. This is similar to calcining. This method of
preparation increases the herb's ability to inhibit and stop
bleeding. It is often combined with other herbs for irregular menstrual bleeding or the passage of pus and blood in
dysenteric disorders. The charred herb can also be used as

lowish fluid, and for moist eczema.

englishReference.commentary:
Slightly warm, such that it unblocks; slightly acrid, such
that it disperses; and red, such that it enters the blood level.
Carthami Flos (hong hua) has a light, harmonious, yet
very rapid effect on the movement of blood that spreads
throughout the body to transform stasis and stop pain. This
speed is due to its light weight, which also allows it to assist
the expression of measles, but it is also very commonly
used in gynecological disorders. Many materia medica
texts mention its ability to moisten dryness, and that ir
large doses it breaks up blood, while in small doses it gently
moves and nourishes the blood. This is known as harmonizing the blood', which has the indirect effect of soothing
Liver constraint.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica observes:
Sweet, slightly bitter, slightly acrid, and a little cool: within
yin it is slightly yang. It solely enters the blood vessels, and
is mainly used in gynecology. In small doses it invigorates
the blood and induces menstruation; in large doses it
breaks up and unbiocks blood stasis. It can drive a dead
fetus downiward, and also treat fainting from blood [stasis
following parturition]. It thrusts out pox and sores due to]
blood heat that have trouble expressing, and scatters rashes
and spots due to stagnant blood that will not disperse.
It moistens dryness, invigorates the blood, stops pain,
unblocks menstruation, and also eliminates toxic swellings
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances is
much more specific:
If big doses of 9 to 12g are used, it will be too acrid and
warming, it will make the blood disperse and travel [outside its normal pathways] ... if small doses of 2 to 2.5g are
used, it will soothe the Liver qi and reinforce the sea of
blood, greatly tonifying blood deficiency: this is its adjusting, facilitating, and harmonizing of blood. If only .5g to 1g
are used,it will enter the Heart to increase Heart blood and
relieve pathogenic fire in the Heart channel by dispersing
it, adjusting and harmonizing the blood; this is its ability
to enrich, nourish, and generate blood. The significance of
these different doses is not amenable to shallow explanations
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica explains its]
qualities, while confirming the view above:
Because its color is red and its substance is light, raising
dredging, and thrusting out, it enters the blood level to
dredge and unblock the channels and collaterals, invigorate
the blood, and reduce obstruction .. [however] used in
excess it can cause continuous bleeding,and can cause the
blood to ascend--one must know this. The important thing
is that its nature is warmly harmonious, and that it is acrid
and dispersing, so that it specifically governs all stasis and
stagnation internally, and lack of movement in the chan
nels and collaterals. However, it travels without an ability
to restrain, rapidly thrusting out to the four [extremities].
Thus,one should not use it alone in large doses to achieve
results, but rather utilize its ability to dredge, spread, and
harmonize the blood in small doses: this will then cause no
problems.

Both herbs invigorate the blood and dispel stasis. In smal

Carthami Flos (hong hua) is best for promoting the movement of blood and unblocking menstruation; Sappan Lignum (su mu) is best for invigorating the blood, unblocking

Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances

Carthami Flos (hong hua) excels at unblocking and facilitat.
ing fiow in the channels and collaterals, and is a herb that
addresses the qi within the blood. It can drain as well as
tonify, and in each action there is a particular significance
... with Sappan Lignum (su mu) the combination drives

invigorating the blood.
This combination is very often used for traumatic injury where there is painful swollen bruises or hematoma.

englishReference.commentary:
4
Bitter, acrid, warm, and drying, Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) enters the Lungs, Large Intestine, Spleen
and Stomach channels. It promotes the flow of qi, directing it downward to calm wheezing, disperse sensations of
fullness, warm the middle, and dry dampness. When the
dampness and fullness have been eliminated, the Lung
qi will descend smoothly to facilitate breathing, and the
wheezing will simply cease.
A special characteristic of this herb is that, while it
disperses the formless stagnation of cold-damp qi, it alsc
reduces problems with form such as food blockage and
stopped-up phlegm. Thus it can be used to treat food
stagnation and qi stasis, which causes distending pain in
the chest and abdomen and dry clumped stools; dampness
stagnating and disrupting the digestion, leading to nausea
vomiting, diarrhea and dysentery; and phlegm and thin
mucus that obstructs the Lungs and thereby prevents its qi
from descending, leading to cough and wheezing.
Li Gao observed that the bitterness of this herb "drives
qi downward, thus draining fullness due to excess; [its]
warmth augments qi, thus dispersing fullness due to damp
ness." Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica elaborates:
Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) is a herb that eases
the middle burner, transforms stagnation, and calms
Stomach qi. Whenever qi stagnates in the middle, becom
ing constrained and unable to disperse, or food accumulates in the Stomach, delayed in its movement, or dampness
becomes constrained, accumulated and unable to depart ..
use the warmth of Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) to

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH AURANTII FRUCTUS IMMATURUS (zhi shi)
The combination of these two herbs greatly enhances the
effect of breaking up qi stagnation, eliminating fullness
mobilizing phlegm, and reducing focal distention. Because
one herb is warm while the other is cold, they can be used
whether the disorder is hot or cold. This combination can
be used for any distention of the abdomen or chest, epigastric focal distention, wheezing, shortness of breath, nausea
or rebellious qi, or constipation--regardless of whether
the etiology involves heat, cold, dampness, or phlegm-as
long as the failure of clumped qi to move is at the root of
the problem. Due to its qi-mobilizing action, however, this
pair should be used with caution in patients who are less
than robust.
>WITH ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) is bitter and warm, and
enters the Lung channel to direct qi downward and dis-

472 7 / Aromatic Herbs that Transform Dampness
perse phlegm-dampness, thereby stopping cough and
calming wheezing. Together the two herbs strongly direct
downward and have a significant effect in drying dampness
and dispersing phlegm, thereby calming wheezing. This
pair excels in the treatment of cough and wheezing resulting from phlegm-dampness lingering internally, leading to
stagnant qi that impairs the descent and dissemination of
the Lung qi, with resulting upward rebellion.
This pair is also often used in the treatment of damp.
ness constrained in the upper and middle burners, where
it causes a stifling sensation in the chest, and epigastric
and abdominal distention with a sensation of fullness. This
is because the two herbs together promote the flow of qi,
expel dampness, and disperse fullness. For these reasons,
this combination plays an important role in the formula
Three Nut Decoction (san ren tang).
> WITH ATRACTYLODIs RHIZOMA (cang zhu); see page 469
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. AURANTII FRUCTUS IMMATURUS (zhi shi)
Both herbs are used in the treatment of obstruction due to
food, dampness, or phlegm, which leads to such symptoms
as fullness and distention in the chest and abdomen, and
constipation. However, Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi
shi) is cold, and its function is to break up qi stasis; when
qi flows properly the phlegm will disperse, and when qi
flows smoothly the Intestines will function normally, and
the obstruction will be guided out of the body. The focus
of Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) is to direct the qi
downward, while its warmth dries dampness and thereby
strengthens the Stomach and Spleen, and its acrid flavor
disperses clumped qi to eliminate the distention and fullness.
>Vs.ATRACTYLODIs RHIZOMA(cang zhu)
Both herbs are acrid, bitter,warm, and enter the Spleer
and Stomach channels, and both dry dampness in orde
to treat damp obstruction in the middle burner. However
Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) is especially drying. In.
ternally it strengthens the Spleen; and by inducing sweat
ing, it also releases the exterior and dispels wind-damp
ness. Furthermore, if combined with the bitter and cold
Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai), it treats damp-heat in the
lower burne
Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po), by contrast,
excels at directing qi downward and thereby eliminating
epigastric and abdominal distention and fullness. Its dis
tinction, however, lies in its ability to treat fullness due to
an accumulation with form,such as constipation,as well a
fullness resulting from formless constrained dampness. It
also treats wheezing through its ability to direct rebellious
qi downward.
In sum, Atractylodis Rhizoma (cang zhu) is an aromat
ic, drying herb, while Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po)
mainly promotes the flow of qi while drying dampness.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
>GINGER MAGNOLIA BARK(# jiang hOu po)
The sliced herb is boiled with ginger juice until the juice
is absorbed, then it is removed and dried in the sun. It
can also be dry-fried after soaking in ginger juice, which
is called ginger-fried magnolia bark (#* # jiang chao
hou po). Both of these ginger preparations reduce the mild
throat-irritating property of Magnoliae officinalis Cortex
(hou po), and enhance its dampness-transforming action,
which harmonizes the Stomach. Extension of the Materia
Medica notes that "If it is not prepared with ginger, it irritates the throat and tongue." And the Materia Medica for
Decoctions advises "For abdominal distention, use ginger
magnolia bark."
>PREPARED MAGNOLIA BARK(zhi hOupO)
The herb slices are soaked in the decocted juice of Perillae
Folium (zi su ye) and Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng
jiang), or simply boiled with them. Once the juice is
absorbed, the other herbs are removed, and the Magnoliae
officinalis Cortex (hou po) is either dried in the sun or
baked dry. This method of preparation also has the effect
of reducing throat irritation and harmonizing the Stomach,
but it especially enhances the ability of the herb to promote
the flow of qi, and is thus appropriate for cases of rebellious
qi causing wheezing and nausea.

englishReference.commentary:
Tigris Os (hui gu) is warm and yang in nature, with an
acrid flavor that contains sweetness. It excels at searching
out wind, stopping pain, and strengthening the bones and
sinews. It has been an important medicinal for treating
wandering pain in the joints due to overabundant wind,
as well as cold pain in the feet and knees from Liver and
Kidney yang deficiency. It has also been used for spasms
of the limbs due to wind, paralysis, childhood convulsions,
anal fistula, and prolapsed rectum.
The Grand Materia Medica observes:
All the bones in a tiger can be used: the bones of the skull
to treat childhood convulsions, warm malarial sores and
swellings, and head wind; the tibia for wind in the hands
and feet; and the vertebra for any wind affecting the lower
back and spine.

causing pain in the sinews and bones, this should be used

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
The general substance tiger bone is subdivided into head
bones ( tou gu), neck bones ( jing gu),skeletal
bones (T shen gu), and bones of the extremities ( Ak
si zhi gu). The first and last of these categories are preferred.
especially the last. Of the various bones of the extremities.
the tibia ( jing gu) is highly valued, while the patella
(* xi gu) is the most prized, often available only at auc
tion. Although tiger bone is typically used in medicinal
wines, as well as pills and powders, it is generally toasted in
oil or vinegar before using.

be used for medicinal purposes.

englishReference.commentary:
Succinum (hu po) is sweet and neutral, and enters the
blood level of the Heart and Liver to suppress fright, quiet
the spirit, unblock blood stasis, and promote urination.
To suppress palpitations, fright, or tremors, and treat
insomnia, it is usually combined with mineral or metallic
medicinals that anchor, settle, and calm the spirit. When
used to promote blood movement and break up blood
stagnation, it is usually combined with warm, acrid herbs
that. encourage the movement of blood. For unblocking
painful urinary dribbling, and to facilitate the urethral orifice, it is usually combined with bland, leaching herbs that
facilitate urination.
In one of the earliest records of its therapeutic proper.
ties, the Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians states:
"Primarily quiets the five yin organs, settles the ethereal
soul and the corporeal soul, eliminates static blood, and
unblocks the five painful urinary difficulties."
The Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Zi notes: "Fortifies the
Heart, brightens the eyes and eradicates superficial visual
obstructions, stops Heart pain and pathogenic withdrawal,
breaks up clumping and fixed abdominal masses.
englishReference.comparisons:
Vs. PoRIA (fu ling)
Both substances calm the spirit and facilitate urination.
However, Succinum (hu po) enters the blood level with a
tendency to drain, while Poria (fu ling) enters the qi level
with a tendency to tonify. Both treat disorders of the spirit
and resolve, but Poria (fu ling) is most appropriate when
the Heart lacks nourishment, or pathogenic water disturbs
the Heart, while Succinum (hu po) is most appropriate when ascendant yang or overabundant fire disturbs
the Heart. Succinum (hu po) transforms stagnation and
unblocks the orifices, and is best when painful urinary dribbling is associated with obstruction of damp-heat or qi and
blood stagnation in the Bladder, and the symptoms involve
scanty, painful, and bloody urine. Poria (fu ling) augments
the qi and leaches dampness, and is thus best for qi defi
ciency failing to transform the fluids, leading to edema and
scanty urine.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:

taken by those with yin deficiency internal heat, fire blaz
ing, or water depletion. If the blood is deficient and urinating is difficult, consuming it will cause an adverse acute
irritation. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Standards of production vary across the many places that
produce amber, and thus the quality of the natural product
also varies widely. Quality is measured by the degree of
contamination due to infiltration by its matrix and soil, and
the extent to which the product has been cleaned.

14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
Specifying true amber (# zhen hu po) in a prescription emphasizes that pure amber is desired. This will
be uniformly amber, transparent, shiny, and friable, with.
out other material infiltration. It crackles and sparks when
set alight, with a slight aroma of pine. That which is blood
red is called blood amber (6 xue hu po or fn xue
po) and is highly prized. The best quality amber is consid
ered to be from Yunnan province, giving rise to the name
Yun[nan] amber ( yun hu po.Amber formed in
close proximity to a coal deposit, or picked out of the coal
itself, is called coal amber ( mei hu po), and apart
from being relatively harder to crush, is otherwise similar
in appearance and effect to standard amber, although of
lower quality
Generally, amber should not be subjected to heat, either
from decoction or calcination. It should be powdered and
added to the decoction just before it is consumed, or used
in powders or pills. For this reason it is often referred to as
amber powder ( hu po mo) or amber filings (
hu po xie).
If the amber is ground in water to a fine pure paste, it is
called amber flour (hu po mian)

englishReference.commentary:
Talcum (hua shi) is bland, to leach out dampness; sweet,
to harmonize the Stomach qi, and to alleviate irritability
and thirst; slippery, to facilitate the functions of the lowe
burner; and cold, to disperse accumulated heat. These
qualities enable it to promote urination, unblock painful
urinary dribbling, and clear heat and summerheat. It is a
very commonly used herb at the height of summer, and is
most appropriate for irritability and thirst due to pathogenic summerheat causing one to feel overheated, along
with dark, scanty urine that feels rough to pass, or contains
blood. It is also good for damp-heat diarrhea, dysenteric
disorders, jaundice, edema, or leg qi. Applied topically
it dispels dampness and heals sores, and is an important
external herb in the treatment of eczema, damp sores, and
toxic rashes
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
describes this mineral:
The substance of Talcum (hua shi) is slippery, which pri
marily facilitates [the functions of] the orifices; its flavor
is bland, which primarily leaches out dampness, so it can
scour and wash the six yang organs without the drawback
of exhausting [the qi]. It primarily treats irritability and
thirst due to summerheat, accumulated obstruction in the
Stomach, cloudy urine with rough [flow] and pain, blocked
milk flow during breastfeeding, and children's pox and
rashes with thirst. All are through its power of benefiting
the orifices and leaching dampness!
Zhang Jie-Bin elaborates on the qualities of this mineral:
[It] treats thirst, but is not actually directly treating the
thirst. In fact, it helps the orifices leach away damp-heat,
and thereafter the Spleen qi is centered and harmonious, so
that the thirst ceases naturally. If the heavens bring about a
season of excessive pernicious dampness, people may suffer from urinary difficulty associated with thirst. This substance is just right to leach and drain out [the dampness]-
the thirst will not appear! If, however, there is no dampness, and the urine flows freely but there is still thirst, then
one knows that dryness and heat exist internally. Dryness
should be [treated by] enriching and moistening. If Talcum
(hud shi) is consumed in error, it will further devastate the
Yin and yang fluids, and the thirst will become worse.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH DIOSCOREAE RHIZOMA (shan yao)
Talcum (hua shi) is sweet, cold, slippery, and facilitating.
It expels summerheat, disperses heat, promotes urination
and removes dampness. Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao) is
sweet and neutral. It tonifies the Spleen and Stomach, and
benefits the Lungs and Kidneys. It is particularly valued
because, while tonifying, it does not cause obstruction.
When used together, one herb clears the excessive dampheat, while the other supplements insufficiency; thus, the
pair clears without causing damage, and tonifies without
generating dampness.
An awkward clinical situation occurs when a constitutionally weak patient suffers summerheat and dampness,
with low fever, spontaneous sweating, irritability, thirst
(but only takes small sips of fluids), urinary difficulty, and
constant diarrhea or loose stools. If one attempts to tonify,
the pathogenic influence could be trapped internally, yet
expelling the pathogen carries the danger of further weakening the normal qi. The combination of Talcum (hud shi)
and Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao) is particularly appropriate for this type of presentation, as its gentle tonification
supports the normal qi, while dampness is gently cleared.
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting
the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun describes his experience with
this combination:
If, in an externally-contracted disorder, whether cold or
warm, there is upper burner dryness and heat and excessive lower burner diarrhea, this is an extremely dangerous
presentation. Around 30g each of Talcum (hud shi) and
Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao) can be decocted and con.
sumed; this will clear the upper burner heat, while halting
the lower diarrhea--this has never lacked for efficacy!
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
While both herbs clear heat and alleviate thirst, Talcum
(hud shi) alleviates thirst by harmonizing the Spleen and
Stomach, while also leaching out dampness. It is especially
appropriate for thirst due to summerheat with dampness
and dark urine that passes only with difficulty. It is inappropriate for thirst due to dry heat.
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) alleviates irritability and
thirst by clearing intense heat at the yang brightness stage,
so that fluids can be replenished when the heat has been
eliminated. Thus, it is best used when pathogenic heat has
entered the yang brightness stage and dried out the fluids.
which can only be restored by removing the pathogenic
heat.
Externally, both substances can be applied topically to
dispel dampness and inhibit sores. Talcum (hua shi) tends
to be better for eczema, toxic rashes, and weeping skin
conditions with severe itching, while Gypsum fibrosum
preparatum (duan shi gao) is better for chronic.sores which
have not healed over. They can also be used together for
these purposes.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "slippery rock"
Usually this substance will be dispensed either as the
original cleaned mineral, or as powder. When talc stone is
cleaned and shaped into marble-sized balls, it is also known
as unprepared talc ( sheng hua shi),or talc lumps
(i hua shi kuai or kuai hua shi). Talc powder
may simply be ground into a relatively fine powder, or it
can be made into an extremely fine powder through aqeous
trituration (see next item).
>FLYING TALCUM(# fei hua shi
Aqeous trituration is the process of using water to reduce
a substance to an extremely fine powder. In the case of
Talcum (hua shi), the mineral is first ground into a relatively coarse powder, then it is placed in an appropriate grind.
ing vessel, water is added, and it is stirred. The material that
is suspended in the water is poured off and retained, while
the coarser material settles to the bottom. The retained
material is ground again, water is added, and the process
is repeated several times. All of the retained material is
combined and allowed to settle, the water is poured off
and then the powder is dried. This gives an extremely fine
powder that is most amenable to internal use.

Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai) is bitter, cold, and directs
qi downward. It is best for draining fire from excess affecting the Kidneys, and clearing lower burner damp-heat. I

heat, vaginal discharge, turbid painful urinary dribbling
hemorrhoids, and hematuria.
The Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Med
ica says that Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai) controls
clumped heat in the organs, Stomach and Intestines, jaundice, and hemorrhoids; alleviates diarrhea and dysen
teric disorders, gynecological red-and-white discharge!
and ulceration of the vulva." In his writings, Zhu Dan-Xi
implied that Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai) tonified the

When water is dried up, how could bitterness tonify? Yin

The Materia Medica of Combinations describes how Phellodendri Cortex (huang bai) "tonifies" the yin, and then how

to expel it. If [however] the true water of the Kidneys is
insufficient so that the true fire floats deficiently upward,
then Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di hudng) and Rehmanniae
Radix preparata (shu di huang)-must be used to enrich
the Kidneys. When the water is sufficient, fire will natu
rally return to its place of containment. If Anemarrhenae

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH EvODIAE FRUCTUS (wui zhu yu)
This is a combination of cold and hot herbs. It treats heat in
the Liver channel causing Liver and Stomach disharmony.
The Heart is the child of the Liver, and, as the adage goes,
"When excessive, drain the child"; thus, the bitter, cold
Heart-draining action of Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian)
cools the Heart and clears Liver heat. This also prevents
fire from overcoming metal, such that metal in turn can
control Liver wood; once wood is calmed, the fire will be
directed downward. At this point, the effects of the small
amount of the acrid, bitter, and very hot Evodiae Fructus
(wu zhu yu) come into play: directly entering the terminal
yin, it promotes the flow.of qi to release constraint, and
guides heat downward. This assists the nausea-calming
action of Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian), and also prevents
the bitterness and cold of the latter herb from injuring the
Stomach. The combination is thus very effective for vomiting, belching, and acid regurgitation. This view is confirmed
in Mirror of Medicines, which describes the combination as
"a marvelous formula for acid regurgitation!"
Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian) and Evodiae Fructus
(wu zhu yu) are combined in a ratio of six to one in the
formula Left Metal Pill (zuo jin wan).
> WITH CINNAMOMI CoRTEX (rou gui)
This combination specifically reestablishes harmonious
communication between the Heart and Kidneys. Coptidis
.Rhizoma (huang lian) is bitter and cold, draining Heart
fire to control the ascent of excessive yang, reining in the
Heart yang and directing it downward to the Kidneys.
Cinnamomi Cortex (rou gui) is acrid, sweet, and very hot. It
warms the Kidney yang to guide fire back to its origin, and
transforms the Kidney yin so that it might rise-and benefit
the Heart. This combination is thus used for palpitations
that worsen at night, insomnia with disturbing dreams, and
irritability, which are due to the inability of the Heart fire to
descend and warm the Kidney yang, and the inability of the
Kidney water to be transformed so that it can rise to nourish the Heart yin.
WITH ASARI HERBA (xi xin)
This pair also combines cold and hot, acrid and bitter properties, each of them intense. Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian)
is intensely bitter and cold, draining and cooling Heart fire;
Asari Herba (xi xin) is intensely acrid and hot, dispersing
constrained pathogenic fire and alleviating pain. Together,
the acrid flavor disperses, the bitter flavor directs downward, and the coldness controls heat; the combination is
thus very effective when Heart channel fire blazes upward,
causing painful ulcers of the mouth and tongue. It is useful
as well for swollen eyes and deafness, and for red eyes with
photophobia, due to Liver fire blazing upward, and for
toothache, swollen gums, halitosis and dental disorders due
to Stomach fire blazing upward.
>WITH AUCKLANDIAE RADIX (mu xiang)
Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian) is bitter, cold, and yin in
nature; it cools the Intestines and alleviates dysenteric disorders. Aucklandiae Radix (mu xiang) is acrid, warm, and
yang in nature, with a strong ability to promote the flow of
qi and break up stagnation. The combination of one yin
and one yang herb, one cold and one hot, one opening
(acrid flavor) and one downward-directing (bitter flavor)
creates a powerful heat-clearing and dampness-drying
effect that facilitates the flow of qi to guide out obstruction
It is very effective for dysenteric disorders from the accumulation of damp-heat obstructing the Intestines.

urination and reducing edema. With its strong ascending
nature, it raises prolapse and alleviates uncomfortable sensations of dragging downward. It can also stop bleeding

its specific strengths, so it is really marvelous for all disorders involving exterior deficiency.

to travel internally, where it tonifies the qi and raises the
yang.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH GINSENG RADIX (ren shen)
When these two strong qi tonics are combined, each complements the other, Astragali Radix (huang qi) contributing
its quick, ascending quality, which particularly strengthens
the exterior, while Ginseng Radix (ren shen) prolongs the
action, supporting the deeper areas of the body, and also
nourishing and protecting the yin. There is thus a broad
range of actions for this combination: if the Lung protective
qi is deficient,it tonifies the qi to secure the protectiveif the
Spleen and Stomach qi is weak, it can stimulate and raise
the middle burner qi; if the Heart qi is deficient, it tonifies
the Heart and unblocks the vessels. In fact, this combination can be used for any pattern of qi deficiency, and while
it often achieves good results on its own, it provides the
foundation for a long list of formulas, among them Tonify

12 / Tonifying Herbs
the Middle and Augment the Qi Decoction (bu zhong yi qi
tang), All-Inclusive Great Tonifying Decoction (shi quan
da bu tang), Lift the Source Decoction (ju yuan jian), and
Sage-like Healing Decoction (sheng yu tang), to name just
a few. The same things can be said about the combination
of Astragali Radix (huang qi) and Codonopsis Radix (dang
shen).
>WITH CIMICIFUGAE RHIZOMA (sheng ma)
In this combination, Astragali Radix (huang qi) augments
and raises the primal qi of the Spleen, assisted by Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma). About this herb, Zhang YuanSu notes that "Herbs that tonify the Spleen and Stomach
will be ineffective without Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma)
to guide their use." After middle age the Spleen qi tends fo
sink, and the use of herbs that raise up-becomes essential.
Li Shi-Zhen points out:
In general, for people over fifty years of age, their qi is being
dissipated more, and generated less; more qi is descending
and less is rising. The nature of autumn in their lives predominates, rather than springtime. Those whose constitu
tion is weak and whose primal qi is sinking would benefit
from Cimicifugae Rhizoma (sheng ma) used adroitly in
their treatment.
When these two herbs are used together, the clear yang qi

lead to such disorders as chronic diarrhea, dragging sensa.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GINSENG RADIX (ren shen)
Both herbs are important primal qi tonics. Ginseng Radix
(ren shen) is sweet, slightly bitter, and neutral in nature.
tonifying the primal qi and also nourishing the yin; its tonic
effect is stronger and longer lasting than that of Astragali
Radix (huang gi).Astragali Radix (huang gi) is sweet and
warm, and while it tonifies the primal qi, it also supports
the yang, with a quick, ascending quality that in Ginseng Radix (ren shen) is less pronounced. Astragali Radix
(huang qi) is most appropriate for those disorders of the q
dynamic which involve sinking of the clear qi, which wil
benefit from its ability to raise the yang. Astragali Radix
(huang qi) also stops sweating, promotes the discharge
of pus, generates flesh, and facilitates urination, none of

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
This herb is both cultivated and wild-crafted. In recent
years the cultivated product is more common.
>DRY-FRIED AsTRAGALUs (k## chao huang qi)
The sliced herb is dry-fried or baked with bran until slightly
yellow. This enhances its warming and tonifying properties toward the Spleen and Stomach. Spraying with a bit
of water, then frying or baking, will help it tonify without
being cloying; this is known as clear prepared astragalus
(#qing zhi huang gi).
>WrNE-FRIED AsTRAGALUS (##jiu chao huang qf)
The herb is mixed with yellow rice wine, left covered briefly
as it is absorbed, then dry-fried or baked until dry. This
method of preparation enhances its ability to reach the
exterior, and allows it to tonify without being cloying. It is
also viewed by some as using the acrid warmth of the wine
-to better treat qi deficiency patterns involving cold, such as
wheezing due to qi deficiency with cold in the Lungs, or qi
deficiency with cold in the Stomach causing diarrhea.
> HONEY-PREPARED ASTRAGALUS
##mi zhi huangqi)
Honey is first slowly brought to a boil, and the froth and
any residual wax or extraneous matter is scraped from the
surface. The honey is then poured through a filter. It is
returned to the wok, and again brought to a boil, which is
maintained at 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles and
the honey no longer stretches between the fingers.
Boiling water is then added to thin the honey. It is then
poured slowly over slices of astragalus and left covered
briefly. The herb is then dry-fried at a low temperature until
deep yellow and no longer sticky to the touch.

22 12 / Tonifying Herbs
This common method of preparation, which is also
simply called prepared astragaluszhi huangqi
induces the astragalus to primarily travel internally, and to
specifically tonify and raise the clear qi of the middle burner. It is also somewhat moistening and is therefore more
appropriate when the pattern involves blood deficiency, or
dryness of the Spleen.

englishReference.actions:
. Clears heat and dries dampness: a major herb for damp.
heat in the Stomach or Intestines, which manifests as diarrhea or dysenteric disorder; damp-warmth, which presents
with fever, stifling sensation in the chest, and thirst but with
an inability to drink; or for damp-heat in the lower burner
with painful urinary dribbling. An auxiliary herb for dampheat jaundice.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitterness dries dampness, and coldness clears heat; these
are the two attributes of Scutellariae Radix (huang qin),
whose actions focus primarily on the Lungs, and somewhat less directly on the Large Intestine. However, if
matched properly with other herbs, it can clear fire, heat, or
damp-heat from the Spleen, Liver, Gallbladder, and Small
Intestine channels.
Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is often used in the
treatment of persistent irritability with fever in febrile
disorders, damp-heat focal distention, jaundice, diarrhea,
and dysenteric disorders due to damp-heat. It is a noted
fetal-quieting herb, benefiting both the mother and the
fetus when heat disturbs the pregnancy. For this purpose,
it is best used dry-fried or baked, so that its bitterness and
coldness are moderated. It is often used for bleeding from
internal heat, nosebleed, sores and swellings, and red, swol.
len, sore eyes.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica
observes:
Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is a very bitter and very cold
herb which generally treats all damp-heat. Its nature is quite
similar to Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian), thus, in its main
sphere of therapeutics it is often combined to act together
with Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian). Furthermore, while
its bitter flavor is directed straight downward, its aroma is
light and clearing; thus, it penetrates both above and below
reaching all the organs internally, while externally reaching
the muscles, flesh, and skin.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH CoPTIDIS RHIZOMA (huang lian)
Both are bitter, cold herbs that clear heat, dry dampness,
drain fire, and resolve
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
below). This combination
is therefore often used for damp-heat that has accumulated
in the Intestines leading to explosive diarrhea with a sensation of burning in the rectum, or fetid, filthy stools and
abdominal pain.
In addition, Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) cools the
blood in order to quiet the fetus in pregnancy, while
Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian) clears heat to alleviate nausea. The combination is therefore useful in pregnancy when
nausea occurs with heat disturbing the fetus. However, due
to their bitter, cold properties, the combination should be
used in small doses for only a short period of time, and
should be discontinued when the desired effect is achieved.
Preparation with wine guides the actions of these herbs
into the upper body, enhancing their ability to clear upper
burner heat and fire. Thus, when the prepared herbs are
combined, they treat red, swollen, and painful eyes, ulcers
of the mouth and tongue, or constrained heat in the blood
level leading to irritable restlessness, bleeding, and sores.
>WITH GARDENIAE FRUCTUS'(zhi zi)
Gardeniae Fructus (zhi zi) clears fire and constrained heat
from the Triple Burner, expels dampness, breaks up toxic
accumulation, and directs fire downward. Scutellariae Radix
(huang qin) is bitter, cold, and enters the qi level to clear
heat and drain fire, acting particularly on the upper and
middle burners. Together they powerfully clear and drain
lurking heat from the Lungs associated with such symptoms
as fever, sensation of fullness in the chest, cough with yel.
low sputum, and nosebleed or spitting up blood. The pair is
likewise effective for damp-heat and jaundice, sores due to
heat toxin, and irregular gynecological bleeding due to constrained Liver channel fire. Charred Gardeniae Fructus (zhi
zi) is better for entering the blood level to expel constrained
heat and thus stop bleeding, while Scutellariae Radix (huang
qin), when fried in wine, is better for draining Lung fire and
upper burner damp-heat.
>WITH ATRACTYLODIS MACROCEPHALAE RHIZOMA
(bai zhu)
This is a well-known fetal-quieting' combination advocated by Zhu Dan-Xi. Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is bitter)
cold, and clears fetal heat to prevent bleeding from excessive

2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
heat in the blood. Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma
(bai zhu) is bitter and warm, which enables it to dry dampness, but is also sweet, which tonifies the middle burner and
thereby enables the Spleen qi to control the blood. This pair
of herbs thus pursues two avenues for stopping bleeding in
early pregnancy: reducing the heat to quiet the blood, and
strengthening the Spleen's ability to keep the blood within
the vessels. Note that if the heat is from yin deficiency, the
sweet, neutral tonifying properties of Dioscoreae Rhizoma
(shan yao) can be substituted for Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu), thereby avoiding its warmth and
tendency to dry, while still strengthening the Spleen and
tonifying the Kidneys.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Both of these medicinals cool Lung heat and drain fire from
excess at the qi level. Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is bitter
and cold, and focuses on clearing heat and drying damp
ness, but it also cools the blood to stop bleeding, and quiets
the fetus when heat disturbs pregnancy.
By contrast, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is acrid, sweet,
and very cold. It focuses on cooling, releasing, and venting
heat in the muscle layer. Its strongest suit is its ability to
eliminate heat so that ffuids can regenerate. Its sphere of
influence is primarily qi-level heat from excess and drying
heat in the Lungs and Stomach.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica explains
that, despite all the virtues of Scutellariae Radix (huang
qin), "still its bitterness can harm the Stomach because
of its downward-directing [action], and thus it necessarily depletes generative qi." It goes on to comment on the
general use of this herb in pregnancy, made popular by
Zhu Dan-Xi:
Dan-Xi established Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma
(bai zhu) and Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) as sage-like
herbs for quieting the fetus. He said that during pregnancy.
the heat should be cleared and the blood should be cooled.
so that the blood did not move chaotically, as only then
could it nourish the fetus. His theory is not incorrect, but
later physicians came to regard Scutellariae Radix (huang
qin) as an essential herb for the pregnant mother, and it
even became a common folk remedy that was invariably
used in pregnancy. Yet constitutions are not inevitably
hot--what is the reason for its general use? Zhang Lu (in
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica]
stated that Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) is appropriate for
fetal heat leading to restless raising movement, but for fetal
13
cold leading to descent, or for poor appetite and diarrhea, it
should not be rashly employed---this is accurate.

(huo ma ren) enters the Spleen to enrich the yin fluids
and transform dry clumps; it excels at moistening the
Intestines and unblocking constipation. This herb is particularly appropriate for dry constipation in the elderly and

Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances

Cannabis Semen (huo ma ren) moistens the bowels and

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PERILLAE FRUCTUs (zi su zi)
Although they belong to different categories, both of these
herbs share the ability to moisten the Intestines and unblock
constipation, and are often combined for this purpose.
Cannabis Semen (huo ma ren) is a yang brightness herb,
specific for constipation due to deficiency of blood and
fluids. Perillae Fructus (zi su zi) is a greater yin herb, acrid
and warm, but also heavy and moist in texture; it excels
at directing rebellious qi downward, and easing the diaphragm and Intestines, with the ability to gently restore
normal rhythmic qi movement to the bowel. Together
the pair moistens Intestinal dryness, and is thus appropriate for elderly or weak patients with blood deficiency,
especially if--at the same time--the Lung qi fails to properly descend, manifesting in constipation with cough and
wheezing.
>WITH PRUNI SEMEN (yu li ren)
Cannabis Semen (huo ma ren) enriches the fluids and
moistens the Intestines in cases of constipation due to
blood deficiency or parched fluids. Pruni Semen (yu li ren)
more strongly directs downward to clear constipation. This
combination has been used for centuries, at least as far back
as Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica, to treat constipation with dry, hard stool.

englishReference.cautions: Because of this herb's acrid, dispersing, and draining qualities, it is contraindi. cated for chronic cough from yin deficiency or in patients with a tendency to cough up blood. See ToxiCiTY below.
englishReference.actions:
Opens up and disseminates the Lung qi, dispels phlegm.
and benefits the throat: for cough or wheezing with profuse
sputum, throat pain, and loss of voice. Can be used for
cough with profuse sputum from either cold or heat.
-With Perillae Folium (zi su ye) and Armeniacae Semen
(xing ren) for wind-cold leading to cough with watery sputum, nasal congestion, chills, and headache, as in Apricot
Kernel and Perilla Leaf Powder (xing su san).

430 6 / Herbs that Transform Phlegm and Stop Coughing
- With Mori Folium (sang ye) and Chrysanthemi Flos (ju
hua) for wind-heat leading to cough with mild fever and
thirst, as in Mulberry Leaf and Chrysanthemum Decoction
(sang ju yin).
-- With Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao) for hoarseness, pain,
and swelling of the throat caused by wind-heat. Scutellariae
Radix (huang qin) is often added.
- With Perillae Caulis (zi su geng) for cough, wheezing, or
stifling sensations in the chest and diaphragm due to Lung
qi constraint.
- With Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he), Arctii Fructus
niu bang zi), and Cicadae Periostracum (chan tui) for
hoarseness and sore throat from wind-heat.
- With Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) for
cough due to externally-contracted wind-cold or a longstanding phlegm-dampness disorder.
- With Aurantii Fructus (zhi ke) and Trichosanthis Pericarpium (gua lou pi) for discomfort and a stifling sensation
in the chest due to phlegm obstruction and qi stagnation.
- Pushes out pus: for expelling pus associated with Lung
abscess or throat abscess. The traditional disease of Lung
abscess is marked by fevers, chest pain, coughing of yellow
sputum with a fishy smell, along with coughing up of blood
and pus.
-With Trichosanthis Semen (gua lou ren), Houttuyniae
Herba (yu xing cao), and Coicis Semen (yi yi ren) for Lung
abscess.
- With Angelicae dahuricae Radix (bai zhi) for ulcerated
abscess where pus is being discharged slowly.
With Fritillariae Bulbus (bei mu) and Crotonis Fructus
(ba dou) to enhance its ability to promote the discharge of
pus.
- Opens up and raises the Lung qi while also directing the
actions of other herbs to the upper regions of the body:
used not only to reinforce the actions of other herbs that
clear and drain the upper burner, but also whenever the
actions of a formuia should be focused on the upper
regions of the body.
englishReference.commentary:
With an acrid flavor that disperses, and bitterness that
drains, Platycodi Radix (jie geng) is also quite lightweight,
which gives it an ascending quality. Overall, it has an
ascending and dispersing nature which raises and opens
the Lung qi, releases the exterior, benefits the throat, transforms phlegm, and expels pus.
Ancient writings say that "Platycodi Radix (jie geng) is
like a boat: it lifts the other herbs upward." Thus the herb
is customarily used for problems above the diaphragm.
The following passage was quoted by Zhang Yuan-Su,
who explained that it can be used to raise the actions of
herbs that would otherwise descend--such as Rhei Radix
et Rhizoma (da huang)--into the chest or higher: "These
herbs are like iron or stone entering a river: they cannot
be carried along without a boat." But Zhang cautioned
that if Platycodi Radix (jie geng) is improperly prescribed
with these herbs, it will prevent their actions from properly
descending. In addition, this raising action can be used
judiciously for lower burner problems, for example, as a
means to treat tenesmus in dysenteric disorders, or (via the
effect of the Lung qi on the water pathways, and the ascent
and descent of the qi dynamic) for urinary blockage. In this
regard, Zhu Dan-Xi noted:
Dysenteric disorders with abdominal pain are constraint of
Lung metal qi in the Large Intestine, which [first] requires
unbinding with the use of bitter Platycodi Radix (jie geng)
and only then can herbs that are specific to dysenteric dis.
order be used. This herb can raise and unbind the qi and
blood, and should accordingly be used with other qi herbs.
Chen Shi-Duo examined this tendency and pointed out its
corollary:
It raises by nature, but why are there still some herbs which
it cannot carry upward? The reason that they are not car
ried upward is always because of improper use of the herbs.
Despite the ascending tendency of Platycodi Radix (jie
geng), if descending herbs are used at the same time for
purging or tonifying [the lower burner], this ascending
tendency will attempt to manifest but fail ... they will cancel each other out, and neither will move. They will remain
stuck in the middle burner, unable to rise, unable to fall.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
While both are Lung channel qi-level herbs, Armeniacae
Semen (xing ren) primarily directs rebellious qi downward
alleviates cough, and calms wheezing, while Platycodi
Radix (jie geng) raises and disseminates the Lung qi,
benefits the throat, and expels phlegm. Because of these
complementary ascending and descending actions, the
two herbs can be used together to restore normal qi flow
when the circulation of Lung qi has been affected either by
an externally-contracted pathogenic factor, or by internal
accumulation of phlegm or thin mucus.
> Vs. STERCULIAE LYCHNOPHORAE SEMEN (pang da hai);
see page 406
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
It is, after all, an herb that raises, and should not be used
whenever pathogenic qi rushes rebelliously upward, unable
to descend,or if lower burner vin is deficient and float
ing, or if there is a pathogen in the lower burner. It should
also not be used with herbs intended to purge or to tonify
the lower burner. If used incorrectly, it will certainly cause
wheezing, rebellious qi, and other changes. When there is
an excess disorder in the upper burner, with no disorder
in the lower burner,it should then be accompanied by
Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao). (Harm and Benefit in the
Materia Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
A variety of names have been coined to emphasize certain
desirable qualities in this herb, such as bitter platycodon
(# ku jie geng), white platycodon ( bai jie
geng), and powdery platycodon (*## fen jie geng)
Because the herb harvested in autumn is generally consid.
ered to be superior, autumnal platycodon ($ qiu jie
geng) is sometimes specifically prescribed.
>DRY-FRIED PLATYCODON (&# chao jie geng)
The herb is dry-fried or baked until slightly yellow. This
method of preparation moderates its acrid, dispersing
qualities and also reduces its tendency to irritate the stom.
ach and cause nausea. Thus it is preferred for treating
elderly or weak patients with cough due to phlegm or thin
mucus.
> HONEY-PREPARED PLATYCODON
(+ K+ mi zhi jie geng)
Also simply known as prepared platycodon (&#*# zhi
jie geng), the herb is mixed with honey then fried until the
honey is absorbed and the herb has turned yellow. Thi
increases its moistening and tonifying qualities, as it is used
for chronic or dry cough from Lung deficiency.
>CHARRED PLATYCODON (#jie geng tan)
The herb is fried or baked at a high temperature until
black but not misshapen. Because it enters the Lung channel, and the Lung and Large Intestine are related, charred
platycodon can be used for dysenteric disorders when pus
and blood appear in thestool as a result of Lung heat being
passed on to the Large Intestine.
