englishReference.cautions: Contraindicated where there is deficiency of the exterior, fully-erupted measles or open sores, or an absence of pathogenic wind of any kind. See ToxiCITY below.
englishReference.actions:
- Releases the exterior and dispels wind: for exterior patterns
of either wind-cold or wind-heat (depending on the herbs
with which it is combined). Also for carbuncles or boils
when they first erupt, especially when accompanied by
chills and fever.
- With Saposhnikoviae Radix (fangfeng) and Notopterygii
Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) for exterior wind-cold with

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
chills, fever, and lack of sweating, as in Schizonepeta and
Saposhnikovia Powder to Overcome Pathogenic Influences
(jing fang bai du san).
-With Menthae haplocalycis Herba(bo he), Forsythiae
Fructus (lian qiao), and Lonicerae Flos (jin yin hua) for
exterior wind-heat, as in Honeysuckle and Forsythia
Powder (yin qiao san).
-With Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) and Chrysanthemi
Flos (ju hua) for eye inflammation associated with windheat.
-With Pogostemonis/Agastaches Herba (huo xiang) and
Eupatorii Herba (pei lan) for externally-contracted damp
disorders.
- With Platycodi Radix (jie geng) and Glycyrrhizae Radix
(gan cao) for acute cough associated with externally-contracted disorders.
- Vents rashes and alleviates itching: for the initial stage of
measles and pruritic skin eruptions.
With Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) for itching
from wind due to blood deficiency, as in Eliminate Wind
Powder (xiao feng san). Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan
xiong) is often added to strengthen the effect.
With Arctii Fructus (niu bang zi and Cicadae Periostracum (chan tui) for the initial stage of measles.
-With Equiseti hiemalis Herba (mu zei) and Eriocauli
Flos (gu jing cao) for pruritic rash.
-With Phaseoli Semen (chi xiao dou) for itchy wind rash
and swollen toxic sores.
- Stops bleeding: as an auxiliary herb for hemorrhage, e.g..
blood in the stool or uterine bleeding. Best used charred
for this action, as in Sophora Japonica Flower Powder (huai
hua san).
-With Sophorae Flos immaturus (hudi mi) for blood in

englishReference.commentary:
Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) is quite harmonious in
nature: acrid, but not overly dispersing, slightly warm, but
not drying. Its light, ascending qualities, which enter the
Liver and Lungs, allow it to be used for both wind-heat and
wind-cold, and also for venting wind from the blood. This
latter action is so marked that Treasury of Words on the
Materia Medica lauds it as
the herb for wind in the midst of the blood ... each and
every wind toxin condition--just at the threshhold of
manifesting, but not completely; about to disperse, but not
dispersing--can be cleared up with the use of unprepared
Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie).
15
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica explains its interac.
tion with Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng). Schizonepetae
Herba (jing jie), it says.
is not like Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng), whose qi is not
light and lifting, and which must enter into the flesh and
bones to drive out wind. Thus, in order to dissipate and
disperse the wind pathogen, when one uses Saposhnikoviae
Radix (fang feng) it is necessary to also use Schizonepetae
Herba (jingjie). This is because Schizonepetae Herba (jing
jie) can enter the muscles and skin to dissipate and disperse (and thus complement Saposhnikoviae Radix's (fang
fengl deeper action]. Furthermore, since Schizonepetae
Herba (jing jie) also enters the Liver channel--the wind
and wood organ-and the Liver is the realm of blood stor.
age, Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) is also able to unblock
and facilitate the blood vessels to treat such symptoms as
nosebleed,Intestinal wind, irregular menstrual bleeding
puerperal fainting, toxic swollen sores, and blood heat.
[Resolution of] all of these [symptoms] relies on its light
lifting, as a tool for dissipating and draining. How could
one regulate the qi in the organ of wind and wood, but not
treat the blood as well?! Therefore, while Schizonepetae
Herba (jing jie) enters the qi aspect of the Liver, it also
enters its biood aspect.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ANGELICAE SINENSIS RADIX (dang gui)
Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) harmonizes the blood
by tonifying and moving it. Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie)
expels wind from the blood; in its charred form, it regulates
blood flow and stops bleeding. Treasury of Words on the
Materia Medica notes: "For any pattern of bleeding, if it
tends to stop and start, seeming to flow but not properly
then charred Schizonepetae Herba (jing jie) can be used to
Stop it."
When used together, each of these herbs complements
the other such that the blood is nourished and regulated,
wind is expelled from the blood, and the bleeding is stopped
This is appropriate and very effective for conditions such as
Intestinal wind with bleeding from the rectum.
One ancient emergency formula listed in Fine Formulas
for Women for postpartum collapse and coma, called
Concurrent Powder (& jiao jia san), instructed that
the two herbs be powdered, then decocted, with some wine
added before administration. This combination is now
frequently used for wind resulting from blood deficiency
with such symptoms as tremors of the hands and feet, or
itching of the skin.
>WiTH SoPHORAE FLOs (hudi hua)
Sophorae Flos (huai hua) is bitter and slightly cold, with the
specific function of cooling the blood and stopping bleed

ing, particularly in the bowels. When the two herbs are used
together, the hemostatic action of charred Schizonepetae

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.PERILLAE FOLIUM (zi su ye)
Both are exterior-releasing and sweat-inducing herbs.
But while Perillae Folium (zi su ye) disperses wind-cold,
Schizonepetae Herba (jingjie) is both stronger at dispelling
wind, and can also be used for either wind-cold or windheat. Perillae Folium's (zi su ye) other actions make it the
herb of choice for treating wind-cold when there are middle
burner issues, qi stagnation, or pregnancy. Schizonepetae
Herba (jing jie) also acts to disperse wind-heat from the
blood and relieve spasms.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH MENTHAE HAPLOCALYCIS HERBA (bo he)
Both are wind-heat dispersing herbs. Chrysanthemi Flos
(ju hua), which is sweet, bitter, and slightly cold, has a
superior wind-expelling and heat-cooling effect. Menthae
haplocalycis Herba (bo he) is light, cooling, and dispersing, and ideal for releasing pathogenic wind-heat, cooling
heat, and soothing the throat. Combined, the wind-heat
dissipating effect is greatly enhanced, especially around
the head and eyes. The pair is commonly used for the early
stages of exterior wind-heat causing fever, chills, headache,
dizziness, sore eyes, and sore throat. Yellow Chrysanthemi
Flos (huang ju hua) is the variety to use for this purpose.
Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) and Menthae haplocalycis
Herba (bo he) both enter the Liver.channel, and both cool
the Liver. But Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) also nourishes
the Liver, while Menthae haplocalycis Herba (bo he) moves
the Liver qi. The combination is therefore ideal for Liver qi
blockage turning to fire blazing upward, with such symptoms as blurry vision, dizziness, headache, and red, swollen
eyes. For this purpose, White Chrysanthemi Flos (bai ju
hua) is the better variety.
> WrTH SAPOSHNIKOVIAE RADIX (fang feng)
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fangfeng) is acrid, sweet, and warm.
Its specialty is dispelling wind, particularly wind-cold.
Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) is sweet, bitter, and slightly
cold, and although it is a wind-heat dispersing herb, its
wind-expelling action is much weaker than its heat-cooling
action. With Saposhnikoviae Radix (fangfeng) as a partner,
the ability of Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) to expel wind is
enhanced, while the warmth of Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang
feng) is cooled by Chrysanthemi Flos (jui hua). Because of
this mutual enhancement and control, this is a good combination for treating wind-heat irritating the exterior, with
such symptoms as slight chills and mild fever, headache,
and itchy eyes.
>WITH CICADAE PERIOSTRACUM (chan tul)
Cicadae Periostracum (chan tut) is sweet and cold, brightens the eyes, and eliminates superficial visual' obstructions. Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) not only expels wind

and disperses heat, it is also excellent for cooling the Liver
and improving the vision. Together, they are often used
for accumulation of wind-heat causing superficial visual
obstructions. Today the combination is most often used
for red, watery eyes and superficial visual obstructions
associated either with Liver channel wind-heat or residual
heat toxin remaining from measles or other rashes. The
combination of these two herbs has been known as Cicada
and Chrysanthemum Powder (chan ju san) at least since its
inclusion in the Grand Materia Medica. Equal parts of each

decocted and mixed with a bit of honey before drinking.
This combination can also be used for superficial visual
obstructions following trauma to the eye.
>WITH LYCII FRUCTUS (gou qi zi)
Lycii Fructus (gou qi zi) is sweet and neutral, nourishing and tonifying the Liver and Kidneys, increasing the
essence, and thereby brightening the eyes. Chrysanthemi
Flos (ju hua) is sweet, bitter, and cool, and is basically a
wind-expelling, cooling, and toxin-relieving herb, which
also has Liver-cooling and vision-improving properties.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes: "Only
Chrysanthemi Flos's (ju hua) cooling, bitter draining and
its ability to direct downward can draw the deficient [but
risingl yang back to its base below; this is why it is an
important herb for eye diseases." In the treatment of Liver
and Kidney deficiency, where the essence and blood are
unable to rise and nourish the eyes, or for Liver yang or
Liver wind rising, the tonifying effect of Lycii Fructus (gou
qi zi) supplements the root, while the Liver-cooling and
Liver-pacifying actions of Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) treat
the branch.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, sweet, and neutral, Raphani Semen (lai fu zi) is best
at facilitating the flow of qi. In its unprepared (raw) form, it
raises the qi, but when dry-fried, it directs the qi downward
and wheezing with profuse phlegm, or abdominal distention, belching, loss of appetite, and diarrhea with tenesmus
due to food and qi stagnation.
In its unprepared form, its raising action is strong.
driving out wind-phlegm and relieving the upper burner
stifling sensation in the chest. However, it often causes
vomiting, a feature which is exploited in cases of windstroke with phlegm welling upward and food stagnating
in the middle burner. Often a single regurgitation of the
obstructing pathogenic influence will provide great relief.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica provides
a helpful discussion of this herb:
When unprepared [it] is slightly acrid and neutral in
nature; when dry-fried it is aromatic and warm in nature.
Its power both raises and directs downward; when unpre.
pared its raising is greater than its downward-directing;
when dry-fried it directs downward more than it raises.
Use it unprepared for unbinding the qi and transforming
phlegm; use it dry-fried when directing qi downward and
reducing food stagnation. On investigation, regardless of
whether unprepared or dry-fried, it can smooth [the flow
of] qi and unbind constraint, reduce distention and eliminate fullness: it is a herb that transforms qi, not one that
breaks up qi.
Most physicians believe that it as able to break up qi, and
therefore [something that] should not be taken in high
doses or for long periods of time, but this is quite incorrect. All herbs that regulate the qi injure the qi if [the herb
is] taken alone or for a long time, but Raphani Semen (lai
fu zi), if dry-fried and powdered, can be taken after every
meal in doses just over one qian [approximately 4g] in
order to reduce food stagnation and smooth the qi. It does
not injure the qi at all, because it assists the intake of food
and drink so that the qi aspect obtains nourishment. If used
to expel fullness and unbind constraint, it can be assisted
by such herbs as Codonopsis Radix (dang shen), Astragali
Radix (hudng qf), and Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma
(bai zhu); then, even if taken in higher doses or for a long
time, how could it injure the qi aspect?

englishReference.commentary:
The bitterness of Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao) drains fire
its coldness cools heat, and its light weight conducts patho.
gens outward, thereby enabling it to vent heat. Thus, it disperses heat from both the exterior and interior, particularly
the Heart and upper burner. Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao)
is used to treat externally-contracted wind-heat or a warm
pathogen disease entering the Pericardium causing irrita.
bility, fever, delirium, or rashes due to blood heat.
The twelfth-century physician Zhang Yuan-Su concisely summarized the actions of this herb in his book Pouch of
Pearls: "Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao) has three uses: one
is to drain heat that has lodged in the Heart channel; the
second is to dispel various types of heat from the upper
burner; as for the third, it is the sage-like herb for sores."
Basic Questions notes that "All painful, itchy sores
derive from the Heart. Forsythiae Fructus lian qiao
excels at clearing Heart fire, and also encourages the
smooth flow of qi and blood. It disperses clumped blood
and the accumulation of qi, thereby reducing swellings;
thus, it is used in treating toxic swollen sores, scrofula
and clumps such as swollen lymph nodes. It also facilitates
urination, and is used for anuria due to clumped heat, or
painful urinary dribbling.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica explains
the reasoning underlying its functions:
Forsythiae Fructus (lian qiao) is bitter, thus [it] cools
heat. Its shape is round and pointed, empty inside with a
chamber very much like the heart, thus it specifically cools
heat in Heart patients. These are inherent, natural characteristics, not forced or appended sophistry. Furthermore.
all herbs which are light in weight and empty or soft inside
must have opening, draining, disseminating, and unblocking functions, thus it can also disperse clumps while draining and transforming heat in the collateral channels.

: Settles anxiety and calms the spirit: for such problems as
palpitations with anxiety, withdrawal-mania, and insomnia
with dream-disturbed sleep.

pararadicis (fu shen) for seizures secondary to fright or

englishReference.commentary:
Astringent and cool, Fossilia Dentis Mastodi (long chi)
enters the Liver and Heart channels to suppress fright.
quiet the spirit, and eliminate irritability and heat. The
Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians says that it
"treats childhood convulsions with the body so hot that it is
unapproachable, and in adults, chills and fever at the level
of the bones.
It is particularly effective for insomnia due to dream.
disturbed sleep and palpitations. Discussion of Medicinal
Properties points out that it "sedates the Heart, quiets the
ethereal and the corporeal souls." Encountering the Sources
of the Classic of Materia Medica concurs, quoting Xu ShuWei: "The Liver stores the ethereal soul, allowing the ability
to transform. If the ethereal soul is unsettled and strays,
treat this with Fossilia Dentis Mastodi (long chi).
The Materia Medica Arranged by Channel provides a
reasonable summary: "Astringent and neutral, it pertains
to wood, and governs the Liver, sedates the Heart, quiets
the ethereal soul, and treats childhood convulsions and
epilepsy."
englishReference.combinations:
> WiTH MARGARITIFERAE CoNCHA USTA (zhen zhu mu)
Both substances are heavy spirit-settling substances, and
both enter the Heart and Liver channels. Margaritiferae
Concha usta (zhen zhu mu) also cools heat and clears
Liver fire, while Fossilia Dentis Mastodi (long chi) strongly
anchors the spirit and restrains the Liver yang. Together
this combination has two major uses: it strongly calms and
anchors the spirit, and inhibits the floating upward of Liver
yang. Not often used by itself, this combination is usually
included in a larger prescription designed to treat forgetfulness, insomnia with dream-disturbed sleep, palpitations
with anxiety, or ascendant Liver yang with red eyes, dizziness, tinnitus, and even seizures.

Literal English translation: "dragon teeth"
Fossilia Dentis Mastodi (long chi) are the fossilized teeth
of such mammals as cattle, horses, deer, rhinoceros, and]
elephants. Traditionally, the best quality are blue-green
dragon teeth (# qing long chi), which have a greyish
green cast, followed by white dragon teeth (t bai
long chi), which are yellowish white and somewhat harder
in texture, and finally block teeth ( ya dun), which are
the remnants of the jaw with cavities where the teeth have
fallen out. In most cases, these types are mingled in supply.
When not calcined, they are known as unprepared dragor
teeth (# sheng long chi)
>CALCINED DRAGON TEETH( duan long chi
The dragon teeth are placed in a calcining container and
heated at a high temperature until red hot, then removed
and pulverized. This method of preparation reduces their
coldness and moderates their ability to cool heat and suppress fright, but increases their restraining, binding, and
securing actions, and especially their power to calm the
spirit and make the mind tranquil. They are thus most
often used in the treatment of insomnia with dream-disturbed sleep.

>ScORCHED GENTIAN#jiao l6ng dan
2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
Adulterants
Sections of the cleaned herb are baked or dry-fried over
high heat until scorched black, but not completely charred.
They are then sprayed with water to extinguish any embers,
and dried. This is also called charred gentian ( dan
cao tan). This method of preparation guides the actions of
the herb into the blood level in order to cool blood and alle.
viate bleeding, while also preventing its extreme bitterness
from injuring the Spleen and Stomach or overly drying and
injuring the yin or blood. It is often used for blood in the
urine or stool from alcohol poisoning or Intestinal wind.
> WINE-FRIED GENTIAN
jiu chao long dan cao
The cleaned sections are sprayed with alcohol and mixed
thoroughly, then baked or dry-fried over moderate heat
until dry. This method of preparation guides the actions of
the herb upward in order to clear toxic fire in the head or
face, and is often used for swelling, redness, and pain of the
eyes, ringing in the ears, and bitter taste: It also moderates
the herb's coldness and tendency to cause obstruction, so
that within its cold, congealing aspect there is still movement. It is thus most effective when fire from excess in the
Liver and Gallbladder is associated with pain in the ribs due
to qi stagnation. This is the form of preparation appropriate for Gentian Decoction to Drain the Liver (long dan xie
gan tang).

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, astringent, slightly cold, and heavy in weight, Fossilia
Ossis Mastodi (long gu) enters the Heart, Liver, and Kidney
channels. Interestingly, Medicinal Combining notes that
it also "treats disorders of the Girdle vessel." Astringency
restrains and holds back to secure what is leaking out, while
heaviness eliminates trepidation and anchors the floating
yang, hence Fossilia Ossis Mastodi (long gu) restrains and
secures the primal qi, calms the spirit, and inhibits loss and

14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
leakage. One of its special characteristics is its ability to
secure the normal qi while not inhibiting the elimination of
pathogenic qi. It is also noted for its effects in the treatment
of seizures and epilepsy due to Liver qi rebelling upward
carrying phlegm.
Fossilia Ossis Mastodi (long gu) is often used when
the yin is unable to control the yang, causing palpitations.
insomnia with dream-disturbed sleep, palsy of the face,
spasms of the limbs, restlessness, and dizziness and vertigo;
or for the yang being unable to secure the yin, leading to
excessive sweating, nosebleed, vomiting of blood, blood in
the stool or urine, loose stools, urinary incontinence, continuous uterine bleeding, or spermatorrhea.
Applied externally, it restrains dampness, stops bleeding, and assists the healing of sores.
The Grand Materia Medica notes that
Astringency eliminates abandonment [disorders], thus
Fossilia Ossis Mastodi (long gu) restrains and holds back
the normal.qi that has floated upward and outward, stabi.
lizes the Large Intestine and sedates fright; it also governs
disorders of the Girdle vessel.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica
observes:
Although its nature is binding, it also enters the Liver to
break up clumping: mobile and fixed abdominal masses
and firm clumping are all accumulations of blood in the
Liver channel. ... It also governs disorders of the Girdle
vessel causing ceaseless vaginal discharge or continuous
uterine bleeding, with fullness in the lower abdomen, and a
flowing sensation around the waist, as if sitting in water.
The early twentieth-century writer Zhang Xi-Chun stated
that "This medicinal only preserves normal qi, it does
not inhibit [expulsion of] pathogenic qi. He went on to
explain that its
flavor is slightly acrid, and within its conserving and inhibiting is the power to unbind and unblock, which is why the
Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica states
that [on the one hand] it treats diarrhea and dysentery with
blood and pus, while [on the other hand] it also treats fixed
abdominal masses and solid clumps.

Calcined dragon bone is most often used in the treat-

Section 3
HERBS THAT TONIFY THE YANG
The herbs in this section are used for patterns of yang
deficiency, primarily of the Kidneys, Spleen, and Heart,
which underlies the qi-transforming functions of the body.
They are also known as herbs that assist the yang (
zhu yang). Because the Kidneys are the seat of the primal
yang--the basis of all the body's yang---the most important
use of this class of herbs is to tonify the Kidney yang.
The principal manifestation of Kidney yang deficiency
is systemic exhaustion and lack of warmth. The most com
mon associated symptoms are withdrawal into oneself, fear
of cold, cold extremities, sore and weak lower back and
lower extremities, pale tongue, and a deep and weak pulse
Other related problems include impotence, spermatorrhea,
watery vaginal discharge, infertility, enuresis, polyuria,
wheezing, and daybreak diarrhea.
Herbs that tonify the yang are divided into three prin.
cipal classes: those that are very potent and very expensive,
usually animal products such as Cervi Cornu pantotrichum (lu rong) and Gecko (ge jie); those-the most commonly used--that reliably strengthen the yang and are
not too expensive, such as Morindae officinalis Radix (ba
ji tian) and Psoraleae Fructus (bu gu zhi); and those that
have a secondary function of nourishing the yin, such as
Cordyceps (dong chong xia cao) and Eucommiae Cortex
(du zhong).
Most of these herbs are warm and drying, which can
injure the yin and assist fire. For this reason they should not
be used in those with fire from yin deficiency.

The Grand Materia Medica recites its major indica

nausea and rebelliousness that prevents food intake, heat in

Wang Ang elaborates on this mechanism:
The Lungs are the upper source of water. The Spleen
distributes essence, which ascends and enters the Lungs.
Only then can the Lungs unblock and regulate the fluid
metabolism and transport to the Bladder. Kidneys are the

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. IMPERATAE RHIZOMA (bai mdo gen)
Phragmitis Rhizoma (lu gen) clears heat, generates fluids)
and promotes urination. These properties are shared by
Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mdo gen). However, Phragmitis
Rhizoma (lu gen) excels at clearing qi-level heat, which is
why it is classified as an herb that drains fire.In particular
it cools the Lungs, drains the Stomach, guides out phlegm.
heat, and has the ability to vent and disseminate pathogenic
inffuences from the exterior. It focuses on-the Lungs and

Stomach. Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mao gen) is better for
clearing blood-level heat and cooling the biood in order
to stop bleeding. Its actions are not restricted to the Lungs
and Stomach; it also guides Heart fire downward and out
through the urine. It focuses on the Heart, Lungs, Stomach,
and Bladder.
These differences are reflected in what each medicinal
treats. Thus, while Phragmitis Rhizoma (lu gen) treats
cough from Lung heat, Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mao gen)
treats nosebleed, spitting up blood, and blood in the urine.
And while Phragmitis Rhizoma (lu gen) treats externallycontracted disorders, or the failure of measles to express,
Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mdo gen) treats jauindice due to
damp-heat.
Nevertheless, one should not make too much of these
differences. Zhang Xi-Chun, an expert in the use of both
herbs, said about Phragmitis Rhizoma (lu gen) that its
nature is quite similar to Imperatae Rhizoma (bai mdo gen)
so that whenever the fresh root of Imperatae Rhizoma (bai
mdo gen) is unavailable, one can always use the fresh root of
Phragmitis Rhizoma (lu gen) as a substitute."

englishReference.commentary:
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) is strongly acrid, dispersing and warm, and enters the channels of the Lungs and
Bladder, both of which relate to the exterior of the body.
The dispersing action of the herb is thus expressed in the
exterior, by opening up the interstices and pores to induce
sweating and drive out pathogenic influences. The acrid,
dispersing action of Ephedrae Herba (md huang) opens
up the Lungs to disseminate and facilitate the Lung qi, and
thus alleviate coughs and calm wheezing. It also enters the
greater yang, both the channel and the Organ (Bladder).
This is why the herb is able to release the exterior while
also promoting urination. As Zhang Xi-Chun observed,
"Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) treats the pathogen in the

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
greater yang channel by inducing sweating, and the pathogen in the greater yang Organ by releasing it through urination.
The acrid, dispersing character of Ephedrae Herba (ma
huang) is also utlized in other ways. Because it is warm as
well as strongly dispersing, it can be used to drive out cold
pathogens in cases of wind-damp painful obstruction, and
combined with other herbs to expel wind-dampness.
It is also used for deep-rooted toxic sores without a head
caused by localized accumulation of dampness (or phlegm)
and cold, which prevents nourishment from reaching
the area, and thereby causing a breakdown in the tissues.
Combined with herbs that restore nourishment, the warm.
of Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) can bedispersing a6f11
instrumental in breaking up the congealing of the gathered
yin pathogens, thus allowing nourishment to reach the area
and repair the tissues. Finally, it can be added to external
medications for the specific purpose of opening the pores
to allow the medication to be absorbed more quickly
When used properly, the warming dispersal of Ephedrae
Herba (ma huang) can be a powerful and versatile agent.
but its use requires familiarity with the qualities of the local
environment and population. A dosage appropriate in one
place may be excessive in another. Chinese physicians have
been debating the relationship between locality and dosage
of this herb for a long time, as reflected in the following
passage from Lu Jiu-Zhi, quoted by Zhang Xi-Chun in
Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting
the Western:
[For] Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) to promote sweating at
several tenths of a gram is perhaps possible in southerners.
but difficult to achieve in the north. The weather is warm
in the south, the people's skin thin: they sweat easily. Thus.
a southern proverb warns, Ephedrae Herba (ma huang),
no more than one gram.' In the north, outside the [Great]
Wall, the climate is freezing, the people's skin tough and
thick, especially in those who work outside exposed to the
wind and frost. When it is also in the middle of winter.
then a sweat could only be produced if repeated doses of
20 grams or more are used. Thus, the Way of Herbs values
adapting the approach in accordance with the time, place.
and people, adroitly changing with the circumstances, and
not hobbled by set views [about dosage].
Li Shi-Zhen also provided some advice regarding the man.
agement of common, mild reactions to this herb:
If ingestion of Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) causes continuous spontaneous sweating, use cold water to soak the scalp!
then pat Ephedrae Radix (ma huang gen) powder over the
area of sweating and it will stop. After using any medicine containing Ephedrae Herba (mi huang), drafts must
be avoided for one day, otherwise the illness will recur.
The problem of red eyes can be avoided by always using
Scutellariae Radix (huang qin) as an accompaniment to
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang).
englishReference.combinations:
>WrTH CINNAMOMI RAMULUS (gul zhi)
Both of these herbs are acrid and warm, and both enter
the greater yang channel. The combination is used when
pathogenic cold has attacked and lodged in the exterior,
especially in winter. Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) travels
best at the protective level; it strongly disperses cold by
promoting sweating. Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi) moves
best at the nutritive level, where it warms the channels and
releases the muscle layer, but its sweat-inducing action
is much less than that of Ephedrae Herba (ma huang).
The diaphoretic effect of Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) is
enhanced by the addition of Cinnamomi Ramulus (gut
zhi), and the latter can lead a pathogen lodged at the nutritive level out to the exterior, where it is dispersed.
When using this combination, caution must be exer.
cised to prevent excessive sweating, which could injure the
qi and fluids. However, one must be equally careful not to
induce less sweating than needed, since this will have no
effect. Generally, pathogenic cold lodged in the exterior
requires only a mild sweat to release it, but the intensity of
the sweating required depends upon an evaluation of the
strength of the patient and the strength of the pathogen.
A strong patient with a strong wind-cold pathogen
requires Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) at twice the dose
of Cinnamomi Ramulus (gui zhi), as in Major Bluegreen
Dragon Decoction (da qing long tang). If the dose is equal,
or there is only slightly more Ephedrae Herba (ma huang),
there will be a moderate sweating effect. More Cinnamomi
Ramulus (gui zhi) than Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) induces only a slight sweat, which is often useful in treating older
or weaker patients, who may also benefit from combining
these herbs in lower dosages, as in Two-parts Cinnamon
Twig Decoction and One-part Ephedra Decoction (gul zhi
er ma huang tang).
>WITH ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
Both herbs enter the Lung channel and excel at alleviating
cough and calming wheezing. However, their mechanisms
of action differ. Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) disseminates
and facilitates the flow of Lung qi, while Armeniacae
Semen (xing ren) primarily drains and directs the Lung qi
downward. Because these various actions exactly match
the Lung's own movements in disseminating and moving
downward, this pair can restore normal Lung function and
so is frequently found in ancient formulas. For example,
in Records of Thoughtful Differentiation of Materia Medica,
Zhou Yan offers this explanation:
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) is known as the 'right hand
of Ephedrae Herba (md hudng). Ephedrae Herba (ma

1 1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
huang) unbinds the muscle layer, while Armeniacae Semen
(xing ren) opens the collaterals of the Lungs. Ephedrae
Herba (md huarig) is hard by nature, while Armeniacae
Semen (xing ren) is soft. Ephedrae Herba (md huang)
spreads externally, while Armeniacae Semen (xing ren)
directs downward internally. When the two are combined.
the pathogen is completely eliminated.
As this passage suggests, regardless of whether a pattern is
hot or cold, this combination is still useful, with the appropriate additions. What is more, because Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang) and Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) also release
the exterior, the pair is strong enough to use as a two-herb
formula when a wind-cold exterior pattern is causing
cough, sensations of fullness in the chest, and wheezing.
> WITH REHMANNIAE RADIX PREPARATA (shu di huang)
This combination benefits the Kidneys while calming
wheezing. It is most suitable when the Kidney qi is not
secure and cannot accept qi, which manifests as chronic
wheezing characterized by difficult inhalation with prolonged exhalation. The patient is often emaciated and
fatigued. The Lungs control the qi, while the Kidneys
are its root. Thus, if the Kidneys are weak and have difficulty accepting inhaled qi, the qi will not remain stable
at the deeper levels (below the navel) but instead will rebel
upward with wheezing. Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu
di huang) nourishes the true yin, generates essence, blood,
and primal qi, thus enhancing the Kidney's ability to accept
the inhaled qi. Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) helps the Lungs
redirect the qi downward instead of accumulating in the
upper body, and so settles the wheezing.
Together these herbs also warm and unblock the channels and collaterals. Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu di
huang) is tranquil and nourishing, while Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang) is mobilizing: it can enter deeply into accumulated phlegm and blood stagnation. This is an illustration of
the adage "tranquility requires movement for motivation."
This combination can be used in the treatment of cold from
defiency in the nutritive level blood, where cold, congealed
phlegm has stagnated and caused deep-rooted toxic sores
without a head, as in Yang-Heartening Decoction (yang
he tang).
>WITH GINSENG RADIX (ren shen)
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) has a strong dispersing action,
possibly too strong for those with externally-contracted
wind-cold who also have weak primal qi or temporary
qi deficiency due to overwork. Ginseng Radix (ren shen)
restores the primal qi so that the dispersing action of
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) will be able to dispel the
pathogen without inducing profuse or continuous sweating. Ginseng Radix (ren shen) is the most fitting of the qi.
supplementing herbs to prescribe with Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang). Astragali Radix (huang qi) is less suitable, for
although it also tonifies the primal qi, it tends to secure the
exterior and work against the action of Ephedrae Herba
(ma huang). Codonopsis Radix (dang shen) tonifies the
Spleen qi rather than the primal qi, and would therefore
also not be the best choice.
One occasionally hears the statement that "tonifying
herbs should not be used with exterior patterns" for fear of
strengthening the pathogen. In Precepts for Physicians, Yu
Chang discusses this at length. He concludes that this is a
problem only if there is no existing deficiency, as there is
then nowhere for the tonification to be received other than
by the pathogen. However, if there is significant deficiency,
tonification is indicated and there is no impediment to its
Use:
There are situations of cold damage where Ginseng Radix
(ren shen) should be included in the prescription: the primal qi will then flourish and the external pathogen will be
carried outward by its power. If the person's primal qi is
weak, even though the [force of the] herbs themselves move
toward the exterior, the qi remains passively ini the middle
In mild cases, a pathogen will be half expelled, leaving half
to remain and cause difficulties; a severe pathogen will follow the primal qi as it withdraws inward, causing endless
fevers. Thus, weak deficient people must have Ginseng
Radix (ren shen) in with their exterior [releasing] herbs: it
makes the herbs powerful so that, with a single gush, the
pathogen is thrust out. This is definitely not a matter of
tonification'.
>WITH GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Both are acrid, dispersing and enter the Lungs, but Ephedrae
Herba (md hudng) is warm and works on the exterior while
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is very cold and works more
deeply at the muscle layer and interior. Together they act
strongly to disseminate the Lung qi, cool the heat, and calm
the wheezing, and are particularly appropriate for exterior
pathogens which have moved internally, transformed into
heat, and clogged the Lungs. This pattern presents with
such symptoms as prolonged fever, cough, and wheezing.
This pair of herbs is the basis for the formula Ephedra,
Apricot Kernel, Gypsum, and Licorice Decoction (ma xing
shi gan tang)
Beyond this, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) can lead
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) to the interior while moderating its sweat-inducing effect; the Gypsum fibrosum (shi
gao) itself clears heat which is trapped within pathogenic
water and dampness. The pair is thus highly effective in
treating wind-edema. However, the dosage of Ephedrae
Herba (ma huang) must be greater than normal in this case,
between 10 to 15g, in order to move fluids, while the dosage

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
of Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is somewhat smaller than
normal, 20-30g being sufficient.
> WITH GINKGO SEMEN (bai guo); see page 892
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Its nature is light, lifting, and very dispersing, and is most
rapid at releasing the exterior ... excessive sweating devas.
tates yang and can endanger a person's life--be on guard!
From the end of spring through summer until the beginning of autumn, the,standard approach is to forbid it; only
in the winter when symptoms appear,showing that a truly
cold pathogen has injured the nutritive [level], is it of ben
efit. If not during the winter months, or the symptoms are
not those of a cold pathogen,or are those of a cold pathogen in the interior, or those of pathogenic wind injuring the
protective [level], then Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) is not
suitable, even though there may be fever and chills: there
will not be aching and stiffness of the head and body, and
no floating and tightness in the six pulse positions.
When the condition is right for sweating, it must not be
excessive. Sweat is the fiuid of the Heart,excessive sweating
will agitate the Heart blood, or cause great loss of yang, or
cause bleeding--and this then becomes a major affliction.
(Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)
englishReference.toxicity:
This herb contains central nervous system stimulants and
may cause high blood pressure, restlessness, and insomnia
It should be used with caution in treating patients with high
blood pressure. Do not use in conjunction with cardiac gly
cosides, as cardiac arrhythmias may occur. Allergic reac
tions in the form of cutaneous eruptions combined with
slightly elevated temperature and measles-like erythema
have been reported. Because ephedrine stimulates the
sphincter muscle of the bladder, long-term administration
may cause oliguria or anuresis.
The toxic dose is approximately 30-45g. Symptoms
of acute toxic reaction include palpitations, insomnia,
restlessness, diaphoresis, chest pain, elevated temperature
and tremor. Extreme overdoses can lead to blurred vision,
dilated pupils, coma, dyspnea, dysuria, convulsions, respiratory arrest, cardiac failure, bradycardia, and ventricular
fibrillation.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "hemp yellow"
>CLEANED EPHEDRA (M#jing ma huang)
This has the nodes on the stalks removed, as well as the
roots, as both are generally considered to reduce the herb's
diaphoretic effect. The nodes. can be left if the herb is not
to be used to induce sweating. For example, the formula Three-Unbinding Decoction (san ao tang) specifically
calls for Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) without the nodes
removed, since the desired effect is to disseminate the Lung
qi and calm wheezing, rather than sweating.
>EPHEDRA CoTTON(##ma huang rong)
Cleaned ephedra is brought to a boil until it rolls over'
in the water ten times, or simply infused in boiling water
until froth rises; it is then removed and dried. Once dried,
it is ground until the fibers become soft. It is then called
ephedra cotton.
Usually, when cleaned ephedra is used to promote
sweating, the patient first boils it, then removes the froth.
as it can cause agitation. Ephedra cotton saves this trouble.
The diaphoretic effect, however, is slightly less than cleaned
ephedra, while stronger than prepared ephedra.
>PREPARED EPHEDRA(#zhi mahuang)
Cleaned ephedra is stir-fried with water. This method of
preparation reduces the herb's diaphoretic action, but
strengthens its effect in calming the Lungs. Discussion
of Cold Damage says to remove the froth after boiling
According to Materia Medica of Combinations, this is
because the froth "makes one irritable"; however, "frying
with honey before use will also work."
> HONEY-PREPARED EPHEDRA
(mi zhi mahuang)
Honey is first brought to a boil slowly, and the froth and
any residual wax or extraneous material scraped from the
surface. The honey is then poured through a filter. It is
returned to the wok, and again brought to a boil, which is
maintained at 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles and
the honey no longer stretches between the fingers.
Boiling water is then added to thin the honey, which is
then poured slowly over cleaned ephedra and left covered
briefly. The amount of cooked honey should be approximately one-fifth the amount of herb, while the amount of
water should be approximately one-third the quantity of
honey; too much water and the herb will become overly
damp and difficult to dry after preparation. The herb is
then dry-fried at a low temperature until deep yellow and
no longer sticky to the touch.
When ephedra is prepared with honey, the diaphoresis
is modified by the sweetness of the honey. Not only is the
intensity of its acrid, dispersing qualities moderated, but
the duration of its action is lengthened in a kind of timerelease' manner. Sweetness pertains to the earth phase and
thus brings harmony. Honey preparation also moistens
the Lungs and protects this tender Organ from the drying
effects of the acrid, warm qualities of the unprepared herb

englishReference.actions:
- Disperses wind and clears heat: for externally-contracted
wind-heat, especially when the major complaint is headache or eye pain.

62 1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
- With Tribuli Fructus (ci ji li) for headache and dizziness
due to wind-heat.; Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) and Cicadae
Periostracum (chan tut) are often added.
- Clears and benefits the head and eyes: for Liver channel
wind-heat manifesting as excessive tearing, red, painful, or
swollen eyes, or spots in front of the eyes.
With Ginseng Radix (ren shen) and Astragali Radix
(huang qi) for eye disease, tinnitus, dizziness, and deafness
due to deficiency.
Drains dampness and expels wind: as an auxiliary herb for
wind-dampness in the limbs causing stiffness, numbness,
cramping, or heaviness.
- With Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng), Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao), and Chaenomelis Fructus (mi
gua) for pain and spasms of the extremities due to winddampness.
--With Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo)
Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo), and Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) for superficial wind-dampness with a
heavy and painfui head and generalized heaviness, as in
Notopterygium Decoction to Overcome Dampness (qiang

englishReference.commentary:
Viticis Fructus (man jing zi) is slightly cold with a clear,
acrid, and light floating nature. It moves upward and disperses. It is best at raising and dispersing wind-heat in the
face and head, e.g., in cases of externally-contracted wind.
heat leading to headache, dizziness, red eyes, or swollen,
painful gums and teeth. It also has a certain ability to expel
wind-dampness, enabling it to unblock and facilitate the
movement of the joints.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica describes the
varied indications of this herb:
[Although] Viticis Fructus (man jing zi) is regarded as a
herb for wind disorders of the face and head,our ancient
forebears used it to unblock the nine orifices and facilitate
the joints, brighten the eyes and firm up the teeth, expelling
wind-cold and wind-heat. ... Thus it is now used for damp
painful obstruction, cold bulging disorder, or leg qi. It is
used in decoction or powders--- the results are always reli.
able, and not limited to the face and head!
Zhou Yan, however, disagreed. In Records of Thoughtful
Differentiation of Materia Medica, he used Viticis Fructus
(man jing zi) to illustrate the difficulties in truly under
standing the nature of a herb:
Viticis Fructus (man jing zi), according to the Miscellaneous
Records of Famous Physicians, mainly treats wind headaches
and ringing in the brain, and its results are indeed quite
often remarkable. However, all regard Viticis Fructus (man
jing zi) as an acrid, cold herb; they do not know that its
bitter warmth is greater than its acrid cold. In the Divine
Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica it says that its
fiavor is bitter and slightly cold-the word "slightly" is used
deliberately. Miscellaneous Records amended this to acrid,
neutral, and warm, which is closer to the whole picture. But
here we should look closely at the significance of this. ..-
Viticis Fructus (man jing zi) grows in the water margins,
the fruit is black and mottled: it is most appropriate for
entering the Kidneys. Furthermore, its nature is acrid and
cold as well as bitter and warm, which similarly imitates the
greater yang's quality of qi transformation: based in cold,
but manifesting as heat, able to go from yin out to yang.
and using yang to transform yin.
Viticis Fructus (man jing zi) is light and empty so that
it rises upward, and despite the statement in the Divine
Husbandman that it can treat painful obstruction and
spasms from cold, heat, and dampness in the sinews and
bones by transforming dampness so as to unblock the
obstruction, in the final analysis, Viticis Fructus (man jing
zi) simply does not have the fortitude to take on this duty
of searching out and expelling. This is why very few ancient
formulas use it for this purpose.
Only wind headaches and tinnitus are really its specialty.
When it is ineffective, this is because people have not investigated carefully.
On reflection, I have come to realize that the scarcity of
those who thoroughly understand Viticis Fructus (man
jing zi) is not a new phenomenon. Xu Zhi-Cai stated that it
disperses yang brightness channel wind-heat--surprisingly
viewing it as no different than Menthae haplocalycis Herba
(bo he) or Arctii Fructus (niu bang zi). Zhang Yuan-Su
called it yin within yang, when actually it is yang within yin,
stating that it cools the blood in all channels, when actually
it is a qi herb, not a blood herb at all! The only ones with
true knowledge of it were Li Shi-Zhen, who said it mainly
treats wind from deficiency of the head and face, and Zhang
Lu [in Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia
Medica] who said that it was forbidden for blood deficiency
with fire-but even here,the reasons behind these state
ments were not clarified.
What difficulties there are in clearly understanding the
materia medica!

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
This is a fragrant oleo-gum resin from East Africa and
Arabia. If well-cleaned of extraneous material, with amberlike transparency, it is called bright myrrh (# ming
mo yao) or clean myrrh (# # jing mo yao). Because historically it has been imported and is expensive, adulterants
and substitutes are not unknown, and the term true myrrh
(# zhen mo yao) reflects this.
Unprepared myrrh (% # sheng mo yao) is generally
used externally or in pill form, as it has a tendency to irritate the stomach and cause nausea. In pill form, it is usually
prepared with either rice paste or honey, both of which act
as buffers. In addition, pills dissolve slowly and therefore
have less impact than does a decoction. Prepared myrrh is
preferred for use in decoctions and internal powders.
PREPARED MYRRHzhimOyao
Clean myrrh is dry-fried at a medium temperature until it
starts to smoke and melt. It is then sprayed with rice vinegar, while still stirring and frying, until the surface appears
oily and glistening. It is then quickly removed from the wok
and spread out to cool. This is also known as vinegar myrrh
cumo yao.
This method of preparation reduces its disagreeable
effects on the digestion and improves its taste. It also
strengthens its ability to invigorate the blood, stop pain,
restrain and inhibit, and generate flesh. It is easier to pulVerize.

also possess blood-invigorating properties which prevent

frequently used pair for cooling the blood and dispersing

warm pathogen diseases entering the nutritive and blood

its strong pain-reducing and stasis-clearing actions, this

nels. In abandonment of qi, [Chaenomelis Fructus (mu
gua)] can restrain; in stagnation of qi, it can harmonize."
Chaenomelis Fructus (mu gua) is specifically indicated for the abdominal cramps associated with sudden
turmoil disorder, or gastroenteritis, but is also very effective for muscular cramps of the leg, which can result from
blood deficiency, or cold invasion leading to contraction.
Regardless of the causative factor, the pathological mechanism which brings about cramping always involves the
deprivation of nourishment to the muscles and sinews.
Chaenomelis Fructus (mu gua) is sour and warm, regulates
the Spleen and Stomach, alleviates vomiting and diarrhea,
and thereby prevents further loss of qi and fluids. The sour
flavor itself mobilizes the sinews and relaxes cramping
spasms.
Extension of the Materia Medica offers the following
explanation:
Chaenomelis Fructus (mu gua) obtains the normal qi of
wood, thus it enters the sinews. This substance enters the
Liver, thus it augments the sinews and blood. For disorders
of the lower back and Kidneys, when the feet and knees
have no strength, this herb cannot be omitted.
However, in his Grand Materia Medica, Li Shi-Zhen reject.
ed this explanation:
Chaenomelis Fructus (mu gua) primarily treats sudden
turmoil disorder with vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, and leg
qi: All of these are disorders of the Spleen and Stomach, not
the Liver. Although the Liver governs the sinews, cramps
result from pathogenic damp-heat or cold-dampness
harming the Spleen and Stomach,which is why cramps
always start in the calves. The calves pertain to yang bright.
ness,and the [mechanism of] treatment of cramps with
Chaenomelis Fructus (mu gua) is not by augmenting the
sinews, but by regulating the Spleen and hewing the Liver
Earth in disorder [causes]weakness of metal and prepon
derance of wood. Thus,the use of sour warmth restrains
the depleted dispersal of the Spleen and Lungs, while it
mobilizes the sinews, so that pathogenic wood is calmed.
This is draining wood from within earth in order to assist
metal. When wood is calmed, earth regains command and
metal is shielded.

>Vs.PAEONIAE RADIX ALBA (bai shao)
Both herbs treat disorders of the sinews, and are commonly used together in the treatment of cramping and
spasms of the muscles and sinews. However, Chaenomelis
Fructus (mu gua) focuses on transforming dampness to
relax the sinews, which is why it is primarily associated
with conditions in which dampness predominates, such as
sudden turmoil disorder, or damp painful obstruction with
restricted movement of the joints. Paeoniae Radix alba (bai
shao), on the other hand, nourishes the blood, preserves
the yin, and softens the Liver to relax the sinews, and is thus
more often used for spasms, cramping, and pain resulting
from malnourishment of the muscles and sinews due to yin
and blood insufficiency.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ALISMATIs RHIZOMA (ze xie)
An ancient adage says toUse Akebiae Caulis(mu tong)
for sovereign fire, use Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) for
ministerial fire. Although similar in facilitating the water
[pathways], their usage is different in each case." The
"sovereign fire" here refers to Heart fire, and "ministerial
fire" to Kidney fire. Thus, while both herbs promote flow
in the fluid pathways and are commonly used together in
the treatment of internal stoppage of water and dampness
due to obstruction in the smooth flow of fluids, there are
differences between them. Akebiae Caulis (mu tong) clears
fire from the Heart and Small Intestine channels,while also
unblocking the flow of qi and blood. By contrast, Alismatis
Rhizoma (ze xie) clears ministerial fire in the Kidney chan.
nel.
>Vs.SUCCINUM (hu pd)
Li Gao observed: "Akebiae Caulis (mu tong) mobilizes
downward, draining fire from the Small Intestine, and
promoting urination: the same effects as Succinum (hu po).
There are no other herbs that can compare." Both of these
are excellent medicinals for clearing the congestion of fire
in the Small Intestine channel, which causes rough urination and blood in the urine. Both of them also clear fire
from the Heart channel. However, when Akebiae Caulis
(mu tong) clears Heart fire, it is primarily used for such
symptoms as ulcers of the mouth and tongue, red eyes, and
irritability. By contrast, Succinum (hu po) clears the Heart
and settles fright, and is mainly used for such symptoms as
spasms and seizures due to heat from constraint, and also
palpitations, insomnia, and disturbing dreams.
Both substances also dredge and unblock the blood
vessels, and can be used for amenorrhea due to blood stasis. Akebiae Caulis (mu tong), however, is able to promote
lactation, and treats damp-heat painful obstruction, while
Succinum (hu po) addresses hematoma due to trauma as
well as sores and toxic swellings. While the two substances
have an unusual number of corresponding actions, their
unique qualities should be taken into account.

distention.
disorders and diarrhea, especially when accompanied by

: Strengthens the Spleen and prevents stagnation: used with

useful when the transformative and transportive functions

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, and warm, with a strong, rich aroma, Auc.
klandiae Radix (mu xiang) enters the Spleen, Stomach, and
Large Intestine channels. It is best at promoting the flow of
qi in the Stomach and Intestines to reduce distention and
alleviate pain, and also strengthening the Spleen and reducing food stagnation. Thus its primary indications include
poor digestion, loss of appetite, abdominal distention, and
diarrhea. It can be used for dysenteric disorders due tc
damp-heat if combined with cooling herbs. It is also helpful
when combined with tonifying herbs, as it can assist diges
tion and prevent obstruction due to greasiness.
The aroma of Aucklandiae Radix (mit xiding) can unblock
the flow of qi, harmonize the five organs, and is an important herb for regulating all of the qi. When it treats focal

9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
distention, stifling sensation in the chest, belching, edema,
abdominal distention, or leg qi, all of this is the effect of
regulating obstruction and dispersing qi. (Transforming the
Significance of Medicinal Substances)
The Grand Materia Medica is even more explicit:
Aucklandiae Radix (mu xiang) is a herb of the Triple
Burner qi level, raising and directing downward all of the
qi. All pent-up constrained qi pertains to the Lungs [says
Basic Questions], thus the reason for using it for upper
burner qi stagnation is to drain metal constraint. All lack
of transport of the middle qi pertains to the Spleen, thus it
is appropriate for middle burner qi stagnation because the
Stomach enjoys fragrant aromas. When the qi of the Large
Intestine is obstructed there is tenesmus; when the qi of the
Bladder does not transform there is urinary blockage or
painful urinary dribbling; when the qi of the Liver is constrained there is pain--thus the reason for using it for lower
burner qi blockage is to unblock that which is plugged.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ARECAE SEMEN (bing lang)
Both herbs promote the flow of qi, but Aucklandiae Radix
(mu xiang) warms the middle to promote transportation and dries dampness, while Arecae Semen (bing lang
reduces accumulation and guides out stagnation, and.can
kill parasites.
Combining these two herbs not only enhances their
ability to promote the flow of qi and stop pain, but also
guides out obstruction, reduces distention, dries damp.
ness, and kills parasites. Thus it is often used in the treatment of qi blockage in the Stomach and Intestines due
to food stagnation, leading to abdominal distention and
fullness, loss of appetite, aversion to the smell of food,
nausea but inability to vomit, and an uncomfortable urge
to move the bowels which is often unsuccessful. Intestinal
parasites can lead to a pressing pain around the umbilicus,
and intermittent focal distention in the abdomen, for which
this combination is often used. Finally, the two herbs are
combined to relieve tenesmus, and the passage of mucus,
in dysenteric disorders.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.CYPERI RHIZOMA (xiang fu)
Both herbs are bitter and acrid, both promote the flow of
qi and stop pain, and more importantly, both enter the
Triple Burner channel. The difference is that Aucklandiae
Radix (mu xiang) particularly mobilizes clumped qi in the
Stomach and Intestine channels and reduces food stag
nation; it is thus specifically indicated for epigastric fullness, abdominal distention, and diarrhea. Cyperi Rhizoma
(xiang fu), by contrast, dredges and disperses qi stagnation
531
in the Stomach and Liver, and is especially good at relieving
constrained Liver qi, regulating menstruation, and stopping pain; it is specifically indicated for emotional constraint, distending pain of the ribs and flanks, and irregular
menstruation.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Aromatic, drying, and tending toward yang, it is contrain.
dicated for those with Lung deficiency and heat, or parched
blood dryness. It is also forbidden in all cases of swelling
and pain involving fire, and primal qi loss or yin deficiency with internal heat. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia
Medica)
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "wood fragrance"
This herb was originally grown in India and the Middle
East. It is now an endangered plant species in India, and
a ban was imposed by CITES on its international trade.
However, the species has been widely cultivated in Yunnan
province over the last half-century, and it is this cultivated
product from China that is now used. It is also known as
Yunnan mu xiang( yun mu xiang). Trade is permit
ted for the cultivated product. In its unprepared form, it is
known as unprepared Aucklandiae Radix (mu xiang) (#
sheng mu xiang.The Grand Materia Medica says
that "Whenever used as a qi-regulating herb, it should be
unprepared; when used to firm the Intestines, it should be
baked in flour and taken prepared."
>BAKED AUCKLANDIA( wei mu xiang)
Slices of the herb are covered with rough absorbent paper.
upon which is placed another layer of herb slices covered
with paper, and so on until several layers have been built
up. These are placed next to a stove or in a drying room
until a portion of the volatile oil in the herb has been
absorbed by the paper. The slices can also be baked in a
flour bag, with the same effect. The flour is then sifted out.

532 9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
This is occasionally known as prepared aucklandia (
zhi mu xiang). Some places simply dry-fry the slices with
bran until yellowed but not scorched; this is known as dry.
fried aucklandia (k chao mu xiang).
These methods of preparation reduce the oil content
and the acrid, dispersing quality of the herb, and endow it
with a drying, inhibiting action that makes it most appropriate for awakening the Spleen and stopping diarrhea, or
for those with Spleen yin deficiency who may otherwise
require the use of Aucklandiae Radix (mu xiang). It still
mildly promotes qi movement.
>BLUE-GREEN mu xiang(# qing mu xiang)
This term now refers exclusively to the dried root of
Aristolochia debelis. or A. contorta, although it original.
ly referred to Aucklandia lappa. Because of their toxic
properties, both should be carefully differentiated from

englishReference.additionalProductInformation:
Two products can be distinguished. One is the imported product,
called Guangdong aucklandiaguang mu xiangas it
comes into China via Guangdong province. This can be further
subdivided into the product from India and Syria, which is known
as old mountain aucklandia ( lao shan mu xiang), and
that from Burma, Thailand, and Laos, which is known as new
mountain aucklandia (#ru xin shan mu xiang). The other type
was originally introduced to cultivation in China in Yunnan province
and is called Yun[nan] aucklandia (# yun mu xiang), even
though it is also cultivated elsewhere.
Traditionally,the imported old mountain aucklandia was regarded
as the best quality, followed by new mountain aucklandia.
However, because the plant is now listed as an endangered spe
cies in those areas, it is no longer imported to China. Today the
best quality comes from the oldest cultivation areas in Lijiang.
Yunnan province. The products of Hunan, Sichuan, and Gansu are
less oily and therefore of inferior quality.
Aucklandia lappa is listed under Appendix I1-of the Convention on
International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora
(CITES), which requires a permit both for export fromChina and
import to other countries, and may therefore be difficult to obtain.

> VARIANT NOMENCLATURE
As a very broadly distributed plant, its leaves and root were
common fodder for cattle, and it was thus known as cattle
vegetable (niu cai) or cattle burdock (niu bang)
Because cattle are strong, its seeds became known as great
power seeds (K h -7 da li zi). The seed pods are prickly
and tend to stick annoyingly to clothing-and even to rats
fur-thus noxious fruit ( # e shi) and rat-adhering seed
(##-7shu nian zi) are other nicknames that are quite
common in ancient texts, especially the latter.
>DRY-FRIED ARCTIUM (k} 4#7 chao niu bang zi)
Fry until popping and yellow. It has an appetizing aroma
that emerges upon grinding. Frying tends to somewhat
reduce its cold, slippery properties so that it does not
injure the middle burner yang qi, for example, in elderly or
weaker patients.
>PROCESSED ARCTIUM(#7 zhi niu bang zi) or
COOKED ARCTIUM (# 4# 7- shu niu bang zi)
Both names are commonly used when this herb is fried or
steamed with wine; the process borrows the rising action of
the wine. Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia
Medica observes: "Wine-frying raises it, enabling it to roam
all twelve channels, expel wind from the skin, and eliminate
toxic rashes."

>DRY-FRIED ACHYRANTHES(kchao niu xi)
The sliced herb is dry-fried until it swells. This method of
preparation eliminates the slippery, downward-draining
problem associated with unprepared achyranthes, and
enhances its ability to tonify the Liver and Kidneys.
>SALT-FRIED ACHYRANTHES (% yan chao niu xi)
The sliced herb is soaked in a mixture of water and table
salt, set aside briefly to absorb the mixture, then dry-fried
until dry. This has the effect of guiding the herb directly
into the Kidney channel to tonify the Kidneys and nourish
the sinews and bones. It is often used for lower backache
and leg atrophy due to Kidney deficiency and exhaustion
of essence.
>WINE-FRIED ACHYRANTHES (ji niu xi)
The herb is mixed with yellow rice wine, left covered briefly
to absorb the mixture, then dry-fried until dry. It can also
be dry-fried in bran that has been soaked in wine. This
method exploits the acrid-dispersing quality of the wine to
enhance the herb's ability to invigorate the blood, unblock
the collaterals, stop pain, and unblock menstruation, and
is thus used to treat disorders such as mobile and fixed
abdominal masses, difficult labor, and retained placenta.
>CHARRED ACHYRANTHEs(niu xi tan)
The herb is placed in the wok with a small amount of wine
and water, then dry-fried until the surface is scorched and
the interior is dark yellow. This is often used to treat fire
from deficiency blazing upward to cause such disorders as
bleeding gums, toothache, and nosebleed.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, astringent, and neutral, Nelumbinis Nodus rhizomatis (ou jie) enters the Lung, Stomach, and Liver channels.
It restrains and inhibits and stops the overflow of blood
while at the same time reducing stasis and generating new
blood. It is this movement in the midst of its ability to
stop bleeding, and its neutral nature, that make it useful
in the treatment of a wide variety of bleeding. It is not very
strong, however, and generally plays an adjunctive role in
prescriptions to stop bleeding of all types. The Detailed
Materia Medica says that "the nodes are astringent in flavor
and neutral. Pounded into juice and consumed, it stops all
bleeding."
"[Nelumbinis Nodus rhizomatis (ou jie)] can stop
coughing of blood, expectoration of blood, bloody painful
urinary dribbling, blood-in the urine [without pain], bleeding in dysenteric disorder, and continuous vaginal bleeding." (Grand Materia Medica)
Petiolus (zong lu pi) is bitter and astringent and is thus
more strongly binding and restraining than Nelumbinis
Nodus rhizomatis (ou jie). It is used primarily for bleeding that is not associated with blood stasis, and it also
dries dampness, which makes it appropriate for the treatment of vaginal discharge. By contrast, Nelumbinis Nodus
rhizomatis (ou jie) is sweet and astringent. It both stops
bleeding and reduces blood stasis; when fresh, it also cools
blood heat.

likewise be used to direct turbid pathogens downward and
out of the Stomach in cases of continuous vomiting due to
externally-contracted damp-warmth or other contagious
toxins.
The Grand Materia Medica describes the main thera
peutic action of this herb:

6 / Herbs that Transform Phlegm and Stop Coughing
Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye), in treating Lung and
Stomach disorders, is generally used for its ability to direct
rebellious qi downward. When qi is driven downward, fire
will then descend and phlegm is smoothly [eliminated].
Thius, rebelliousness is curbed, nausea is quelled, thirst is
quenched, and the cough is alleviated.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH MoRI FoLIUM (sang ye)
Lung metal normally controls Liver wood, but if the Lungs
are weak or the Liver overbearing, the situation can be
reversed. This is particularly likely when cosmic factors
favor the growing and ascending yang energy of wood, as
occurs during the spring. This ascending wood energy all
too easily upsets the descending metal energy of the Lungs,
causing the Lung qi to tend upward instead of downward,
leading to cough and other symptoms.
This pair of herbs provides an excellent basis to redress
the balance. Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) is bitter, cooling, and enters the Lung and Stomach channels. Best at
descending, it cools the Lung heat to transform phlegm
and stop the cough, and can also cool Stomach heat and
stop nausea. Mori Folium (sang ye) is light, ascending
cooling and moistening, sweet, bitter, and cold; it can thus
disperse wind-heat, but also cool and drain both the Lungs
and the Liver. While both of these herbs are cooling, Mori
Folium (sang ye) gently ascends and thus smooths the flow
of Liver qi, while its bitterness drains away pathogenic heat
Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) descends and thereby soothes
the Lungs and helps direct its rebellious qi downward.
Just these actions would be sufficient to harmonize
the two organs, yet there is a further subtlety based on the
relationships among the five phases: wood controls earth
but earth produces metal, which in turn controls wood.
The ability of Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) to harmonize
Stomach earth will in turn allow greater nourishment to be
supplied to the Lungs, effectively tonifying metal and helping restore its normal function of controlling wood.
> WITH BLETILLAE RHIZOMA (bai ji); see page 587
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.CYNANCHI STAUNTONII RHIZOMA (bai qian)
Both herbs are good for directing rebellious Lung qi
downward. Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye), however, is
cooling and moistening and thus best for dry cough or
phlegm which is hard to expectorate. By contrast, Cynanchi
stauntonii Rhizoma (bai qian) is warming and parching
and is thus best for externally-contracted pathogenic qi
which has bound up the Lungs, causing sensations of fullness in the chest and the sound of phlegm in the throat
47
Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) also stops nausea, which
Cynanchi stauntonii Rhizoma (bai qian) does not do.
>Vs.PINELLIAE RHIZOMA PREPARATUM (zhi ban xia)
Both herbs treat Lung and Stomach conditions, but their
nature is different: Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) cools
the Lungs to stop coughs and transform phlegm and is
thus used for phlegm-heat and cough from dryness in the
Lungs. The effect of Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zh
ban xia) on the Lungs is in fact mediated via the Spleen,
transforming dampness and phlegm, and is thus better for
cough with profuse sputum from phlegm-dampness.
The ability of Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) to treat the
Stomach derives from its cooling of Stomach heat, preventing the Stomach qi from being carried upward by excessive
yang activity. The action of Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum
(zhi ban xia) is different in that it transforms dampness
and phlegm so that Stomach qi is free to properly descend,
thereby preventing nausea.
To summarize their differences, Eriobotryae Folium (pi
pa ye) is cool and moistening, while Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) is warm and parching; Eriobotryae
Folium (pi pa ye) mainly brings down the heat in the Lung
and Stomach channels, while Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) mainly parches dampness and transforms
phlegm. Together, moist and dry are both represented,
cold and heat balance each other, and the effect of directing
qi downward is considerably enhanced. Furthermore, the
moistening action of Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) allows
phlegm to be more easily moved by Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia).
The combination of Eriobotryae Folium (pi pa ye) and
Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) is frequently
used for cough and wheezing, but the marked efficacy of
the pair in alleviating nausea and calming the Stomach is
often ignored.

or cough due to wind-cold." These conditions can still be
treated with this herb, however, if the leaves are prepared
with ginger, and other appropriate herbs are added.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, acrid, and neutral, Typhae Pollen (pu huang) enters
the blood aspect of the Liver, Heart, and Spleen channels.
Because it is sweet, and neither warming nor cooling, it
harmoniously removes blood stasis and stops bleeding,
while also promoting urination. It is one of the herbs that
stops bleeding without leaving foci for subsequent blood
stasis. It is particularly good in the treatment of hematuria,
and is also widely used for bleeding from the nose, mouth,
intestines, and uterus. It can also be applied topically. It can
be used for pain from blood stasis, for example, in cases of
thoracic painful obstruction, and postpartuim obstruction.
The Grand Materia Medica says that it "Stops all pain in the
Heart and abdomen.
The Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica observes that it is "Sweet, neutral, governs cold and
heat in the Heart, abdomen, and Bladder, facilitates uri
nation, stops bleeding, and eliminates stagnant blood."
With respect to the aforementioned "cold and heat,"
563
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica
explains that the nutritive and protective qi is unable to
circulate in the places where blood clumps, and this causes
sensations of heat and cold due to disharmony in the nutri.
tive and protective qi. Typhae Pollen (pu huang) disperses
this clumping, thus restoring harmony and eliminating the
sensations of cold and heat.
Since at least the Song dynasty this herb has been
regarded as slippery in its unprepared form, and astringent when dry-fried. Thus the unprepared herb is used for
breaking up blood stasis, reducing swelling, and promoting urination, while the dry-fried herb is used for stopping
bleeding. This is echoed in Materia Medica Arranged by
Channel: "Used unprepared, its nature is slippery, promoting blood movement and eliminating stasis; if fried black,
its nature is astringent and stops bleeding." However,
recent pharmacological and clinical research has cast some
doubt on these views, and currently the herb is generally
used in its unprepared form.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica ob.
serves:
If there are disorders such as ulcers of the mouth and
tongue or itching damp skin.diseases, apply the fine powder of the unprepared herb and the disorders will be cured.
This utilizes its fine, sticky, congealing [properties], which
naturally have the power to generate flesh,as well as its
clearing and cooling properties.

>WITH CIRSII HERBA (xiao ji)
Both herbs stop bleeding, but also promote urination, and
Cirsii Herba (xiao ji) cools heat in the blood. The combina.
tion is therefore particularly effective for bloody urine in
painful urinary dribbling due to heat in the blood.

englishReference.commentary:
The bitter nature of Peucedani Radix (qian hu) facilitates
the downward direction of qi, while its acrid flavor helps

6 / Herbs that Transform Phlegm and Stop Coughing
it spread and disseminate. Thus, while it drains Lung heat
by eliminating phlegm and directing qi downward, it also
expels externally-contracted pathogens by assisting in the
spreading of the Lung qi. It is therefore most appropriate
in treating the cough, headache, and constrained Lung
heat that results from externally-contracted pathogenic
wind-heat, or the cough and wheezing with thick sputum
that results from Lung qi failing to properly descend.
When these two co-exist--thick phlegm and externallycontracted heat--Peucedani Radix (qian hu) is especially
indicated. Many texts warn, however, that it should not be
used for externally-contracted disorders in the absence of
phlegm accumulation.
The Grand Materia Medica s observes:
The merit of Peucedani Radix (qian hu) lies primarily in
directing qi downward, for when qi descends then fire will
descend, and phlegm will also descend. Peucedani Radix
(qian hu) can be credited with driving out the old to bring
forth the new, and is a valued herb for the treatment of qi
and phlegm.
The expression "driving out the old to bring forth the new"
in descriptions of this herb appears in many textbooks of
materia medica. It refers to the restoration of normal qi
that results when obstructing phlegm is eliminated. There
is also a somewhat greater emphasis in the ancient literature, compared to more recent textbooks, on its ability to
disperse epigastric clumped qi and enhance digestive function, for example, in the treatment of childhood nutritional
impairment. Several works also mention that it enters the
Liver and Gall Bladder; Essentials of the Materia Medica
goes so far as to say that "Wind-phlegm in the Liver and
Gall Bladder channels cannot be expelled without [the use
of] Peucedani Radix (qian hu).
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH BUPLEURI RADIX (chai hu)
Both herbs dispel wind and relieve the stifling sensation
and distention in the chest and epigastric area. Separately,
Peucedani Radix (qian hu) transforms phlegm and reestablishes the normal downward flow of Lung qi; it is therefore
used for the more obvious symptoms of cough associated
with externally-contracted disorders. Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu) releases constraint, and is very lightweight; it ascends.
lifts, and disperses, draining heat and dredging the exte
rior. Together, Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) lifts and releases
the constraint, while Peucedani Radix (qian hu) directs qi
downward; one rises while the other descends. These paired actions regulate the ascending and descending aspects of
the qi dynamic. In this way the Lung qi is disseminated and
the wind-heat dispelled much more effectively than if only
herbs to direct Lung qi downward were used.
3
The ability of this combination to dispel the pathogen
while stopping the cough accounts for its common usage
when wind-heat constrains the Lungs, leading to a stifling
sensation in the chest and a productive cough. So frequent.
ly are the two herbs prescribed together that sometimes
just the words "two hu" (=-* er hu) are written on the
prescription.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
Both herbs enter the Lung channel and cause rebellious
Lung qi to properly descend. Peucedani Radix (qian hu)
is cool, drains away Lung heat, and expels wind-heat; it
is better for treating sticky, yellow phlegm. By contrast.
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) is warm and dispels wind
cold while alleviating wheezing in cases of copious white
phlegm.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
According to some traditional sources, this herb counteracts Veratri nigri Radix et Rhizoma (li lu).
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Med.
ica notes that the herb is indicated for "wind-phlegm with
excess qi; it is forbidden for phlegm which is disturbed
by fire from yin deficiency, or for patients with audible
phlegm that does not result from an externally-contracted
disorder."
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "before barbarians"
While the herb's present name qian hu, means
"before barbarians," according to some sources it was
originally written with a similar looking character,
jian, which means "wash," as in "wash away filth or evil
practices." This probably relates to its ability to scour away
phlegm and reduce fullness. The character # hu most
likely relates to its origin outside the central part of China.

: Strengthens the Spleen and stops diarrhea: for chronic
diarrhea caused by weakness in the transportative func.
tion of the Spleen (internal accumulation of dampness)
Especially useful in children.
-With Nelumbinis Semen (lian zi), Poria (fu ling), and
Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu) for chronic
diarrhea due to Spleen deficiency.
-With Lablab Semen album (bian dou), Dioscoreae Rhi

Stabilizes the Kidneys and secures the essence: for Kidney
