englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, astringent, and neutral, Euryales Semen (qian shi)
tonifies and restrains the Spleen and Kidneys, while eliminating dampness. Thus it is particularly effective for vaginal
discharge due to Spleen and Kidney deficiency. It secures
the essence to treat spermatorrhea, stops chronic diarrhea.
and contains urinary incontinence due to loss of Bladder
control. Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica describes
the therapeutic scope of this herb:
How can Euryales Semen (qian shi) tonify the Spleen? It is
due to its sweet flavor. How can it stabilize the Kidneys? Its
astringency. It is only its sweet tonification of the Spleen
that enables it to facilitate [removal of] dampness, thus
treating diarrhea and abdominal pain; it is only its astringent stabilization of the Kidneys that enables it to close up
[the Kidney and Bladder] qi, so that leaking vaginal discharge and dribbling urine are both cured.
The Grand Materia Medica says that it "alleviates thirst,
augments the Kidneys, treats urinary incontinence, spermatorrhea, cloudy urine, and vaginal discharge."
In New Compilation of Materia Medica, Chen Shi-Duo
says that it
may appear unremarkable, but it is highly beneficial. Most
herbs that tonify the Kidneys are moist, and thus inevitably
contribute somewhat to the dampness. Euryales Semen
(qian shf) tonifies the middle and eliminates dampness, but
its nature is not drying, so it can expel pathogenic water

884 13 / Herbs that Stabilize and Bind
while tonifying the true water. If it is used with other yin
tonifying herbs, it notably assists in the supplementation of
essence, without any fear of increasing the dampness.
The northern Song poet, administrator, and polymath Su
Shi (also known as Su from the Eastern Slope, or #
Su Dong-Po), who was no mean physician in his own
right, developed an elegantly simple combination of diet
therapy and qi gong that he claimed contributed to his own
longevity and continued effectiyeness into old age. This
prescription was noted in his Jottings from the Eastern Slope
and involves boiling 10-20 seeds of Euryales Semen (qian
shi), after which they are slowly and finely chewed, one by
One. If done every day, he says, "this is sufficient to circulate
the water of the upper pool, so that those who eat Euryales
Semen (qian shi can make the essential fluids (# hua
ye) flow unceasingly."

Some may ask why I extol this common substance wher
there is nothing exotic about it-for augmenting the

Even if the patient has lost essence to the point of emaciated exhaustion, within ten days the spermatorrhea will have
stopped and the spirit will be flourishing! The most moderate of herbs actually have the most remarkable effects-but

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.NELUMBINIS SEMEN (lian zi)
Both herbs are seeds that tonify and bind, with sweet, neutral, and astringent properties, and both enter the Spleen
and Kidney channels to tonify those organs and to treat
chronic diarrhea and spermatorrhea. However, Euryales
Semen (qian shi) can also eliminate dampness, which
Nelumbinis Semen (lian zi) does not do, and is therefore
better at treating deficiency disorders in which dampness predominates, such as vaginal discharge, for which
Nelumbinis Semen (lidn zi) is less capable. By contrast,
Nelumbinis Semen (lian zi) nourishes the Heart, reestablishes harmonious communication between the Heart and
Kidneys, and treats incessant uterine bleeding, none of
which is within the therapeutic scope of Euryales Semen
(aian shi).

>DRY-FRIED EURYALE SEEDS (kchao qian shi
The cleaned seeds are dry-fried at a moderate heat until
slightly yellow. While the unprepared seeds tonify, restrain.
and eliminate dampness, and are neutral in nature, when
dry-fried they become warming. Rectification of the Mean
ing of Materia Medica says that "Unprepared, it is sweet
and neutral; dry-fried it is warm." Dry-frying also enhances
its ability to tonify the Spleen and Kidneys, to stabilize.
and to conserve. It is most appropriate for treatment of
spermatorrhea due to failure of the gate of essence to close.
which results from Kidney deficiency.
>BRAN-FRIED EURYALE SEEDS (#k}X#fu chao qian shi)
Bran is heated until it begins to smoke slightly, then cleaned
euryale seeds are added and dry-fried until slightly yellow.

The bran is then sifted out. This method of preparation also
changes its nature to warm, and enhances the herb's ability

Essentials of the Materia Medica observes that Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang hu6) is most appropriate for
Governing vessel disorders involving muscular tetany (

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH SAPOSHNIKOVIAE RADIX (fang feng)
Saposhnikoviae Radix (fang feng) has a thin qi and an
ascending nature and is neither harsh nor drying. It is very
effective for dispelling wind. Notopterygii Rhizoma seu
Radix (qiang hu6) is very drying and effective in dispersing
exterior cold, with its focus on the upper and more super
ficial aspects of the body. Combining these greater yang

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
wind herbs provides a synergistic effect and is particularly
helpful in dispelling wind, dispersing cold, and overcoming
dampness to stop pain, as in externally-contracted wind
dampness. In addition, because both herbs ascend and
disperse by nature, when used in a very small dosage, their
combination can raise sunken middle qi.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ANGELICAE PUBESCENTIS RADIX (du huo)
In ancient times, Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang
huo) and Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo) were not
differentiated. In fact, a passage in Divine Husbandman's
Classic of Materia Medica refers to one as just a different
name for the other: "du huo, also named qiang huo."
The actions of these two herbs are indeed similar: both
expel wind-dampness, eliminate painful obstruction, and
alleviate pain. However, Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix
(qiang huo) has a clear, strong aroma which travels best
at the qi level, which makes it better for treating the more
yang or superficial aspects of the body. It is also warmer
and more drying than Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du
huo), which has a heavier aroma and more moderate
warmth, travels more slowly, and more readily enters the
blood level. Because this herb tends to move downward,
it is better for lower limb and lower back wind-dampness
which has penetrated deeper into the body.
This combination is thus able to treat wind-dampness
at any level, above or below, and is better at relieving pain
than is either herb by itself.
Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica makes the
following comparison: "Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix
(qiang huo) is more purple, masculine, and harsh in nature,
and better able to regulate wandering wind; Angelicae
pubescentis Radix (du huo) is more yellow, moderate, and
better able to regulate lurking wind."
>Vs.LIGUSTICI RHIZOMA (gao ben)
Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix's (qiang huo) powerful
aroma rises to expel ambulatory wind in the muscles and
exterior. It is best for neck and shoulder pain, but also
for freeing the joints by venting pathogens from between
the sinews and bones. Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix
(qiang huo) and Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) both enter the
Governing vessel, but Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix's
(qiang huo) tendency to move upward is stronger; while
Ligustici Rhizoma (gao ben) can reach the vertex, it is better than Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) for
treating lower body disorders. Notopterygii Rhizoma seu
Radix's (qiang huo) ability to enter the Liver and Kidney
channels refers primarily to its effect at the sinew (Liver)
and bone (Kidney) levels of the joints.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Both Notopterygii Rhizoma seu Radix (qiang huo) and
Angelicae pubescentis Radix (du huo) are wind herbs,
important for expelling wind, dispersing cold, and elimi21
nating dampness. Both, however, are forbidden for internal
injury causing blood-deficient headache and generalized
pain, resulting in chills and hot flushes, because these wind
herbs can dry the blood. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia
Medica)

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, and slightly cold (rated neutral' in some
sources), Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) enters
the Spleen and Liver channels. Acridity disperses and bitterness drains; Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao)
therefore dispels wind and drains dampness from these
channels, unblocking the flow of nutrients to the sinews
and muscles, and thereby eliminating painful obstruction
disorder. It also treats damp-heat jaundice. By eliminating yang brightness dampness, the pathogenic heat has no
material impediment to its dispersal. In this way, it halts the
process that leads to steaming bones and tidal fevers.
Although it is a wind-expelling herb--which are usually drying-its bitterness does not dry excessively, and its
nature is relatively harmonious. This has given rise to the
adage, "All wind herbs are drying, but only Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) tends to be moistening." In this
context, "moistening really means less drying, such that
when it dispels wind and dampness, it does not severely
damage the yin or fluids. It can therefore be used in the
treatment of steaming bones, heat from consumption, heat
during pregnancy, and the constrained heat involved in
childhood nutritional impairment.
englishReference.combinations:
> WiITH TRIONYCIS CARAPAX (bie jia)

heat, while dispersing nodules.
Together these herbs are very effective in venting muscle-layer heat, and cooling tidal fevers associated with consumption, in the treatment of which this pair is fundamental. They are especially appropriate for wind-consumption,
which involves wind attacking those with severely weakened constitutions who are unable to prevent the wind
from invading deep within the body. Because wind is
yang in nature, it readily transforms into heat, which dries
the yin and blood. Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin
jiao) expels the wind toward the exterior, while Trionycis
Carapax (bie jia) augments the essence and blood, and
nourishes the yin fluids. By eliminating the pathogen, the

englishReference.comparisons:
Vs.CLEMATIDIs RADIX (wei ling xian)
Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) and Clematidis
Radix (wei ling xian) both treat pain and limited move
ment due to wind-dampness, especially in the lower body
Yet Clematidis Radix (wei ling xian) is warm and highly
mobilizing, and is thus best suited for painful obstruction
disorder with pronounced pathogenic cold causing marked
pain and limitation of movement, or even paralysis. By
contrast, Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) tends to
be cooling, and its primary action is to expel dampness. It
is therefore best suited for wind-dampness with a tendency
toward heat; the greater the dampness, the more appropriate is the use of this herb.
Beyond these differences, Clematidis Radix (wei ling
xian) also softens hardness, and can thus be used to reduce
clumping, or even fish bones stuck in the throat. Gentianae
macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) can also be used for steaming
bones due to exhaustion, as well as damp-heat jaundice.
> Vs.GENTIANAE RADIX (l6ng dan cao)
Both herbs are species of Gentiana. They both eliminate
dampness and reduce heat, and are used for damp-heat
jaundice. However, Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin
jiao) expels wind and dampness, but is not overly drying.
It is mainly used in the treatment of wind-damp painful
obstruction and steaming bone disorder with tidal fever. By
contrast, Gentianae Radix (long dan cao) is very bitter and
very cold. It primarily drains fire from excess in the Liver
channel, lower burner damp-heat, or Liver fire leading to
red eyes, vertigo, and tinnitus; cramps and spasms due to
Liver heat disturbing wind; or vaginal swelling and itching
due to damp-heat lodged in the lower burner.

Detailed Materia Medica provides this description
Fraxini Cortex (qin pi): Its effect in the treatment of the
eyes and childhood convulsions is derived from its ability
to calm the Liver; its effect in the treatment of dysenteric
disorders, irregular uterine bleeding, and vaginal discharge
is derived from its ability to restrain and inhibit; its ability
to benefit the [sperm-] essence is derived from its bind
ing and tonification. Dysenteric disorders make the lower
burner deficient, thus the bitterness of Fraxini Cortex
(qin pi) can be used to fortify. It should be used sparingly
for patients with cold from deficiency of the Spleen and
Stomach.
Zhang Bing-Cheng, however, disagrees with this assessment:
Because its nature is cold, it specifically clears Liver and
Gallbladder damp-fire. Every single one of its main indications is caused by Liver and Gallbladder damp-fire. As for
its ability to benefit the [sperm-] essence, this too is a result
of [its ability to] expel pathogenic heat. The essence natu
rally benefits [from this].
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PULSATILLAE RADIX (bai t6u weng)
Pulsatillae Radix (bai tou weng) enters the blood level,
while Fraxini Cortex (qin pi) enters the qi level. Pulsatillae
Radix (bai tou weng) eliminates heat toxin, cools the blood,
and stops dysenteric disorder, while Fraxini Cortex (qin
pi) cools the Large Intestine, dries dampness, and likewise
stops dysenteric disorder. Thus, one herb treats the blood,

148 2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
the other treats the qi, and together they are very good for
cooling heat toxin and drying dampness, which is a good
match for hot-type red-and-white dysenteric disorders.
Red-and-white dysenteric disorders refers to the expulsion of pus and blood in the stool. This was described as
early as the seventh century in Discussion of the Origins of
the Symptoms of Disease:
Cold and heat intermingle, thus red and white are mixed
together; when severe it appears like thick nasal mucus with
mixed blood, when mild the mucus only has streaks of thin
blood, like a fatty brain.
This disease is usually the result of damp-heat obstruction
blocking the Stomach and Intestines, affecting both the
blood and qi levels. The treatment is to cool heat and transform dampness, regulate the qi, and move the blood. This
pair of herbs is prominently featured in a formula which
does just that: Pulsatilla Decoction (bai tou weng tang)

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
>CHARRED FRAXINUS(qin pi tan)
The herb is dry-fried or baked with high heat until blackened but not completely turned to ash. This moderates its
cold nature while enhancing its ability to enter the blood
level to restrain and inhibit bleeding and alleviate dysenteric disorder. In fact, this method of preparation invests
Fraxini Cortex (qin pi) with a restraining and inhibiting
property which in its unprepared form exists only as a
potential. Thus, it is often used for passage of mucus, pus,
and blood in the stool in dysenteric disorders; it can also be
used for Intestinal wind and irregular uterine bleeding.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, cold, and aromatic, Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing
hao) enters the Liver and Gallbladder channels. While its
bitterness and coldness clear heat, its aroma vents and
disperses; it is thus ideal for clearing Liver and Gallbladder
heat, and cooling heat in the blood. It vents heat in the yin
level outward, bringing the pathogen from the yin level out
to the yang level.
This herb is often used for summerheat with low fever,
headache, dizziness, and a stifling sensation in the chest!
fevers due to yin or blood deficiency, especially those that
worsen at night, and malarial disorders with alternating
chills and fevers. It can also cool the blood to treat purpuric
rashes, and stop bleeding such as nosebleeds
Furthermore, its aroma is mild in effect, and its bitter
coldness does not harm the Stomach nor injure the yir
and blood; it is therefore particularly appropriate for heat
disorders in patients with blood deficiency.
The New Compilation of Materia Medica notes that
Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao) specifically resolves
steaming bones and consumptive heat, and is outstanding
for draining the fire of summerheat---but in so draining
it does not exhaust the qi or blood. Thus, it is particularly
indicated for yin deficient patients who have externally.
contracted pathogens.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica elaborates:
Its clear aroma seeps through the forehead, and therefore
brightens the eyes and also disperses wind-heat--it does
not only work through its bitter-coldness, clearing and
directing downward! Its sprout appears very early [in the
spring] so that it receives the qi of spring that commands
raising and bringing forth, and thus it enters both the Liver
and the Gallbladder channels to clear heat from the blood.
The reason that it can treat heat remaining within the bones
and joints is that it enters deeply into the blood and dredges
constrained fire outward. Its present use for resolving sum.
merheat during the hottest days of the season relies on its
bitter coldness to clear heat, as well as its beautifully aromatic and chilling qi, which enables it to awaken the Spleen
and Stomach, and regulate damp-heat. When Encountering
the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica observes that]
it can facilitate the water pathways in a manner that is not
dissimilar to Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen), that is
correct.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH TRIONYCIS CARAPAX (bie jia)
Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao) is cold by nature, and
bitter with an aroma that clears heat, vents the collaterals,
and leads fire from within the bones out to the exterior
Ievel of the muscles and flesh. Trionycis Carapax (bie jia)
is salty and cold, and excels at tonifying the water of the
deepest yin.
While the properties of these two herbs are different, they nicely complement each other. With Trionycis
Carapax (bie jia), Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao)
is directed deep into the yin levels where it can rout the
pathogens from the depths; Trionycis Carapax (bie jia)
then replenishes the yin that was hitherto ravaged by the
pathogenic influence. This can occur in the final stages of
a warm pathogen disease when the yin fluids have already
been damaged, and the pathogen still lurks deep within
the yin level. This manifests in such symptoms as night
fever with chills in the morning, the fever receding without
sweating, emaciation, rapid pulse, and a red tongue with
little coating.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.BUPLEURI RADIX (chai hu)
Both herbs enter the Liver and Gallbladder channels, and
both treat malarial disorders and alternating chills and
fevers. The differences are that the nature of Bupleuri
Radix (chai hu) is raising and dispersing, which is excellent for spreading Liver qi constraint and raising the clear
yang. However, overuse of Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) tends
to injure the yin. Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao), by
contrst, has a light, clearing, cooling aroma that is excellent
for resolving summerheat without injuring the yin. Thus,
it is often used for fever from yin injured by warm and
summerheat pathogens, or for steaming bones due to yin
deficiency or consumptive heat.

and abdominal distention and pain.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica describes
the herb as follows:
Bitter in flavor, slightly sour; the fullness of its flavor [indi
cates that it] sinks. Yang within yin. Its bitterness expels
obstruction, sourness enters the Liver as well as the lesser
yang: Triple Burner and Gallbladder organs. It reduces
firm lumps, dispels pain in the hypochondrium, relieves
constraint and anger, treats bulging disorders, dredges the
Liver, breaks up stagnant qi, and expands the chest.
In Essentials of the Materia Medica, after quoting the
statement that Citri reticulatae viride Pericarpium (qing
pi) dredges the Liver and drains the Lungs, Wang Ao
makes an interesting observation: "Bupleuri Radix (chai
hu) dredges upper burner Liver qi, and Citri reticulatae
viride Pericarpium (qing pt) calms lower burner Liver qi;
any herb that drains qi is said to drain the Lungs."
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH BUPLEURI RADIX (chai hu)
Both herbs dredge Liver qi, but Bupleuri Radix (chai hu)
is light in weight with a very mild flavor, and thus relieves
constraint in the upper burner. Citri reticulatae viride
Pericarpium (qing pi) has a strong flavor and nature, and its
bitterness makes it drain downward, thus dredging Liver qi
in the lower burner. Together, the ascent and descent of the
qi dynamic is restored, the qi circulation between the upper
515
and lower burners resumes, and the clumping is thereby
dispersed. In cases of long-term Liver qi stagnation which
eventually involves blood stasis, where the pain is fixed in
location with occasional palpable lumps (e.g., in the breasts
or in bulging disorders), this combination is appropriate
as a foundation upon which herbs to invigorate the blood
or soften areas of hardness can be added. However, the
combination must be used with caution in cases of blood
deficiency.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. CITRI RETICULATAE PERICARPIUM (chen pi)
Originating from the same fruit but at different stages
of development, it wasn't until the eleventh century that
these two medicinals were differentiated. They are very
similar in nature but the action of Citri reticulatae viride
Pericarpium (qing pi) is more fierce. It primarily enters the
Liver and Gallbladder channels to break up qi stagnation,
reduce accumulation, and transform obstruction. By contrast, Citri reticulatae Pericarpium (chen pi) is more moderate in nature, promoting qi movement, strengthening
the Spleen, drying dampness, and transforming phlegm
The immature Citri reticulatae viride Pericarpium (qing pi)
possesses the just-ripening energy characteristic of spring
time wood, and so relates to the Liver, while the mature
Citri reticulatae Pericarpium (chen pi) has the harmonious
nature of earth, and so relates to the Spleen. Essentials of the
Materia Medica observes:
Citri reticulatae Pericarpium (chen pi) raises and foats,
entering the Spleen and Lungs, and treats what is high
above; Citri reticulatae viride Pericarpium (qing pi) sinks
and directs downward, entering the Liver and Gallbladder.
and treats what is low.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Straight Direction from [Yang] Ren-Zhai warns that this
herb "cannot be used for those with sweating." The Grand
Materia Medica elaborates: "[For] reducing accumulation
in children, usually Citri reticulatae viride Pericarpium
(qing pi) is used, which very readily induces sweating:
[therefore] it cannot be used for those who are [already]
sweating." Essentials of the Materia Medica explains it from
another standpoint: "Peels can reach the skin, acrid flavors
excel at discharging and dispersing."
Hidden Aspects of Materia Medica concludes that, for
the "aged, weak, deficient, or emaciated, the best is total
abstinence [from this herb]."
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "green peel"

516 9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
Generally cultivated, the small (1-2cm), immature fruit
is picked in early summer, or collected if already fallen,
cleaned of extraneous material, washed, and dried in the
sun. These are known as small unripe tangerine peels (l
#& xido qing pi) or fine unripe tangerine peels (m # & xi
qing pi) and are usually regarded as superior in quality. The
fruit may be whole or sliced in half. Some prefer fruit that
is all the same small size, and thus call for uniform unripe
tangerine peels jun qing pi
When, in late summer, the larger but as yet immature
fruit with green peels are chosen, they are soaked briefly in]
boiling water, then cut into quarters without completely
severing the peel. The flesh and rind are removed, and the
peels dried in the sun. These are called four-flowers unripe
tangerine peels ( t & si hua qing pi). If the peels are
separated, they are called unripe tangerine peel slices (#
&H qing pi pian).
>DRY-FRIED UNRIPE TANGERINE PEEL
(k#& chao qing pi)
The peel is dry-fried, sometimes with bran, over moderate heat until slightly scorched yellow. This method of
preparation moderates its fierce nature, especially if bran is
used, enhancing its ability to harmonize the Stomach. It is
particularly appropriate for treating distention and pain in
the chest and flanks, poor appetite, and abdominal fullness
due to Liver and Stomach disharmony.
> VINEGAR-FRIED UNRIPE TANGERINE PEEL
cu chao qing pi
The slices are left to soak briefly in rice vinegar until some
has been absorbed, then dry-fried over moderate heat until
deep yellow. This is also known simply as vinegar unripe
tangerine peel (# # & cu qing pi). Dry-frying with vinegar
directs the actions of the herb specifically into the Liver
channel, and enhances its ability to dredge and break up
constrained Liver qi.
Essentials of the Materia Medica points out that "dry.
fried with vinegar, this is [in line with] the classical adage,
The Liver desires dispersal, quickly consume acrid to
disperse it, use sour to drain it, and use bitter to direct it
downward."
> WINE-FRIED UNRIPE TANGERINE PEEL
(#jiu chao qing pi
Soaked in yellow rice wine, the slices are then dry-fried
until deep yellow. This is also known simply as wine unripe
tangerine peel ( # jiu qing pi). Preparing with wine
enhances its acrid-dispersing qualities. This method of
preparation is thus often used in combination with herbs
that promote the flow of qi and blood in the treatment of
such disorders as abdominal masses.
>CHARRED UNRIPE TANGERINE PEEL(##qingpi tan)
The slices are dry-fried using high heat until scorched
and blackened, quickly sprayed with water to cool, then
removed and dried in the sun. After this procedure its
ability to break up qi is weakened, but it can still reduce
food stagnation, transform obstruction, and harmonize
the Stomach. Thus it can be used in the treatment of accumulated food stagnation causing epigastric distention and
belching. It is often used in combination with other herbs
that relieve food stagnation.

englishReference.commentary:
Salty, acrid, neutral, and toxic, Scorpio (quan xie) has a
piercing, opening nature that enters the Liver channel to
strongly extinguish internal wind, halt spasms, unblock the
collaterals, track down externally-contracted wind lodged
internally, and stop pain. The Grand Materia Medica
explains:
Scorpions come from the east, are green in color, and pertain to wood: a medicinal of the leg terminal yin channel.
They therefore treat disorders of the terminal yin: all wind
vertigo and dizziness, cramping, spasms, chills and fever in
malarial disorder, poor hearing and deafness--all of these
are terminal yin wind wood [conditions].
985
As an important wind-extinguishing substance, Scorpio
(quan xie) is used in the treatment of seizures, spasms,
convulsions, wind-stroke, facial paralysis, muscular tetany,
tremors of the hands and feet, twitching, and torticollis. However, it is also effective for wind-damp painful
obstruction, headache, and migraines. Consistent with the
theory of "using toxin to attack toxins," it is also applied
externally to treat scrofula, toxic sores, and mumps.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica states that it
specifically enters the Liver channel to expel wind. It is
used in all cases of children's fetal wind convulsions, adult
hemiplegia, paralysis of the face and mouth, impaired
speech, spasms of the hands and feet, chills and fever due
to malarial disorders, tinnitus, and vaginal discharge, when
these are due to external wind lodging internally.
The contemporary physician Xiao Xi-Fang describes his
experience with this substance:
Animal medicinals can be used in the treatment of stub.
born headaches according to the dictum 'early [stage]
disorders are in the channels, long-term pain enters the col
laterals.' They can be added to the original prescription to
unblock the collaterals and stop pain with good results. Of
these, Scorpio (quan xie) is an essential item; the scorpion
tail is especially effective. Generally, five to seven tails are
used for adults [combining as follows]: for wind-damp]
ness, add Bombyx batryticatus (bai jiang can); for cold with
dampness, add Scolopendra (wiu gong); for Liver yang and
heat constraint, add Pheretima (di long); and for severe
continuous pain, scorpion tail should be combined with
Pheretima (di long), Bombyx batryticatus (bai jiang can).
and Scolopendra (wu gong).

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH GECKO (ge jie)
Both substances are strongly tonifying in patterns of Lung
deficiency, Ginseng Radix (ren shen) affecting the Lung
qi, and Gecko (ge jie) strongly warming the Kidneys and
enhancing their ability to grasp the qi. Because Gecko (ge
jie) is an animal substance, it can have a deeper effect on
the structural aspects of the body, including the Kidney
essence. The Grand Materia Medica notes that its ability"to
tonify the Lung qi and to settle wheezing is the same as that
of Ginseng Radix (ren shen).
Patterns of deficency marked by wheezing usually
involve both the Lungs and the Kidneys, as the Lungs
govern the qi and control breathing, while the Kidneys are
the root of qi and govern the grasping of qi. When Lung qi
is deficient the breathing will lack strength, causing shortness of breath, cough, and wheezing. When the Kidneys
are deficient there is less ability to grasp the qi; inhalation
will then be weaker than exhalation, and the wheezing will
worsen with exertion.
In this combination, Ginseng Radix (ren shen) tonifies
the qi, while Gecko (ge jie) restores the Kidney's ability to
grasp the qi. In this way, metal and water are mutually supportive and the proper interaction between the Lungs and
Kidneys is restored.
> WITH REHMANNIAE RADIX PREPARATA (shu di huang)
This combines one of the strongest qi tonifying herbs with
one of the strongest blood and yin tonifying herbs, taking
advantage of the fact that when qi is sufficient, blood can
be generated, and when blood is sufficient, there is a basis
for the transformation of qi. Ginseng Radix ren shen
is yang and mobile in nature, augmenting the qi, while
Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu di huang) is yin and
quiescent in nature, augmenting the blood. Thus this combination is often used in the treatment of qi and blood or qi
and yin deficiency patterns. In Rectification of the Meaning
of Materia Medica, Zhang Jie-Bin explains:
Qi and blood are the basis of human life: qi is primarily yang and mobile, blood is primarily yin and still. Tc
tonify the qi, Ginseng Radix (ren shen) is primary, with
Astragali Radix (huang qi) and Atractylodis macrocephalae
Rhizoma (bai zhui) acting as assistants. To tonify the blood,
Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu di hudng) is primary,
with Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) and Chuanxiong
Rhizoma (chuan xiong) acting as assistants. Yet there ar
situations in which Astragali Radix (huang qi), Atractylodis
macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu),Chuanxiong Rhizoma
(chuan xiong), and Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui)
should be avoided, but Ginseng Radix (ren shen) and
Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu di huang) are compulso
ry for qi and blood [deficiency treatment]. Thus, whenever
there is yang-qi deficiency in any of the channels, one can
not do without Ginseng Radix (ren shen); whenever there
is yin-blood deficiency in any of the channels, Rehmanniae
Radix preparata (shu di huang) must be used.

Other similar forms of ginseng include forceful ginseng
(h da li shen), where the fresh roots are boiled in hot
water for a very short time and then sun-dried, and active
ginseng (A hu xing ren shen), which are freezedried fresh roots.
RED GINSENGhong shen)
These are the the fresh roots that are first steamed and later
sun-dried or dried by heating. This is warmer in nature
than white ginseng, and is used for treating patterns of qi
and yang deficiency. Most Korean ginseng is processed red
713
ginseng. It is usually considered stronger than that from
China.
>GINSENGNECKren shen lu
This is the neck of the ginseng plant, traditionally con.
sidered to be a mild emetic. It is used to induce vomiting
if there is an abundance of food stagnation and phlegm,
together with deficiency. In central and southern China,
however, this part of the plant is used as a mild tonic.
Commentators believe this may be due to differences in the
type of ginseng used.
>GINSENG LEAF(# ren shen ye)
The leaf of this plant is bitter, slightly sweet, and cold. It
clears summerheat, generates fluids, and treats heat or fire
from deficiency. It is often used in treating summerheat
with thirst, injury to the fluids due to febrile diseases,
hoarseness associated with Lung heat, insufficient Stomach
yin, and toothache due to fire from deficiency. It is also
used for alcoholic intoxication.

englishReference.commentary:
Most of the herbs named dou kou are acrid, warm
aromatic, and drying, but only Myristicae Semen (rou dou
kou) also possesses an astringent, binding quality. Note that
this binding action is only a property of the roasted variety:
unprepared nutmeg can actually cause diarrhea in addition
to a variety of other serious problems. The comments here
concern only the roasted form of the herb.
Affecting particularly the middle and lower burners,
this herb warms the Spleen and Stomach, restores smooth
circulation to the qi dynamic, and binds up the Intestines.
Grand Materia Medica says that it "warms the Spleen and
Stomach, and stabilizes the Large Intestine." It is most
often used in patterns of cold from deficiency of the Spleen
and Kidneys leading to unstable slippage in the Intestines.
with such symptoms as chronic diarrhea or dysenteric disorders. It is also used for epigastric distending pain, loss of
appetite, nausea, and vomiting due to cold from deficiency
with qi stagnation in the Stomach and Intestines. Hidden
Aspects of Materia Medica notes that, when used for dysenteric disorders, it should be taken with white rice congee.
and when used for vomiting and diarrhea, it should be
taken with fresh ginger tea.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Med.
ica observes:
Spleen earth favors fragrant aromas, so Myristicae Semen
(rou dou kou) is extremely suitable for the Spleen and
Stomach. As to its ability to drive qi downward, the reason for this is the strengthened transportation derived
from tonifying the Spleen and Stomach; it is not like the
drastic action of Magnoliae officinalis Cortex (hou po) and
Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shf).
However, in Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica.
Zhang Jie-Bin has a different explanation:
As to its stabilization of the Large Intestine, this means
that the primal qi does not run out of the Intestines, and
the Spleen qi is naturally strengthened. Thus, when it is
said that it regulates cold from deficiency of the Spleen and
Stomach, it is not actually tonifying deficiency.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH PsORALEAE FRUCTUS (bu gui zhi)
Daybreak diarrhea occurs because dawn is the time that the
yang is just beginning to emerge through the preponderant
yin, but if the Kidney yang is deficient, this emergence will
9
fail to occur: the tendency of the yin to sink and contract
gathers within and then pours downward. This manifests
as diarrhea because the Kidney yang fails to support the
Spleen yang's transportive and transformative functions,
giving rise to such accompanying symptoms as abdominal
distention and loss of appetite.
In describing the pathogenesis of this disorder, Zhang
Lu, in Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia
Medica first quotes Sun Si-Miao: "Tonifying the Kidneys is
not as good as tonifying the Spleen." Then he counters with
a passage from Xu Shu-Wei: "Tonifying the Spleen is not as
good as tonifying the Kidneys." Zhang then comments:
When the Kidney qi is weak and deficient, and the yang qi
is depleted and unable to steam the Spleen and Stomach
this causes fullness in the Spleen and reduced food intake
It is like a cooking pot without a fire underneath: [the food
can remain] all day and still not be cooked; similarly, if the
Yang qi is depleted, food and drink will remain undigested.
Myristicae Semen (rou dou kou) warms the Spleen and
Kidneys, binds up the Intestines and halts diarrhea, and
so is often combined with other herbs that warm the
Kidneys and Spleen, such as Psoraleae Fructus (bu gu zhi).
Acrid, bitter, and very warming, Psoraleae Fructus (bu
gu zhi) tonifies the yang of both the Spleen and Kidneys.
Furthermore, its astringent nature acts on the Kidneys to
secure the primal yang, while binding the Spleen to stop
diarrhea. These two herbs are the foundation pair for
the four-herb formula Four-Miracle Pill (si shen wan)
designed by Xu Shu-Wei.

>VINEGAR-PREPARED FRANKINCENSE
cu zhi ru xiang
Clean gum olibanum is dry-fried at a medium temperature
until it starts to smoke and melt; it is then sprayed with
rice vinegar, while still stirring and frying, until the surface
appears oily and glistening. It is then quickly removed from
the wok and spread out to cool. This is also known simply
as prepared frankincense (#L zhi ru xiang)

englishReference.commentary:
Mori Folium (sang ye) enters the Lung and Liver channels.
It is bitter, sweet, and cold, and light in weight to clear heat
and wind from the head and face, disperse Lung heat, and
cool exuberant Liver fire.
Overall this herb is light, cooling, and dispersing, while
also being sweet, cold, and moistening. It can disperse
wind-heat from the exterior, but this effect is rather weak;
its action is more specific to cooling and clearing the Lungs
and Liver. It is often used to treat such symptoms as headaches, fever, and cough from externally-contracted windheat, or dry cough from drying heat injuring the Lungs, as
well as sore, red, swollen eyes from wind-heat or exuberant
Liver fire.
As it cools the Liver, Mori Folium (sang ye) also cools
the blood. This action requires a dosage between 15-30g to
be effective. While commonly used for vomiting or spitting
up of blood, its gentle moistening nature makes it a fre
quent choice of gynecologists in the central coastal areas of
China as an adjunct herb to stop vaginal bleeding.
It is surprising how many of the early materia medica
texts gave scant attention to Mori Folium (sang ye), which
is completely overshadowed by the mulberry root bark.
Mori Cortex (sang bai pi). Until the seventeenth century
few texts mentioned it at all, and those that did included it
merely as a footnote to Mori Fructus (sang shen) or Mori
Cortex (sang bai pi).
In the section describing Mori Cortex (sang bai pi), the
Illustrated Classic of the Materia Medica says: "The best

56 1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
leaves are those which sprout again in the summer and
autumn, then picked after the first frost. Boil into soup and
wash the hands and feet, as it is particularly effective for
painful obstruction from wind.c
Zhu Dan-Xi, as always, favored clinical observation
over tradition. In Teachings of [Zhu] Dan-Xi, he observes:
"Green mulberry second-growth leaves, dried and powdered, mixed with thin rice water and taken on an empty
stomach, is exceptional for stopping nightsweats."
The Grand Materia Medica reiterates the indications
cited above, and adds the following: "Mori Folium (sang
ye) is an arm and leg yang brightness channel herb; if the
juice is decocted and used as a tea substitute, it can stop
Wasting and thirsting disorder."
It appears that the first major breakthrough for Mori
Folium (sang ye) came in the formula Eliminate Dryness
and Rescue the Lungs Decoction (qing zao jiu fei tang)
which was published in the book Precepts for Physicians
The author, Yu Chang, who designed this formula, stressed
the importance of Mori Folium (sang ye) in the formula:
"Mori Folium (sang ye), following the frost, obtains the
metal qi [of autumn], remaining soft and moist without
withering, so it is selected [here] as the chief herb.
Yu Chang's inspiration for this formula seems to have
come from an influential clinician and expert herbalist
Miao Xi-Yong, who lived the century before, and whose
list of favorite herbs featured Mori Folium (sang ye). In
his book, Yu Chang defended Miao against those who
criticized his techniques as "strange and generally inap
plicable":
I say it is not this way at all: there are many who suffer from
diseases of dryness in the world; Miao Xi-Yong liked to use
moistening prescriptions, and in treating dryness seems to
have single-handedly opened a new way of treatment.
Ye Tian-Shi, in Case Records as a Guide to Clinical Practice
gave Mori Folium (sang ye) considerable exposure, including it in formula after formula. He extended the "soft and
moist" approach to far more than the treatment of parched
Lungs, prescribing it for a vast array of problems including exterior patterns, stroke, abdominal swelling, diarrhea,
women's diseases, pediatric conditions, and various types
of pox. One reason seems to be that Ye Tian-Shi used
Mori Folium (sang ye) as a Liver herb; this is suggested in
Materia Medica of Combinations, where it is said to "drain
excesses of the east. Ye often combined Mori Folium.(sang
ye) with Chrysanthemi Flos (ju hua) to calm the Liver, and
with Moutan Cortex (mu dan pi) and Gardeniae Fructus
zhi zito cool and clear lesser yang constraint
From that time on, Mori Folium (sangye) was accepted
as an important part of the materia medica. It seems likely
that its rise paralleled that of the warm pathogen disease
school. It is also possible to trace its usage to the influence
of just three individuals: the idea to use it was first attributed to Miao Xi-Yong, it was then incorporated into a very
influential formula by Yu Chang, and then its scope was
further enlarged by Ye Tian-Shi.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH CHRYSANTHEMI FLOs (ju hua)
This is a commonly used pair for expelling wind and
dispersing heat. It first appeared in the late eighteenthcentury work Systematic Differentiation of Warm Pathogen
Diseases as the formula Mulberry Leaf and Chrysanthemum Decoction (sang ju yin). The two herbs both dispel
wind-heat in the exterior, and act synergistically, especially
in early stage wind-heat or warm pathogen disease patterns
with fever, headache, cough, and sore throat.
In addition, this pair is commonly used to cool and
calm the Liver when patterns of Liver channel wind-heat
or Liver fire blazing upward cause such symptoms as red,
swollen, painful eyes, and watery eyes that are sensitive to
light. It is also often used for vertigo and dizziness from
ascendant Liver yang, with reliable results.
>WITH ARMENIACAE SEMEN (xing ren)
Mori Folium (sang ye) is bitter, sweet, and cold, light, clearing, and dispersing, and is good at dispersing wind-heat
and draining Lung heat. Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) is
sweet, bitter, and slightly warm; it directs qi downward
while also moistening dryness, benefiting the Lungs, and
stopping cough. Together the lightness of both herbs will
disseminate Lung qi and disperse the pathogen, while their
softness and moistness obviates the usual concerns regarding damage to the yin fluids. Each supports the other:
one disseminates and the other directs downward, thus
regulating the ascent and descent of Lung qi. It is therefore
an excellent combination for headache, fever, and dry,
non-productive cough in warm-dryness exterior patterns,
such as those indicated for the formula Mulberry Leaf and
Apricot Kernel Decoction (sang xing tang)
> WITH GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is acrid, sweet, and cold, and
is an important herb for relieving qi level heat from excess,
specifically clearing heat from the Lungs and Stomach.
This combination--one herb of which disseminates while
the other clears-is very effective in cooling Lung/metal
dry-heat. This pairing of acrid, cold and sweet-cold allows
the heat to be cleared without injuring the fluids, which can
happen when bitter, cold herbs are used. Also, the combination disseminates the Lung qi and disperses the pathogen
without exhausting the qi. For this reason, the pair is often

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
used for dry, non-productive cough arising from drying heat injuring the Lungs, as in Eliminate Dryness and
Rescue the Lungs Decoction (qing zao jiu fei tang).
>WITH SESAMI SEMEN NIGRUM (hei zhi ma)
Sesami Semen nigrum (hei zhi ma) is sweet, neutral, and
rather cloying so that it nourishes the yin and blood, with a
strong Liver and Kidney moistening quality. Mori Folium
(sang ye) cools and calms the Liver. This combination
treats the blurry vision and dizziness associated with Liver
and Kidney yin deficiency failing to control ascendant Liver
yang. Sesami Semen nigrum (hei zhi ma) nourishes water
and wood, thus treating the root, while Mori Folium (sang
ye) cools the Liver fire and calms the Liver yang, to treat the
branch. It is particularly effective if the symptoms include
a bitter taste, red eyes, and constipation with dry stools.
This combination, with these indications, first appeared in
Precious Mirror for Advancement of Medicine, where equal
parts of frost Mori Folium (sangye) and fried Sesami Semen
nigrum (hei zhi ma) are powdered and made into pills with
glutinous rice powder, 12-15g to be taken each day.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.MoRI RAMULUS (sang zhi)
Both herbs originate from the mulberry, but their effects
are quite different. Mori Folium (sang ye) is best for dispelling wind from the exterior; it focuses on the head and
face. Mori Ramulus (sang zhi) has a pointed, thrusting-out
nature which enables it to not only cool heat and expel
wind, but also to open the collaterals and relieve pain. Mori
Ramulus (sang zhi) tends to move into the limbs and is
ideal for cooling wind-heat in the joints.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Traditionally, the old leaves collected after the first frost
are considered the most potent for dissipating wind and
cooling heat. These are called winter mulberry leaves (
#dong sang ye),frost mulberry leaves (##shuang
sang ye), or old mulberry leaves (*# # lao sang ye).
Generally, the best time for collection of winter mulberry
leaves is midway between the autumnal equinox and the
winter solstice.
Some, however, prefer the tender young leaves of
spring, called tender mulberry leaves (nen sang ye) or new
mulberry leaves (xin sang ye). It is said that they embody
the springtime qi, and thereby specifically enter the Liver
channel where they cool the Liver and brighten the eyes. It
must be said that at least as good a case could be made for
the winter leaves, since they embody the metal qi, which
should control Liver wood; and because mulberry leaves
5
also enter the Lungs, they support that organ's ability to
.direct downward as a means of controlling the ascending
Liver qi.
> HONEY-PREPARED MULBERRY LEAVES
#mi zhi sangye)
Honey is slowly brought to a boil, then the froth and any
residuai wax or extraneous material is scraped from the
surface. The honey is poured through a filter, then returned
to the wok, and again brought to a boil, maintaining the
temperature at 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles and
the honey no longer stretches between the fingers.
Next, boiling water is added to thin the honey, which
is then poured slowly over sliced sections of mulberry leaf
and left covered.briefly. The leaves are then dry-fried at a
low temperature until they become deep yellow and are
no longer sticky to the touch. This is also called honey
mulberry leaves (#mi sang ye), or prepared mulberry
leaves (&# zhi sang ye). Prepared in this manner, while
the leaves still retain the ability to dredge wind and clear
heat, their moistening action is enhanced so that they can
moisten dryness and nourish the Lungs in cases of warmdryness accosting the Lungs.

englishReference.commentary:
Amomi Fructus (sha ren) is strongly aromatic, warming.
drying, and comfortably spreading, thus it warms the

480 7 / Aromatic Herbs that Transform Dampness
Spleen and Stomach, disseminates the qi, transforms turbid
dampness, improves the appetite, stops nausea, alleviates
diarrhea, and mobilizes stagnant qi to be expelled from
the bowels. When the qi dynamic flows smoothly, and the
middle burner is harmonious, the placenta is naturally
calm. This is the rationale behind the use of this herb to
calm the fetus.
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
observes: "Its aromatic qi harmonizes the five organs, and
follows guiding herbs to unblock and mobilize all channels." The Grand Materia Medica says that it "promotes
qi movement and stops pain; when fetal qi is injured and
disturbed, the pain is unbearable." Seeking Accuracy in
the Materia Medica elaborates: "As to the statement that it
stops pain and calms the fetus ... this too is the significance
of harmonizing the middle and smoothing the flow of qi.
This herb can be used alone as a powder to regulate
the qi, calm the fetus, awaken the Spleen, and unbind the
Stomach. It is used both for restless fetus disorder as well as
diarrhea from Spleen cold.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH MAGNOLIAE OFFICINALIS CORTEX (hOu po)

Cortex (hou po) directs the qi downward, and Amomi
Fructus (sha ren) primarily unbinds the Stomach by dry
ing dampness. When used together, these actions are

englishReference.comparisons:
> Vs. AMOMI FRUCTUS ROTUNDUs (bai dou kou); see also
TsAOKo FRUCTUs (cao guo)
Both herbs have similar flavors and properties. However,
Amomi Fructus rotundus (bai dou kou) unblocks and disseminates Lung qi and has a clear, fragrant aroma that is
somewhat less drying than Amomi Fructus (sha ren). It is
therefore primarily used for phlegm-dampness obstruct
ing the Lungs with a stifling sensation in the chest, and for
mild cases of cold-dampness lurking and constrained in the
middle burner.
The aroma of Amomi Fructus (sha ren) is strong and
full. It is warmer and more drying than Amomi Fructus
rotundus (bai dou kou). Amomi Fructus (sha ren) is also
more focused on the Spleen and Stomach so that it is
usually utilized for more serious cases of congealed colddampness obstructing the middle burner. It also calms the
fetus.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet and neutral, harmonious and moderating in nature
Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao) both tonifies the qi and
nourishes the yin. Moreover, it has no cloying quality at
all, which means that it does not obstruct the digestion. It
nourishes the yin of the Lungs, Spleen, and Kidneys, and
has a mild astringent quality that stops diarrhea, secures
the essence, and inhibits urinary frequency. Not only does
Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao) directly tonify the Lungs,
Spleen, and Kidneys, it also has an indirect, cumulative
effect resulting from the gradual strengthening of metal,
which then generates earth, which in turn generates water.
Because of its mild astringent quality, which inhibits and
restrains, these gains are retained as essence and not lost
Although the herb thus has a wide range of actions, it
is most appropriate for diarrhea and poor appetite due to
Spleen and Stomach deficiency, cough and wheezing due
to Lung qi and yin deficiency, and urinary frequency or
spermatorrhea due to Kidney qi and yin deficiency. It is
also used for vaginal discharge, and for wasting and thirsting disorder.
Nevertheless, the relative strength of Dioscoreae Rhiz.
oma (shan yao) must be borne in mind. It is a commonly
consumed food as well as a medicine, which means that its
nature is particularly harmonious. And like all foods that
serve as herbs, one should not expect quick results. That
is what is meant when the Divine Husbandman's Classic

12 / Tonifying Herbs
emphasizes that long-term consumption is appropriate.
Taken over an extended period of time, the effects will
gently accumulate.
The Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica states that the herb
governs injury to the middle, tonifies deficiency, eliminates
cold and hot pathogenic qi, tonifies the middle and augments the power of qi, and increases the muscie. Long-term
consumption sharpens the hearing, brightens the eyes, and
lightens the body.
The Grand Materia Medica says that it can "augment the
Kidney qi, strengthen the Spleen and Stomach, stop diarrhea and dysenteric disorders, transform phlegm and
thick saliva, and moisten the skin." Rectification of the
Meaning of Materia Medica notes that it "strengthens the
Spleen, tonifies deficiency, enriches the essence, secures the
Kidneys, treats all deficiency, and remedies consumption
and [internal] injuries."

Literal English translation: "mountain herb
The original name for Dioscoreae Rhizoma (shan yao)
was # # shu yu, meaning potato or yam. This is still the
Chinese botanical name, but over the course of its history
this name was twice changed because of a taboo against
using a character that was found in the name of the emper
or. The first time was during the reign of the Tang Emperor
Dai Zong, whose personal name was #Yu. The herb's
name was therefore changed to # #shu yao, literally "yam
herb. However, during the Song dynasty, the Emperor
Ying Zong had the personal name # Shu, which required
that the herb's name be changed again, this time to lt
shan yao, meaning "mountain herb."
725
This herb is often called huai shan yao. Even in Chinese
grocery stores where it is sold as a "food herb" for cooking
tonic foods, it is most often labeled as hudi shan. Although
the pronunciation is the same, there are two different characters used for the first syllable of this name. One is H# hudi,
as in # L # huai shan yao, which refers to the plant from
Henan province that is big, fleshy, and powdery with a fine
texture---this is the best. The other huai is #, as in L
huai shan yao, which is from Jiangxi province, and is also
of reasonable quality.
>DRY-FRIED DIOSCOREA (&L#chao shan yao)
The sliced herb is dry-fried or baked, often with bran, until
it turns golden brown. Prepared in this manner, it more
strongly augments the Spleen, harmonizes the Stomach,
and tonifies the Kidneys to secure the essence. It is used
to stop diarrhea, loose stools, vaginal discharge, or spermatorrhea.
>EARTH-FRIED DIOSCOREA(L#tu chao shan yao)
Terra flava usta (zao xin tu) is heated in a wok, then the
sliced herb is added and fried until the surface is the color
of dirt. This method of preparation is especially good for
tonifying the Spleen and harmonizing the Stomach. It is
most often indicated for cases of weak Spleen with poor
appetite, fatigue, and diarrhea, but is equally suitable for
vaginal discharge.

englishReference.commentary:
Sour, sweet, andslightly warm, Crataegi Fructus (shan zha
awakens the Spleen, unbinds the Stomach, promotes food
intake, and assists digestion. It is particularly useful for
problems due to overindulgence in meat and greasy foods
For this purpose it can be used alone as a decoction. It stops
diarrhea and dysenteric disorders. It also enters the Liver
channel blood level to disperse stasis, invigorate the blood,
transform clumps, and reduce distention. In this way it
treats food stagnation, epigastric and abdominal distention, childhood nutritional impairment, watery diarrhea,
and dysenteric disorders. Because it invigorates the blood.
it is also used for amenorrhea, abdominal masses, blood
stasis following parturition, and prolonged lochia.
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun explained that this
herb
has the most sour flavor, is slightly sweet, and is neutral
in nature. Its skin is red and its flesh reddish yellow, thus
it excels at entering the blood level as an important herb
for transforming stagnant blood: ... Because its flavor is
sour but slightly sweet, it tonifies and assists the acid juices
within the stomach, thus it digests food accumulation and
is particularly good for digesting accumulation of meat. Its
power to transform stagnation especially eliminates blockage and stagnation within the Intestines, which is causing
the passage of blood and pus in dysenteric disorders, and it
also enters the qi level to open constrained phlegm clumps,
and treats pain in the Heart and abdominal regions. If
assisted by sweet herbs ... it transforms static blood but
does not injure newly-generated blood, and opens constrained qi but does not harm the normal qi--its nature is
especially harmonious and calm:

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
>DRY-FRIED CRATAEGUS (chao shan zha)
The fruit is dry-fried using moderate heat until the outside
turns pale yellow; if high heat is use'd, it is heated until the
outside becomes a scorched brown and the inside turns
brownish yellow. Dry-frying or scorching enhances the
ability of the herb to reduce food stagnation and guide out

8 / Herbs that Relieve Food Stagnation
obstruction, and endows it with the ability to stop diarrhea. Thus it is often used for obstruction in the Spleen and
Stomach due to overeating coupled with diarrhea.
>PREPARED CRATAEGUs(Lzhi shan zha
The fruit is mixed with honey or sugared water, then dry.
fried until no longer sticky to the touch. This method of
preparation relies on the sweetness to prevent injury to the
blood or normal qi that might otherwise occur as the herl
transforms blood stagnation and guides out obstruction.
>CARBONIZED CRATAEGUs (#shan zha tan)
The fruit is dry-fried over high heat until carbonized but
not deformed; this is also simply known as # zha tan.
Its blackness enables it to more easily enter the blood level
to transform stagnation, and also halt bleeding, and thus it
is often used for postpartum abdominal pain, prolonged
lochia, and red dysenteric disorder.

englishReference.commentary:
Sour and slightly warm in nature, Corni Fructus (shan
zhu yu) augments the Liver and Kidneys, while binding
and securing so that the benefits of this augmentation are
retained without loss. The Miscellaneous Records of Famous
Physicians says that it "Strengthens the yin, augments the
essence, quiets the five organs, brightens the eyes after
long-term consumption, strengthens vigor, and lengthens
life." Grandfather Lei's Discussion of Herb Preparation adds
that it "fortifies the primal qi. When the essential qi and
the yin are strong, the organs will naturally function at
a better level, particularly the Kidneys and Bladder. The
Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Zi says that the herb "Warms
the lower back and knees, and assists the water organ."" But
its benefit extends to other aspects of the Kidneys as well:
Discussion of Medicinal Properties says that it "Treats brain
and bone pain, halts irregular periods, tonifies the Kidney
qi, excites the way of yang [male sexual function], replenishes the essence and marrow, remedies tinnitus ... and
stops incontinence in the elderly."
This herb is not only beneficial to the Liver, it also
benefits the Heart through the Liver. Pouch of Pearls says
that it "Warms the Liver." Transforming the Significance of
Medicinal Substances elaborates:
[It] enriches the yin and augments the blood, primarily
treating blurred vision, tinnitus, bitter taste, dry throat,
greenish tinge to the complexion with loss of color, sweating followed by shaking chills--this is a fine herb for
tonifying the Liver and assisting the Gallbladder. Now, the

13 / Herbs that Stabilize and Bind
Heart is the child of the Liver. The Heart can be afflicted by
chaotic dispersal, but favors conservation and containment
when contained, it is quietly tranquil; when quiet, it is clear
and harmonious. Using [this herb] to restrain the dissipation of the Heart can treat frail, deficient Heart qi with
palpitations--this is the concept of cin deficiency, tonify the
mother.' At the same time, the Kidneys are the mother of
the Liver. The Kidneys favor moisture and abhor dryness,
and must store the essential qi. One uses the sourness of
this [herb] to conserve loss, holding in the water to generate yang fluids, and thereby treating spermatorrhea and
cloudy urine, impotence, incontinence, weak softness of the
lower back and knees, and sore aching of the feet--this is
the concept of the child making the mother strong.
According to several materia medica texts, such as Wu Pu's
Materia Medica (where the idea is attributed to Qi Bo in the
Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) and Discussion of Medicinal
Properties, this herb also has an acrid flavor that enables
it to mildly disperse. Thus,

Without further preparation this herb is called unprepared

shan yu). Traditionally, the seeds are removed, as they are
thought to cause spermatorrhea. This leaves the fruit flesh,
called shan zhu yu rouwhich is often simplified
to shan yu rou. It is also called cleaned cornus (

>WINE-PREPARED CORNUS ( L#jiu shan yu)
The fruit is mixed with yellow rice wine, then sealed in a
container which is placed in water and boiled until the wine
is absorbed. This is also known as prepared cornus(
zhi shan yu). The effect of this is to make the herb warmer,
and its flavor slightly acrid and somewhat less sour and
astringent; thus, while tonifying the Liver and Kidneys, it
also harmonizes the blood and invigorates the collaterals.
This form of preparation is often used in the treatment
of aching lower back due to Kidney weakness, or chronic
pain in the ribs due to Liver deficiency failing to nourish
the local collaterals.
>STEAMED CoRNUS(#L# zheng shan yu)
The fruit is steamed until it turns black, then dried in the
sun. Because its appearance then resembles black date
skins, it is known as date skin ($& zao pi). In its unprepared form this herb primarily stabilizes and secures, but
after steaming, it primarily tonifies the Liver and Kidneys,
while still stabilizing and retaining the essence. It is mainly
used to treat vertigo, impotence, premature ejaculation,
frequent and profuse urination, and excessive uterine
bleeding due to deficiency.

Bitter and cold, Belamcandae Rhizoma (she gan) clears heat
toxin, resolves swelling and pain of the throat, transforms
Rhizoma (she gan) directs downward, which explains its
importance in ancient formulas for treating sore throat
and painful obstruction in the throat." Rectification of the
Meaning of Materia Medica observes: "The main therapeutic effects of Belamcandae Rhizoma (she gan) may
seem to be many, but they can be subsumed under these
two: 'directs downward to unbind phlegm' and breaks up
clumps to drain heat'." Thus, Belamcandae Rhizoma (she
gan) is used for swelling and pain of the throat from either
wind-heat or phlegm-heat obstruction, and for phlegm
leading to coughing and wheezing. By cooling the heat in
the Lungs, the yang fluids of the Lungs no longer thicken,
thereby reducing the accumulation of phlegm, and facilitating its expulsion.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica suggests that Belamcandae Rhizoma (she gan) also possesses an acrid flavor, and explains its functions:
The primary indications in the Divine Husbandman are
cough and upward rebellion of qi, and painful obstruction
of the throat that does not let up. It disperses clumped qi,
rebellious qi within the abdomen, and over-consumption
of very hot food or drink. To clarify: bitterness can drive
downward and drain, acridity can disperse upward, so all
of the indications in the Divine Husbandman involve its
clump-dispersing effect--and it is indeed an important
medicinal for painful obstruction of the throat.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, such that it disperses, warm , such that it unblocks.
and fragrantly aromatic, such that it travels through and
pierces, Moschus (she xiang) mobilizes and unblocks all
of the twelve channels. While it opens the orifices, it also
unblocks channels and collaterals where there is retained
accumulation, and awakens the spirit. It serves as the chief
herb in formulas for loss of consciousness due to patterns
of wind-stroke, phlegm collapse, and high fever.

15 / Aromatic Substances that Open the Orifices
This substance is also very important in trauma medicine and external medicine. Because of its ability to invigorate the blood, reduce swelling, unblock stagnation, stop
pain, and prevent necrosis and reduce inflammation, it is
very effective in the treatment of toxic swollen sores and
abscesses, injuries from trauma, swelling and pain from
stagnant blood, mobile and fixed abdominal masses, and
amenorrhea.
The Grand Materia Medica observes:
The piercing mobility of Moschus (she xiang) unblocks
every orifice that lacks free passage, opens channels and
collaterals that are clogged; in disorders of wind, qi,blood
pain, seizures, and mobile and fixed abdominal masses
that clog and close the channels and collaterals and impair
facilitation of the orifices, there is every reason to use this as
a guide to open and unblock them.
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang
Jie-Bin explains how this substance works:
The most important aspect in the use of Moschus (she
xiang) can be found in the words copens every orifice'.
When illness involves clogging, clumping, or closure, one
should treat from the root;how else can one proceed other
than to open the clogged [area], disperse the clumping, and
unblock what is closed?
Recently, the synthetic form of this substance has been
ingested, inhaled, or applied as a plaster over the precordium and BL-15 (xin shu) for coronary artery disease.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "musk deer fragrance"
The musk deer is known as she, a word composed of the
character for deer written above the character meaning 'to
shoot out' like an arrow. This is explained in the third cen.
tury B.C. compendium, Approaching the Refined: "The fragrance of the musk deer penetrates a great distance [like an
arrow], hence the name." In fact, the character that means
to shoot out' ( she) is sometimes used as an abbreviation for musk deer, and the name for this substance is then
written as shooting fragrance'( she xiang). In a still
more abbreviated form, just the right side of the character
for shooting, cun, meaning inch, is substituted for the
character musk deer, and the shortened name is then written as inch fragrance' (- cun xiang).
Musk is a waxy, brownish substance secreted from the
navel musk gland of male musk deer that are over the age of
one year. The word musk derives from the ancient Indian
word muskah, meaning testicles, as the walnut-sized gland
is located very close to the male deer genitals. Traditionally,
it is collected by killing the deer, and collecting the pouch
or pod, known in Chinese as the aromatic sac (% # xiang
nang), which is also considered valuable. Before the musk
is removed from the sac, it is called furry sac musk (
mao ke she xiang).
Close to the autumn mating season, musk begins to
form in the deer as a yellowish secretion that fills the musk
sac; within a month it ripens into a highly aromatic, reddish brown substance. When the gland is extracted from
the animal and dried, this substance turns into darker
powdery granules, known as powdery musk (#* san
she xiang), musk kernels ((= xiang ren), or musk seeds
( xiang zi).
Since 1958, methods to remove the musk without killing the deer have been under development in China. While
the animal is anesthetized, a spatula is inserted into the
musk sac through an opening, and the musk is removed.
The musk is then sealed in an airtight container, and an
antibiotic cream is applied to the sac orifice. Approximately
18g (10g dry weight) of musk can be harvested each year
from captive deer, generally up to the age of 14 years.

948 15 / Aromatic Substances that Open the Orifices
Musk is a very valuable substance. The per-ounce price
in Europe during the past decade reached three to five
times that of gold. It is estimated that three to five musk
deer---including juveniles and females--are killed to capture a single male with approximately 25 grams of raw
musk. We therefore recommend that either musk from
farmed animals, or the synthetic product, be used. Musk
is currrently listed in CITES II. In fact, at the present time,
basically all commercially available products use synthetic
Moschus ( he cheng she xiang), which is a reddish
brown or dark brown, oily, granular powder.

Massa medicata fermentata (shen qu) is acrid, sweet, and
warm, but its acrid flavor does not overly disperse, its
sweetness does not accumulate or obstruct, and its warmth
does not dry. It is highly valued for its ability to promote
the flow of qi, regulate the middle, reduce food stagnation,
and unbind the Stomach. It is most appropriate for food
stagnation due to overconsumption of starch and grains.
leading to qi stasis with abdominal distention and diar

phlegm, warms the Stomach, and transforms thin mucus

acrid, sweet, and warm; disperses qi, regulates the middle.

and reduces stagnation. In children it tonifies the Spleen.

diarrhea and distention: "[It treats] all disorders of diarrhea, dysentery, distention, and fuliness." (Grand Materia

englishReference.combinations:

HoRDEI FRUCTUS GERMINATUS (mai ya)
Together these are known as the three immortals (=
san xian), a term used directly in prescriptions. This is a
very common combination used for food stagnation due
to overeating, which leads to qi stasis with such symptoms
as belching, epigastric and abdominal distention and discomfort, as well as diarrhea, loss of appetite, and lethargy

include this combination in many of their formulas, believing that the modern diet predisposes most patients to food

This is a nonstandardized preparation consisting of a fer
mented mixture of wheat flour, bran, and the various herbs
listed under STANDARD SPECIES above, as well as other
herbs, depending on the particular mixture that is chosen.
Because there are generally four or six herbal constituents
in the fermented mixture, the terms four-spirit cake (gs
si shen qu) or six-spirit cake ( liu shen qu) or
simply six cake ( liu qu) are often used. Note, however,
that the term four cake ( # si qu) sounds to Chinese ears
Iike "dead and gone," and is therefore not used.
Generally, the aged product is regarded as the best
quality, thus the terms aged medicated leaven
chen shen qu) or aged leaven (* chen qu) are used.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica
explains that "The effect of Massa medicata fermentata
(shen qu) is specifically to digest accumulations of grain
and wine--the best has been aged for a long time."
If there is no further preparation beyond the fermenta
tion and drying process, it is called untreated medicated
leaven (#h sheng shen qu). In many areas of China, if
this is the desired method of preparation, it must be specifically written on the prescription; otherwise, dry-fried
medicated leaven will be dispensed.

englishReference.commentary:
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) is bitter, sweet, and
cold and enters the Heart, Liver, and Kidney channels.
Its bitter coldness drains heat, while its cold, sweet, and
moistening qualities enrich the yin and moisten dryness.
Because it enters the blood level of the Heart and Liver
it can clear heat from the nutritive and blood levels, and
drain the pathogenic heat from warm pathogen diseases.
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di hudng) treats insatiable thirst,
internal heat, and hot flashes due to yin deficiency, and
also bleeding or rashes due to heat in the blood. It is often
prescribed whenever there is exhaustion of yin, deficiency
of blood, or insufficient fluids.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica describes the
nature of this herb:
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) is used as soon as it
is dug up; its nature has not undergone steaming or baking, and thus it is sweet, bitter, and very cold.... Its power
is directed at cooling heat and draining fire, cooling the
blood, and dissolving stagnation.
The rather surprising reference to "dissolving stagnation"
refers to a particular type of stagnation that is caused by
heat in the blood which dries up its fluid aspect, making
it thick and clotted. Once the heat in the blood has been
cooled and the fluids have been restored through the use
of Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di hudng), there is no longer
cause for stagnation.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica elaborates:
It is purple in its heart-core [to] unblock the Heart, yel.
low in the middle [to] enter the Spleen, and black on the

outside [to] accrue to the Kidneys. Heavy in flavor but light
in aroma, it focuses internally on cooling the blood and
enriching the yin, and externally on moistening the skin,
making it glossy and lustrous. When patients are deficient
and have heat, it should be used.

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) cools the blood, but if
the patient has weak Stomach qi it may impede digestion;
Rehmanniae Radix preparata (shu di huang) tonifies the
blood, but for those with excessive phiegm and thin mucus
it may bind up the diaphragm. It is said that after frying
Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) with wine, it will not
impede the Stomach, and that after preparing Rehmanniae
Radix preparata (shu di huang) with ginger, it will not bind
the diaphragm. In such cases, it is necessary to analyze,
in the patient, the degree of both the primal qi and the
pathogenic qi before using either [herb]. Their use should
be avoided in postpartum patients with poor appetite,
diarrhea, or abdominal pain or clumping; deficiency con.
sumption patients with weak Spleen and Stomach leading
to unformed stools, and excessive phlegm in the chest and
abdomen; and in those where there is a lack of free-flowing qi and obstruction of its ascent and descent. (Seeking
Accuracy in the Materia Medica)
This book also cautions against allowing Rehmanniae
Radix (sheng di huang) to come into contact with iron during its preparation or decoction.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:

>BIGREHMANNIA(da shengdi huang
A variety of names are used to emphasize certain desirable
qualities in this herb. The best quality is fat, big, heavy, and
oily black. The unprepared dried rhizome is not as good
as the freshly harvested rhizome in its ability to generate
fuids.
>SMALL REHMANNIA(Jt# xiao sheng di huang)
This name is derived from the thin but long rhizome
of rehmannia, which is washed, moistened, and sliced.
Because it is thin and small, resembling a root more than a
rhizome, it is often called thin rehmannia (l k xt sheng
di) or root rehmannia (# gen sheng di). Furthermore,
because it is second in quality to big rehmannia, it is also
known as secondary rehmannia (=kt ci sheng di). The
actions of small rehmannia are identical to those of the
large variety, but it is not as oily and moist, which means
that it is not as oppressive to the digestion. The Convenient
Reader of Materia Medica mentions this difference: "Thin
rehmannia is soft, thin, and harmonizes the nutritive qi;
in exterior patterns it can nourish the yin without being
cloying.

2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
>FRESH REHMANNIA(#f#Th# xian sheng di huang
or just mf th xian sheng di)
The fresh rhizome is harvested, but instead of being clean
ed, it is stored in dry mud to be dug up and used as needed
later, after washing and slicing. It can be stored like this
for up to three months. While it is usually decocted, occasionally the fresh rhizome is instead pounded to extract
the juice, which is then directly imbibed. This is the best
form for generating fluids and alleviating thirst. Even when
decocted, fresh rehmannia is better for fluid generation
than are the other forms of the herb.
The term unprepared or raw ( sheng) is sometimes
used instead of fresh (# xian) in the ancient medical lit.
erature, as in this example from Encountering the Sources
of the Classic of Materia Medica: "When the fresh root is
harvested, it becomes sheng di huang. " Present usage, how
ever, is that the term unprepared rehmannia (t # sheng
di huang) refers to the dried but otherwise unprepared rhi.
zome of rehmannia, in contrast to the newly-collected fresh
rehmannia (##th# xian sheng di huang) or prepared
rehm'annia (#h tk # shu di huang).
>WILD-CRAFTED REHMANNIA(f#+ye sheng di
huang)
Rehmanniae Radix is mostly cultivated, but sometimes
herbs collected from the wild can be found. The wild.
crafted herb is smaller, mostly cut into cylindrical pieces
that are 3-5cm long and only Icm in diameter. The taste is
slightly bitter and less sweet than the cultivated variety, but
the quality is considered to be the same.
>DRY-FRIED REHMANNIA (&#+#chdo sheng di huang)
Slices of the dried herb are dry-fried or baked until slightly
charred. This method of preparation reduces both its cooling property and its greasiness, while somewhat enhancing
its ability to nourish the blood. Note that it is much less
cooling for the blood.
>CHARRED REHMANNIA(#shengdihuang tan)
The slices of the herb are baked at moderate to high tem
perature in a covered pan until a piece of white paper
affixed to the top of the cover turns scorched black; the
slices are then removed when cool. Alternatively, the slices
of raw rehmannia can be dry-fried until carbonized, but
not destroyed. This is also known simply as + sheng
di tan. Not only is charred rehmannia still able to cool the
blood, it is more effective at stopping bleeding.
>WINE-FRIED REHMANNIA
i+h#jiu chao sheng di hudng)
The unprepared root is soaked in yellow rice wine for several hours, then it is dry-fried or baked with moderate heat
123
until the wine is completely absorbed. This method was
very popular in the past, but is rarely used now. The purpose of frying it in wine is explained in Orthodox Lineage of
Medicine: "Rehmannia fried with wine no longer harms the
Stomach." Thus, it can be used when there is concern that
the coldness of Rehmanniae Radix (sheng di huang) will
injure the yang qi of the Stomach and Spleen.
