not only bring out and disperse, but also move the yin and
yang fluids of the Spleen in order to harmonize the nutritive and protective qi.
Similarly, in formulas for tonification this pair assists the
digestion of tonifying herbs and prevents them from foster
ing damp accumulation in the middle burner. It also serves
the function of preventing phlegm in phlegm-transforming
formulas.
Interestingly, this combination finds an even more
subtle use in blood-moving formulas such as Unblock the
Orifices and Invigorate the Blood Decoction (tong qiao huo
xue tang), in which Jujubae Fructus (da zao) nourishes the
blood and prevents injury from harsh blood-moving herbs,
while the yang-unblocking action of Zingiberis Rhizoma
recens (sheng jiang) assists the movement of qi.
>WITH CITRI RETICULATAE PERICARPIUM (chen pi)
This herb is warm, acrid, and bitter. It dries dampness.
strengthens the Spleen, regulates the qi, and harmonizes the
Stomach. When the two herbs are combined, the Spleenstrengthening action of Citri reticulatae Pericarpium (cher
pi) is enhanced by the warm yang-unblocking property of
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang), while the nauseasettling action of Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang)
is enhanced by the action of Citri reticulatae Pericarpium
(chen pi) in harmonizing the Stomach. This is the basis
for the Golden Cabinet formula Tangerine Peel Decoction
(ju pt tang) which treats cold-dampness obstructing the
middle where it causes nausea and hiccough.
This pair can also be used for thin mucus blocking
the Lungs, leading to cough and wheezing with profuse
sputum.
>WITH CINNAMOMI RAMULUs (gui zhi)
This herb is acrid, sweet, and warm. It releases the muscle
layer, expels cold, warms the channels, and unblocks yang
qi. Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) is acrid and
slightly warm, with a moderate ability to induce sweating
and release the exterior. Together they have a strong sweat.
inducing effect in treating the chills, fever, body aches, and
absence of sweating that characterize externally-contracted
wind-cold.
Each herb can also move internally. Zingiberis Rhizoma
recens (sheng jiang) is best at warming the Stomach, dis.
persing cold, and driving out pathogenic water and thin
mucus, while Cinnamomi Ramulus (gut zhi) is best at using
its warmth to unblock the yang qi. Together, the ability to
warm and dispel thin mucus in the Stomach is improved,
thus alleviating the usual symptoms of nausea and hic.
cough, stomach pain, and reflux or vomiting of clear fluid
As previously noted, when the two are combined with
Jujubae Fructus (da zao), their ability to harmonize the
nutritive and protective qi is enhanced, thus driving out
the pathogen.
>WITH EPHEDRAE HERBA (ma huang)
Ephedrae Herba (ma hudng) and Zingiberis Rhizoma
recens (sheng jiang) are both acrid, warm, exterior-releasing herbs. Ephedrae Herba (ma huang) has a stronger
sweat-inducing action than Zingiberis Rhizoma recens
(sheng jiang), but this effect is markedly improved when the
two herbs are combined. Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng
jiang) also contributes a Lung-warming action to Ephedrae
Herba's (ma huang) ability to spread and disseminate the
Lung qi, as well as calming the Stomach and reducing
nausea. Thus, the pair is indicated for all externally-contracted wind-cold disorders, especially those in which the
wind-cold has constrained the Lung qi, leading to cough
and wheezing, and the failure of the Lung qi to descend has
allowed the Stomach qi to rebel upward, causing nausea
and vomiting.

The famous poet Su Shi (Su Dong-Po) was also a collector
of folk remedies, and no mean physician in his own right. In
Fine Formulas of Su and Shen, an excellent compilation of
popular medicinal prescriptions from the eleventh century
gathered by Su and the famous natural philosopher Shen

Gua, there is a deceptively simple formula for severe vomiting and diarrhea: ginger and tea leaves. Equal amounts
(about 6g) of both items are used.. They are briefly boiled
together, and the resulting tea is sipped slowly, settling the
stomach and reducing the violence of the diarrhea.
A deeper examination of the theoretical basis for this
prescription reveals a surprising sophistication: Zingiberis
Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) is acrid and warm, alleviating nausea and expelling exterior pathogens; tea leaves are
bitter, sweet, and cooling, dispersing turbid food stagnation and phlegm. So, in this remedy, acrid and bitter are
combined to disperse and drain, sweetness and warmth
replenish the middle, and coolness ensures harmony and
prevents excessive heat.
This is an excellent formula for travellers, as the ingredients are available most everywhere. It is simple to remember and use, and highly effective for symptoms of dysentery
and diarrhea from unclean foods.

>Vs.ZINGIBERIs RHIZOMA (gan jiang) and ZINGIBERIS
RHIZOMA PREPARATUM (pao jiang)
The most common phrase used to describe the actions of
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) is "mobile but
does not conserve" (#rn F zou er bu shou). The word
mobile ( zou) means that a herb has a wide spectrum of
use, and its effect is rapid; conserve ( shou) means that
it has a narrow application, but the effect is prolonged.
This and similar phrases are used to compare the different
preparations of ginger.
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) is acrid and
warm, with a mild aroma and flavor. It is used primarily to induce sweating and expel pathogenic influences. Its
effect is rapid, but does not last very long. Transforming the
Significance of Medicinal Substances therefore concludes
that Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) mainly disperses."
By contrast, Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) is acrid
and hot, with a strong aroma but a mild flavor. Its texture
is compact, and its primary action is to be internally mobile
while warming the middle and dispersing internal cold.
This effect is maintained somewhat longer than that of
fresh ginger. Xu Da-Chun says of it: "Zingiberis Rhizoma
(gan jiang) disperses and can conserve."
By further contrast, Zingiberis Rhizoma preparatum
(pao jiang) is no longer acrid, but has become bitter. Its
nature is warm and harmonious, and its primary action is
warming the middle and stopping diarrhea and bleeding
To summarize, Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (shengjiang)
is mobile but does not conserve, Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan

jiang) is mobile and does conserve, and Zingiberis Rhizoma
preparatum (pao jiang) conserves but is not mobile.

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
As early as the Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia
Medica it was noted that "long-term consumption of
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) unblocks the
clarity of the spirit." Later writers expressed their reserva
tions, however. Tao Hong-Jing, an expert in longevity, felt
that taking Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) over a
long period of time would reduce the will and intelligence,
and injure the Heart qi. In the Tang dynasty, Sun Si-Miao
noted that excessive consumption during the latter part
of summer would lead, during the following spring, to
eye problems and loss of sinew strength; it would reduce
longevity, rather than increase it. Much later, in the Qing
dynasty, the famous warm pathogen disease physician
Wang Meng-Ying noted in Food and Drink Recipes from
the Lay Buddhist Sui-Xi that "Excessive or continuous eating of Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) exhausts the
yin-fluids and damages the nutritive qi." The consensus
view now, however, is that normal people can eat ginger
frequently, but not in excessive amounts, while those who
are ill can consume whatever amount will benefit them.

>BAKED GINGER (+#wei sheng jiang or
wei jiang
Fresh ginger is wrapped in five or six layers of paper and
soaked thoroughly in water, then placed in hot ashes to
bake until the paper is scorched yellow. Alternatively, it can
be placed directly in the ashes without paper. Baked ginger
no longer has a dispersing action, but just descends without
rising; it is stronger for warming the middle and directing
rebelliousness downward, thus harmonizing the middle
and stopping nausea. It is often used for Spleen yang cold
from deficiency leading to abdominal pain and nausea.
Thoroughly Revised Materia Medica observes: "Baked
ginger harmonizes the middle and stops nausea, when
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) would be too dis.
persing and Zingiberis Rhizoma (gan jiang) too drying."

Here the herb is fried over a high flame until black, but not

Slices of the herb are sprayed with vinegar or wine or salt
water, left alone for 30 minutes, then fried until all the liquid
is absorbed. This method was common in ancient times,
but is less used today. The different materia medica texts
do not agree exactly on the effects of this preparation, but
generally, when combined with Ginseng Radix (ren shen)
and Nelumbinis Semen (lian zi), the vinegar-fried herb

involving nausea and difficulty in eating. Frying it in wine
increases its ability to tonify the Spleen and its tendency to
ascend. Frying in salt leads it into the Kidney channel to lift]
and benefit the Kidney qi. Coupled with Kidney tonics, as
well as herbs that secure and bind, frying the herb in salt
can be used for treating spermatorrhea, vaginal discharge,

englishReference.commentary:
Although Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (shi chang pu) is acrid
and warm, its warmth is gentle and harmonious, and it
dredges, disperses, opens, and spreads out due to its fragrant aroma. Entering the middle burner, it disseminates
and transforms turbid dampness, awakens the Spleen and
Stomach, and promotes digestion. Entering the chest and
diaphragm, it dredges and dislodges congealed turbid
phlegm, raises the clear yang, stimulates the consciousness.
and unblocks the sensory orifices to improve hearing.
It is considered essential in the treatment of coma.
withdrawal-mania, or impaired mental function when
these are associated with phlegm-dampness veiling the
consciousness, preventing the clear yang from ascending:
and for deafness, blunted affect, or forgetfulness when due
to the same causes.
Its warming action is quite mild, and may not be sufficient if pathogenic cold is prominent in combination with
dampness. Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica
explains:
Although Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (shi chang pu) is
warming, and this is sufficient in terms of clearing away the
noxious, it will not suffice to warm the middle. This is not
the herb to undertake major responsibility in cases of direct
attack into the three yin [channels] with such symptoms
as severe pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and [the consequent]
cramping and cold sweats, hidden pulse, and cyanosis.
Jottings from Repeated Celebration Hall notes that it
soothes the Heart qi, eases the spirit, delights the emotions.
and augments the mind--a marvelous herb! Used with

medicinals that clear and resolve, it can be depended upon
to expel turbid phlegm-filth and protect the palace [of the
Heart]; used with medicinals that enrich and nourish,it can
be adopted to disseminate clumping in the Heart due to
excessive thinking, and to unblock the consciousness.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica expands on
this, explaining that
In cases where phlegm stops, thin mucus accumulates, or
turbid dampness veils, or in painful obstruction of the chest
due to qi stagnation, with a tongue coating that is white and
greasy with foul filth, or yellow and thick, only the fragrant
aroma of Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (shi chang pu) will
unblock the orifices and restore free passage [of qi].
The ability of Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (shi chang pu)
to enhance digestion is also notable. Thoroughly Revised
Materia Medica says that it: "Drives out phlegm, reduces
accumulation, unbinds the Stomach and eases the middle.
It remedies dysenteric disorders where the patient is unable
to eat or drink.

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, sweet, and very cold, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao)
enters the Lung and Stomach channels. It is very cooling
and dispersing; within its ability to drain fire is a tendency
to clear and release. In the exterior, it releases heat from
the muscle layer, and in the interior,it clears fire and heat
from excess from the qi level of the Lungs and Stomach.
Reducing heat is crucial for the preservation of fluids, and
it is no accident that intense thirst is a signal for the use
of Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao), as is the high fever with
absence of chills and the large, strong pulse.
Other conditions for which this mineral is an excel.
lent choice include Lung heat leading to severe cough and
wheezing, and Stomach fire causing headache, toothache,
bleeding gums, or tooth abscess. If used with herbs that
cool heat in the blood, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) can also
treat symptoms of heat in the qi and blood such as rashes,
delirium, and muddled consciousness.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH ANEMARRHENAE RHIZOMA (zhi mu)
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) is acrid, sweet, and very cool.
ing; it can vent muscle-layer heat and cool Stomach fire,
and while its heaviness directs fire downward, its acrid
flavor allows it to reach the exterior. Thus, it addresses
both the interior and exterior of the body. Anemarrhenae
Rhizoma (zhi mu) is bitter and cold; its bitterness directs
fire downward, while its moistening quality resolves dryness. Together they have a powerful ability to cool heat in
the yang brightness Stomach while protecting the Stomach
fluids that this heat would injure. The associated symptoms
are high fever, profuse sweating, insatiable thirst, large and
strong pulse, red face, and aversion to heat. At this time!
with the pathogenic heat widely spread throughout the
body and not concentrated in the Intestines, treatment
which attempts to clear heat through the Intestines will not
be effective, nor will the use of bitter, cooling herbs, such
as Coptidis Rhizoma (hudng lian) or Scutellariae Radix
(huang qin), which will further damage the fluids. The best
approach is to use acrid, cold flavors combined with bitter
cold, moistening qualities. Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) and
Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) are ideal for this purpose, combining to release heat and eliminate irritability,
as in White Tiger Decoction (bai hu tang)
>WITH LOPHATERI HERBA (dan zhu ye)
The sweet, bland, cooling properties of Lophateri Herba
(dan zhu ye), which cools the Heart and eliminates irritability, combined with the acrid cooling of Gypsum fibrosum
(shi gao), provides a rather gentle heat-clearing effect. It
is much less powerful than the combination of Gypsum
fibrosum (shi gao) and Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu)
to clear qi-level heat from excess. Thus the pair would be
appropriate for the later stages of warm pathogen diseases
when the lingering vestiges of heat still cause insomnia,
irritability, and a dry tongue with scanty coating. The two
herbs can also be used together for mouth ulcers and swollen, painful gums due to Heart and Stomach heat, or for
cough with fever in children.
>WITH AsARI HERBA(xi xin)

This is a combination of cooling and warming herbs. Asari

ity can lift the actions of Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) to clear
heat from the head and face. Together these two substances
clear heat and drain fire while expelling wind and stopping
pain. The pair is best used for Stomach fire blazing upward
or wind-heat attacking the head and causing headache,
toothache, or swelling of the gums.

englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Fundamentally, it is an important herb for releasing heat
from excess, expelling summerheat, alleviating thirst, and
eliminating irritability. It readily makes the Stomach cold
Warm and febrile disorders generally involve the yang
brightness. If there is headache, generalized aching of the
bones, yet no thirst or desire to drink, then the pathogen
is in the greater yang and has not transferred to the yang
brightness, and Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) should not be
used. After seven or eight days, when the pathogen has
already clumped internally and there is parched stools with
alternating chills and fever, this requires purging----do not
use Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao). For summerheat with diarrhea due to dampness and Spleen and Stomach weakness,
do not use it. It should likewise not be used for malaria-like
disorders which are not in the yang brightness and do not
involve thirst. (Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica)

>UNPREPARED GYPSUM(sheng shi gao)
This is the form most commonly prescribed for internal
consumption.
>CALCINED GYPSUM(duan shi gao)
This is generally applied externally as a fine powder. Its
dispersing property has been removed, and it is somewhat
less cold, but its abilities to restrain and to generate flesh are
enhanced. It is frequently used externally for eczema, scalding, and erupted sores or wounds that fail to heal. However,
it is also included in a number of classical formulas for
internal use. Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica notes

92 2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
that calcined gypsum is not as harmful to the Stomach as
the unprepared form, especially if mixed with rock sugar,
but it will be ineffective if used in small doses. However,
Zhang Xi-Chun and others object that once calcined, its
ability to vent and release the muscle layer is lost, and if
used internally for externally-contracted pathogens coupled with heat from excess, it will instead restrain phlegmfire and lead to clumping and other toxic effects. Thus, at
present, calcined gypsum is usually applied externally.

englishReference.commentary:
Salty, cold, and heavy, Haliotidis Concha (shi jue ming)
enters the Liver channel to cool the Liver and calm ascendant Liver yang. The Liver governs wind, and the orifice

Concha (shi jue ming) cool the Liver and anchor the Liver

>CALCINED ABALONE SHELL(T # duan shi jue ming)
The shell is placed in a calcining container and heated at a
high temperature until the color of the shell turns greyish

white or greyish green. This method of preparation reduces

and inhibiting actions, and improves its ability to brighten

SALT-PREPARED ABALONE SHELL

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, bitter, and slightly cold, Pyrrosiae Folium (shi wei)
primarily enters the Lung and Bladder channels. Sweet and
bland fiavors leach and facilitate dampness, bitterness and
cold clear and drain Lung heat from the upper body while
facilitating Bladder function in the lower body. The Lungs
are the upper source of fluids: if the source is clear, the flow
will be also be clear. Thus, while Pyrrosiae Folium (shi wei)
excels at facilitating the fluids and unblocking painful urinary dribbling, it also clears the Lungs and alleviates cough.
In addition, it cools the blood and stops bleeding. Thus,

bling with blood in the urine. It is often used for cough and

helps the essential qi of the Lungs and Kidney, linking

englishReference.cautions: Contraindicated in cases of high fever and coma, and spontaneous sweating and collapse. Use with caution during pregnancy.
englishReference.actions:
- Opens the orifices and penetrates through turbidity to
awaken the spirit: for closed disorder, phlegm collapse,
and epidemic toxic diseases. Especially indicated for cold
disorders.

15 / Aromatic Substances that Open the Orifices
With Moschus (she xiang), Caryophylli Flos (ding xiang)
and Benzoinum (an xi xiang) for'sudden loss of consciousness and coma, chest pain, childhood convulsions, or seizures, especially in cases with phlegm and qi obstruction, as
in Liquid Styrax Pill (su he xiang wan).
- Opens up areas of constraint and clears away filth: for sti
fling sensations, cold, fullness, and pain in the chest and
abdomen. Recently used for such problems as coronary
artery disease and biliary colic. Applied topically for chil.
blain.
- With Borneolum (bing pian), Olibanum (ru xiang), and
Santali albi Lignum (tan xiang) for angina pectoris.
englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, acrid, and warm in nature, with an intense aroma,
Styrax (su he xiang) excels at opening the orifices and clearing away filth, and is used to open closed patterns occurring
with sudden loss of consciousness as a result of wind-stroke
or phlegm collapse. Closed disorders can be hot or cold,
and each type requires an appropriate substance to open
them up: hot opening substances for patterns of cold
closure, and cold opening substances for patterns of hot
closure. Because Styrax (su he xiang) is warm, mobile, and
piercing, it is best suited for wind-stroke or phlegm collapse in patterns of cold-closure and should not be used
for patterns of hot-closure or abandoned disorders from
deficiency.
Encountering the Sources of the Classic of Materia Medica
explains that it
is created by the accumulation of the qi of various [types
of] fragrances; it ventilates every yin organ and orifice, and
clears away every type of abnormal qi. Whenever phlegm
accumulates [leading to] qi collapse, this must first be used
to open and guide--to treat phlegm, first regulate the qi as
the basis [for further treatment]. For the miasmic damp qi
of mountain mists which invades the channels and collaterals causing intermittent cramps and spasms, Styrax (su he
xiang) is imperative for treatment.
Its fragrance is so penetrating that one traditional test for
Styrax (su he xiang) is to rub a small amount into the palm
of the hand; if its fragrance penetrates through to the back
of the hand, it is the genuine article.
englishReference.combinations: > WITH MosCHUs (she xiang); see page 947
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.MosCHUs (she xiang)
Both substances are acrid, warm, and aromatic, and both
open the orifices and awaken the spirit. However, Styrax
(su he xiang) more strongly clears away filth and expels
phlegm, and is thus best used for turbid, filthy qi disturb--
949
ing the body and causing loss of consciousness, and for
wind-stroke with overabundant phlegm causing loss of
consciousness.
Moschus (she xiang), on the other hand, is stronger
than Styrax (su he xiang) at opening the orifices and awakening the spirit, while its mobile, piercing nature unblocks
the channels and thrusts out through the collaterals. Hence
it is also often used for qi and blood stagnation with swell
ing and pain.
> Vs. BENZOINUM (an xi xiang); see page 951

Literal English translation: "revive and join fragrance"
The word styrax is derived from the Arabic word assitirax!
meaning 'sweet-smelling exudate'. The Chinese Styrax (su
he xiang), produced from the tree Liquidamber orientalis, is
equivalent to the international commercial product known
as Levant Styrax, also known as liquid styrax (in Chinese
the liquid' is oil: #h su he you), or just styrax. The latter should not be confused with the balsamic resin derived
from Styrax benzoin, which is Benzoinum (an xi xiang),
also known as benzoin.
This substance is derived from cutting the bark of the
tree in early summer, causing the tree to produce new wood
with resin-secreting ducts. The resin (balsam) saturates the
bark, which is collected in autumn, boiled, then pressed to
collect the balsam, known at this point as crude styrax (
pu tong su he xiang.When dissolved in ethanol
filtered, and then distilled to remove the ethanol, it is called
refined styrax (## jing zht su he xiang). Only the
latter is now imported for use in China.

englishReference.cautions: Use with caution in cases of severe diarrhea or heat from excess. See ToxiCiTY below.
englishReference.actions:
Nourishes the Heart yin, augments the Liver blood, and
quiets the spirit: for irritability, insomnia, and palpitations
with anxiety due to either blood deficiency (inability to
nourish the Heart) or yin deficiency (with upward-flaring
fire).
--- With Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao), Angelicae sinensis
Radix (dang gui), and Polygoni multiflori Radix preparata
(zhi he shou wu) for irritability, insomnia, and palpitations
with anxiety due to Heart blood and yin deficiency.
With Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu and Poria (fu
ling) for insomnia and irritability due to Liver yin defi.
ciency and its accompanying heat, as in Spiny Zizyphus
Decoction (suan zao ren tang).
With Codonopsis Radix (dang shen), Poria (fu ling), and
Longan Arillus (long yan rou) for insomnia, palpitations,
and irritability due to deficiency of the Spleen qi and Heart
blood, as in Restore the Spleen Decoction (gui pi tang)
Prevents abnormal sweating: for both spontaneous sweat.
ing and nightsweats.
--With Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi), Astragali Radix
(huang qi), and Corni Fructus (shan zhu yu) for spontane
ous sweating and nightsweats.
englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, sour, and neutral, the special characteristic of Zizi
phi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren) is its ability to tonify the
interior while inhibiting the exterior: it tonifies the nutritive
blood to quiet the spirit and resolve, while simultaneously
inhibiting the nutritive yin in order to stop sweating. In
Renewed Materia Medica, Ye Gui says that it
Calms the Liver to regulate the qi, moistens the Liver to
nourish the yin, warms the middle to facilitate dampness.
restrains qi to stop sweating, strengthens the resolve to
settle angry outbursts; enhances the hearing and brightens
the eyes.
It is an essential ingredient for prescriptions treating Heart
and Liver blood deficiency depriving the spirit nourish
ment, and chaotic movement of fire from deficiency, which
forces the nutritive yin to drain outward as sweat, with
such symptoms as restless insomnia, palpitations, timidity,
dream-disturbed sleep, being flustered and anxious, and
sweating. Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians says
that it "governs Heart irritability with inability to sleep.
Zhu Zhen-Heng observes that
When blood does not return to the Spleen and causes rest
less sleep, [Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren)] should
be used to amply tonify the Heart and Spleen, after which

14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
the blood will return to the Spleen, the five yin organs will
be peaceful and harmonious, and sleep will become tranquil.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica describes the
wide application of its sour, restraining properties:
[It] tonifies all five yin organs: for example, [it can be used
for] insufficiency of Heart qi with palpitations and failure
to contain the consciousness; for insufficient closure of
the pores and interstices with spontaneous sweating and
nightsweats; for insufficiency of Lung qi with shortness of
breath and trepidation, and dry cough without phlegm; for
insufficiency of Liver qi with contracture and spasms of the
sinews and bones, and dry, splitting nails; for insufficiency
of Kidney qi with spermatorrhea, nocturnal emissions, and
dribbling urine; for insufficiency of Spleen qi with clumped
gathering of hot and cold, and emaciation of the muscles
and flesh; for insufficiency of Gallbladder qi with trembling
palpitations, fear, and restlessness from deficiency and
inability to sleep. All of these cases are disorders of los
in the five yin organs--when they receive the sour, sweet
warmth of Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren),it quiets
and calms the qi and blood, restraining so as to allow circulation.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ANEMARRHENAE RHIZOMA (zhi mu)
The Liver stores the blood, which returns for replenishment to the Liver during sleep, as it is no longer needed
to nourish the sinews and eyes. If the Liver blood is insufficient, the ethereal soul-can no longer be contained by the
Liver, leading to insomnia with dream-disturbed sleep
If the Heart blood is deficient or disturbed by fire from
deficiency, the spirit will lack nourishment, causing anxiety
and insomnia, palpitations, and forgetfulness.
This combination addresses both aspects of this situa.
tion: the sourness of Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren)
enters the Liver, augments the Liver blood, and tonifies
Liver deficiency. When the Liver blood is replenished, the
Heart blood also flourishes (as wood generates fire), and
both the ethereal soul and the Heart spirit become tranquil.
Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is bitter, cold, and moistening; it cools heat, enriches the Kidney yin, and direct the
Heart fire downward.
Together the sour and bitter flavors each match their
respective organ: the Liver blood is supplemented, the
Heart yin is enriched, and the fire from deficiency is cleared
and directed downward, leaving no basis for disturbance
of the spirit.
>WrTH PoLYGALAE RADIX (yuan zhi); see page 932
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.PLATYCLADI SEMEN (bai zi ren) and
PoLYGALAE RADIX (yuan zht); see also page 932
92
All three herbs enter the Heart channel, calm the spirit, and
treat fright palpitations and insomnia. However, Ziziphi
spinosae Semen (suan zao ren) and Platycladi Semen (bai
zi ren) are sweet and neutral, and nourish the Heart yin and
Liver blood; thus, they are more appropriate for irritability and insomnia from deficiency. Of the two, Platycladi
Semen (bai zi ren) primarily treats the Heart, while Ziziphi
spinosae Semen (suan zao ren) primarily treats the Liver.
Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi), by contrast, is acrid-dispersing,
bitter-draining, and warm so that it unblocks; it assists the
Heart yang and augments the Heart qi, reestablishing harmonious communication between the Heart and Kidneys
to calm the spirit and strengthen the resolve. Polygalae
Radix (yuan zhi) is thus more appropriate for palpitations
and insomnia due to loss of communication between the
Heart and Kidneys, as well as confusion, loss of mental
concentration, and forgetfulness.
Moreover, the sour flavor of Ziziphi spinosae Semen
(suan zdo ren) restrains and inhibits, inhibiting sweating
and generating yang fluids, so that it can be used in the
treatment of thirst due to injured fluids, and profuse sweating resulting from deficiency. Platycladi Semen (bai zi ren)
moistens and lubricates the Intestines, and can thus be
used to treat dry constipation. Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi)
disperses stagnation and expels phlegm, reduces swellings
and disperses sores, and can thus be used for cough due to
cold-phlegm, and for cold congealing and obstructing the
qi such that phlegm and dampness enter the collaterals and
cause toxic swollen sores.

Literal English translation: "sour date seed"
Generally wild-crafted, the mature fruit is gathered in late
autumn or early winter, and the seed is extracted. If this is
done too early, the fruit will be pale and not yet filled out,
thus affecting quality. The fruit is also simply known.as date
seeds#= zao ren. When cleaned and dried, they are

928 14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
known as unprepared spiny zizyphus, literally, unprepared
sour date seeds (m $= sheng suan zao ren). The seeds
should be pulverized before dispensing.
> DRY-FRIED SPINY ZIZYPHUS
=chao suanzao ren
Also known as prepared spiny zizyphus (#t #(= shu zao
ren), the seeds are dry-fried at a moderate temperature
until they begin to pop and their color darkens. The dryfrying should then cease. Seeking Accuracy in the Materia
Medica cautions: "Dry-frying too long will dry out the oil
and cause loss of aroma, so that when it is pulverized the
aroma and flavor are lost; it will then be hard to see results."
Research has confirmed that while moderate dry-frying
enhances the availability of the constituents to extraction in
water, extended frying until scorched or blackened reduces
their availability to below that of the raw fruit.
Traditionally, this method of preparation is thought to
change the nature of the seeds from neutral to warmly tonifying, thereby enhancing their ability to nourish the Heart
and restrain the Liver. The seeds should be pulverized
before dispensing, a process which is much easier and more
complete after dry-frying. This increases the full utilization
of the herb, and thus improves its efficacy.
Traditionally (from the twelfth century onward) the
prepared fruit was thought to calm the spirit and facilitate
sleep, while the unprepared fruit was thought to awaken
the spirit and treat drowsiness. For example, the Materia
Medica Arranged According to Pattern advises, for "exces
sive sleep, use it unprepared; unable to sleep, prepare it by
dry-frying." The Grand Materia Medica concurs: "Used
prepared, it remedies patterns of Gallbladder deficiency
with inability to sleep, irritable thirst, and sweating from
deficiency; used unprepared, it remedies Gallbladder heat
with excessive sleep." Research in China has shown that
decoctions of both the prepared and unprepared forms of
the herb are equally calming. Whether this results from the
heat of the decoction, which is similar to the heat used in
the process of dry-frying, has not yet been tested.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
The fruit is harvested in autumn when it is mature and the
kernels are full and solid; the kernels of the summer fruit
are too small to use. The flesh of the fruit is removed and
the. seeds collected, from which the kernels are extracted
by striking the side of each seed until it splits. This is called
cleaned peach kernel (#= jing tao ren). The procedure
is mechanized in large-scale production. Peach kernels are
also known as #t# = tao he ren. .
>STRIPPED PEACH KERNEL (#k=guang tao ren)
In some place the outer coat is not removed. But when they
are, the cleaned peach kernels are boiled in water for ten
minutes until the seed coat wrinkles, then placed in cold
water and the seed coat is rubbed off. They are then dried in
the sun, and any blackened kernels or extraneous material
is removed.
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
explains the traditional view of this procedure:
If used without removing the seed coat, in large doses, it
then travels to the Liver channel and primarily breaks down
the build-up of blood, drives out menstrual biood, [treats]
pain all over the body, numb painful obstruction of the four

10' / Herbs that Regulate the Blood
limbs, and hemiplegia ... If used with the coat removed.
in small doses, and pulverized, it then enters the Small
Intestine, treats blood dryness constipation and difficult
stool, because it moistens, cools, and harmonizes the blood,
and has the power to open clumps and unblock stagnation.
When the kernels are ground into a paste before using,
they are called peach kernel paste (#= tao ren ni) or
broken-up peach kernels (& #k(= po tao ren). This method
facilitates decoction.
>DRY-FRIED PEACH KERNEL (&#k{=chao tao ren)
The peach kernels are dry-fried until yellow. Dry-frying
strengthens their ability to break up blood stasis; there is
also the view that it increases the moistening quality of the
kernels. Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica advises:
"To moisten dryness, remove the tip and seed coat, then
dry-fry."
>DEFATTED PEACH KERNEL, lit. peach kernel frost'
=tao ren shuang
Cleaned peach kernels are wrapped in oil-absorbent paper
and then pressed. The paper is replaced and the process
repeated until no more oil can be expressed. This defatting
process completely eliminates the Intestinal-moistening
effect without reducing its ability to invigorate the blood
and dispel stasis. It is appropriate for blood stagnation in
patients with loose stools due to Spleen deficiency

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.TRICHOSANTHIs RADIX (tian hua fen)
Both herbs generate fluids and alleviate thirst, nourish the
yin and clear heat, and enrich the Stomach. They are often
used together as their actions are mutually complementary. However, Dendrobii Herba (shi hu) is sweet, bland,
slightly salty, and cold by nature, whereas Trichosanthis
Radix (tian hua fen) is sweet and cold. Dendrobii Herba
(shi hu) enters the Kidneys and Stomach, enriching the
Kidney essence, and its ability to cool heat from deficiency
is superior to that of Trichosanthis Radix (tian hua fen)
By contrast, Trichosanthis Radix (tian hua fen) primarily
enters the Lungs and Stomach, more strongly generates
fluids, and also directs phlegm-fire downward, expels pus
and reduces swelling.
>Vs.GLEHNIAE/ADENOPHORAE RADIX (sha shen) and
POLYGONATI ODORATI RHIZOMA (yu zhu)
All three of these herbs enter the Stomach channel and clear

830 12 / Tonifying Herbs
heat, nourish the yin, and generate fluids, and all are used
in the treatment of Stomach yin and fluid insufficiency with
such problems as dry mouth, thirst, and wasting and thirst.
ing disorder. Both Glehniae/Adenophorae Radix (sha shen)
and Polygonati odorati Rhizoma (yu zhu) also enter the
Lung channel and are therefore used to treat coughs due to
Lung yin deficiency.
However, each of these herbs has its own particular
strengths. Glehniae/Adenophorae Radix (sha shen) is best
at clearing the Lungs and moistening what is dry. It is
most effective for dry coughs with little sputum or bloodstreaked sputum. Polygonati odorati Rhizoma (yu zhu) is
better at enriching and moistening. Because it nourishes
the yin without being greasy, its effect in retaining patho
gens is slight, hence it is used for those with underlying yin
deficiency who also have an externally-contracted disease.
Dendrobii Herba (shi hu) is better at clearing heat and is
frequently used when a febrile disease has injured the fluids. It is also effective in reducing heat from yin deficiency.
and can be used for visual disorders, dizziness, and weakness in the lower back and legs.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH TRICHOSANTHIS PERICARPIUM (gua lou pi)
Although these two herbs are derived from the same
plant, their actions are not identical. Trichosanthis Radix
(tian hua fen) is better at directing fire downward, moistening dryness, and generating fluids to alleviate thirst.
Trichosanthis Pericarpium (gua lou pi) is better at facilitat
ing the movement of qi, easing the chest, and transforming
and cooling phlegm-heat
Together each exercises its particular properties in a
complementary fashion so that heat is cooled, fluids are
generated, the chest is made comfortable, and clumping
is dispersed. This combination also generates fluids and
moistens without obstructing the flow of qi. In this way, the
fluids do not accumulate to form thin mucus. It promotes
the movement of qi in such a way that the fluids are in no
danger of further injury, which would exacerbate the dry
ness. This combination is an ideal choice for treating the
cough which results from injury to the Lung fluids in the
aftermath of a febrile disease. The cough produces either
scanty or no sputum, and often presents with thirst resulting from rebellious qi and a stifling sensation and discomfort in the chest.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, neutral, and moist, with a nature that is slightly
moistening and tonifying, Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian ma)
enters the Liver channel to nourish the yin fluids, calm the
Liver, and extinguish wind. Considered a sage-like herb
for wind, it treats all forms of internal wind, including
problems such as wind-stroke, wind-seizures, tingling and
numbness, headache, vertigo, and dizziness. Transforming
the Significance of Medicinal Substances says that it "is harmonious and moderate in nature. The [Inner] Classic says
"when the Liver suffers restlessness, use sweetness to moderate it'---this is used to moderate the Liver qi."
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica says that it
"governs head wind, headache, dizziness and vertigo, epi
lepsy with strong convulsions, spasms in the four limbs,
difficulty in speech, and all wind-stroke and wind-phlegm."
Li Gao observes:
91
When the Liver is deficient, use Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian
ma) and Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) to tonify it.
The functions of Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian ma) are four
it remedies wind-heat headaches in adults, wind-seizures,
palpitations with anxiety in children, all wind tingling,
painful obstruction, and numbness, and wind-heat affecting speech.
The Grand Materia Medica says that it
is a herb of the Liver channel qi level. Basic Questions says:
'All wind and dizziness belongs to wood', and therefore,
because Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tiain ma) enters the leg terminal yin channel, it can treat all [these types of] disorders.
According to Luo Tian-Yi [a student of Li Gao]:Darkening
of the vision with dizziness is due to the internal activity of
deficiency windwithout Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian ma) it
cannot be treated.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes an
internal contradiction in the traditional presentation of
the attributes of Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian.ma): on the one
hand, it was originally described as acrid and warm, and
thus
drives out wind, overcomes dampness, and warms to
unblock movement in areas of painful obstruction. Yet all
the commentators also say that it governs wind from deficiency headaches and dizziness, so that it calms the Liver
and extinguishes wind, which is quite opposite to the method of expelling wind and unblocking painful obstruction.
The book's author, Zhang Shan-Lei, goes on to say that if
it is indeed acrid and warm, would this not aggravate the
internal wind symptoms?
And yet Luo Tian-Yi says that darkening of the vision with
dizziness cannot be treated without Gastrodiae Rhizoma
(tian md). From this we know that patterns such as painful
obstruction or paralysis due to wind,cold, or damp patho
gens cannot be effectively treated with Gastrodiae Rhizoma
(tian md). For the texture of Gastrodiae Rhizoma (tian ma)
is heavy, thick, and solid, transparent, glossy and moist,
rich in oils, and therefore it is calm and quiescent, sedating
and settling, nourishing the yin fluids in order to extinguis
internal wind; hence the [alternate] name settle wind herb
dingfeng cao

exceeds 80 percent.

englishReference.commentary:
Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao) guides heat downward
and out through the urine, unblocking the fluid pathways
and facilitating urination. In the Stomach channel, it raises
qi to the breast to promote lactation. This dual ability to
raise and direct downward is a special characteristic of
Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao). It is often used in the
treatment of urinary difficulty and dark urine due to damp.
warm disorders, urinary dribbling due to damp-heat, as
well as edema and obstructed lactation.
The Grand Materia Medica notes that it
enters the greater yin Lung channel to guide heat down.
ward and facilitate urination; enters the yang brightness
Stomach channel to unblock the ffow of qi [so that it]
reaches upward and promotes lactation. It is cold, which
directs qi downward; it is bland, which raises.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica elaborates:
The word 'sweet' does not mean intensely sugary.--it is
actually bland---but rather like the sweetness of spring
water, rice, or other grains, which are examples of this type
of sweetness. This substance has neither aroma nor flavor;
it is used for its blandness. Its power to unblock and direct
downward is therefore moderate, without being drasti.
cally harsh. Although it unblocks and facilitates, it does not
greatly injure the yin, and is appropriate for damp-heat that
is not too severe.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.AKEBIAE CAULIS (mu tOng)
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes that
Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao)

4 / Herbs that Drain Dampness
is used for its blandness, thus it can unblock and promote
the flow in the channels and collaterals, cool heat, and
promote urination, with a nature that is similar to Akebiae
Caulis (mu tong), but without its bitterness. Its power
to unblock and direct downward is therefore moderate,
and without the drastic harshness [of Akebiae Caulis (mi
tong)]. Although it unblocks and facilitates, it does not
greatly injure the yin, and is appropriate for damp-heat that
is not too severe. For disorders of accumulated blocked
clumps, however, it cannot compare with the prompt effciency of Akebiae Caulis (mit tong).
Thus, Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao) enters the Lungs to
drain and direct downward the heat that is blocked in the
Lungs in order to facilitate urination. It is most often used
for the symptoms of damp-heat disorders. By contrast,
Akebiae Caulis (mu tong) is bitter and cold. It clears and
directs downward the fire in the Heart and Small Intestine
to facilitate the fluid pathways, and is therefore used more
for symptoms such as mouth and tongue ulcers, rough urination, and blood in the urine. Both medicinals promote
lactation, and can also be used for amenorrhea and painful
obstruction disorders. Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao) is
easier to take in stews and other home remedies, as it is not
bitter.
In terms of the direction of their actions, Tetrapanacis
Medulla (tong cao) raises the qi while Akebiae Caulis (md
tong) is bitter and drains downward. Although the latter
herb too' can affect the upper body because it is light in
weight, its bitterness does not raise the qi, but rather directs
it downward and promotes the movement of blood. This
ability to promote blood flow is what makes it effective in
promoting lactation. Zhang Shan-Lei observed: "When
breastfeeding and the milk does not flow, although one
may say that the [flow in the] collaterals is not facilitated, in
fact, it is usually due to lack of suffusion of the blood fluid!"
Zhang explained that while herbs such as Akebiae Caulis
(mu tong) and Vaccariae Semen (wang bu liu xing) rapidly
promote movement, this may lead to problems later, unless
they are combined with substances like pig's feet (ham
hocks), because they can also injure the blood and yin. By
contrast, because Tetrapanacis Medulla (tong cao) is gentle
and bland, it does not injure the yin.

englishReference.commentary:

(wang bu liu xing) enters the blood aspect and excels at
facilitating movement in the blood vessels, transforming
stasis, and dispersing swelling and distention. Its bitterness
adds a downward-draining action that is quite strong, and
many of its notable clinical effects derive from this, such as
unblocking menstruation, inducing labor, and promoting
the flow of breast milk. It is often used in the treatment of
amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea due to stagnation of qi and
blood, delayed initiation of labor, and postp artum obstruction of the collaterals of the breast, causing breast distention and preventing sufficient milk flow.

Rapid stirring is continued for a short time until most of
the seeds appear white and popped; they are then removed
and cooled. Heating the wok first ensures that all the seeds
begin popping at roughly the same time, otherwise those
seeds which have popped first will be burnt while others are
still closed. This method of preparation changes the nature
of the herb from neutral to warm, and strengthens its abil.
ity to invigorate the blood and promote menstruation. It
is commonly used in the treatment of amenorrhea due to
blood stasis.

englishReference.commentary:
Clematidis Radix (wei ling xian) is acrid, and thus dispersing, with a strong mobilizing tendency, and a warm,
unblocking, and facilitating nature that promotes flow
in all the channels, although it tends to favor the lower
limbs. Externally, it disperses pathogenic wind; internally,
it transform dampness, unblocks the channels, and extends
its reach through the collaterals:
Guiding and disseminating, Clematidis Radix (wei ling
xian) is an important herb for pain due to wind, It is indicated for painful obstruction disorder due to wind, dampness, or cold leading to restricted movement of the joints,
numbness of the muscles and flesh, and aches and pains in
the sinews and bones. It is also used for phlegm-water in
the vicinity of the diaphragm, as well as for gynecological
pain due to qi and blood obstruction.
Clematidis Radix (wei ling xian) is also salty; it softens
areas of hardness and disperses clumps. It is therefore used
for abdominal masses, breast lumps, and other clumping.
Traditionally, it has even been used alone to soften bones
lodged in the throat.
However, because of its very yang and mobilizing
nature, it is also drying and tends to exhaust the normal qi.
It must therefore not be used for extended periods of time,
or in weaker patients.
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
explains that this herb
is violently urgent in nature, mobilizing without preserv
ing, disseminating and unblocking all twelve channels and
collaterals. It primarily treats wind, dampness, and phlegm
accumulated in the midst of the channels and collaterals
leading to painful wind and painful joints that may be swolHen or numb.
englishReference.comparisons:

Both herbs dispel wind and eliminate dampness and treat
pain and restricted movement due to wind-dampness;
especially in the lower limbs. However, Clematidis Radix
(wei ling xian) is warm, piercing, and mobilizing, and is
therefore better for treating painful obstruction disorder
with an emphasis on cold characterized by marked pain.
numbness,and restricted movement (even paralysis)
Although Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao) is
regarded as neutral in nature, it tends to be slightly cooling.
and primarily dispels dampness. Thus, in the treatment of
327
painful obstruction disorder, it is better where pathogenic
wind and dampness are accompanied by heat, and dampness predominates.
Clematidis Radix (wei ling xian) also softens areas of
hardness, while Gentianae macrophyllae Radix (qin jiao)
cools heat and clears steaming bones in such disorders as
damp-heat jaundice, or steaming bones consumption.

englishReference.actions:
* Disperses blood stasis and alleviates pain: for a variety of
disorders caused by blood stasis, including amenorrhea,
dysmenorrhea, postpartum abdominal pain, and epigastric
Pain.
- With Leonuri Herba (yi mu cao) and Corydalis Rhizoma
(yan hu suo) for dysmenorrhea and other menstrual disor.
ders associated with blood stasis.
- With Typhae Pollen (pu huang) for postpartum'retained
lochia and abdominal pain. This combination is also used
for stabbing pain in the chest and epigastrium due to blood
stasis, as in Sudden Smile Powder (shi xiao san).

ciency and stagnant blood.

and blood stasis, as in Pinch Powder (shou nian san)
Transforms stasis and stops bleeding: for uterine bleeding
and retained lochia due to blood stasis.
-With Notoginseng Radix (san qi) and Rehmanniae
Radix (sheng di huang) for prolonged menstrual bleeding
with dark blood, many clots, and stabbing pain in the lower
abdomen.

englishReference.commentary:
Salty, Trogopterori Faeces (wu ling zhi) enters the blood
aspect of the Liver channel to disperse blood stasis and congealed stagnation. Warm in nature, it unblocks the blood
vessels and invigorates the blood. Its best quality is its outstanding ability to stop pain resulting from blood stasis.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica explains:
It has a meaty, unpleasant odor, and a flavor that is bitter.
sour, and acrid. Because of its meaty, unpleasant odor, it
can enter places where blood has congealed and become
fetid, and treat the illness originating there. Because of its
bitter, sour, and acrid flavors, it can enter the Heart and
Liver to drain their stagnation. Therefore, disorders such
as stabbing pain in the Heart from blood and qi [stasis],
women's postpartum lower abdominal pain, and phlegm
mixed with blood to form pockets, congealed blood causing
pain, superficial visual obstruction that moves around--for
all of these it must be used to promote the movement of qi
At the blood level.
The reference to superficial visual obstructions comes
from a case history of Kou Zong-Shi,author of Extension
of the Materia Medica, in which he says: "This is an illness
of the blood. The Liver must receive blood before sight is
possible; to treat the eyes without treating the blood goes
against this principle." Kou used Trogopterori Faeces (wu
ling zhi) to successfully resolve the case.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH TYPHAE PoLLEN (pu huang)
In combination these substances powerfully disperse blood
stagnation and thus stop intense pain and reduce swellings.
The Grand Materia Medica says that Typhae Pollen (pu
huang) "used together with Trogopterori Faeces (wu ling
zhi) can treat all pain around the Heart and abdomen.
Clinically, the combination is used for qi and blood stasis
causing severe pain in the chest, epigastrium, and abdomen, dysmenorrhea, and pain following birth.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. TYPHAE POLLEN (pu huang)
Both herbs invigorate the blood, disperse stasis, and stop
pain. However, Typhae Pollen (pu huang) is acrid, aro.
matic, and dispersing; it breaks up blood stasis, while also
stopping bleeding. By contrast, Trogopterori Faeces (wu
ling zhi) is bitter and warm, invigorates the blood, and
strongly stops pain. Typhae Pollen (pu huang) primarily
stops bleeding, while Trogopterori Faeces (wu ling zhi
primarily stops pain.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:

vertigo due to excessive blood loss during parturition, pain
due to Heart deficiency with fire,or any disorder due to
blood deficiency without stasis or blockage. (

"Because it receives the spirit of the five phases, and its

Materia Medica)
Trogopterus xanthipes, also known as the complex.
toothed flying squirrel, is native to China. Although the
animal is an endangered species, collection of its feces does
not constitute a danger to the animal. It feeds nocturnally
upon young branches, twigs, and leaves of the cypress or
similar trees, and the medicinal substance in its unprepared
form carries aromatic traces of cypress leaf. The use of the
feces of other species is not official (see ADULTERANTs).
>DRY-FRIED FLYING SQUIRREL FECES
(h chao wu ling zhi)
The dried material is dry-fried until scorch marks appear.
This method of preparation reduces any objectionable
odor, increases its ability to invigorate the blood, but also
endows it with the ability to stop bleeding. Transforming
the Significance of Medicinal Substances notes:
Use fried to regulate all bleeding disorders: it leads blood
to naturally return to the channels and not move recklessly.
and has a uniquely encompassing ability to treat continuous uterine bleeding, threatened miscarriage, and bleeding
dysenteric disorders in the Intestine.
> WINE-FRIED FLYING SQUIRREL FECES
H jiu ling zhi
The material is sprayed with yellow rice wine, then fried
at a low temperature until dry. This further strengthens
its ability to harmonize the blood and stop pain, and it is
often used in the treatment of dysmenorrhea, or pain in the
chest or abdomen. The dry-frying process, again, enables
it to stop bleeding. Rectification of the Meaning of Materia
Medica recommends: "If there is continuous uterine bleeding in women, or ceaseless red vaginal discharge, one
should use equal amounts of [this substance] dry-fried and
unprepared, mixed with wine and consumed."
> VINEGAR-FRIED FLYING SQUIRREL FECES
cu ling zhi
The material is sprayed with rice vinegar, then dry-fried at
a low temperature until dry. Prepared in this manner allows
it to directly enter the Liver channel, and increases its abil.
ity to stop pain, harmonize the blood, and stop bleeding

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, and thereby dispersing, bitter, and thereby downward-directing, very warm but violently drying, Evodiae
Fructus (wu zhu yu) is best at warming the Liver and
Stomach to stop nausea, but is also very effective for dredg.
ing Liver constraint, promoting the movement of qi, and
alleviating pain. It appears in several classical formulas in
Discussion of Cold Damage and Essentials from the Golden
Cabinet, where it is used to disperse cold, direct rebellion down.
ward, alleviate pain, and warm the yang. In the middle
burner, its major indications involve nausea and vomiting
particularly of turbid thin fluid, due to cold from deficiency
of the Spleen and Stomach. When headache is involved
this is usually a vertex headache that includes the temples,

11 / Herbs that Warm the Interior and Expel Cold
and is due to Liver cold accosting the Stomach, causing
turbid yin to rebel upward. Zhang Zhong-Jing relied on its
acrid warmth to disperse cold in the middle burner, and its
bitter flavor to direct rebellious turbid yin downward, in
the formula Evodia Decoction (wu zhu yu tang).
This herb warms the Liver and relieves constraint from
pathogenic cold, and thus promotes the movement of qi
and alleviates pain. In the Golderi Cabinet it is used to treat
pain in the chest, combined with other warming herbs.
Later generations prescribed it for painful bulging disorders along the Liver channel. In gynecology it is used for
lower burner cold causing irregular menstruation, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. See, for example, the Golden Cabinet
formula Warm the Menses Decoction (wen jing tang).
In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang Bing
Cheng states that the herb
is acrid, bitter, and warm, aromatic and drying. It is basi.
cally a Liver governing herb,but also enters the Spleen
and Stomach, because the Spleen likes aromatic dryness.
and the Stomach likes downward-direction. By nature, its
downward-directing of qi is most rapid, and it remarkably
disseminates and spreads what has been constrained and
clumped. It therefore treats constrained stagnation of Liver
qi which has allowed cold turbidity to reside below, causing
such conditions as abdominal pain, bulging disorders, and
fixed abdominal masses. In cases where the pathogenic disorder has moved downward to an extreme, and thereafter
ascends, where it forms nausea, vomiting, acid regurgita.
tion, and sensations of fullness in the chest--it can treat all
of these.

englishReference.commentary:
The ability of Asari Herba (xi xin) to induce sweating
is rather weak, so it cannot serve as the chief herb in an
exterior-releasing formula. Similarly, when used to warm
the Kidney yang it is also generally used in an adjunctive capacity. The perfect example of this is the formula
Ephedra, Asarum, and Aconite Accessory Root Decoction
(ma huang xi xin fu zi tang), where externally it assists the
sweat-inducing action of Ephedrae Herba (ma huang),
while internally helping Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata
(zhi fu zi) warm the Kidneys.
Chen Shi-Duo says of this herb:
[It] benefits the orifices and clears phlegm, alleviates watery]
eyes from wind ... but Asari Herba (xi xin) can only be
used in small doses, not large, and it can only be used in
coincert [with other herbs], not by itself. An excessive dosage will exhaust the qi and increase the pain; used alone it
will finish the qi and end life-- there is no room for carelessness.
It might be asked: Since Asari Herba (xi xin) can warm the
Kidneys, it must be tonifying, how then can it disperse qi?
The answer is that Asari Herba (xi xin) is a yang herb, rising not sinking. Although it warms the fire of the Kidneys
below, it does not warm the water of the Kidneys. The
nature of fire is to flare upward; Asari Herba (xi xin) warms
the fire and thus causes it to ascend- this is why it cannot]
be used in large doses.
Others may inquire: If Asari Herba (xi xin) disperses true
qi, how can it be effective for headaches? The answer is that
the head is the capital of true yang; if clear qi rises and turbid qi descends, then the head and eyes are clear and crisp.
It is only if turbid qi rises and clear qi descends that the
eyes and head are heavy, aching, and painful. Asari Herba's
(xi xin) qi is clear and not turbid, thus it brings down tur.
bid qi and lifts clear qi; this is why it cures headaches so
miraculously.
However, its flavor is acrid and its nature is dispersing
one must use it with herbs that tonify the blood, so that
there is blood to prevent qi from dispersing excessively.
There is an adage about this herb to the effect that it should
not be used in a dosage larger than one qian (3g). However,
this was taken out of context. The source of the adage
Alternative Statements in Materia Medica, refers to the use
of the herb by itself as a powder. There are physicians who
report good results in difficult cases using a large dosage of
Asari Herba (xi xin), but those without extensive experience in the use of this herb should be wary and err on the
side of caution.
Some traditional herbal pharmacies use Asari Herba (x)
xin) as a non-toxic alternative to camphor for the preserva-

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
tion of herbs, especially ginseng. Small portions are simply
wrapped in a cotton cloth and placed in the corners of the
storage space.
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH ACONITI RADIX LATERALIS PREPARATA (zhi fu zi)
This pair is frequently used for dispersing cold and stopping pain. As explained in Rectification of the Meaning of
Materia Medica:
Asari Herba's (xi xin) aroma is most potent, therefore it
excels at opening clumped qi, and disseminating constraint
and stagnation; it can reach the vertex, unblock the eyes
and ears, and reach laterally to the hundred articulations.
There is no subtle area it does not reach: internally it
dredges the collaterals and channels in order to unblock
the joints, exteriorly it mobilizes the orifices of the pores in
order to directly vent the muscles and skin.
When the two herbs are used together, their common
warmth combines, their ambulatory nature facilitates
movement, and the effect is to disperse cold and alleviate
pain. Internally, Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zhi fu
zi) warms while Asari Herba (xi xin) draws out the cold
and disperses it; exteriorly, Asari Herba (xi xin) dredges up
the pathogen while Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zhi
fu zi) encourages and supports this action. Thus, cold at
any level can be completely eliminated. Clinically, besides
treating cold damage involving both the exterior and interior marked by aversion to cold, headache, and generalized
body aches with aching joints, the pair can also be used in
treating painful obstruction from wind, dampness, and
cold leading to spasms of the joints and intolerable pain.
However, caution must be exercised in the use of these
herbs due to potential side effects--if the condition is not
one of cold from excess, this pair should be used only with
considerable caution.
> WITH SCHISANDRAE FRUCTUS (wu wei zi)
This herb is sour, warm, and specifically used for contracting and preserving. It is particularly good at restraining the
Lungs and alleviating cough.
Together with Asari Herba (xi xin), whose acrid, dispersing property opens the Lungs, the sour, restraining
quality of Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi) preserves the
Lung qi: the first herb opens the Lungs without risk of
exhausting its qi, while the second herb closes the Lungs
without risk of mistakenly trapping the pathogenic qi
Thus, the pair is ideal for regulating the opening and clos--
ing of the Lungs, alleviating cough, and calming wheezing
It is used for patients with existing thin mucus, who are further exposed to externally-contracted wind-cold, leading to
acute wheezing and coughing up of thin clear sputum.
29
The relative dosage of each of the two herbs should be
based upon the duration of the disorder and the strength of
the pathogen. Generally speaking, recent or early stage dis.
orders have a stronger pathogen, in which case Asari Herba
(xi xin) should be emphasized. In more chronic cases the
pathogen will have weakened, but so will the patient, and
Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi) should be emphasized
in order to take advantage of its Lung-preserving action
These rules are reflected in the adage, "For a new cough.
use more Asari Herba (xi xin); for an old cough, use more
Schisandrae Fructus (wu wei zi)."
>WITH CHUANXIONG RHIZOMA (chuan xiOng)
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) is acrid, and ideal for
moving and dispersing. It can travel upward to the head.
eyes, and vertex with a relatively powerful wind-expelling
action to relieve pain. It is considered an essential herb for
headaches. Asari Herba (xi xin) also reaches the crown, and
excels at unblocking the nose and ears, expelling wind-cold.
and relieving pain. Together, the pain-relieving actions of
these herbs are strengthened synergistically, especially for
wind-cold headaches: This use has been extended to pain
from wounds as described in Rectification of the Meaning
of Materia Medica:
Chuanxiong Rhizoma (chuan xiong) excels at dispersing
and also travels in the Liver channel: a qi herb that moves
blood. ... Thus, it disperses wind-cold, treats headache,
breaks up stagnation, unblocks the blood vessels,releases
clumped qi, eliminates pain, expels pus, dissolves swelling.
drives out blood, and unblocks the channels. ... Decocted
together with Asari Herba (xi xin), it treats pain from
wounds caused by metal.
This pair can treat swelling and pain from sores and boils.
or from trauma. Other herbs should be added based upon
the nature of the disorder: hot, cold, excessive, or deficient.

englishReference.commentary:
The subtle flavors and qualities of Cyperi Rhizoma (xiang
fu have multiple uses. It is acrid, and thus disperses

528 9 I Herbs that Regulate the Qi
blocked qi, and slightly bitter, enabling it to direct rebel.
lious qi downward. It is neutral and can thus be used for
either hot or cold disorders, and while it mainly enters the
qi aspect of the Liver and Triple Burner, it has the effect of
promoting qi flow in all twelve channels. Cyperi Rhizoma
(xiang fu) is known for its ability to promote the movement of qi at such a deep level that it strongly influences the
movement of blood, and so is known as a herb that 'moves
qi within the blood.
It is appropriate in the treatment of emotional con.
straint, Liver and Stomach qi stagnation, distending pain
in the chest and flanks, food stagnation, nausea, vomiting
and acid regurgitation. It is equally useful when Liver constraint affects blood flow, causing stasis and amenorrhea,
dysmenorrhea, and postpartum disorders due to residual
obstruction.
The Grand Materia Medica states that it
is neutral in quality, rather than cold. Its aroma can pierce.
Its flavor is mainly acrid to disperse, slightly bitter to direct
downward, and slightly sweet to harmonize. It is a primary
herb for the qi level of the leg terminal yin Liver and arm
lesser yang Triple Burner, but likewise unblocks the qi level
of all twelve channels. It is the commander-in-chief of qi
disorders, and for gynecology, the supreme leader.
Li Shi-Zhen quotes Wang Hao-Gu as saying that it
is yin within yang, a herb for the qi within the blood; when.
ever qi constrains qi and blood it must be used. Fried black
it stops bleeding and treats continuous uterine bleeding--it
is an immortal herb for women!
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica elaborates,
noting that it
has a particularly intense acrid flavor and a very rich
aroma, and all its effects are through the qi. Thus it specifically treats disorders due to qi clumping. However, as its
color contains purple, its center is relatively black, its sub.
stance is firm, solid, heavy, and weighty, so even though its
qi prevails, it is still different from other acrid, warm, lightweight, raising and lifting herbs. This is why it enters the
blood aspect, and reaches downward to the Kidneys and
Liver. When Wang Hao-Gu says that it is yin within yang
and a qi-within-blood herb, this is a marvellously deep
grasp of the innate law of its nature.

englishReference.commentary:
Allii macrostemi Bulbus (xie bai) is acrid, bitter, warm,
and slippery. Its acridity disperses while its bitterness
and warmth dry dampness, and its slipperiness benefits
the orifices. Acting on the Lung channel, it unblocks the

9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
chest and disperses pathogenic cold so that chest yang can
extend, and it expels phlegm-dampness so that the qi flow
is smooth and unblocked. Thus, Allii macrostemi Bulbus
(xie bai) is an excellent herb for unblocking the chest yang.
scouring turbid phlegm, adjusting the flow of qi, and opening painful obstruction of the chest.
In addition to effectively treating painful obstruction
of the chest, and its associated symptoms of wheezing.
coughing up sputum, pain through the chest and back,
and shortness of breath, it can also reach down to move
stagnant qi in the Large Intestine in order to treat tenesmus
with dysenteric disorder. Miscellaneous Records of Famous
Physicians notes that it "warms the middle and disperses
clumped qi."
The special quality of this herb is its ability to reach
into areas of congealed constraint, whether this is unbinding painful obstruction of the chest in the upper body, or
draining Large Intestine qi stagnation in the lower body.
Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica provides a
good description of the herb's actions based on its flavors.
and more:
Allii macrostemi Bulbus (xie bai) is acrid in flavor, so it
disperses; this dispersing immediately reduces cold stagnation in the upper body. Its flavor is bitter so that it directs
downward, which immediately drives out cold stagnation
below. Its nature is warm so that again it disperses; this
dispersal expels cold stagnation in the middle. Its texture is
slippery so that it unblocks; this unblocking releases longstanding stubborn cold stagnation. Thus dysenteric disorder below is eliminated. ... Wang Hao-Gu says to use Frigid
Extremities Powder (si ni san) plus Allii macrostemi Bulbus
(xie bai) to drain blockage. Stagnant blood is dispelled;
acute wheezing can be stopped; it can be applied externally
as a paste for wind-cold type fluid retention; and cures
painful obstruction of the chest with stabbing pain---use
Zhang Zhong-Jing's Trichosanthes Fruit, Chinese Garlic,
and Wine Decoction (gua lou xie bai bai jiu tang). It can
also treat cold stagnation problems during late pregnancy
or surrounding labor. He also says that for scalds or burns
it can be mixed with honey and applied externally
Many of the earlier materia medica texts note that Alli
macrostemi Bulbus (xie bai) is warmly tonifying, although
some dispute was occasioned by the Illustrated Classic of
the Materia Medica, which states that it is cool and tonify
ing. Li Shi-Zhen discussed this at length, but settled the
argument by quoting from "Chive Poem" (## xie shi),
written in 759 by the famous poet Du Fu:
Autumn day: Hermit Ruan sends thirty stalks of garlic chives
Hermit, within a brushwood fence.
Bed upon bed of autumn vegetables surround the house.
Even before my note arrived, you sent
A full peck of dew-moist garlic chives.
Stalks tied, greener than green;
Heads bundled neatly as jade chopsticks
Old I am, weak in years, cold in joint and belly:
Two stalks of warming flavor will soothe my woes.

englishReference.commentary:
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) is bitter, warm, and slightly
toxic. The bitterness directs downward, the warmth opens,
and its moist property moistens dryness in the Lungs
and Large Intestine. In addition to directing rebellious
qi downward to stop the cough and settle the wheezing,
Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) can also disperse wind-cold
and phlegm-dampness in the Lung channel.
Zhang Bing-Cheng elaborates in his Convenient Reader
of Materia Medica:
When we investigate the nature of Armeniacae Semen (xing
ren), it appears that it does not have an acrid flavor, and
apparently only has a moistening, downward-directing
action without any ability to release or disperse. Yet when
the exterior is encumbered by wind-cold such that Lung qi
accumulates and rebels,we cannot do without using this
bitter herb to direct the rebellious qi downward, making
the qi flow smoothly.--the only way that the exterior can be
released.
Li Shi-Zhen notes that this herb can
disperse and direct qi downward, thus it releases the muscle
layer and disperses wind, directs qi downward and moistens dryness, and reduces accumulation-for which latter
effect it should be used with herbs that treat injury and
trauma. It treats sores and kills parasites by virtue of its
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PERILLAE FRUCTUS (zi su zi)
The bitterness of Armeniacae Semen (xing ren) directs
downward, its warmth opens, and its moist nature moist.
ens dry Lungs or Large Intestine. In addition to directing
rebellious qi downward to alleviate cough and calm wheezing, its dispersing action can affect wind-cold and phlegmdampness in the Lung channel. Perillae Fructus (zi su zi) is
acrid, warm, and heavy so that it descends, eases the dia-
.phragm, reduces phlegm, directs rebellious qi downward,
and calms wheezing. It is moistening rather than drying,
and facilitates bowel movements.
Both herbs enter the Lung channel and their combined
actions alleviate cough and wheezing, since once the rebel.
lious qi is directed downward, the phlegm will be cleared.
Furthermore, because the Lungs and Large Intestine have
an interior-exterior relationship, when the Lung qi fails to
properly descend, the qi of the Large Intestine also fails in
its rhythmic movement, causing difficulty in the passing of
stool. This pair of herbs restores the descent of Lung qi and
moistens the Intestines, treating both the upper and the
Iower. It can also be used for other types of constipation.
>WITH PERSICAE SEMEN (tao ren)
Both are fruit kernels which moisten the Intestines, but
the focus of treatment for Armeniacae Semen (xing ren)
is the upper body, and for Persicae Semen (tao ren) the
lower body. This provides a remarkable trickle down
effect which first facilitates peristalsis above by directing
the Lung qi downward, and then continues in the lower
body through the moistening, blood-invigorating action of
Persicae Semen (tao ren) on the Large Intestine. This combination works best when constipation is caused by Lung
qi constraint, wherein the Lungs fail to provide normal
rhythmic descent to guide the Large Intestine.
Zhang Bing-Cheng notes that while these kernels are
similar in nature, "one moves into the Liver channel at the
blood level, the other moves into the Lung channel at the
qi level." Thus the pair addresses movement of both the qi
and blood, and because the flow of qi supports the movement of blood, this combination can be used when blood
stasis leads to pain in the chest, abdomen, or throughout
the body.
While the knowiedge that Armeniacae Semen (xing
ren) enters the Lungs and calms wheezing is commonplace,
the fact that Persicae Semen (tao ren) also possesses this
action is less well known. Yet one of the earliest discussions
of materia medica; the Miscellaneous Records of Famous
Physicians, records that Persicae Semen (tao ren) can "alleviate cough and direct rebellious qi downward." Thus the
pair is also effective for wheezing and cough due to Lung
qi constraint.
>WrTH AMOMI FRUCTUS ROTUNDUS (bai dOu kOu) and
COICIS SEMEN (yi yi ren)

symptoms as heaviness of the head and body, .stifling

open the Lung qi in the upper burner, and, combined with

virtue of its dampness-dispersing aroma. The bland Coicis

provide a route for the now-transformed dampness to leave

englishReference.commentary:
Scrophulariae Radix (xuan shen) is sweet, bitter, salty,
and cold, with a moistening nature. It enters the Lung,
Stomach, and Kidney channels. Its sweet-coldness enriches
the yin, its bitter-coldness drains fire and eliminates toxins
and its salty-coldness softens areas of hardness and moistens dryness. Because it is cool and moistening, it nourishes
the Kidneys, controlling the fire which is floating upward.
Yet it also transforms phlegm-heat. In Rectification of the
Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang Shan-Lei describes this
wel:
Scrophulariae Radix (xudn shen) has a bitter and sweet
flavor: bitterness can cool fire, sweetness can nourish the
yin, and because of its sweet flavor, its descending nature
is mild. The [Divine Husbandman's Classic of the] Materia
Medica says that it only enters the Kidney channel, but [the
writer] did not know that it especially enters the Lung yin
Organ, and can therefore resolve rootless floating fire, and
disperse clumps of phlegm and generalized sores due to
heat.
In Essays on Medicine Esteeminig the Chinese and Respecting
the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun describes his experience with
this herb:

2 / Herbs that Clear Heat
All my life I have used it to treat postpartum heat from
excess due to externally-contracted pathogenic influences;
when it is severe I use White Tiger plus Ginseng Decoction
(bai hii jia ren shen tang), except that Scrophulariae Radix
(xuan shen) is substituted for Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi
mu). ... I am aware of the principle that cool herbs should
not be used after parturition, but when an externally-contracted pathogen has indeed led to heat from excess,there
is nothing that will do except to use cooling herbs to clear it.
[Of all the cooling herbs, however,] only the two herbs
Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) and Scrophulariae Radix (xuan
shen) are explicitly mentioned in the Divine Husbandman's
Classic of the Materia Medica for treating postpartum conditions; thus, I am encouraged to dare use them.
Zhang goes on to note, however, that Ginseng Radix (rer
shen) must be used with Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao), and
blood-tonifying herbs with Scrophulariae Radix (xuan
shen), to address the underlying condition of the patient.
"This is being careful while being courageous," he says.

The word xuan means black as well as mysterious; this
herb is therefore also known as black root ( hei shen)
or black dark root (hei xuan shen). The given name
of the Kangxi emperor (r. 1654-1722) was Xuan Ye,
and thus, for the duration of the Qing dynasty, both of the
words in his name (one of which is the same character as
xuan in this herb's name) became taboo and could not be
used. During this time the herb was referred to as primal
root (it $ yudn shen), a name which is still occasionally
used.
Because the best quality is large, black, and moist, a
variety of nicknames are used to emphasize these desirable
qualities: big scrophularia ( da xuan shen), crowblack scrophularia ( wu xuan shen), and moist
scrophularia ( run xuan shen).

sliced and dried. Alternatively, it can be washed, soaked
briefly, steamed thoroughly, then dried in the sun until
three-quarters dry. It is then soaked again and left covered
until both inside and outside are equally black.
Most commentators believe that the non-steamed form
is colder and therefore better for clearing heat, draining

In Convenient Reader of Materia Medica, Zhang BingCheng states that it
