Literal English translation: "extended barbarian rope"
The name 3 # yan hu suo is often shortened to 3
yan hu, or more commonly * yuan hu. The origina
name was xudn hu suo, ordark barbarian rope.
However, because the given name of an early Qing dynasty
emperor (the Kangxi Emperor) was # Xuan Ye, for the
duration of the Qing dynasty, both of these characters were
taboo and could not be used for any other purpose. The
character xuan in the name of this herb was therefore
changed to 3 yan, and this is still the most commonly
written form today. Yet any of these names can be used in
writing a prescription.
> DRY-FRIED CORYDALIS (k3# # chao yan hu suo)
Dry-fried over a moderate flame until the color changes;
this moderates its blood-invigorating action so that its
nature tends more to regulate the flow of qi and blood. It
is thus used in the treatment of milder cases of menstrual
irregularity, or in epigastric dull ache from clumped qi in
the Spleen and Stomach, when a less robust treatment is
indicated
VINEGAR-FRIED CORYDALIS
cu chao yan hu suo)

10 / Herbs that Regulate the Blood
The sliced rhizome is soaked in rice vinegar overnight, then
stir-fried over a moderate flame until just dry. Alternatively, it can be boiled together with vinegar until the vinegar
is absorbed, then gently dried over a mild flame. It is also
called processed corydalis 3# zhi yan hu suo
Vinegar-fried corydalis enters the Liver channel more
directly, better regulates menstruation and stops pain, and
is thus often used in gynecological disorders, particularly
dysmenorrhoea.
There are those who think that the sour-constricting
effect of the vinegar helps stop bleeding, without affecting
the stagnation-removing action of the herb. Be that as it
may, modern research has shown that vinegar-fried coryd.
alis has much increased alkaloid solubility, which means
that this method of preparation promotes the availability
of corydaline and the other major active ingredients in this
herb (see NoTe at the end of this section).
WINE-FRIED CORYDALIS
jiu chdo yan hu suo)
The herb is mixed evenly with yellow rice wine, set aside
briefly to facilitate absorption, then dry-fried until slightly
charred. This method of preparation was traditionally held
to broaden the scope of activity of the herb, so that it could
rise to the head as well as descend, and reach the surface as
well as the interior.
SALT-FRIED CORYDALIS
yan chao yan hu sio)
Sprayed with salt water until mixed evenly, then fried at a
moderate temperature until slightly charred. Prepared in
this manner, the action of the herb is traditionally said to
move mainly downward, which is regarded as especially
good for the treatment of pain associated with bulging
disorders.
Note: There is a large difference in alkaloid availability
from the various methods of preparation. If total alkaloids
are 100%, decoction of the unprepared herb gives 25.06%
availability, wine-fried 22.66%, and vinegar-fried 49.33%
Some other non-traditional methods produced even higher
levels. In clinical studies, the vinegar-fried corydalis provided the best analgesic effect, except in the treatment of
coronary artery disease, for which the unprepared hert
worked best.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet and neutral, Polygoni multiffori Caulis (ye jiao teng)
enters the blood level of the Heart and Liver channels. The
Heart governs the blood and stores the spirit, and the Liver
stores the blood and governs wind. Hence this herb nourishes the blood and calms the spirit, while expelling wind
and unblocking the collaterals to stop itching. It is used
whenever blood deficiency leads to insomnia, restlessness,

940 14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
palpitations, and disturbing dreams; or aching soreness of
the limbs; or itching skin disorders when blood deficiency
has allowed encroachment of pathogenic wind.
Its now common use for calming the spirit is a rather
late historical development. In the Grand Materia Medica,
Li Shi-Zhen has only: "Wind sores and itching scabies,
decoct and use as a wash." Later, Ye Gui, in his nineteenthcentury work Renewed Materia Medica, says: "Tonifies the
middle qi, promotes movement in the channels and col
laterals, unblocks the blood vessels, quiets the spirit, and
expedites sleep.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes
that Li Shi-Zhen
only mentions the use of the vine and leaves for the treatment of wind [patterns] causing sores, and scabies, and that
it is particularly effective when the decoction is used as a
wash. The present use, to treat lack of good sleep at night,
relies on its ability to guide the yang into yin.
The phrase guide the yang into yin' refers to the ability
of Polygoni multiflori Caulis (ye jiao teng) to nourish the
blood, and thereby provide a balance to excessive yang
activity.

Aromatic Substances that Open the Orifices
HE SUBSTANCES IN THIS chapter are used to open
up the sensory orifices and awaken the spirit.
The Heart governs the spirit. When pathogenic influences
envelop and veil the clarity of the sensory orifices, the spirit
becomes locked up and the patient becomes delirious or
even comatose. This is the presentation of the closed or
locked-up' disorder ( bi zheng), a type of wind-stroke
which manifests as coma, locked jaw, clenched fists, rigid
limbs, and a forceful pulse.
These substances are also used for treating turbid
phlegm veiling the sensory orifices, which has a similar
presentation and may include seizures. These problems
usually fall under the traditional rubric of collapse ( jue)
Closed disorders may be further subdivided into two
major categories:
HOT CLOSED DISORDERS: Symptoms include delirium, irritability, convulsions, red face, heavy breathing, yellow
tongue coating, rapid pulse, and usually a high fever. This
occurs when warm pathogen diseases enter the nutritive
level, as in meningitis, encephalitis, severe pneumonia, and
the toxic stage of suppurative infections. It can also occur
in heat stroke, end-stage liver disease, uremia, and cerebrovascular accidents.
- COLD CLOSED DISORDERS: Symptoms include an ashen or
cyanotic face, cold body, white tongue coating, and a slow
pulse. This disorder is sometimes heralded by a sudden
collapse or foaming at the mouth, which is usually seen in
coma associated with cerebrovascular accidents or poisoning.
Aromatic substances that open the orifices are scattering' by nature and can drain the source qi. They are used
for treating the manifestation, not the root, of a disorder.
For this reason, they should only be used for short periods
S
of time. They should not be used for treating abandoned
patterns (#t tuo zheng), when delirium or coma follows
excessive sweating, excessive vomiting, or hemorrhage; or
if the patient is weak or in shock with such symptoms as
severe sweating, cold limbs, flaccidity, loss of bladder and
bowel control, and a minute, weak pulse. In such cases,
substances that warm the middle burner and rescue devastated yang would be appropriate.
Aromatic substances are almost always combined with
others to achieve the optimal effect: for hot closed disorders, substances that clear heat and resolve

Section 2
HERBS THAT TONIFY THE BLOOD
The herbs in this section are used for treating patterns of
blood deficiency; they nourish the blood (#m yang xue).
Among the primary manifestations of blood deficiency are
pallid face and lips, dizziness, vertigo, diminished vision,
Iethargy, palpitations, dry skin, menstrual irregularities,
pale tongue, and a fine pulse. Because the sinews and bones
depend on the blood for nourishment, those with blood
deficiency are often weak and thin. In traditional Chinese
medicine, the three organs most affected by this disorder
are the Heart, which directs the blood and governs the
blood vessels, the Spleen, which controls the blood, and
especially the Liver, which stores the blood.
These herbs are usually not very effective when used
alone. To potentiate their actions, they should be combined
with other herbs that tonify the yin. Moreover, because qi
and blood deficiency often occur at the same time, these
herbs are often combined with others that tonify the qi.
-It is important to remember that because most of these
herbs are cloying in nature, overuse causes indigestion. To
counteract this effect, herbs that strengthen the Stomach
are often added to prescriptions for tonifying the blood.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, slightly cold, and with a clearing, fragrant aroma,
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) facilitates the
removal of dampness, clears heat, and reduces jaundice. It
is an essential herb for these purposes.
Jaundice results from the accumulation of dampness
and heat in the Spleen and Stomach, which is unable to
vent outward or downward. Rather, it is constrained; it
steams and fumes the Gallbladder until the bile is forced
outward to the skin and downward to the Bladder, so that
both the skin and the urine turn yellow. When the skin
is a bright yellow-orange, the dampness and heat are of

4 / Herbs that Drain Dampness
equal strength; this is yang jaundice. If the yellow is darker
this represents overabundant cold-dampness coupled with
yang deficiency; this is yin jaundice.
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) can be used
for both types of jaundice. For yang jaundice, it should be
combined with bitter, cold herbs, and for yin jaundice, with
acrid, hot or sweet, warm herbs that tonify the Spleen. If the
jaundice is accompanied by edema and urinary difficulty,
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) should be combined
with bland herbs that leach dampness out of the body.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica notes
that this herb provides
a specific treatment for damp-heat in the Spleen and
Stomach. In damp jaundice or jaundice due to alcohol, the
body is yellow and the urine is dark like a sauce. These are
the signs of accumulated dampness and gathered heat in
the Stomach earthi. This has been the primary herb since
ancient times; its effect is very rapid. It washes out the
Intestines and Stomach, thrusts out to the skin--it cannot
be done without.
englishReference.combinations:
WITH GARDENIAE FRUCTUS (zhi zi)
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) clears damp-heat
from the Spleen and Stomach to treat jaundice. Links to the
Origins of the Records of Materia Medica observes:
The special ability of Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin
chen) to bring out the old and create the new is unlike
other herbs that drive out damp-heat; as to those herbs
that act by leaching and facilitating, they cannot compare
[with Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen)]. In jaundice,
if damp qi predominates, the jaundice is smoky and dark;
if heat predominates, the jaundice is orange and bright.
Dampness holds in and steams the heat, heat likewise thick
ens the dampness, and both are based in the middle earth
damp toxin; Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) is thus
suitable for both.
Gardeniae Fructus (zhi zi) is bitter and cold with a down
ward-directing nature. Thus, it cools heat, drains fire,
and facilitates the water pathways of the Triple Burner
Discussion of Medicinal Properties says that it "relieves the
five types of jaundice.
When used together, Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin
chen) is the principal herb and Gardeniae Fructus (zhi zi
assists by guiding damp-heat out through the urine. This
provides a much stronger jaundice-relieving action than
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) alone, and explains
why the pair is fundamental to many formulas that treat

> WITH ACONITI RADIX LATERALIS PREPARATA (zht fu zi)
Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) is bitter. It drains
and directs downward, cooling and clearing dampness tc

eliminate jaundice. Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zhi fu

disorders, warming the Kidneys and Spleen, driving out

With the added warmth of Aconiti Radix lateralis preparata (zhi fu zi), Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) is
able to treat cold-dampness, while retaining its ability to

tion is thus the foundation for many formulas that treat

The combination of these two herbs facilitates the elimination of both stool and urine, which is helpful in the treatment of damp-heat jaundice. Rhei Radix et Rhizoma (da
huang) is bitter and cold. It unblocks the Intestines to guide

Adding Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) enhances

such symptoms as fever, urinary difficulty, constipation

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs. LYSIMACHIAE HERBA (jin qian cdo)
Both herbs cool heat, facilitate the removal of dampness,
clear Liver heat, and benefit the Gallbladder, and thus are
often combined when damp-heat affects these two organs.
However, Lysimachiae Herba (jin qian cao) is sweet, salty,
and slightly cold, with a tendency to soften hardness, expel
stones, and assist the Gallbladder. By contrast, Artemisiae
scopariae Herba (yin chen) is bitter, cold, descending and
draining, and much more fragrant than Lysimachiae Herba
(jin qian cao); these properties enable it to better break up
turbid dampness. It thereby reduces jaundice and promotes
urination, and assists the Liver more than the Gallbladder.
> Vs. ARTEMISIAE ANNUAE HERBA (qing hao)
Both herbs are aromatic and resolve damp-heat. They are
commonly used together in the treatment of jaundice due
to damp-heat, damp-warm disorders, and summerheat
warmth. However, Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen)

312 4 / Herbs that Drain Dampness
enters the Spleen and Stomach and is specific for jaundice.
By contrast, Artemisiae annuae Herba (qing hao) primarily
enters the Liver and Gallbladder, and is better for resolving
steaming bones due to consumption. It is particularly good
for draining pathogenic fire in summerheat-warmth, and
for malarial disorders.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
Although Artemisiae scopariae Herba (yin chen) is a

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.MUME FRUCTUS (wu mei)
The sour, warm properties of Mume Fructus (wu mei)
have a wide variety of therapeutic uses for conditions that
primarily require binding restraint. For example, it enters
the Lungs to alleviate cough from deficiency, enters the
Intestines to stop chronic diarrhea, enters the qi level to

burner. Most importantly, it also secures and stabilizes the

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
The word ying means a small-mouthed jar, which is a
good description of the seed capsule of the opium poppy.
The word # su means a grain crop like millet or maize, and
#t ke means husk. The seed capsule, or husk, of the opium
poppy is collected in mid-spring or early summer, split
open to remove the seeds, and dried. The. Grand Materia
Medica explains its preparation: "To use, wet it thoroughly
remove the calyx and sinewy membrane, choosing only the
outer pericarpium. Dry in the shade, slice thinly, and dryfry with rice vinegar before using; sometimes honey is used
in the preparation." At present, the husk is usually used
with the calyx retained.
>VINEGAR-FRIED POPPY HUSK
cu chao ying suke
The husk is soaked in rice vinegar then dry-fried until
slightly scorched. This method of preparation increases its
ability to bind up the Intestines, while also reducing its tendency to cause nausea. This method is often called for when
the poppy husk is used to treat dysenteric disorders.
HONEY-PREPARED POPPY HUSK
(#mi zhi ying suke)
The honey is first slowly brought to a boil, and the froth and
any residual wax or extraneous material is scraped from the
surface. The honey is then poured through a filter, returned
to the wok, and again brought to a boil. This is maintained
at 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles and the honey no
longer stretches between the fingers.
Boiling water is added to thin the honey, which is then
poured slowly over sliced sections of poppy husk and
left covered briefly. The husks are then dry-fried at a low
temperature until deep yellow and no longer sticky to the
touch.
This method of preparation enhances its ability to
restrain the Lungs, and is often used in the treatment of
chronic cough and wheezing. Encountering the Sources
of the Classic of Materia Medica notes: "Honey-prepared
treats cough, vinegar-prepared stops dysenteric disorders."

englishReference.actions:
Invigorates the blood and stops pain while promoting the
movement of qi and resolving constraint: used topically
and internally for pain related to traumatic injury and to
hasten the healing process of chronic sores as well as such
symptoms as chest, abdominal, flank, or menstrual pain
from constrained Liver qi. Particularly useful for constrained Liver qi patterns with heat signs.
- With Cyperi Rhizoma (xiang fu), Angelicae sinensis
Radix (dang gui), and Paeoniae Radix alba (bai shao) for
flank and abdominal pain associated with menstruation.
-With Aurantii Fructus (zhi ke) for Liver qi constraint
with stifling sensation in the chest, fullness in the epigastrium and abdomen with signs of heat from constraint.
- With Bupleuri Radix (chai hu) for pain and distention
in the flanks, irregular menses, and dysmenorrhea due to
constrained Liver qi and blood stasis.
-With Moutan Cortex (mu dan pi and Achyranthis
bidentatae Radix (niu xi) for purplish maculae, spitting
of blood, and nosebleed due to chaotic movement of hot
blood with blood stasis.
- With jin qian cao (Lysimachiae/Desmodii/etc. Herba)
for pain associated with painful urinary dribbling with
stones.
Clears the Heart and opens the orifices: used when hot
phlegm obstructs the Heart orifices with such symptoms
as anxiety, agitation, seizures, or mental derangement.
Although it is rather effective in clearing the Heart, its ability to open the orifices is weak.
- With Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (sht chang pu) and
Bambusae Succus (zhu li) for damp-heat veiling the clear
orifices marked by focal distention and a stifling sensation
in the chest and epigastrium along with muddled consciousness.
- With Alumen (bai fan) for seizures due to phlegm obstruction.
- Benefits the Gallbladder and reduces jaundice: for gall.
bladder disorders and jaundice.
- With Artemisiae scopariae Herba (vin chen) and Gardeniae Fructus (zhi zi) for jaundice due to damp-heat.
-- With Lygodii Spora (hai jin sha) and Gigeriae galli
Endothelium corneum (ji nei jin) for gall stones.
englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, such that it disperses, bitter, such that it drains
and directs downward, and cold, such that it cools heat,
Curcumae Radix (yu jin) enters the blood aspect of the
Heart and Liver channels to cool heat in the Heart and

10/ Herbs that Regulate the Blood
blood, while also promoting the movement of qi within
the blood in order to dredge and relieve Liver channel qi
constraint and clumping. In Convenient Reader of Materia
Medica, Zhang Bing-Cheng observes:
Relieves constraint and expands the chest, so that the Heart
and Lungs can be unblocked and the Liver restored; acridity disperses,bitterness directs downward,blood stasis is
driven out, and the qi disseminated. Because it is aromatic
and fragrant, it scours out phlegm from the Heart orifice;
because its nature is rather cooling and drying, it treats
withdrawal seizures in Liver patients.
Curcumae Radix (yu jin) is widely used for blood stasis
due to heat, such as dysmenorrhea and clumping in the
hypochondrium, as well as for bleeding disorders due to
heat in the blood, such as nosebleed and blood in the urine.
It facilitates the proper functioning of the Gallbladder to
eliminate jaundice, and because of its ability to cool the
Heart and relieve constraint, it is used for muddled consciousness from warm pathogen diseases, and in cases of
seizures and withdrawal mania.
Essentials of the Materia Medica states that it "promotes
the movement of qi, relieves constraint, cools the blood,
and breaks up stasis. It treats nosebleed, and women with
inverted menses (nosebleed at the onset of menstruation
or instead of menstruation), and pox toxin entering the
Heart."
englishReference.combinations:
> WITH AURANTII FRUCTUs (zhi ke)
While Curcumae Radix (yu jin) acts at both the qi and
blood levels, Aurantii Fructus (zhi ke) is a strong qi-level
herb, expanding the chest and promoting the movement
of qi. Together they have a strong ability to release qi
constraint, disperse clumped qi, invigorate the blood, and
dispel blood stasis, thus the combination can be used not
only for Liver qi constraint causing stifling sensations in the
chest, fullness in the epigastrium and abdomen, but also
for stabbing pain in the chest, flanks, and abdomen due
to blood stagnation. However, because both herbs tend to
be somewhat cold, this combination is best used when the
stasis or obstruction involves some heat. If pathogenic cold
is responsible, either do not use this combination, or add
much warmer herbs that also promote the movement of qi
and blood.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.CURCUMAE LONGAE RHIZOMA (jiang huang)
Curcumae Radix (yu jin) is cold and enters the blood level
so that it cools blood heat while also breaking up blood
stasis and promoting the flow of qi at the blood level. Cur111
cumae longae Rhizoma (jiang huang) likewise promotes
the flow of both qi and blood, but it is warm rather than
cold, and treats wind painful obstruction, which Curcumae
Radix (yu jin) does not do. Both herbs facilitate the Gallbladder to eliminate jaundice, but Curcumae Radix (yu
jin) is stronger in this regard. Curcumae Radix (yu jin) also
clears Heart heat and relieves constraint, which Curcumae
longae Rhizoma (jiang huang) does not do.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "constrained gold"
Li Shi-Zhen speculated that the name constrained gold
( yu jin) is due to its long-established usage for Liver
qi constraint: "The ancients used this to treat disorders of
constraint, [the qi] trapped and unable to ascend, perhaps
the name is because of this." The twentieth-century sinologist Edward Shafer had a different idea, believing that it
meant "a golden substance as sweet-smelling as the yi
plant used in making sacrificial wines in antiquity." It is
occasionally written as jade gold ( yu jin), which has
the same pronunciation, but can be written with many less
strokes in classical characters. Because of its yellow color, it
is occasionally called yellow constraint gold ( huang
yu jin).
The identification and parts used of the herbs derived
from the Curcuma species is complex. See Curcumae longae Rhizoma (jiang huang) for a brief discussion of these
Issues.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, juicy, soft, and moist, Polygonati odorati Rhizoma
(yu zhu) is best for nourishing the yin, tonifying without
being cloying, generating fluids injured by the processes
of a febrile disease, and clearing and nourishing without
retaining these pathogens or preventing their dispersal.
Hence it is often used in the later stages of a febrile disease
when the pathogen is weak, but the injury to the body's flu.
ids has already occurred. It can begin to restore the fluids.
without preventing the final eradication of the pathogens
which more cloying yin tonics might do. It is used for thirst
from Stomach yin deficiency, and dryness of the Lungs
with chronic cough and thickened phlegm, or dry cough.
It is considered to be a gentle, harmonious tonic which
requires frequent consumption or larger doses for its
effects to become noticeable.
Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica observes
that, "Although Polygonati odorati Rhizoma (yu zhu) is
moistening, it does not injure the Spleen [or cause] diar
rhea."
The Materia Medica of Ri Hua-Zi says that it can
eliminate irritable stifling sensations in the chest, stop
thirst, moisten the Heart and Lungs, tonify those with the
five types of consumption and seven types of [internal]

Literal English translation: "jade bamboo"
In ancient times the name of this herb was luxuriant foliage (# wei rui). At present, because the larger, fleshier
semi-transparent rhizomes are considered superior, the
names fat Solomon's seal (HEL+ fei yu zhu) and clear
Solomon's seal ( ming yu zhu) are used.

12 / Tonifying Herbs
Without any further preparation, this herb is known
as unprepared Solomon's seal (#+ sheng yu zhu). It
clears heat and generates fluids to alleviate thirst. Because it
increases the fluids without interfering with the expulsion
of pathogens, this is the appropriate form of the herb fo
injured fluids in the later stages of a febrile disease.
>PROCESSED SOLOMON's SEAL(# E+ zhi yu zhu)
The cleaned rhizomes are placed in a bamboo steamer,
then steamed and left to sit. This process is repeated three
or four times, until the surface and interior are evenly
black. This is also known as steamed Solomon's seal (
+ zheng yu zhu). While this process increases the herb's
cloying nature somewhat, it enables the herb to also tonify
the qi of the middle burner. With this method of preparation its effects are quite similar to those of Polygonati
Rhizoma (huang jing), and is most appropriate for the later
stages of a warm or febrile disease when heat has injured
both the qi and yin, and for consumptive disorders.
> DRY-FRIED SOLOMON's SEAL (kY +F chao yu zhu)
Slices of the herb are dry-fried, sometimes with bran, until
slightly yellow; the bran is then sifted out. Prepared in this
manner, it nourishes the yin without being cloying, and
also strengthens the Spleen and harmonizes the Stomach.

englishReference.actions:
Calms the spirit and quiets the Heart: for insomnia, palpitations with anxiety, restlessness, and disorientation.
Most effective in cases related to excessive brooding or constrained, pent-up emotions as well as those related to lack
of communication between the Heart and Kidneys.
--With Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zdo ren), Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu), and Angelicae sinensis Radix (dang gui) for palpitations and insomnia
due to qi and blood deficiency, as in Restore the Spleen
Decoction (gui pi tang).
With Ginseng Radix (ren shen), Poria (fu ling), and
Acori tatarinowii Rhizoma (shi chang pu) for forgetfullnes
and to calm the spirit, as in Mantis Egg-Case Powder (sang
piao xiao san).
-With Astragali Radix (huang qi), Angelicae sinensis
Radix (dang gui), and Longan Arillus (long yan rou) for
forgetfulness, palpiations and insomnia
-. Expels phlegm, clears the orifices, and stops coughs: used
when phlegm envelops the orifice of the Heart with such
manifestations as emotional and mental disorientation
spasms, or seizures. Also used for phlegm affecting the
Lungs with copious sputum, especially when it is difficult
to expectorate. Recently, it has also been used for angina
pectoris.
- A decoction of this herb may be mixed with a little rice

englishReference.commentary:
Acrid, bitter, and slightly warm, the nature of Polygalae Ra
dix (yuan zhi) disseminates, drains, unblocks, and thrusts
outward to assist in the free movement of the Heart qi,
opens constraint, and guides the Kidney qi upward to
reach the Heart, thereby re-establishing,harmonious communication between the Heart and Kidneys. Rectification
of the Meaning of Materia Medica says that "the actions
of Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi) focus on the Heart and
Kidneys", and Wang Hao-Gu says that these actions "enter
the qi level of the Kidneys."
The herb's acrid flavor disperses, while its bitter flavor
drains, thereby opening the orifice of the Heart and expelling the turbid phlegm that occludes the spirit. It is thus
most appropriate for symptoms of disturbed consciousness
associated with phlegm blocking the Heart orifice, such as
forgetfulness, palpitations, and insomnia. These qualities
also make it suitable for cough due to Liver constraint, or
phlegm-dampness obstructing the channels and collaterals, such as may occur with swollen and painful breasts
Polygalae Radix (yuan zht) can be powdered and applied
topically for this complaint, as well as other swellings and
sores.
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
provides an excellent description of this herb:
Polygalae Radix (yuan zht) is acrid, heavy, and robust, an
herb to enter the Heart, open the orifices, disseminate and
disperse. Whenever phlegm lurks in the Heart, it clogs
and plugs the Heart's orifice, causing heat from excess in
the Heart qi and leading to confusion, mental blankness,

932 14 / Substances that Calm the Spirit
impaired ability to speak, restless sleep, disorientation,
fright, forgetfulness, disturbing dreams, and children
who remain upset after seeing strangers. Briefly use [it to]
dislodge the phlegm,facilitate the orifices, and open and
unblock the Heart qi so that the spirit and ethereal soul
naturally become tranquil.
In Rectification of the Meaning of Materia Medica, Zhang
Shan-Lei gives a detailed explanation of the proper use of
this herb to restore communication between the Heart and
Kidneys and what may happen if it is not used properly.
Communication is disrupted, he says, when the
Heart yang is not stimulated, the clear qi sinks and
descends, while at the same time the Kidney qi is deficient and cold, and unable to rise up. The warm, raising
Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi) is then used to lift what has
sunken down, and prompts the Kidney yang to rise--this
is the proper treatment. . . . Yet most people do not investi.
gate [the situation]: as soon as they encounter the failure of
the Kidney yang to be contained, in a pattern such as noc.
turnal emissions, they declare this to be a loss of relations
between [the trigrams] kan and li--Polygalae Radix (yuan
zhi) must be used to prompt the reconnection of fire and
water!' But this simply causes the ministerial fire to float
upward even more, and renders the Kidneys less able to
contain. The ability to facilitate the nine orifices' [from the
Divine Husbandman's description of Polygalae Radix (yuan
zhi)] then applies: this makes the essence orifice leak, and
[the herb's] ability to 'benefit the essence' soon becomes,
instead, the loss of essence.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH ZIZIPHI SPINOSAE SEMEN (suan zao ren)
This combination is not only commonly used in the clinic,
appearing in such formulas as Restore the Spleen Decoc
tion (gui pi tang), it also illustrates an important but rarely
elucidated therapeutic principle: when treating the spirit,
there must be a balance between sour-restraining herbs
that contract, and acrid-dispersing herbs that free the
movement of the spirit. Extroversion and introversion,
in modern terms, describe the poles of this movement as
manifestations of the activity of the spirit. When it is harmonious, as in most people, it is simply a tendency toward
one pole or the other. But when this tendency goes beyond
harmony, the person can no longer function normally.
Over-expansion of the spirit may be as mild as insomnia, or
as extreme as psychosis or mania; over-contraction of the
spirit may be as mild as an inability to 'open up' with other
people, or as extreme as withdrawal and catatonia
It is important that this mechanism be recognized so
that spirit-quieting herbs can be prescribed in the proper
measure. Excessive sour-restraining herbs in an overlyintrospective person will cause them to feel withdrawn,
while prescribing excessive acrid-dispersing herbs. in an
individual whose spirit is already un-rooted will often
cause racing thoughts that they cannot control. Usually
a combination of sour-restraining and acrid-dispersing
herbs--such as this combination--is the best approach.
Here, the sour-restraining Ziziphi spinosae Semen
(suan zao ren) restrains excessive dispersal of the spirit,
while the acrid-bitter Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi) assists
the dissemination of Heart yang and qi, thus preventing
over-inhibition of the spirit, while also eliminating phlegm
that may occlude the orifice of the Heart. At the same time,
Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren) generates fluids to
prevent excessive drying by Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi),
and Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi), in turn, ensures that these
fluids do not form phlegm. In sum, each herb controls the
other and thereby forms a very harmonious combination
that ensures the proper balance of openness and sobriety
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.ZIZIPHI SPINOSAE SEMEN (suan zao ren)
Both herbs enter the Heart channel, calm the spirit, and
treat palpitations with anxiety and insomnia. However
Ziziphi spinosae Semen (suan zao ren) is sour, sweet, and
neutral. It nourishes the Heart yin and Liver blood, and is
thus more appropriate for deficiency irritability and insom
nia, in which its sour-contracting nature both generates
fluids and restrains excessive dispersal of the spirit.
Polygalae Radix (yuan zht), by contrast, is acrid-dis.
persing, bitter-draining, and warm. These properties en
able it to unblock, assisting the Heart yang and augmenting
the Heart qi, reestablishing harmonious communication
between the Heart and Kidneys and thereby calming the
spirit and strengthening the resolve. Polygalae Radix (yuan
zhi) is thus more appropriate for palpitations and insomnia due to loss of communication between the Heart and
Kidneys, and also confusion, lack of concentration, and
forgetfulness.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "profound will"
Many of the materia medica texts suggest removing the
heartwood of the root before the herb is used medicinally
as it was thought to cause restless feelings in the chest. For
this reason, traditionally, the best quality polygala is a rela
tively large hollow tube. This is known as tubular polygala
( yuan zhi tong). When the roots are too small for
the heartwood to be removed, the cortex is simply peeled
away from the heartwood in pieces, which are called poly
gala flesh ( yuan zhi rou). And when the roots are
very small, the heartwood is simply retained; this is called
polygala sticks (*# yuan zhi gun).
Modern research, however, suggests that the medicinal
actions of the heartwood are similar to those of the cortex,
but much less potent, and thus the object in its removal is
simply to increase the herb's potency by weight. Because
removal is highly labor intensive, nowadays the heartwood
is usually retained.
Unprepared polygala ( sheng yuan zhi) tends to
irritate the throat, and is therefore more commonly used
for external application.
>PROCESSED POLYGALA(zhi yuan zht)
The cleaned polygala is added to a concentrated decoc.
tion of Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao), left covered briefly
then slowly boiled until most of the liquid is absorbed. It is
then removed and dried in the sun. This is also called clear
polygala qing yuan zhtThe ancient directions
described this method as "using sweetness to moderate it
and make it discharge upward." This method of prepara
tion reduces the herb's drying property and numbing taste,
along with its tendency to irritate the throat, while enhanc.
93
ing its ability to calm the spirit. Research has shown that
this method also increases it effectiveness.
>HONEY-PREPARED POLYGALA
(+& mi zhi yuan zhi)
Honey is first slowly brought to a boil, and the froth and
any residual wax or extraneous material is scraped from the
surface. The honey is then poured through a filter, returned
to the wok, and again brought to a boil which is maintained
at a temperature of 116-118C until the whole wok bubbles
and the honey no longer stretches between the fingers.
Boiling water is added to thin the honey, which is then
poured slowly over the Polygalae Radix (yuan zhi), and left
covered briefly. The herb is then dry-fried at a low temperature until deep yellow and slightly scorched, and no longer
sticky to the touch.
This method of preparation strengthens the herb's
ability to transform phlegm and stop coughs, and is best
used for cough with profuse phlegm that is difficult to
expectorate.

englishReference.commentary:
Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) is sweet, bland, and cold.
Coldness drains fire and overcomes heat, while blandness
leaches and facilitates the removal of pathogenic water. As
it enters the Kidney channel, it excels at draining Kidney
channel ministerial fire; as it enters the Bladder channel, it
also excels at leaching out dampness through the Bladder.
With these properties, this herb can be used for a wide variety of disorders, including urinary difficulty with burning
pain and dark urine due to the internal collection of dampheat; dizziness and vertigo due to water and thin mucus
will the use of this substance be appropriate: by clearing
damp-heat, it will allow the dragon minister to rest naturally.
Ministerial fire is supported by Kidney water, but expresses
itself through the Liver, and by its warmth activates the
transformation of fluids by the Triple Burner qi. This is the
basis for Zhang's references to "dredging drainage" and
"dragon minister." The function of ministerial fire relies
on its steady, charcoal-like static nature, maintained in its
proper location. If this bank of stable fire is agitated into
flaring up by pathogenic lower burner damp-heat, one of
the first results is spermatorrhea, as the quiescent essence is
mobilized by the now pathogenic ministerial fire.

Cheng Lin elaborates:
The sweet,bitter Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma
(biai zhu) tonifies the Spleen, so that phiegm is not gener.
ated; the sweet, salty Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) enters the
Kidneys, so that thin mucus does not gather. (These two
herbs combine to make] a small formula which treats mild
cases of prodding thin mucus.
The halting of thin mucus in the Stomach is usually due to
the failure of the clear yang to raise, and the turbid yin to
descend. Atractylodis macrocephalae Rhizoma (bai zhu)
strengthens the Spleen in order to restore the ascent of

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.PoLYPORUs (zhu ling)
Both herbs enter the Kidney and Bladder channels to clear
heat and promote urination, and are commonly used
together in the treatment of edema with scanty, difficult
urination. However, Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) is cold
and therefore better -at cooling heat than Polyporus (zhu
ling); it is especially indicated for blazing ministerial fire.
By contrast, Polyporus (zhu ling) more strongly facilitates
the removal of pathogenic water. Both herbs treat spermatorrhea, but of different types: Polyporus (zhu ling)
treats spermatorrhea due to lower burner damp-heat, with
dampness predominant, which means that the urine will
be turbid; Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie) also clears dampheat, but with heat predominant, especially heat disturbing
the essence chamber due to blazing ministerial fire in the
Kidney channel.
Treasury of Words on the Materia Medica elaborates:
Polyporus (zhu ling) facilitates the removal of pathogenic
water with its ability to separate out and drain pathogenic
influences from the exterior; Alismatis Rhizoma (ze xie)
facilitates the removal of pathogenic water with its ability to
disseminate and unblock dampness in the internal organs.

>DRY-FRIED ALISMAchao ze xie
Slices of the herb are dry-fried (sometimes with bran) or
baked until slightly yellow. This method of preparation
somewhat moderates its cold nature to avoid injuring the
middle burner qi. If bran is used in the dry-frying process.
it imparts the property of harmonizing the Stomach. This
method is often used when fluid retention is due to Spleen
and Stomach yang deficiency.
>SALT-FRIED ALISMA( yan ze xle)
Salt water is sprayed evenly over the slices of the herb,
which are covered and briefly left to stand to allow the salty
water to be absorbed. The slices are then baked or dry-fried
with moderate heat until the surface is slightly yellow, then
they are removed and thoroughly dried. This method of
preparation utilizes the relationship of the salty flavor to
the water phase and the Kidneys in order to enhance the
herb's ability to facilitate urination while reducing injury
to the yin.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, sweet, cold, and moistening, Anemarrhenae Rhizoma
(zhi mu) primarily acts through the Lung, Stomach, and
Kidney channels. Bitter and cold, it drains fire, while its
sweet, cold, and moistening qualities enrich the yin and
moisten what is dry. This clearing and moistening quality
is the principal advantage of Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi
mu): in the upper burner it clears Lung heat, in the middle
burner it cools the Stomach, and in the lower burner it
drains ministerial fire, while also enriching the yin of the
Kidneys, Lungs, and Stomach. Therefore, it can be used
in situations of both excess and deficiency when heat has
dried the yin fluids, such as wasting and thirsting disorder.
Divine Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica
explains that Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) "governs
wasting and thirsting, heat in the middle, expels pathogenic
qi, and, by driving water downward, treats floating edema
of the limbs. It tonifies insufficiency and benefits the qi.
("Heat in the middle" refers to Stomach yin deficiency.)
The pathogenic qi that Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu)
expels is pathogenic heat that has entered the body, particularly at the yang brightness stage. This herb drives water
downward because its cold, moistening qualities drain the
Spleen.
Grand Materia Medica explains why Anemarrhenae
Rhizoma (zhi mu) can act on both the Lungs and on the
Kidneys:
When the Kidneys suffer dryness, acrid [substances] should
be imbibed to moisten them;when the Lungs suffer rebel.
lion [upward],bitter [substances] should be imbibed to
drain them. Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is acrid, bitter, and cold, so that below, it moistens Kidney dryness and
enriches yin; above, it clears Lung metal and drains fire.
It acts at the qi level of both channels. . . . To lead into the
channel above, fry with wine then bake it dry; to move it
downward, soak in salt water then bake.
93
In an interesting further comment, Li Shi-Zhen notes
that Astragali Radix (huang qi) acts at the blood level of
the Kidneys, which is why the two herbs should be used
together."
Zhang Xi-Chun points out that "Anemarrhenae
Rhizoma (zhi mu) is not intrinsically extremely cold, nor
is it very bitter." He tasted and compared Anemarrhenae
Rhizoma (zhi mu) with an equal amount of Astragali Radix
(huang qi) and found little perceptible difference in temperature sensations. Then he boiled Anemarrhenae Rhizoma
(zhi mu) and Glycyrrhizae Radix (gan cao) together, and
found the result to be mainly sweet:
Thus, we know that Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is
neither extremely cold nor extremely bitter.However,it
does have copious fluid with which to enrich yin. Some say
that Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu can only cool heat
and is unable to enrich yin: this is viewing Anemarrhenae
Rhizoma (zhi mu) too superficially. When I treat condi.
tions of heat from excess with a rapid pulse,I always use
Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu).Formulas which use
Astragali Radix (huang qi) to tonify qi can be too hot
for some patients; use Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu)
as a supporting herb. Its fluids, however, lubricate the
Intestines, and so it should not be used if the stools are
loose.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH COPTIDIS RHIZOMA (huang lian
Both of these herbs are bitter and cold, and both clear
Stomach heat and direct fire downward.However,Coptidis
Rhizoma (huang lian) is drying by nature, and while good
for eliminating dampness, it readily harms the yin. On the
other hand, Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is moistening and nourishes the yin while cooling heat. Together
they act strongly to clear Stomach heat and direct fire
downward, while concurrently drying dampness without
harming the normal yin fluids. This pair is most often used
for symptoms of blazing Stomach fire such as voracious
hunger, continual thirst, dry stools, a dry, yellow tongue
coating, and a slippery, rapid pulse.
Jottings from Repeated Celebration Hall--a text passed
down through the family of the celebrated Wang MengYing, which focuses on the implications of yin deficiency---notes that: "Great predominance of Stomach heat will
cause the yin to be insufficient in harmonizing the yang.
Fluids, both yin and yang, will dry, leading to a parched
inability to break down foods." This pair can reduce the
predominance of Stomach heat and prevent further injury
to the Stomach fluids.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.GYPSUM FIBROSUM (shi gao)
Both medicinals cool the Lungs and Stomach, and both
clear heat from the yang brightness qi level. This pair is
therefore appropriate for treating the irritability, thirst,
and fever, and the large, strong pulse that characterize this
condition. They are often combined in the treatment of
Lung and Stomach heat leading to such symptoms as thirst
or cough.
There are, however, significant differences between
them. Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) primarily clears
heat and moistens, and besides cooling the Lungs, alsc
cools the Kidneys and nourishes the yin. Owing to its acrid
flavor, Gypsum fibrosum (shi gao) primarily clears heat
and disperses, which extends its effect to the exterior; its
heavy property enables it to reach the interior. Gypsum
fibrosum (shi gao) protects the fluids by draining fire,
while Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) benefits the yin by
directly generating fluids.
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
A passage in Harm and Benefit in the Materia Medica
observes:
Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) injures the Stomach and
lubricates the Intestines, giving people diarrhea; it is forbidden for anyone with disorders such as impotence coupled
with quick arousal and quick ejaculation, weak Spleen,
inability to digest food, Stomach deficiency with no thought
of eating, or Kidney deficiency diarrhea.
This passage goes on to quote Xu Shu-Wei, who reminds
us that Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) is bitter and cold
and thus shares the qualities of autumn and winter, which
are inappropriate for long-term tonification;"yet people
ignore these aspects and focus on its ability to enrich the
yin."
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
Literal English translation: "know about mother"
Li Shi-Zhen says: "Alongside the main root, the accessory
roots have the appearance of insect larvae, larvae crawling
toward their mother. [Larvae are called # chi] and this
gradually became zhi, hence # zhi mu--know about
mother."
A variety of names are used to emphasize certain desir.
able qualities in this herb, such as fat anemarrhena (e tr
fei zhi mu), because the best quality herb is big, fat, and
moist. Unprepared anemarrhena has a powerful fire-draining action, and so is often used for conditions of heat from
excess in the Lung and Stomach with high fever and restlessness, thirst, and a large, tidal pulse. It is appropriate in
such formulas as White Tiger Decoction (bai hu tang).
>DRY-FRIED ANEMARRHENA (&chao zhi mu
The herb is dry-fried over a medium flame until slightly
browned. The heavy, bitter, cooling qualities of anemarrhena readily injure the Stomach and Intestines and cause
diarrhea. Frying reduces its cooling nature and moderates
its fire -draining effect. Some fry it with wheat chaff to protect the digestion, especially for those patients with both
fire from deficiency and Spleen and Stomach deficiency.
>HONEY-PREPARED ANEMARRHENA
(&k#mi zhi zhimu)
Honey-prepared Anemarrhenae Rhizoma (zhi mu) aims to
protect the Spleen and Stomach by moderating its bitter
draining, and cooling nature, while adding sweetness to
tonify the middle. This form is best for those with damaged
fluids and blood, or those who are too weak to take strong,
bitter, cooling herbs.
> VINEGAR-FRIED ANEMARRHENA
cu chao zhi mu
Slices of anemarrhena which have been soaked in vinegar
are dry-fried or baked until slightly brown, which focuses
the herb's actions on the Lungs. Origins of Medicine notes:
"To raise to the head, or to lead into its channels, prepare
with vinegar." The anemarrhena then cools Lung metal
and drains fire, e.g., when lurking heat in the Lungs causes
symptoms such as coughing or spitting up of blood, nose
bleeds, irritability from deficiency, cough, and wheezing.
>SALT-FRIED ANEMARRHENA(kK#yan chao zhi mu)
Slices of the herb are briefly dry-fried, then sprayed with
salt water, then dry-fried again or baked until dry. The
saltiness promotes its affinity for the Kidneys and increases
its downward-directing action. Thus, salt-fried anemarrhena nourishes the yin, moistens dryness, and cools and
drains ministerial fire.
>WINE-FRIED ANEMARRHENA (%u#jiu chao zhi mu)
Slices of the herb are soaked in rice wine, then dry-fried or
baked until somewhat browned. This has the effect of guiding the herb's actions upward, and lessens its cold, draining
qualities.

englishReference.commentary:
Bitter, draining, sinking, and downward-directing, Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) is an important herb for
promoting qi flow and unblocking plugs. The Grand Materia Medica notes that "Its functions are summed up in the
phrase 'facilitating the movement of qi..
Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
states that without it, "one cannot treat excess fullness
around the navel and abdomen, reduce phlegm clumps,
expel tarried water, drive out harbored food stagnation.
break up clumping in the chest, or unblock constipation."
Both Essentials from the Golden Cabinet and Emergency
Formulas to Keep Up One's Sleeve mention the efficacy of
Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) in the treatment of
chest painful obstruction and pain around the region of the
heart, in some cases even used as a stand-alone herb.
englishReference.combinations:
>WiTH AURANTII FRUCTUS (zhi ke)

5 18 9 / Herbs that Regulate the Qi
Used together, it enhances their ability to promote qi flow
and break up clumps, and extends their scope of application
beyond that of either acting alone. Thus both the upper and
lower parts of the trunk are unblocked, and the flow of qi is
unimpeded throughout. When the qi descends, wheezing
due to phlegm stops; when the flow of qi is restored, foca
distention is eliminated; when the movement of qi is facilitated, tenesmus is alleviated, and the qi dynamic throughout the Triple Burner flows firmly and unhindered.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.AURANTII FRUCTUs (zhi ke)
This is actually the same herb, but at different stages of
development: Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) is the
unripe fruit, and Aurantii Fructus (zhi ke) is the almost ripe
Both break up qi, disperse clumps, promote the dispersal of
phlegm, and reduce focal distention. However, while their
effects are similar,the two herbs act on different parts of the
body and at a different rate. As Wang Hao-Gu explains:
Aurantii Fructus (zht ke) governs the heights, Aurantii
Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) governs below ... thus Aurantii
Fructus (zhi ke) governs disorders of the chest, diaphragm,
skin, and body hair, while Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi
shi) governs disorders of the Heart, abdomen, Spleen, and
Stomach.

englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
When not prepared in any special manner, it is known as
unprepared unripe bitter orange ( sheng zhi shi).
Because they are smaller than Aurantii Fructus (zhi ke), this
herb is also known as small unripe bitter orange (
xiao zhi shi). And because the older the product, the more it
is valued, the term aged unripe bitter orange ( chen
zhi shi) is often specified.
>DRY-FRIED UNRIPE BITTER ORANGE
(kh# chao zhi shi)
The sliced fruit is dry-fried (occasionally with bran) until
slightly scorched. This method of preparation slightly
warms its coldness, and moderates its very strong nature!
so that it can be used in both hot or cold disorders. In some
parts of China it is believed that unprepared unripe bitter
orange breaks up qi too strongly and harms the normal
qi, and for this reason will dispense dry-fried unripe bitter
orange unless the unprepared variety is specified.
> DRY-FRIED GOOSE-EYED UNRIPE BITTER ORANGE
chao e yan zhi shi
The small whole fruit is placed in previously heated sandy
earth, and continually heated until it begins to bubble and
slightly split at the skin. The sandy earth is sifted away, and
the fruit is then cooled. It is pounded before dispensing.
The actions are the same as those of dry-fried unripe bitter orange except that the aroma has not dispersed, and its
efficacy is therefore somewhat superior.
>CHARRED UNRIPE BITTER ORANGE (#zhi shi tan)
The sliced fruit is dry-fried until scorched and blackened
externally, and the interior has turned dark yellow. It is
also known as scorched unripe bitter orange (# ## jiao
zhi shi). This method of preparation greatly moderates the
cold quality of the fruit and allows it to enter the blood level
to stop bleeding. It is often used for qi blockage disorders
associated with bleeding, for example, Intestinal wind.

englishReference.commentary:
Sweet, bland, and neutral, Polyporus (zhu ling) enters the
Kidney and Bladder. It opens the interstices, facilitates the
function of the lower orifices, leaches out dampness, and
strongly promotes urination. It is used in the treatment of
turbid painful urinary dribbling, anuria, and the distention and fullness of edema, damp-heat jaundice, leg qi
edema, and chronic diarrhea. According to Transforming
the Significance of Medicinal Substances, Polyporus (zhu
Ling)
is bland in flavor: blandness primarily leaches. It enters
the Spleen to unblock the water pathways and is the single
fastest treatment for watery diarrhea and damp diarrhea,
unblocking painful urinary dribbling and expelling damp
ness, reducing edema, and treating jaundice.
The Grand Materia Medica notes that it is bland and
leaching; its qi raises but also directs downward; thus, it can
open the interstices and pores while facilitating urination."
In Hidden Aspects of Materia Medica, Chen Jia-Mo
elaborates:
When using it, the black cutis must be removed; it enters
the Bladder and Kidney channels to unblock painful urinary dribbling, reduces edematous fullness, expels dampness, and facilitates urination. This is because its bitterness
[sic] drains stagnation, while its blandness facilitates the
orifices.

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH PORIA (fu ling)
When Polyporus (zhu ling) and Poria (fu ling) are combined, their ability to leach out dampness and facilitate the
removal of pathogenic water is strengthened. This combination can be used for any problem due to an internal
stoppage of water and dampness, including edema, scanty
urine, diarrhea, loose stools, painful urinary dribbling,
vaginal discharge, jaundice, and leg qi. At the same time,
the Spleen-strengthening action of Poria (fui ling) assists the
recovery of Spleen qi, thereby preventing the further forma.
tion of dampness. Although the pair is rarely used by itself,
if combined with tonifying herbs, it strengthens the Spleen;
if combined with warming herbs, it warms the Spleen; and
if combined with cooling herbs, it clears damp-heat.
englishReference.comparisons:

Bladder channels. It promotes urination more strongly

Materia Medica says that Polyporus (zhu ling)mobilizes
water and facilitates [the lower] orifice; the actions are the
same as those of Poria (fu ling), but without tonification."
While its effect in promoting urination is relatively mild.
Poria (fu ling) also tonifies the Spleen, harmonizes the
middle, and calms the spirit. These multiple actions explain
its wider therapeutic scope in comparison to Polyporus

Circulating in the Lungs, Bambusae Caulis in taeniam (zhu

and stops nausea and reflux; entering the Gallbladder, it

Transforming the Significance of Medicinal Substances
provides the following description of this herb: "Its lightness can expel excess, its coolness can expel heat, and its
bitterness can direct downward--an admirable herb for
calming the spirit and relieving constraint!
In Essays on Medicine Esteeming the Chinese and Respecting the Western, Zhang Xi-Chun describes some of
the less commonly recognized applications of Bambusae
Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru):
As the bark of the bamboo, it is both cooling and directs
downward; thus, while cooling the Lungs and facilitating
[the removal of] phlegm, it disseminates and unblocks the
fiuid passageways of the Triple Burner, and below unblocks
the Bladder. Therefore, it is an important herb for unblocking and facilitating the flow of urine, similar to bamboo
leaves, but superior to the leaves in its power. It also excels

ing and pain due to trauma and blood stasis will find the

englishReference.combinations:
>WITH CoPTIDIS RHIZOMA (huang lian)
When Bambusae Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru) is joined with
the cold, bitter, downward-directing actions of Coptidis
Rhizoma (huang lian), its ability to clear Stomach heat and
alleviate nausea is greatly augmented; it can also dry damp.
ness and transform phlegm. This pair can thus be utilized
when Stomach heat is the sole cause of hiccough, nausea, or
dry retching, or when phlegm-heat obstructs the Stomach
causing vomiting of mucous sputum or acid regurgitation.
But the combination is also appropriate for palpitations.
insomnia, irritability, and stifling sensation in the chest
due to Gallbladder fire and phlegm disturbing the Heart
This is because Bambusae Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru) enters
the Gallbladder, while Coptidis Rhizoma (huang lian)
enters the Heart; both organs are thus harmonized. This is
the mechanism underlying the formula Coptis Warm the
Gallbladder Decoction (huang lian wen dan tang)
> WITH DENDROBII HERBA (shi hu)
Bambusae Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru) is sweet and slightly
cold. Entering the Lungs, it cools and transforms phlegm
to treat coughs; entering the Stomach, it cools heat and
directs rebellious qi downward, thereby alleviating nausea
and vomiting; entering the Gallbladder, it clears and drains
Gallbladder fire. Dendrobii Herba (shi hu) is sweet, bland
and cooling. Its salient characteristic is its ability to nourish the Stomach yin while eliminating heat from deficiency
from within the Stomach. It has an excellent fluid replenishing action, which alleviates thirst.
Both herbs clear Stomach heat, and as a pair they
harmonize the Stomach qi by directing rebellious qi down.
ward and replenishing the Stomach yin fluids; thus, there is
clearing in the midst of tonification, and tonification in the
midst of clearing. This combination is most suitable when
the patient is hungry but cannot eat very much, and also
experiences recurrent nausea and vomiting or dry retching,
thirst, and dry mouth. This is due to Stomach yin insufficiency, which causes heat from deficiency and the resulting
loss of harmony in the smooth descent of Stomach qi.
>WITH AURANTII FRUCTUS IMMATURUS (zhi shi)
Aurantii Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) breaks up qi and
mobilizes phlegm. With the addition of these qualities, the
ability of Bambusae Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru) to transform
phlegm is both strong and vigorous. Conversely, Aurantii
Fructus immaturus (zhi shi) benefits from the coolness
and the bitter, downward-directing qualities of Bambusae
Caulis in taeniam (zhu ru), which enhances its ability to
transform phlegm and quickly direct Stomach qi downwa.
This combination is especially effective when phlegm
and heat have combined to obstruct the flow of qi, leading
to focal distention in the chest and epigastrium, hiccough,
dry retching, nausea, and the regurgitation of acidic fluids.
However, it is also very useful in treating the palpitations,
irritability, insomnia, and emotional lability that results
from Gallbladder constraint coupled with phlegm disturb.
ing the Heart. Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia)
is usually added to this combination.
englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.PINELLIAE RHIZOMA PREPARATUM (zhi ban xia)
Both herbs transform phlegm, alleviate nausea, and calm
the spirit; indeed, they are often combined to mutually
enhance these qualities. However, Bambusae Caulis in tae.
niam (zhu ru) is moistening and cooling, and is biased
toward the treatment of phlegm-heat and nausea from
Stomach heat; it also excels at relieving constraint and
dispersing clumped phlegm-heat affecting the Gallbladder.
By contrast, Pinelliae Rhizoma preparatum (zhi ban xia) is
acrid, warm, and drying, and is biased toward the treatment
of cold-phlegm, damp-phlegm, and thin mucus, especially
affecting the Spleen, Stomach, and epigastrium.

englishReference.commentary:
Cinnabaris (zhu sha) is 'sweet, cold, and heavy in weight
Its coldness directs fire downward ("heaviness suppresses
trepidation", in the oft-quoted words of the sixth-century
physician Xu Zhi-Cai), and its crimson color signals that
it enters the Heart channel. Thus it clears fire, sedates the
Heart,arrests jitteriness and anxiety, and quiets the spirit
Because the Heart governs the spirit and resolve, which
reside in the Heart, suppression of fire restores calm to
the Heart. Cinnabaris (zhu sha) has therefore been used as
an important medicinal for irritability, restless insomnia,
withdrawal-mania, and childhood convulsions.
Applied topically, it treats toxic sores and carbuncles,
breaks up mobile and fixed abdominal masses, and is an
antidote for toxins due to bites from poisonous animals
and insects.

Cinnabar is the primary ore of mercury. In the Divine
Husbandman's Classic of the Materia Medica it is also
known as cinnabar sand (# dan sha). Because Chen
prefecture in modern day Hunan province was especially
well-known as a source of production, from the time of the
Inner Classic to this day it is commonly referred to as Chen
Sand (R chen sha). Yet it should be noted that the term
Chen sand is occasionally used as the commercial name for
artificially-produced cinnabar, otherwise known as divine
sand ( ling sha). As mentioned above, this is very toxic
and is for external use only.
In the process of separating the cinnabar from its matrix
of stone, the small chunks of cinnabar are split off, so it is
also known as cloven sand (# pi sha). These particles
are fresh red in color and semi-transparent, and because
they are shiny like a mirror, they are known as mirror-faced
sand (5n jing mian sha) and brilliant clear sand (a
" guang ming sha). In the past, exceptionally high quality
cinnabar was presented as tribute to the imperial court for
use in longevity medicinals, thus the term tribute cinnabar
(##y gong zhu sha) is specified by those wishing to
emphasize the best quality.

combined and allowed to settle, the water again poured off,
and the powder is then dried in the sun.

englishReference.commentary:
"Its acrid flavor enters the qi level, while its purple color
signals that it enters the blood level." These are the open-

1 / Herbs that Release the Exterior
ing words from the discussion of Perillae Folium (zi su ye)
in Essentials of the Materia Medica. Further description is
found in Seeking Accuracy in the Materia Medica: "[I]ts
aroma can vent wind outward, its warmth can warm the
middle, facilitating the comfort of the whole body. Thus.
it is named revivify (# su). Materia Medica of Food Stuff
adds that it can "bring down floating qi in the chest and
diaphragm."
Most classical texts warn, however, that continued
consumption will drain away true qi (see CAUTioNs &
CoNTRAINDICATIONS above). The same caveat applies to
all acrid, dispersing herbs.
englishReference.combinations:
>WITH CYPERI RHIZOMA (xiang fu)
This two-herb combination is excellent for treating exterior wind-cold where there is pre-existing qi constraint
This will present with exterior symptoms such as chills
and fever, headache, and lack of sweating, with concurrent
symptoms of qi stagnation such as stuffy chest, burping,
and flatulence. This combination can be used alone or as
part of a larger formula such as Cyperus and Perilla Leaf
Powder (xiang su san), but the choice of which herb shall
serve as chief depends upon which symptoms are primary.
Perillae Folium (zi su ye) releases the exterior, but also
has the ability to move middle burner qi. The addition of
the acrid, mobilizing quality of Cyperi Rhizoma (xiang
fu) assures that the congealing cold which is blocking the
protective qi is released, and that the pathogen will thereby
be dispersed via the exterior. Cyperi Rhizoma (xiang fu)
however, contributes more than just facilitating qi move
ment; it also moves the qi at the blood level. When one
considers that the locus of disruption in an invasion of the
exterior is the disharmony between the protective and the
nutritive qi, and that the latter is intimately associated with
blood, the elegance of this apparently simple combination
becomes apparent.
>WITH ZINGIBERIS RHIZOMA RECENs (shengjiang)
Both herbs release the exterior and can induce sweating.
The acrid, warm nature of Perillae Folium (zi su ye) dis
perses, with a light qi that unblocks and a light flavor that
can drain. In this way it disperses exterior pathogens while
clearing the head and eyes, drains the Lung qi and unblocks
the interstices and pores, thereby treating invasion of either
wind or cold.
Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng jiang) is acrid and
warm. While it can disperse exterior wind-cold, its sweatinducing action is rather weak by itself; combined with
Perillae Folium (zi su ye), it is much stronger.
This combination is very effective in treating wind-cold
13
exterior patterns with symptoms of chills, fever, headache.
nasal congestion, and, most importantly, the absence of
sweating.
Interestingly, both Zingiberis Rhizoma recens (sheng
jiang) and Perillae Folium (zi su ye) can be used indi.
vidually as an antidote to seafood poisoning: together, this
effect is increased. The pair is therefore often used for the
vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that results from
this kind of food poisoning.

englishReference.comparisons:
>Vs.EPHEDRAE HERBA (ma huang)
While Perillae Folium (zi su ye) is acrid and can disperse
while inducing sweating, it is not as strong as Ephedrae
Herba (ma huang) in this regard. Yet its aroma promotes
the movement of Lung and Spleen qi, harmonizes the
middle, and calms the fetus, qualities which are lacking in
Ephedrae Herba (ma huang).
englishReference.traditionalContraindications:
In Extension of the Materia Medica, Kou Zong-Shi observed
that
Nowadays people drink perilla soup morning and night.
but it is not good for them, just as the old medical saying
has it that 'aromatic plants cause diseases which steal away
riches'-this is one such case. For example, in people with
Spleen and Stomach cold, it often causes runny diarrhea
without their realizing it.
In the centuries since this was written, most materia medica
texts repeated or paraphrased this passage in their discus.
sion of Perillae Folium (zi su ye). Chen Shi-Duo, in New
Compilation of Materia Medica, was the first to question
whether this herb necessarily causes diarrhea in those with
Spleen and Stomach cold:
[Kou] Zong-Shi has a saying that *people with Spleen and
Stomach cold who consume Perillae Folium (zi su ve)usu
ally have diarrhea.'But do they really? I say:Perillae Folium
(zi su ye) is a wind herb, good at calming the Liver. If earth
is [excessively] controlled by wood then people will often
have diarrhea, but once wood is calmed, then earth will
obtain the nourishment it needs. It goes without saying that
Perillae Folium (zi su ye) is acrid and warm, acridity can
expel dampness while warmth can expel cold; so people
with Spleen and Stomach cold should really not have any.
problem--how could it cause diarrhea? It is only that acrid,
aromatic flavors are able to disperse a person's true qi.
Short term this is no problem, but long term it will cause
injury; this should also be kept in mind.

Its flavor is acrid and warm, a plant that is pure yang. Thus,
any patient with qi deficiency or weakness of the exterior
should not take it, nor should those with heat from yin defi.

englishReference.toxicity:
A large dosage of this herb can raise blood sugar levels, and
should not be used in those suffering from diabetes.
englishReference.nomenclaturePreparation:
>DRY-FRIED PERILLA LEAVES (k##chao zi su ye)
The leaves are fried lightly and briefly over a warm flame.
For prepared perilla leaves (zhi zi su ye) they are sprayed
with a honey-water mixture before lightly frying dry. These
methods both reduce the aroma and pungency of Perillae
Folium (zi su ye) so that the leaves are less sweat-inducing.
This is an advantage in treating older, weaker, or yin-deficient patients who would be injured by excessive sweating.
Nowadays, however, the leaves are almost always used
in their unprepared (raw) state; if less sweating is needed.
the dosage is reduced or herbs to support the normal qi are
added. For best results, when used for releasing the exterior, Perillae Folium (zi su ye) should be added at the very
end of boiling the decoction.
